バンドギャップ.desc: The energy difference between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band. About 1.12 eV for silicon at room temperature. A larger band gap means better tolerance to high temperatures and voltages.

about.p: The band gap Eg sets which light a semiconductor absorbs or emits, via λ (nm) ≈ 1240 / Eg (eV): silicon at about 1.12 eV absorbs out to about 1.1 µm, germanium at about 0.66 eV to about 1.9 µm, and GaAs at 1.42 eV emits near 870 nm. It also sets the intrinsic carrier density, ni ∝ T^(3/2)·exp(−Eg/2kT), about 1×10^10 cm^-3 for silicon at room temperature, versus about 2×10^13 for germanium and 2×10^6 for GaAs. A small ni keeps junction leakage low and lets light doping control conductivity. The gap itself shrinks slightly with temperature, about 0.3 meV/K in silicon.

In a direct-gap semiconductor such as GaAs or InGaN, the conduction-band minimum and valence-band maximum occur at the same crystal momentum, so an electron and hole can recombine by emitting a photon efficiently. Silicon has an indirect gap, so radiative recombination needs a phonon as well and is weak; recombination instead proceeds mainly through deep-level traps (Shockley-Read-Hall recombination). That is why LEDs and lasers use compound semiconductors: InGaN for blue and, with more indium, green; AlGaInP for red near 1.9–2.0 eV; AlGaN for deep ultraviolet.

Wide-bandgap semiconductors, roughly 3 eV and above, tolerate high fields and high temperatures because few carriers are thermally excited. 4H-SiC (about 3.26 eV) and GaN (about 3.4 eV) have breakdown fields near ten times silicon's, so a SiC drift layer for the same voltage can be about one tenth as thick and about 100 times more heavily doped, sharply cutting on-resistance. Ultra-wide-bandgap Ga2O3 (about 4.5–4.9 eV) and diamond (about 5.5 eV) go further. Insulators sit higher still: SiO2 is about 9 eV and HfO2 about 5.8 eV.

Alloys tune Eg continuously: AlGaAs rises from 1.42 eV while staying lattice-matched to GaAs, In0.53Ga0.47As on InP gives about 0.75 eV for 1.55 µm photodetectors, and HgCdTe spans nearly 0 to 1.5 eV for infrared detectors. Heterojunctions such as the narrow-gap SiGe base of an HBT exploit gap differences. Very heavy doping narrows the apparent gap, while quantum confinement in fins or nanosheets a few nanometers thick widens it. The gap also sets the about 33% Shockley-Queisser limit for single-junction solar cells, and a bandgap reference circuit outputs about 1.2 V, close to silicon's gap extrapolated to 0 K.

faq.q: What is a band gap in simple terms?
faq.a: It is the minimum energy needed to free an electron from a bond so it can conduct, equal to the energy difference between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band. Metals have no gap at the Fermi level, semiconductors have a moderate one and insulators a very large one.

faq.q: How do you convert a band gap to a wavelength?
faq.a: Use λ (nm) ≈ 1240 / Eg (eV). For silicon's 1.12 eV this gives about 1.1 µm, the longest wavelength silicon absorbs efficiently.

faq.q: What is the difference between a direct and an indirect band gap?
faq.a: In a direct gap the band edges align in crystal momentum, so electrons and holes recombine efficiently by emitting light, as in GaAs. In an indirect gap, such as silicon's, a phonon is also required, so light emission is weak.

ドナー.desc: An impurity that supplies electrons to a semiconductor. For silicon, group V elements such as phosphorus (P) and arsenic (As) act as donors and make n-type semiconductors.

about.h: How a donor supplies an electron
about.p: Phosphorus, a group V atom, replaces a silicon atom and uses four of its five valence electrons for bonds. The fifth is bound only weakly, because the surrounding silicon screens the ion's charge, so the system behaves like a large, shallow hydrogen atom. Its donor level lies about 0.045 eV below the conduction band for phosphorus and about 0.054 eV for arsenic, small compared with room-temperature thermal energy of about 0.026 eV, so nearly every donor ionizes. Each one releases a mobile electron and becomes a fixed positive ion in the lattice.

about.h: Carrier concentrations and the Fermi level
about.p: With all donors ionized, the electron density equals the donor concentration, and the law of mass action, n·p = ni², sets the holes: 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ donors with ni = 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ leave only 10⁴ holes per cm³, yet these minority carriers govern junction leakage and bipolar action. The Fermi level moves toward the conduction band by about 60 mV per decade of doping, and at very high doping enters it, making the material degenerate. Doping is extremely effective: silicon has about 5 × 10²² atoms/cm³, so 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ is one atom in five million, yet resistivity falls to roughly 0.5 Ω·cm.

Electron density stays close to the donor concentration only over a middle temperature range, the extrinsic region where devices are meant to operate. Below roughly 100 K in silicon, thermal energy is too small to free electrons from donors, and carrier density drops sharply in what is called freeze-out. At high temperatures, intrinsic carriers generated across the band gap grow steeply and eventually exceed the donor density, so doping no longer controls conduction. Even before that, the rising minority-carrier density increases leakage, one reason hot chips leak more.

Phosphorus and arsenic are the workhorse donors in silicon. Arsenic is heavier and diffuses more slowly, making it suitable for shallow n+ source and drain regions, and antimony is also used where slow diffusion is wanted, such as heavily doped substrates and buried layers. Donors can also appear unintentionally: oxygen in Czochralski silicon can form thermal donors during heating around 450 °C. In compound semiconductors, behavior can depend on the lattice site; silicon in GaAs normally sits on gallium sites and acts as the standard donor.

faq.q: Why does phosphorus act as a donor in silicon?
faq.a: Phosphorus has five valence electrons, one more than silicon needs for its four bonds. The extra electron is weakly bound, about 0.045 eV below the conduction band, so it is freed at room temperature and makes the silicon n-type.

faq.q: How do you calculate the hole concentration in n-type silicon?
faq.a: Use the mass-action law p = ni²/n with n ≈ ND. For ND = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ and ni = 10¹⁰ cm⁻³, p = 10⁴ cm⁻³.

faq.q: What is carrier freeze-out?
faq.a: At cryogenic temperatures, below roughly 100 K in silicon, there is too little thermal energy to ionize donors, so electrons stay bound and the free-carrier density falls sharply.

アクセプタ.desc: An impurity that accepts electrons from a semiconductor and creates holes. For silicon, group III elements such as boron (B) act as acceptors and make p-type semiconductors.

about.h: How an acceptor creates a hole
about.p: Silicon atoms share four valence electrons with their neighbours. A group III atom such as boron substitutes for silicon but has only three, leaving one bond incomplete. With very little energy, an electron from the valence band fills that bond, so the boron becomes a fixed negative ion and a mobile hole appears in the valence band. Boron's acceptor level lies about 0.045 eV above the valence band, small compared with room-temperature thermal energy, so nearly all acceptors are ionized and the hole concentration roughly equals the acceptor concentration. At very low temperatures holes freeze back onto the acceptors.

Donors are the mirror image: group V atoms such as phosphorus and arsenic have one extra electron, sit about 0.045–0.054 eV below the conduction band and become fixed positive ions. If both types are present they compensate, and the net doping is their difference. Because the product of electron and hole concentrations stays at ni² in equilibrium, a p-type region has very few electrons, its minority carriers. In compound semiconductors the role can depend on the site: silicon in GaAs is a donor on a gallium site but an acceptor on an arsenic site, so it is called amphoteric.

In a pn junction, the depletion region on the p side holds uncompensated negative acceptor ions, which set the built-in field and junction capacitance. In an nMOSFET, a more heavily doped p-type channel holds more acceptor charge in depletion and has a larger Fermi potential, raising the threshold voltage, which is how channel implants tune Vth. Boron is light and diffuses quickly, so shallow p+ junctions use low-energy or BF2 implants. Heavier indium diffuses slowly and has been used for steep retrograde and halo profiles, but its deeper level of about 0.16 eV leaves it only partly ionized.

Wide-bandgap materials make acceptors harder to use. In GaN the standard acceptor, magnesium, sits about 0.2 eV above the valence band, so only a few percent ionize at room temperature: Mg concentrations above 10¹⁹ cm⁻³ yield only 10¹⁷–10¹⁸ holes per cm³. During MOCVD growth, hydrogen also bonds to Mg and passivates it, leaving the layer highly resistive. Electron-beam irradiation, and later annealing at about 700 °C in nitrogen, were found to activate the acceptors, the step that made practical blue LEDs and lasers possible.

faq.q: What is the difference between an acceptor and a donor?
faq.a: An acceptor (group III in silicon, such as boron) takes an electron from the valence band, leaving a hole and making the material p-type. A donor (group V, such as phosphorus) gives an electron to the conduction band, making it n-type.

faq.q: Why is boron used as the acceptor in silicon?
faq.a: Boron has a shallow level about 0.045 eV above the valence band, so it is almost fully ionized at room temperature, and it is highly soluble in silicon. Its drawback is fast diffusion, which makes very shallow junctions harder to form.

faq.q: Why is p-type GaN hard to make?
faq.a: Its magnesium acceptor is deep, about 0.2 eV, so only a few percent ionize, and hydrogen from growth passivates Mg until an anneal or electron-beam treatment activates it.

移動度.desc: How easily carriers move when an electric field is applied. In silicon, electron mobility is higher than hole mobility.

about.p: At low electric fields a carrier's average drift velocity is proportional to the field, v = μE, and the constant μ is the mobility. Its unit follows directly: (cm/s) divided by (V/cm) gives cm²/(V·s); the SI unit m²/(V·s) equals 10⁴ cm²/(V·s). Physically, mobility is set by two things: how heavy the carrier appears inside the crystal (its effective mass) and how long it travels between scattering events. Lighter carriers and fewer collisions mean higher mobility. Mobility then enters conductivity as σ = q(nμn + pμp), so carrier density and mobility together decide resistivity.

Two scattering mechanisms dominate in bulk silicon. Lattice vibrations (phonons) grow stronger with temperature, so in lightly doped silicon mobility falls roughly as T^(−1.5 to −2.5), which is the main reason MOSFET drive current drops when a chip runs hot. Ionized dopants scatter carriers by Coulomb attraction or repulsion, so mobility falls as doping rises; in compensated material every ionized donor and acceptor counts, not just the net doping. In a MOSFET channel, surface roughness and interface charge add further scattering and can cut mobility to half the bulk value or less.

In lightly doped silicon at room temperature, electron mobility is about 1,400 cm²/(V·s) and hole mobility about 450, a ratio of roughly three caused mainly by the heavier hole effective mass. Electron mobility drops to around 100 cm²/(V·s) near 10¹⁹ cm⁻³ doping. GaAs electrons reach about 8,500 and InSb about 77,000 cm²/(V·s). The linear v = μE picture fails at high fields: for silicon electrons, velocity growth slows above roughly 10⁴ V/cm and saturates near 10⁷ cm/s, a regime that short MOSFET channels operate in.

about.h: Where mobility shows up in practice
about.p: Because holes are slower, a CMOS pMOS is usually drawn two to three times wider than its nMOS partner to balance rise and fall times, and advanced processes add compressive strain from SiGe to speed up pMOS holes. Through the Einstein relation D = μkT/q (kT/q ≈ 26 mV at room temperature), mobility also fixes the diffusion coefficient, about 36 cm²/s for electrons in silicon. Mobility is commonly measured by combining a Hall measurement, which gives carrier density, with resistivity, using μ = 1/(qnρ).

faq.q: Why is electron mobility higher than hole mobility in silicon?
faq.a: Holes in silicon behave as if they had a larger effective mass than electrons, so the same field accelerates them less between collisions. At room temperature and low doping this gives roughly 1,400 versus 450 cm²/(V·s).

faq.q: What is the difference between mobility and drift velocity?
faq.a: Drift velocity is the actual average speed of carriers in a field, while mobility is the proportionality constant linking the two (v = μE). The relation holds only at low fields; at high fields the velocity saturates even as the field keeps rising.

faq.q: Does mobility increase or decrease with temperature?
faq.a: In lightly doped silicon near room temperature it decreases, because phonon scattering grows. In heavily doped material or at low temperature, ionized-impurity scattering dominates and weakens as temperature rises, so mobility can increase over that range.

空乏層.desc: A region near a PN junction boundary that contains almost no carriers. It widens under reverse bias.

about.p: When p-type and n-type regions meet, electrons diffuse from the n side and holes from the p side, recombining near the junction. They leave behind fixed charges: positive ionized donors on the n side and negative ionized acceptors on the p side. These charges set up a built-in electric field pointing from n to p that pushes carriers back and stops further net diffusion. The resulting built-in potential is typically about 0.6 to 0.9 V for silicon junctions, depending on doping. The region is also called the space-charge region, because its defining feature is uncompensated fixed charge.

about.h: Width and how doping divides it
about.p: Charge neutrality requires NA·xp = ND·xn, so the depletion layer extends further into the more lightly doped side. For an abrupt junction the total width is W = √(2ε(Vbi + V)/q × (1/NA + 1/ND)), where V is the reverse bias. In a p+n junction this reduces to W ≈ √(2ε(Vbi + V)/(qND)), and almost the whole layer lies on the n side. Typical widths are about 0.1 to 1 µm; for example, ND = 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ at zero bias gives roughly 0.3 µm. Quadrupling Vbi + V doubles the width.

Because the region contains almost no mobile carriers, it behaves like the insulator of a parallel-plate capacitor with C = εA/W. As reverse bias widens W, the capacitance falls, roughly as (Vbi + V)^-1/2 for an abrupt junction. Varactor diodes exploit this voltage-controlled capacitance for tuning. The same relation is used in capacitance-voltage profiling: plotting 1/C² against reverse bias gives a slope from which the doping on the lightly doped side can be extracted. Junction capacitance also loads every transistor's drain and source, adding to circuit delay.

The concept appears throughout device physics. A gate voltage depletes the silicon under a MOS gate before inversion occurs. Polysilicon gate electrodes deplete too, adding roughly 0.3 to 0.5 nm of equivalent oxide thickness, which is why high-k/metal gate technology replaced them. Photodiodes collect light-generated carriers efficiently within the depletion region, so PIN diodes insert a wide intrinsic layer. Power devices use lightly doped drift layers so a wide depletion region can hold high voltage. Note that the sharp-edged picture is the depletion approximation; real edges taper over a few Debye lengths.

faq.q: Why does the depletion region widen under reverse bias?
faq.a: Reverse bias adds to the built-in potential, so more fixed charge must be uncovered to support the larger voltage. Since the dopant density is fixed, the only way to expose more charge is to deplete a wider region, with width scaling roughly as the square root of the total voltage.

faq.q: Is the depletion region the same as the space-charge region?
faq.a: Yes. Both names describe the same zone around the junction where mobile carriers are nearly absent and the ionized dopants leave a net fixed charge.

faq.q: Does a PN junction have a depletion layer with no voltage applied?
faq.a: Yes. It forms in thermal equilibrium through diffusion and recombination of carriers, supported by the built-in potential. Forward bias narrows it and reverse bias widens it.

ツェナーダイオード.desc: A diode that provides a constant voltage by using the nearly fixed reverse breakdown voltage.

about.h: How it is used: reverse bias in breakdown
about.p: A Zener diode is connected with its cathode more positive than its anode and operated beyond its reverse breakdown voltage. In that region the current can change greatly while the voltage changes very little, meaning the dynamic resistance is low, so the diode acts as a voltage reference. The datasheet Zener voltage is specified at a stated test current, and the diode regulates best near that current. Below breakdown only a tiny leakage current flows. In the forward direction it behaves like an ordinary silicon diode and conducts at about 0.6 to 0.7 V.

The breakdown voltage is set by doping. Heavily doped junctions have very thin depletion layers and very strong fields, so electrons tunnel directly from the valence band on the p side to the conduction band on the n side; this true Zener breakdown dominates below about 5 V and has a negative temperature coefficient. More lightly doped junctions break down by avalanche multiplication, dominant above roughly 5 V, with a positive temperature coefficient. Parts near 5 to 6 V mix both mechanisms, whose coefficients partly cancel, so they tend to show the smallest drift with temperature.

The basic regulator places a resistor between the input and the Zener, with the load in parallel with the diode. The resistor limits current and absorbs input variation as its own voltage drop. Choose R = (minimum input − Vz) ÷ (maximum load current + minimum Zener current). For a 9 to 12 V input, a 5.1 V Zener, a 10 mA load and 5 mA minimum Zener current, R ≈ 260 Ω. Then check the worst case: at 12 V with no load, about 26 mA flows through the diode, dissipating about 0.14 W. Because current flows continuously, this circuit is inefficient and suits only small loads.

Zener diodes also clamp voltages. Placed across a sensitive input, one conducts only when the voltage exceeds its rating, protecting against overvoltage. In a relay driver, a plain flyback diode across the coil clamps the turn-off spike to about one diode drop but makes the relay release slowly; adding a Zener in series lets the voltage rise to a controlled higher level, dissipating the coil's energy faster for quicker release. Transient voltage suppressor (TVS) diodes are related avalanche devices optimized for absorbing large surge energy rather than for precise regulation.

faq.q: Can a Zener diode be used in the forward direction?
faq.a: It conducts forward like an ordinary diode at about 0.6 to 0.7 V, but that is not its intended use. For voltage regulation it must be reverse biased beyond its breakdown voltage.

faq.q: How do I choose the series resistor for a Zener regulator?
faq.a: Use R = (minimum input voltage − Zener voltage) ÷ (maximum load current + minimum Zener current), then check that the Zener's power rating is not exceeded at maximum input with the lightest load.

faq.q: What is the difference between a Zener diode and a TVS diode?
faq.a: Both operate in reverse breakdown, but a Zener diode is designed for a precise, steady reference voltage at small currents. A TVS diode is built to absorb brief high-energy surges and clamp them, with less emphasis on voltage accuracy.

電流増幅率(hFE).desc: The ratio of collector current to base current (IC/IB) in a bipolar transistor.

about.p: Current gain can be expressed two ways. The common-base gain α = IC/IE is slightly less than 1 because a small fraction of the emitter current is lost in the base. The common-emitter gain, written β or hFE = IC/IB, follows as β = α/(1 − α). With α = 0.99, β = 99; with α = 0.995, β = 199, so a tiny change in α makes a large change in hFE. In the active region IC ≈ hFE × IB: a 10 µA base current with hFE = 100 gives about 1 mA, provided the collector circuit can supply it.

about.h: What sets hFE inside the transistor
about.p: Base current consists mainly of holes injected back from the base into the emitter and of electrons that recombine while crossing the base (for an NPN device). A heavily doped emitter makes injection efficiency high by suppressing the back-injected holes, and a base much thinner than the minority-carrier diffusion length lets nearly all electrons reach the collector. Very heavy emitter doping eventually loses effect through bandgap narrowing; heterojunction bipolar transistors (HBTs) solve this with a wider-bandgap emitter. A thin base also raises base resistance and the risk of punch-through.

about.h: Why circuits should not rely on it
about.p: hFE is typically tens to hundreds for small-signal transistors and tens for power devices, but it varies widely between units of the same part, often binned into ranges such as 100–400. It also rises with temperature, roughly 0.5–1% per °C, and it peaks at moderate collector current, falling at low current because of depletion-region recombination and at high current because of high injection and the Kirk effect. Robust bias circuits therefore use an emitter resistor and a resistor-divider base so the operating point is set by resistors rather than by hFE.

Uppercase hFE is the DC ratio IC/IB, used for bias calculations; lowercase hfe is the small-signal ratio ΔIC/ΔIB at the operating point, used for AC gain and input resistance. They are often close but not equal. In switching, the transistor is driven into saturation, where the collector current is limited by the load and IC/IB, the forced beta, is deliberately below hFE. Designers commonly supply 2–10 times IC/hFE(min) as base current to guarantee saturation, at the cost of more stored charge and slower turn-off.

faq.q: What is the difference between hFE and beta?
faq.a: In practice they mean the same quantity, the common-emitter current gain IC/IB. hFE is the h-parameter name used on datasheets for the DC value, while β is the symbol common in textbooks and device physics.

faq.q: What is the difference between hFE and hfe?
faq.a: hFE is the DC current gain IC/IB at a given operating point, while hfe is the small-signal gain ΔIC/ΔIB around that point. Use hFE for bias design and hfe for AC analysis.

faq.q: Why does hFE vary so much between transistors?
faq.a: hFE depends on base width, doping and recombination, which vary from device to device, and it changes further with temperature and collector current. That is why good designs set the operating point with feedback resistors instead of depending on an exact hFE.

しきい値電圧.desc: The gate voltage at which a channel (inversion layer) forms in a MOSFET and current starts to flow. Written as Vth.

about.p: Threshold voltage (Vth) is conventionally the gate voltage at which strong inversion begins, when the surface potential reaches twice the Fermi potential φF and the surface minority-carrier density equals the bulk majority density. For an nMOSFET, Vth = VFB + 2φF + Qd/Cox. The flat-band voltage VFB depends on the gate-to-silicon work-function difference and on charge in the oxide; Qd is the depletion charge. Raising channel doping or thickening the gate oxide therefore raises Vth. In high-k/metal-gate FinFETs and gate-all-around devices, channels are nearly undoped and Vth is set mainly by the gate metal's work function.

An enhancement-mode nMOSFET conducts when VGS exceeds a positive Vth; an enhancement-mode pMOSFET has a negative Vth, around −0.4 V, and turns on when its gate is more than |Vth| below its source, so documents often quote magnitudes. Advanced logic uses about 0.2 to 0.4 V, power devices about 1 to 4 V. Above threshold, a long-channel device in saturation follows ID = ½μCox(W/L)(VGS − Vth)², so the overdrive voltage VGS − Vth sets drive current. Short channels deviate from this square law because of velocity saturation.

Lowering Vth increases overdrive and on-current at a given supply, but below threshold the current falls only exponentially, so off-state leakage grows roughly tenfold for every 60 to 80 mV of reduction. Processes therefore offer low-, standard- and high-Vth transistors, and designers place low-Vth cells only on critical paths. Operating conditions move Vth too: reverse body bias raises it (the body effect), higher drain voltage lowers it through drain-induced barrier lowering (DIBL), and rising temperature lowers its magnitude by about 1 to 2 mV/°C.

Vth is never exactly the same twice. In small transistors, random dopant fluctuation and gate-metal grain effects scatter Vth by tens of millivolts, with the spread scaling roughly as one over the square root of gate area (Pelgrom's law); SRAM cells feel this most. In fins and nanosheets a few nanometers thick, quantum confinement turns thickness variation into Vth variation. Over a product's life, negative and positive bias temperature instability (NBTI, PBTI) and hot carrier injection shift Vth upward and slow circuits, so timing must include aging margin.

faq.q: What is a typical threshold voltage for a MOSFET?
faq.a: Transistors in advanced logic processes typically have threshold voltages of about 0.2 to 0.4 V in magnitude, with several options offered per process. Power MOSFETs are usually around 1 to 4 V so they stay reliably off with noise on the gate.

faq.q: Why is the threshold voltage of a pMOS transistor negative?
faq.a: A pMOS channel is made of holes, which are attracted to the surface of the n-type body when the gate is driven below the source. Turning it on therefore requires a negative gate-to-source voltage, so its threshold is negative.

faq.q: How is threshold voltage measured?
faq.a: It is usually extracted from the measured ID-VG curve, either as the gate voltage where drain current reaches a fixed value scaled by W/L (constant-current method) or by extrapolating the linear part of the curve to zero current. The two methods give slightly different numbers, so the definition should always be stated.

CMOS.desc: A circuit style that combines nMOS and pMOS transistors in a complementary way. Almost no current flows through it in steady state, so power consumption is low.

about.h: How a CMOS gate avoids static current
about.p: In a CMOS (complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor) inverter, a pMOS connects the output to the supply and an nMOS connects it to ground. A low input turns the pMOS on and the nMOS off; a high input does the reverse. In either steady state one transistor is off, so no DC path exists from supply to ground, and the output swings fully to the rails, giving large noise margins. In more complex gates the pull-up and pull-down networks are duals: a two-input NAND has two nMOS in series and two pMOS in parallel.

CMOS power has three parts. Dynamic power, P = αCV²f, is spent charging and discharging load capacitance, where α is the activity factor; halving V cuts it to a quarter, which is why voltage scaling and DVFS are so effective. Short-circuit (crowbar) current flows briefly while the input passes through intermediate voltages and both transistors conduct; with sharp transitions it stays around a tenth of dynamic power or less. Static power comes from subthreshold and gate leakage in off transistors. Once negligible, leakage grew with scaling and lower threshold voltages and is now handled with techniques such as power gating.

Electrons in silicon are roughly two to three times more mobile than holes, so a pMOS of the same size delivers less current than an nMOS. Designers therefore make the pMOS about two to three times wider to place the inverter's switching threshold near VDD/2 and match rise and fall delays. Gate delay is roughly CV/I, the time for drive current I to charge load capacitance C through voltage V. Because series stacks are slow, NAND gates, which stack the faster nMOS, are generally preferred over NOR gates, which stack pMOS. Strained SiGe channels have narrowed the gap.

Placing nMOS and pMOS side by side in wells creates a parasitic PNPN thyristor. If substrate current from noise or an input overvoltage triggers it, the two parasitic bipolar transistors feed each other and a large supply-to-ground current flows until power is removed. Well contacts, guard rings, retrograde wells, p/p+ epitaxial wafers and SOI suppress this latch-up. The near-zero quiescent current of good CMOS also enables IDDQ testing, which flags defects such as bridging shorts by their abnormal standby current, although rising normal leakage has made that test harder to apply.

faq.q: What does CMOS stand for?
faq.a: CMOS stands for complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor. Complementary refers to pairing n-channel and p-channel MOSFETs so that one is always off in steady state.

faq.q: What is the difference between CMOS and NMOS logic?
faq.a: NMOS logic uses only n-channel transistors with a resistive or transistor load, so current flows whenever the output is low. CMOS replaces the load with a complementary pMOS network, eliminating that static current, which is why it became the standard IC technology.

faq.q: Why does CMOS consume power if no static current flows?
faq.a: Every transition charges or discharges load capacitance, consuming dynamic power proportional to αCV²f. In addition, real transistors leak when off, and in advanced processes this static leakage power is significant.

フリップフロップ.desc: The basic element of sequential circuits that stores one bit. A D flip-flop captures its input at a clock edge.

about.p: A D flip-flop samples its D input at the active clock edge and holds that value at Q until the next edge; changes between edges are ignored. Internally it is usually two latches clocked in opposite phases in a master-slave arrangement. A latch, by contrast, is level-sensitive: while enabled it is transparent and passes input straight to output. Edge triggering makes timing far easier to analyze, which is why flip-flops form CPU registers, pipeline stage boundaries, state machines and counters in synchronous designs.

about.h: Setup time, hold time and maximum frequency
about.p: Data must be stable for a setup time before the edge and a hold time after it. On a register-to-register path the clock period must cover clock-to-output delay, logic delay and setup time: with 0.15 + 2.2 + 0.15 ns the minimum period is 2.5 ns, or 400 MHz. Setup violations can be fixed by slowing the clock, but hold violations cannot, because the check compares data launched and captured on the same edge; designers add delay buffers instead. Clock skew that delays the capture clock helps setup but hurts hold.

If data changes inside the setup-hold window, as happens with signals from an unrelated clock, the flip-flop can become metastable, its output lingering between 0 and 1. The chance that it remains unresolved falls exponentially with time but never reaches zero. A synchronizer of two or more flip-flops in series gives the first stage a full clock period to settle, pushing the mean time between failures to thousands of years or more. Multi-bit values cross clock domains through asynchronous FIFOs or handshakes, and CDC (clock domain crossing) verification tools check that these structures are present.

A JK flip-flop sets with J = 1, resets with K = 1, holds with both 0 and toggles with both 1, giving meaning to the forbidden input of an SR flip-flop. Tying the inputs high makes a T flip-flop that toggles every edge, dividing the clock frequency by two with a 50 percent duty cycle; chains of them form ripple counters and dividers. Modern logic uses D flip-flops almost exclusively. For testing, scan design adds a multiplexer at each flip-flop input so the flip-flops can be chained into shift registers to load and observe internal states.

faq.q: What is the difference between a latch and a flip-flop?
faq.a: A latch is level-sensitive and passes its input to the output whenever it is enabled, while a flip-flop is edge-triggered and samples its input only at the clock edge. A typical D flip-flop is built from two latches enabled on opposite clock phases.

faq.q: Why can't a hold violation be fixed by lowering the clock frequency?
faq.a: The hold check compares data launched and captured on the same clock edge, so the clock period does not appear in it. The fix is to add delay to the short path, usually with buffers.

faq.q: How do you calculate the maximum clock frequency of a flip-flop path?
faq.a: Add the clock-to-output delay, the worst-case combinational delay and the setup time, adjusting for clock skew, to get the minimum period; the maximum frequency is its reciprocal. The slowest such path on the chip, the critical path, sets the chip's limit.

オペアンプ.desc: An amplifier with differential inputs and very high gain. Used with negative feedback in amplifiers, filters and more.

about.p: A typical operational amplifier (op-amp) has three parts. The input stage is a differential pair: a tail current source splits its current between two transistors according to the difference of the input voltages, so signals common to both inputs largely cancel, which gives a high common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR). A current-mirror active load converts that stage's output to single-ended form with high gain, a second gain stage adds more, and an output stage supplies load current. A compensation capacitor across the second stage, magnified by the Miller effect, sets the frequency response. Open-loop gain is typically 10^5 to 10^6.

about.h: Negative feedback and the virtual short
about.p: Op-amps are almost always used with negative feedback. The ideal model assumes infinite input impedance, zero output impedance and infinite open-loop gain; with feedback the output settles where the voltage between the inputs is essentially zero, the virtual short. Gain then depends only on components: an inverting amplifier gives −Rf/Ri with input impedance Ri, and a non-inverting amplifier gives 1 + R2/R1 with very high input impedance. With no R2, the voltage follower has a gain of 1 and serves as a buffer. A capacitor in the feedback path makes an integrator; a feedback resistor alone converts current to voltage in a transimpedance amplifier.

An internally compensated op-amp's gain falls at 20 dB per decade, so gain times bandwidth stays roughly constant. With a gain-bandwidth product (GBW) of 1 MHz, a non-inverting gain of 10 leaves about 100 kHz of bandwidth; strictly, divide by the noise gain, 1 + Rf/Ri. Large signals meet a separate limit, the slew rate, the fastest the output can change. A sine of peak amplitude Vp distorts above SR/(2πVp): 0.5 V/µs and 10 V give only about 8 kHz.

Mismatch in the input transistors produces an input offset voltage, a few millivolts in general-purpose parts and tens of microvolts or less in precision or chopper-stabilized types, which appears at the output multiplied by the noise gain. Bipolar inputs also draw bias current, so a resistor equal to Ri in parallel with Rf is placed at the non-inverting input to cancel its effect. A comparator looks similar but is designed to run without feedback, switching fully and recovering quickly from saturation, often with an open-drain output and added hysteresis to prevent noisy chatter.

faq.q: What is the virtual short in an op-amp?
faq.a: With negative feedback and very high open-loop gain, an op-amp drives its output so that the two input voltages are nearly equal, even though they are not connected. This holds only while the output is not saturated and feedback is negative.

faq.q: Can an op-amp be used as a comparator?
faq.a: It can work at low speed, but op-amps are optimized for feedback operation and may recover slowly from saturation or have output levels unsuited to logic. Dedicated comparators switch faster, often have open-drain outputs, and are designed to run open-loop.

faq.q: What is gain-bandwidth product?
faq.a: Gain-bandwidth product is the frequency at which an op-amp's open-loop gain falls to 1, and for a compensated op-amp the closed-loop gain times bandwidth is roughly equal to it. A 10 MHz GBW part, for instance, gives about 100 kHz at a noise gain of 100.

リフレッシュ.desc: The periodic reading and rewriting of DRAM data before the charge in its capacitors is lost through leakage.

about.p: A DRAM cell stores a bit as charge on a small capacitor reached through one access transistor (a 1T1C cell). Even when the transistor is off, charge leaks away through its subthreshold current and through junction leakage at the storage node, including gate-induced drain leakage (GIDL) and defect-assisted generation. Retention time varies from cell to cell, and a small tail of the weakest cells sets the refresh period. Standards therefore require every row to be refreshed within about 64 ms in the normal temperature range. SRAM, by contrast, holds data in a cross-coupled latch and needs no refresh while powered.

Reading a DRAM cell is destructive: the cell shares its charge with the much larger bit-line capacitance, and the sense amplifier resolves a difference of tens of millivolts while writing the full level back. Simply activating a row and closing it therefore refreshes every cell in that row. In DDR4, the controller issues 8,192 refresh commands per 64 ms window, one about every 7.8 µs (tREFI), each refreshing several rows internally. Each command keeps the bank busy for tRFC, which grows with density to several hundred nanoseconds for 16 Gbit devices.

Leakage rises with temperature, and retention roughly halves for every 10 °C as a rule of thumb, so DDR standards halve the refresh interval above 85 °C, to 3.9 µs in DDR4. Larger chips have more rows to refresh, so refresh eats a growing share of time and power, costing several percent up to about 10 percent of performance in dense devices; per-bank refresh keeps other banks available meanwhile. During standby, self-refresh lets the DRAM refresh itself from an internal timer while the controller sleeps, and low-power DRAM adds temperature-aware and partial-array refresh.

Some cells show variable retention time (VRT): a defect switching states makes their leakage jump between values, so a cell that passed testing can later become weak; refresh margin and ECC cover this. Row hammer is another threat: activating one row tens of thousands of times within a refresh window can drain charge from neighboring rows and flip bits, which has been exploited in security attacks. DRAMs and controllers counter it by refreshing the neighbors of heavily activated rows, through mechanisms such as target row refresh and DDR5's refresh management commands.

faq.q: How often does DRAM need to be refreshed?
faq.a: Standard DDR DRAM must refresh every row within about 64 ms at normal temperatures, spread across 8,192 refresh commands. Above 85 °C the interval is typically halved.

faq.q: Does SRAM need refresh?
faq.a: No. SRAM stores each bit in a cross-coupled latch that holds its state actively as long as power is applied. DRAM needs refresh because it stores bits as charge on a leaky capacitor.

faq.q: What is DRAM self-refresh mode?
faq.a: It is a low-power mode in which the DRAM refreshes itself using an internal timer, so the external clock and memory controller can be stopped. It preserves data while a phone or PC sleeps.

センスアンプ.desc: A circuit that amplifies the tiny voltage difference read from a memory cell and decides whether it is 0 or 1.

about.p: Memory cells are made as small as possible, so they cannot drive long bit lines quickly. In DRAM, opening a cell shares its charge with a bit line whose capacitance is several times larger, producing a swing of only about (VDD/2)·Cs/(Cs + Cb), tens to about a hundred millivolts. In SRAM the cell can discharge its precharged bit line only slowly. A sense amplifier detects this small difference and turns it into a full logic level, so the memory does not have to wait for the bit line to swing all the way.

about.h: How a latch-type sense amplifier works
about.p: The common form is two cross-coupled inverters connected across a pair of bit lines, one carrying the cell signal and the other a reference. Both lines are first precharged and equalized. When the sense amplifier is enabled, whichever side is slightly higher pulls the other down, and positive feedback regenerates the small difference to the full supply rails in a short time. Timing matters: firing too early, before enough signal develops, risks a wrong decision, while firing too late wastes access time.

DRAM bit lines are precharged to VDD/2 so a stored 1 or 0 moves them up or down by the same amount. Because charge sharing destroys the stored value, the sense amplifier that resolves the bit line also drives it to full level and rewrites the cell, so activating a row automatically refreshes it. Closing the row and returning bit lines to VDD/2 is precharge, timed by tRP. Folded bit-line arrays place both lines of a pair side by side so coupled noise cancels; open bit-line arrays split them to permit smaller 6F² cells.

Random threshold-voltage mismatch between the latch transistors gives every sense amplifier an input offset, which must stay well below the available signal; this limits how many cells can share a bit line and motivates offset-compensation schemes. Single-ended memories such as flash compare the cell current against a reference current or reference cell, and multi-level cells need several comparisons per read. The same regenerative latch idea appears in the clocked comparators of analog-to-digital converters.

faq.q: Why does DRAM need a sense amplifier?
faq.a: The cell capacitor is much smaller than the bit line capacitance, so reading produces only tens of millivolts of change. The sense amplifier amplifies this to a full logic level and also rewrites the cell, because the read destroys its charge.

faq.q: Why are DRAM bit lines precharged to VDD/2?
faq.a: Starting halfway lets a stored 1 raise the bit line and a stored 0 lower it by similar amounts, so the sense amplifier compares the line against an equal reference. It also halves the bit line swing, saving power.

faq.q: What is the difference between DRAM and SRAM sense amplifiers?
faq.a: Both use regenerative latches, but DRAM sense amplifiers also restore the destroyed cell data and work from a VDD/2 precharge. SRAM sense amplifiers only need to detect a small differential on bit lines precharged near VDD to speed up reads.

NAND型フラッシュメモリ.desc: Non-volatile memory in which memory cells are connected in series. It is dense and easy to scale to large capacities, and is used in SSDs and memory cards.

about.p: A NAND flash cell is a transistor with a charge-storage layer, either a floating gate or a charge-trap film, beneath its control gate. Dozens of cells are connected in series in a string between two select transistors, so the string needs contacts only at its ends, which makes area per bit very small. To read a cell, a read voltage is applied to its word line while all other word lines in the string get a higher pass voltage that turns their cells fully on; whether the string conducts reveals the selected cell's threshold.

Programming applies around 20 V to the control gate so electrons tunnel from the channel through a thin tunnel oxide into the storage layer by Fowler-Nordheim (FN) tunneling, raising the threshold voltage. Incremental step pulse programming (ISPP) raises the pulse voltage a few hundred millivolts at a time and verifies after each pulse for a tight distribution. Erasing raises the cell well to high voltage to pull electrons out of every cell in a block. The erased, low-threshold state reads as 1, so erased flash reads 0xFF.

NAND reads and programs in pages of roughly 16 KB, the cells on one word line, but erases only whole blocks of hundreds of pages, several to tens of megabytes. Programming can only move bits from 1 to 0, so data cannot be overwritten in place. A flash translation layer (FTL) in the controller writes new data to a free page, remaps the logical address and marks the old page invalid; garbage collection later copies valid pages out of a block and erases it. Wear leveling spreads erases across blocks, and strong error-correcting codes handle bit errors.

Storing N bits per cell requires 2^N threshold-voltage levels in roughly the same voltage window: 2 for SLC, 4 for MLC, 8 for TLC and 16 for QLC. Each extra bit lowers cost per gigabyte but narrows the gaps between levels, slowing programming and reducing endurance, because each program/erase cycle slightly degrades the tunnel oxide. Typical figures are about 50,000 to 100,000 cycles for SLC, a few thousand for TLC and around 1,000 for QLC. Modern 3D NAND stacks more than a hundred word-line layers vertically, mostly with charge-trap cells formed around vertical channel holes.

faq.q: What is the difference between NAND and NOR flash?
faq.a: NAND connects cells in series, giving the smallest cell and highest capacity but page-based access, so it is used for SSDs and memory cards. NOR connects each cell in parallel to the bit line, giving fast random reads suited to storing and executing code, at lower density.

faq.q: Why can't NAND flash overwrite data in place?
faq.a: Programming can only add charge and raise threshold voltages, and removing charge requires erasing an entire block. Controllers therefore write updated data to a fresh page and reclaim old blocks later through garbage collection.

faq.q: What do SLC, MLC, TLC and QLC mean?
faq.a: They denote 1, 2, 3 and 4 bits stored per cell, which require 2, 4, 8 and 16 distinguishable threshold-voltage levels. More bits per cell means cheaper capacity but slower writes and lower endurance.

MRAM.desc: Non-volatile memory that stores data as the difference in resistance caused by the magnetization direction of a magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ).

about.h: How a magnetic tunnel junction stores a bit
about.p: The storage element is a magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ): a fixed reference layer and a switchable free layer, both ferromagnetic, separated by an insulating tunnel barrier about 1 nm thick. When the two magnetizations are parallel, electrons tunnel easily and resistance is low; antiparallel gives high resistance. This tunnel magnetoresistance (TMR) distinguishes 0 from 1. Crystalline MgO barriers give TMR ratios of several hundred percent, far above the tens of percent of amorphous Al2O3. Reading passes a small current and compares against a reference; it does not disturb the magnetization, so no write-back is needed.

In STT-MRAM, write current flows through the MTJ itself. Electrons spin-polarized by the reference layer transfer angular momentum to the free layer and flip it; the current direction selects the state. Unlike early MRAM written by magnetic fields from nearby wires, the STT write current shrinks with cell area, which makes scaling possible. The limit is thermal stability: the energy barrier is anisotropy times free-layer volume, and its ratio to kT, called Δ, must be roughly 60 or more for ten-year retention. Raising Δ raises write current, so perpendicular magnetization materials are used to balance the two.

MTJs are built between interconnect layers in the back end of line (BEOL), after the transistors are finished, with only a few extra masks. Embedded flash, by contrast, needs ten or more additional masks for floating gates and becomes impractical beyond about 28 nm or with high-k/metal gates. This makes MRAM a leading replacement for embedded flash in microcontrollers and automotive chips at 22 nm and below. Integration challenges include surviving BEOL thermal steps of about 400 °C and patterning magnetic films without metal redeposition, typically using ion-beam etching.

Compared with flash, MRAM writes in a few to tens of nanoseconds without an erase step and endures over 10¹⁰ cycles, versus thousands to tens of thousands for NAND. Unlike DRAM and SRAM it is non-volatile. Its weaknesses are density and read margin: cells are larger than NAND cells and cannot be stacked in 3D, so cost per bit is far higher, and a 2 to 3 times resistance ratio gives smaller read margins than DRAM or flash. FeRAM stores data in ferroelectric polarization instead, and phase-change memory in crystalline versus amorphous resistance.

faq.q: Is MRAM volatile or non-volatile?
faq.a: MRAM is non-volatile: data is held in the magnetization direction of the free layer, which persists without power, typically for ten years or more. It combines this with fast writes and very high endurance.

faq.q: What is the difference between STT-MRAM and toggle MRAM?
faq.a: Toggle or field-written MRAM flips the free layer with magnetic fields from current in nearby wires, which needs more current as cells shrink. STT-MRAM passes spin-polarized current directly through the MTJ, so write current scales down with cell size.

faq.q: Why is MRAM replacing embedded flash?
faq.a: Embedded flash adds many process steps and is hard to integrate beyond about 28 nm or with high-k/metal gates. MRAM is built in the interconnect layers with only a few extra masks and offers faster writes and higher endurance.

キャッシュメモリ.desc: Fast, small memory placed close to the CPU. It holds frequently used data to bridge the speed gap with main memory. Mostly built from SRAM.

IGBT.desc: Insulated-gate bipolar transistor. Driven by a MOS gate, it achieves a low on-state voltage even at high voltage ratings through conductivity modulation.

about.p: An insulated-gate bipolar transistor (IGBT) looks like a vertical power MOSFET with an extra p+ layer at the back, the collector. The gate forms a MOS channel that supplies electrons into the lightly doped n-drift region, and these act as base current for an internal pnp transistor, so the p+ collector injects holes. The drift region floods with both carriers, and this conductivity modulation sharply lowers its resistance. The price is a junction in the conduction path, which gives the on-state voltage a knee of roughly 0.7 V before current rises.

A silicon MOSFET conducts with majority carriers only, so its drift region must be thicker and more lightly doped as voltage rating rises, and on-resistance increases steeply with breakdown voltage. That keeps silicon MOSFETs mostly below a few hundred volts. The IGBT's conductivity modulation largely breaks this link, so it dominates silicon devices from about 600 V up to 6.5 kV, in electric vehicle inverters, rail traction and industrial drives. At low current, though, the IGBT's knee voltage makes a MOSFET more efficient, and silicon carbide MOSFETs now compete in the 650 to 1700 V range.

Turn-on is quick, but at turn-off the stored minority carriers must be removed, producing tail current while the voltage is already high. This turn-off energy limits silicon IGBTs to switching frequencies of tens of kHz or less. Device design trades on-state voltage against turn-off loss: more stored charge means lower conduction loss but a longer tail. Trench gates and field-stop layers improve this trade-off. Unlike a MOSFET, an IGBT has no internal body diode for reverse current, so inverter modules pair each IGBT with an antiparallel freewheeling diode.

Because the gate is insulated, an IGBT is voltage-driven, typically switched on with about +15 V and held off at zero or a negative voltage for noise immunity, although the gate capacitance still requires a driver able to supply peak currents. Silicon IGBTs typically survive a short circuit for about 10 µs, so drivers watch for desaturation, a rise in collector voltage during conduction, and switch off within that time. The device also contains a parasitic pnpn thyristor, whose latch-up modern cell designs suppress.

faq.q: What is the difference between an IGBT and a MOSFET?
faq.a: Both have an insulated MOS gate, but an IGBT adds bipolar conduction through hole injection, giving lower on-state voltage at high voltage ratings. MOSFETs switch faster and have no tail current, so they dominate at lower voltages and higher frequencies.

faq.q: Why can't IGBTs switch at high frequency?
faq.a: Minority carriers stored in the drift region during conduction must be removed at turn-off, producing a tail current while voltage is high. The resulting turn-off energy grows with switching frequency, which practically limits silicon IGBTs to tens of kHz or less.

faq.q: Why does an IGBT need an antiparallel diode?
faq.a: An IGBT cannot conduct in the reverse direction like a MOSFET body diode, but inductive loads in inverters need a path for freewheeling current. A separate fast diode is therefore placed across each IGBT.

SiC(炭化ケイ素).desc: A wide-band-gap semiconductor with a band gap of about 3.3 eV. Its high breakdown field makes it suitable for high-voltage, low-loss power devices.

about.h: Why the wide band gap matters
about.p: SiC's band gap of about 3.3 eV gives it a critical breakdown field near 3 MV/cm, roughly ten times silicon's. For a given voltage rating the drift layer can be about one tenth as thick and about 100 times more heavily doped, so its resistance falls by a theoretical factor of several hundred. Baliga's figure of merit, εμEc³, captures this because the breakdown field enters cubed. The wide gap also keeps intrinsic carrier density low at high temperature, and SiC conducts heat about three times better than silicon, around 400 W/(m·K).

The workhorses are SiC MOSFETs and SiC Schottky barrier diodes. Being unipolar, they avoid the tail current of silicon IGBTs and the reverse-recovery current of silicon pn diodes, so switching losses drop sharply; SiC Schottky diodes are made at 600–1700 V. Lower losses let designers raise switching frequency and shrink inductors, capacitors and cooling, which is why SiC spread into electric-vehicle inverters, especially 800 V systems. The price of speed is steep dv/dt, tens of volts per nanosecond, which turns small parasitic inductances into voltage surges and EMI, so layout and gate drive matter.

SiC MOSFETs are usually driven at about +15 to +18 V when on and often a negative bias of −3 to −5 V when off. Their threshold voltage is low, around 2–3 V, so the Miller current caused by the opposite switch's dv/dt could otherwise turn them on falsely. Small chips with low thermal capacity mean short-circuit withstand time is typically a few microseconds, versus about 10 µs for silicon IGBTs, so protection must act faster. Kelvin-source packages separate the gate-drive return from the main current path to avoid common-source inductance problems.

about.h: Why SiC is hard to make
about.p: SiC does not melt at normal pressure, so boules are grown by sublimation (physical vapour transport) at 2000–2500 °C at only about 0.1–1 mm per hour, and the extremely hard crystal is slow to slice and polish. Power devices use the 4H-SiC polytype on substrates cut about 4° off-axis for step-flow epitaxy at 1500–1650 °C. Dopants barely diffuse, so junctions are formed by epitaxy and hot ion implantation followed by 1600–1800 °C anneals. Reliability concerns include low channel mobility from carbon-related oxide-interface defects and bipolar degradation, where basal-plane dislocations grow into stacking faults.

faq.q: Why is SiC better than silicon for high-voltage power devices?
faq.a: SiC's breakdown field is about ten times silicon's, so a thinner, more heavily doped drift layer blocks the same voltage with far lower resistance. It also tolerates higher temperatures and conducts heat better, which cuts both losses and cooling requirements.

faq.q: What is the difference between SiC and GaN power devices?
faq.a: Both are wide-band-gap semiconductors with gaps of about 3.3 and 3.4 eV. SiC is grown as native substrates and is used mainly for vertical MOSFETs and diodes at high voltage and current, while GaN power transistors are usually lateral HEMTs grown on foreign substrates such as silicon and excel at very fast switching at moderate voltages.

faq.q: What is 4H-SiC?
faq.a: 4H-SiC is the polytype of silicon carbide with a four-layer hexagonal stacking sequence. It is the standard choice for power devices because it combines a band gap of about 3.26 eV with electron mobility around 1000 cm²/V·s and relatively little anisotropy.

GaN(窒化ガリウム).desc: A III-V compound semiconductor with a band gap of about 3.4 eV. Used in blue LEDs and in high-frequency and power devices.

about.p: Gallium nitride is a III-V compound semiconductor with a direct band gap of about 3.4 eV, corresponding to an absorption edge near 365 nm in the ultraviolet. Like SiC, it is a wide-bandgap semiconductor: it has very few intrinsic carriers even when hot, and a critical breakdown field roughly ten times that of silicon, so a thin layer can block a high voltage. Large native GaN substrates are hard to make, so GaN devices are usually grown epitaxially on foreign substrates such as sapphire, SiC or silicon.

The key power and RF device is the high-electron-mobility transistor (HEMT). At the AlGaN/GaN interface, differences in spontaneous and piezoelectric polarization induce a two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) with a density of about 10¹³ cm⁻² without any intentional doping. With no ionized dopants to scatter them, these electrons reach mobilities around 2,000 cm²/(V·s), giving low on-resistance and fast switching. Because the 2DEG exists at 0 V gate bias, the basic HEMT is normally on; power circuits need normally-off behavior, achieved with a p-type GaN gate or a cascode with a low-voltage silicon MOSFET.

GaN-based InGaN quantum wells made efficient blue LEDs possible, and blue LEDs combined with phosphors give white lighting; a GaN blue LED has a forward voltage of about 3 V. In RF, GaN HEMTs serve as high-power, high-frequency amplifiers for wireless infrastructure and radar. In power electronics, low switching loss lets GaN converters run at higher frequency, which shrinks inductors, capacitors and transformers. The price is very steep voltage edges, tens to 100 V/ns, so layouts must minimize parasitic inductance to control surges and EMI, and dead time can be cut to tens of nanoseconds.

Both are wide-bandgap materials with band gaps around 3.3 to 3.4 eV, but they are used differently. SiC is grown on native SiC substrates and built into vertical MOSFETs and diodes that handle high voltages and currents, typically 1,200 V class and above. GaN power transistors are mostly lateral HEMTs on silicon or other substrates, strongest at up to several hundred volts where their very fast switching pays off. Silicon remains cheaper for low-frequency, cost-driven designs.

faq.q: Why is GaN better than silicon for power devices?
faq.a: Its wide band gap gives a much higher breakdown field, so a thinner drift region can block the same voltage with lower on-resistance. GaN HEMTs also switch very fast with low loss, allowing higher operating frequencies and smaller passive components.

faq.q: Is a GaN HEMT normally on or normally off?
faq.a: The basic AlGaN/GaN HEMT is normally on because its 2DEG channel exists at zero gate bias. Commercial power devices are made normally off with a p-GaN gate structure or by pairing the HEMT with a silicon MOSFET in a cascode.

faq.q: What is the band gap of GaN?
faq.a: About 3.4 eV at room temperature, roughly three times that of silicon (1.12 eV). It is a direct gap, which is why GaN-based materials emit light efficiently.

直接遷移型.desc: A band structure in which the bottom of the conduction band and the top of the valence band are at the same wave number. Electron-hole recombination emits light efficiently. Example: GaAs.

フォトダイオード.desc: A diode that generates charge (current) when it receives light. Used as the light-receiving element in image sensor pixels.

about.h: How a photodiode converts light to current
about.p: A photon with energy above the band gap creates an electron-hole pair. If the pair is generated in or near the depletion region of a PN junction, the built-in field separates the carriers and a photocurrent flows. Reverse bias widens the depletion region and lowers junction capacitance, giving faster response, while zero-bias operation gives lower dark current for precise measurement of weak light. Photocurrent is nearly proportional to light intensity over many decades; silicon's responsivity is about 0.5 to 0.6 A/W near 800 to 900 nm. A transimpedance amplifier usually converts the current to a voltage.

Silicon's 1.12 eV band gap sets an absorption edge near 1.1 µm, and longer visible and near-infrared light is absorbed weakly: the absorption depth is about 1.5 µm at 550 nm, about 20 µm at 850 nm and over 50 µm at 940 nm. Thin photodiodes therefore have poor infrared sensitivity, and germanium or compound semiconductors are used at telecom wavelengths. Dark current, generated thermally through interface states, defects and metal contamination, flows even without light; in image sensors it roughly doubles every 6 to 8 °C, causing noise and hot pixels.

In a CMOS image sensor pixel, a pinned photodiode collects electrons during exposure. Its n-region is buried under a heavily doped p+ surface layer that suppresses interface-state dark current and lets the region fully deplete, so a transfer transistor can move all the charge to a floating diffusion. Sampling before and after transfer, called correlated double sampling, cancels reset noise. Full-well capacity ranges from a few thousand electrons in small pixels to around 100,000 in large ones. Because a photodiode senses only intensity, color requires filters over each pixel.

An ordinary photodiode has no internal gain: one absorbed photon yields at most one electron-hole pair. An avalanche photodiode (APD) is biased near breakdown so that impact ionization multiplies the photocurrent tens to hundreds of times, lifting weak signals above amplifier noise in optical receivers and LiDAR. A single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) is biased above breakdown in Geiger mode, where a single photon triggers a large pulse. The same PN junction operated without bias to deliver power is essentially a solar cell.

faq.q: Why is a photodiode operated in reverse bias?
faq.a: Reverse bias widens the depletion region so more light-generated carriers are collected quickly, and it lowers junction capacitance, speeding up the response. The trade-off is higher dark current than zero-bias operation.

faq.q: What is the difference between a photodiode and an avalanche photodiode?
faq.a: A standard photodiode produces one electron-hole pair per absorbed photon with no gain. An APD is biased close to breakdown so avalanche multiplication amplifies the photocurrent internally, allowing detection of much weaker light.

faq.q: Why can't silicon photodiodes detect 1550 nm light?
faq.a: A 1550 nm photon has about 0.8 eV of energy, below silicon's 1.12 eV band gap, so it cannot create electron-hole pairs. Germanium or InGaAs detectors are used at that wavelength.

CZ法(チョクラルスキー法).desc: A method of making single-crystal silicon by dipping a seed crystal into molten silicon in a crucible and slowly pulling it up while rotating.

about.p: High-purity polysilicon, typically made by the Siemens process, is melted in a quartz crucible, just above silicon's melting point of about 1,414 °C. A seed crystal is dipped into the melt and drawn upward at a few centimetres per hour while seed and crucible counter-rotate. First a thin neck of about 3 to 5 mm is grown so that dislocations from the thermal shock grow out to the surface (Dash necking); the crystal then widens through a shoulder to a constant-diameter body and ends in a tapered tail. A camera watches the meniscus, and pull rate and heater power hold the diameter constant.

The quartz crucible slowly dissolves, so CZ silicon contains oxygen at around 10¹⁸ cm⁻³. This is partly useful: oxygen pins dislocations and strengthens the wafer, and its precipitates, called bulk micro defects, serve as intrinsic gettering sites for metal impurities. Too much oxygen causes defects and thermal donors, so the concentration is controlled. Magnetic CZ (MCZ) applies a magnetic field to the conductive melt, whose Lorentz force damps convection, reducing oxygen transport and growth striations; it is standard for large melts.

Dopants are added to the melt: boron for p-type, phosphorus, arsenic or antimony for n-type. Most have segregation coefficients below 1 (phosphorus about 0.35, antimony about 0.023), so they accumulate in the melt and the later part of the ingot is more heavily doped; boron, at about 0.8, stays more uniform. Only sections within the resistivity specification become product. The ratio of pull rate to temperature gradient, V/G, decides whether excess vacancies (forming voids) or self-interstitials (forming dislocation loops) are frozen in, and growing in the narrow balanced window yields nearly defect-free crystal.

The float-zone (FZ) method melts a narrow zone of a polysilicon rod with RF induction heating and moves it along the rod, never touching a crucible. FZ crystals therefore contain little oxygen and reach resistivities above 1,000 Ω·cm, which suits high-voltage power devices such as IGBTs and radiation detectors, but the method is limited to about 200 mm. CZ scales to 300 mm ingots about 2 m long and weighing hundreds of kilograms, so it supplies most IC wafers. Solar-cell production has also shifted toward CZ monocrystalline silicon instead of cast multicrystalline ingots.

faq.q: What is the difference between CZ and FZ silicon?
faq.a: CZ silicon is pulled from a melt in a quartz crucible, so it contains about 10¹⁸ cm⁻³ oxygen but scales to 300 mm. FZ silicon is crucible-free, with very low oxygen and high resistivity, and is used mainly for power devices and detectors.

faq.q: Why are silicon wafers round?
faq.a: In the CZ method the crystal is pulled while rotating, which evens out the temperature around the axis, so the ingot grows as a cylinder. Slicing it gives round wafers, and processes such as spin coating and CMP also suit a round shape.

faq.q: Why is the bottom of a CZ ingot more heavily doped than the top?
faq.a: Most dopants have segregation coefficients below 1, so the growing crystal rejects them and they concentrate in the remaining melt. As the melt shrinks, later-grown crystal incorporates more dopant and its resistivity falls.

熱酸化.desc: A method of forming an SiO2 film on silicon by heating it in oxygen or water vapor. There are dry and wet oxidation.

about.p: Dry oxidation reacts silicon with oxygen gas, Si + O2 → SiO2, while wet oxidation uses steam, Si + 2H2O → SiO2 + 2H2. Water dissolves in SiO2 several hundred times more than O2, so wet oxidation grows oxide several to ten times faster: about 70 nm dry versus 400 nm wet after one hour at 1000 °C. Wet oxide retains some hydrogen and is slightly less dense, so it suits thick isolation and masking layers. Dry oxide grows slowly with precise thickness control and a low density of interface states, which made it the classic gate oxide.

The Deal-Grove model treats oxidation as oxidant moving from the gas to the oxide surface, diffusing through the oxide and reacting with silicon at the Si/SiO2 interface. Balancing these fluxes gives x² + Ax = B(t + τ). While the oxide is thin, the interface reaction limits growth and thickness rises linearly with time at rate B/A. Once the oxide is thicker than roughly A/2, diffusion limits growth and thickness follows the square root of time, so doubling it takes about four times as long. Higher temperature or oxidant pressure speeds both regimes.

Oxide grows by consuming the substrate: forming a film of thickness x uses about 0.44x of silicon, so 44 percent of the oxide lies below the original surface and 56 percent above. The roughly 2.2 times volume expansion leaves the oxide in compressive stress. Above about 950 °C the amorphous SiO2 can flow viscously and relax this stress; at lower temperatures stress retards oxidation at convex corners and leaves them sharp. Because new oxide always forms at a freshly created interface, thermal oxide has a cleaner interface than deposited oxide.

Oxidation runs at about 800 to 1,200 °C, usually in vertical furnaces holding around 100 wafers. The (111) surface oxidizes faster than (100), by about 1.5 times for thin oxides. Adding a few percent HCl getters sodium and metal contamination and suppresses oxidation-induced stacking faults, which grow from silicon interstitials injected during oxidation. Heavily doped polysilicon oxidizes faster and gives poorer oxide. Thermal SiO2 has a relative permittivity of about 3.9, the reference for equivalent oxide thickness (EOT). For thin, orientation-independent films, ISSG radical oxidation is used.

faq.q: How much silicon is consumed during thermal oxidation?
faq.a: About 0.44 times the final oxide thickness. Growing 100 nm of SiO2 consumes roughly 44 nm of silicon, and the surface rises by about 56 nm.

faq.q: Why is wet oxidation faster than dry oxidation?
faq.a: Water molecules dissolve in SiO2 at a concentration several hundred times higher than oxygen, so far more oxidant reaches the Si/SiO2 interface. This makes wet oxidation several to ten times faster at the same temperature.

faq.q: What is the difference between thermal oxide and CVD oxide?
faq.a: Thermal oxide is grown by converting the silicon substrate itself, giving a dense film and a high-quality interface. CVD oxide is deposited from precursor gases on top of any surface without consuming silicon, which allows lower temperatures and thick films on non-silicon layers but gives a poorer interface.

イオン注入.desc: A technique that ionizes impurities, accelerates them and implants them into the wafer. The dose and depth can be controlled precisely.

about.p: Dopant ions are extracted from a plasma in the ion source, an analyzer magnet selects only the desired mass, an accelerator brings them to the required energy, and the beam is scanned across the wafer, or the wafer moved through it, for uniform coverage. Faraday cups measure beam current, which is integrated to give dose with roughly ±1 percent accuracy and in-wafer variation down to about 0.5 percent. Because positive ions charge isolated gates and resist, a plasma flood gun supplies low-energy electrons to neutralize them. Reaching several MeV needs multistage RF linear accelerators or tandem accelerators.

about.h: Energy sets depth, dose sets concentration
about.p: The projected range Rp, the average stopping depth, grows with energy: boron in silicon stops around 30 to 40 nm at 10 keV and about 0.3 µm at 100 keV, and lighter ions go deeper at equal energy. Dose, counted in ions per square centimetre, spans roughly 10¹¹ to 10¹⁶ cm⁻² and is set independently of depth. Thermal diffusion, by contrast, ties surface concentration to depth and needs high temperatures. Since implantation runs near room temperature, photoresist can serve as the mask, provided it is several times thicker than the ion range.

Ions travelling along crystal rows can slip through open channels and penetrate far deeper than intended. Tilting the wafer about 7° with a twist offset, implanting through a thin screen oxide or pre-amorphizing the surface suppresses this channeling tail. Every implant also displaces lattice atoms, and most implanted dopants land in interstitial sites where they are electrically inactive. A post-implant anneal repairs the damage and activates the dopants; seconds-long rapid thermal anneals and millisecond flash or laser anneals limit the diffusion that would otherwise deepen shallow junctions.

CMOS processes use many implants: wells and retrograde wells, threshold adjustment, source/drain extensions and contacts. MeV implants form deep photodiodes and pixel isolation in image sensors and superjunction pillars in power devices. Hydrogen implantation splits wafers in the Smart Cut process for SOI. Alternatives appear where beamline implantation struggles: plasma doping for high doses at very low energy on 3D fins, and in-situ doped epitaxy for source/drain regions near 10²¹ cm⁻³. In SiC, where dopants barely diffuse, implantation is often done hot and the implanted profile is used as is.

faq.q: What determines the depth of ion implantation?
faq.a: Mainly the acceleration energy: higher energy gives a deeper projected range. Ion mass also matters, since lighter ions penetrate further at the same energy, and channeling can add an unwanted deep tail.

faq.q: What is the difference between ion implantation and thermal diffusion?
faq.a: Implantation shoots accelerated ions into the wafer near room temperature, controlling dose and depth independently and allowing resist masks. Diffusion drives dopants in from the surface at high temperature, coupling surface concentration and depth, and needs oxide masks.

faq.q: Why is annealing needed after ion implantation?
faq.a: Implantation damages the crystal and leaves most dopants on interstitial sites where they are inactive. Annealing repairs the lattice and moves dopants onto substitutional sites, activating them.

アニール.desc: Heat treatment. Used to repair crystal damage after ion implantation and to activate dopants, among other purposes.

about.h: Why implanted wafers must be annealed
about.p: Ion implantation knocks silicon atoms out of place and, at high doses, can make the surface layer amorphous. Most implanted atoms also sit in interstitial positions where they do not donate or accept carriers. Annealing gives the lattice enough thermal energy to regrow its crystal order and move dopants onto substitutional sites, which is called activation. The catch is that heat also makes dopants diffuse: source and drain regions spread laterally under the gate, shortening the effective channel length and adding overlap capacitance. Every anneal therefore trades activation and damage repair against unwanted diffusion.

The total heat a wafer sees is called the thermal budget, set by both temperature and time. Vertical furnaces process about 100 wafers at once over many minutes and suit oxidation, diffusion and long anneals. Rapid thermal processing (RTP) heats one wafer at a time with lamps for seconds, and millisecond anneals using lasers or flash lamps go further, activating dopants while allowing almost no diffusion; advanced nodes rely on these to keep junctions shallow. Fast ramps have a cost: temperature gradients across a large wafer can cause slip dislocations, so ramp rates and wafer support are optimized.

Many anneals have nothing to do with implant damage. A forming gas anneal at about 400 to 450 °C in hydrogen-containing nitrogen passivates dangling bonds at the Si/SiO2 interface, cutting interface states to about 10¹⁰ cm⁻²eV⁻¹. Annealing densifies CVD oxide so its etch rate approaches that of thermal oxide. Magnesium-doped GaN becomes p-type only after annealing near 700 °C in nitrogen drives out the hydrogen that passivates the acceptors. Wafer makers anneal above 1100 °C to form a denuded zone, and briefly above about 650 °C to eliminate oxygen thermal donors.

Required temperatures vary widely with material. Dopants barely diffuse in SiC, so its implants are often done hot, at about 300 to 600 °C, and activation needs 1,600 to 1,800 °C, far beyond silicon practice. At the other extreme, the Smart Cut process for SOI wafers needs only a few hundred degrees for implanted hydrogen to form microcavities that split the wafer. Unintended anneals matter too: holding oxygen-rich CZ silicon near 450 °C generates thermal donors that shift resistivity.

faq.q: What does dopant activation mean?
faq.a: It means moving implanted dopant atoms onto substitutional lattice sites, where they can donate electrons or accept them to create holes. Annealing supplies the energy for this while also repairing implant damage.

faq.q: What is the difference between RTA and furnace annealing?
faq.a: Furnace annealing treats a large batch of wafers for minutes to hours, while rapid thermal annealing (RTA) heats a single wafer with lamps for seconds. The shorter time of RTA gives a much smaller thermal budget and less dopant diffusion.

faq.q: What is a forming gas anneal used for?
faq.a: It is a low-temperature anneal, around 400 to 450 °C, in nitrogen with a few percent hydrogen. The hydrogen passivates dangling bonds at the Si/SiO2 interface, improving threshold stability, subthreshold slope and mobility.

CVD.desc: Chemical vapor deposition. A method of depositing thin films on a wafer through chemical reactions of source gases.

about.p: In chemical vapor deposition, precursor gases flow over a heated wafer, adsorb on the surface, react and leave a solid film while volatile by-products are pumped away. For example, tungsten is deposited by reducing WF6 with hydrogen, releasing HF. This distinguishes CVD from physical vapor deposition (PVD) such as sputtering, where atoms are knocked off a solid target and fly in straight lines without chemical change. Because the film grows by reaction on whatever surface the gas reaches, CVD can coat the sidewalls and bottoms of features far better than PVD.

At relatively low temperature the surface reaction is the slow step, so growth rate follows the Arrhenius law and depends exponentially on temperature; thickness uniformity then depends on temperature uniformity. At high temperature the reaction is fast and the supply of gas limits growth, so gas-flow uniformity becomes critical. Reaction-limited conditions, favored by lower temperature and lower pressure, give the best conformality because gas penetrates deep into trenches before reacting. Under supply-limited conditions, film builds up at openings and can pinch them off, trapping voids.

Low-pressure CVD (LPCVD) at tens to hundreds of pascals coats more than 100 wafers uniformly at about 600 to 800 °C, depositing polysilicon, silicon nitride from dichlorosilane and ammonia, and TEOS oxide. Plasma-enhanced CVD (PECVD) uses plasma electrons to break precursors at about 300 to 400 °C, so it can be used after metallization, at the cost of hydrogen in the film. High-density plasma CVD sputters corners while depositing for gap fill, and epitaxial CVD grows single-crystal layers, at about 1,500 to 1,650 °C for SiC. Atomic layer deposition (ALD) is a self-limiting cousin with near-100 percent step coverage.

CVD fills shallow trench isolation, deposits interlayer dielectrics, spacers and passivation, forms tungsten contact plugs and 3D NAND word lines, and grows epitaxial device layers. Film quality is a recurring concern: CVD oxide is usually less dense than thermal oxide and etches faster in dilute HF, so the wet etch rate ratio (WERR) to thermal oxide serves as a quality index, and annealing densifies the film. Choosing between CVD variants is mostly a balance of temperature limits, conformality, throughput and film purity.

faq.q: What is the difference between CVD and PVD?
faq.a: CVD forms films through chemical reactions of precursor gases on the wafer surface, while PVD, such as sputtering, physically transfers atoms from a solid source without a reaction. CVD generally gives much better step coverage in deep features.

faq.q: Why is PECVD done at lower temperature than LPCVD?
