faq.a: In PECVD, energetic plasma electrons supply the energy to decompose precursors, so the wafer needs only about 300 to 400 °C instead of the 600 to 800 °C of thermal LPCVD. This makes it usable after aluminum or copper wiring is in place.

faq.q: What is the difference between CVD and ALD?
faq.a: CVD supplies precursors together and grows film continuously, while ALD alternates precursor pulses so each cycle adds about one self-limited atomic layer. ALD is slower but gives nearly perfect conformality and atomic-scale thickness control.

ALD.desc: Atomic layer deposition. A deposition method that repeats self-limiting surface reactions of precursor gases to control film thickness one atomic layer at a time.

about.p: Atomic layer deposition (ALD) splits a CVD reaction into two half-reactions separated in time. A precursor such as trimethylaluminum (TMA) is dosed and chemisorbs on surface sites until they are filled; excess gas is purged; a co-reactant such as water then reacts with the adsorbed layer; and a second purge follows. Because each half-reaction stops once the surface is saturated, growth per cycle is fixed, typically about 0.1 nm or less, since bulky precursor molecules block neighboring sites. Film thickness is set simply by counting cycles.

Self-limiting growth only holds within a temperature range called the ALD window. Too cold, precursors condense or react incompletely; too hot, they decompose and grow CVD-like, or adsorbed species desorb. Within the window growth per cycle is nearly constant, about 150–300 °C for Al2O3 from TMA and water. Precursor choice shifts it: HfO2 can be grown from HfCl4, which is stable around 300 °C but may leave chlorine, or from organometallics such as TEMAHf, which react at lower temperature but may leave carbon. Such residues affect threshold voltage and reliability.

about.h: Conformality compared with CVD and PVD
about.p: Because growth is controlled by surface saturation rather than gas transport, ALD reaches nearly 100% step coverage, coating the sidewalls and bottoms of features with aspect ratios of several tens. Sputtering may leave under 10% of the top thickness at the bottom of deep holes, and CVD sits in between. This is why ALD deposits high-k HfO2 gate dielectrics, TiN for metal gates and barriers, ZrO2/Al2O3/ZrO2 stacks in DRAM capacitors, the gate stack wrapped around GAA nanosheets, and the spacers used in self-aligned double and quadruple patterning.

The cost is speed: a cycle takes seconds to tens of seconds, so a few nanometers needs dozens of cycles. Batch reactors and spatial ALD, which moves wafers through separate gas zones, raise throughput. Plasma-enhanced ALD (PEALD) uses radicals in the reactant step to deposit at room temperature to a few hundred °C and to enable films such as SiN, at some cost in conformality inside deep features because radicals recombine. Atomic layer etching (ALE) applies the same self-limiting idea to removing material.

faq.q: What is the difference between ALD and CVD?
faq.a: In CVD all reactants are present together and the film grows continuously at a rate set by temperature and gas supply. In ALD the reactants are supplied separately with purges between them, so each step is self-limiting and thickness is set by the number of cycles.

faq.q: How thick is the film deposited in one ALD cycle?
faq.a: Typically about 0.1 nm, which is one atomic layer or less. A 2 nm film therefore needs on the order of 20 cycles.

faq.q: Why is ALD slow?
faq.a: Each cycle needs two precursor doses and two purges that must fully saturate and then fully clear the surface, taking seconds or longer, yet adds only a fraction of a nanometer.

スパッタリング.desc: A type of PVD in which ions in a plasma bombard a target and the ejected atoms are deposited on the wafer.

about.p: A target plate made of the film material sits at a negative potential of several hundred volts in a low-pressure argon plasma. Argon ions accelerate into the target and knock surface atoms loose by momentum transfer, and the ejected atoms travel to the wafer and condense into a film. No chemical reaction is needed, so sputtering is a form of physical vapor deposition (PVD). The sputter yield, atoms ejected per ion, is roughly 0.5 to 3 for argon at a few hundred eV and rises with ion energy, ion mass and oblique incidence. Deposition rate rises roughly in proportion to target power, so targets are water-cooled.

In magnetron sputtering, magnets behind the target create a field crossing the electric field near its surface, trapping electrons in spiralling paths that ionize more argon. The dense plasma sustains high rates at about 0.1 to 1 Pa and reduces electron bombardment of the wafer. Erosion concentrates where the field is strongest, so magnets are rotated to use the target evenly. Conductive targets can use DC power, while insulating targets need RF power so that positive charge does not build up on their surface. Adding a reactive gas such as nitrogen deposits compounds like TiN from a metal target.

Compared with vacuum evaporation, sputtering preserves alloy composition, because atoms are knocked out physically rather than boiled off at component-dependent rates, and sputtered atoms arrive with several to tens of eV instead of about 0.1 eV, giving denser films with better adhesion. Like evaporation, though, it is line-of-sight: bottom coverage in deep holes can fall below 10 percent, whereas CVD and ALD coat features conformally. Collimators and later ionized PVD, which ionizes sputtered atoms and pulls them vertically with substrate bias, improve bottom coverage. Thornton's structure zone model relates film microstructure to substrate temperature and gas pressure.

Aluminum wiring was deposited by sputtering aluminum alloy targets with about 0.5 percent copper to resist electromigration. In copper interconnects, sputtering deposits Ta or TaN barrier layers and the thin copper seed layer on which electroplating builds the wire, using copper targets of around 6N purity. TiN, titanium and various electrode metals are also sputtered. Targets need high purity and uniform grain structure because impurities and grain variations show up directly in the film.

faq.q: What is the difference between sputtering and evaporation?
faq.a: Evaporation heats the source until atoms vaporize, while sputtering ejects atoms by ion bombardment. Sputtering keeps alloy compositions closer to the target and gives denser, better-adhering films, while evaporation is simpler and gives very pure films.

faq.q: Why is argon used in sputtering?
faq.a: Argon is chemically inert, so it does not react with the film, and its ions are heavy enough to sputter most metals efficiently. It is also inexpensive and easy to ionize in a stable plasma.

faq.q: Why does sputtering have poor step coverage?
faq.a: Sputtered atoms travel in nearly straight lines and barely migrate after landing, so sidewalls and bottoms shadowed from the opening receive little film. Ionized PVD or CVD and ALD are used when deep features must be coated.

フォトレジスト.desc: A light-sensitive material whose solubility in developer changes when exposed. In positive resist the exposed areas dissolve; in negative resist they remain.

about.p: Most resists for KrF (248 nm), ArF (193 nm) and EUV (13.5 nm) lithography are chemically amplified resists, consisting of a base resin, a photoacid generator (PAG), solvent and additives such as quenchers that limit acid diffusion. Exposure releases acid from the PAG; during the post-exposure bake (PEB), each acid molecule catalytically removes many protecting groups from the resin, changing its solubility and greatly raising sensitivity. A positive resist is then developed in 2.38% aqueous TMAH (tetramethylammonium hydroxide), which dissolves the exposed regions. In negative-tone development, an organic solvent dissolves the unexposed regions instead.

Resist is spin-coated to a thickness from tens of nanometers to several micrometers, soft-baked to drive out solvent, exposed, baked again and developed. Supporting films help: a bottom antireflective coating (BARC) suppresses reflections from the substrate, and in ArF immersion lithography a topcoat keeps the immersion water from leaching resist components and keeps the surface hydrophobic during fast stage motion. After the pattern has served its purpose, the resist is removed by ashing, oxidizing it in an oxygen plasma to CO2 and H2O, followed by a wet clean.

about.h: Resist as an etch and implant mask
about.p: The pattern is only useful if the resist survives the next step. For ion implantation the resist must be several times thicker than the ion range, so MeV implants use films from several micrometers to about 10 µm. High-dose implants carbonize the resist surface into a hard crust; ashing it hot right away can make gas from the soft resist underneath burst the crust, called popping, so stripping starts at low temperature or uses hydrogen-based plasmas. For deep etches that would consume a thin resist, the pattern is first transferred into a hard mask of nitride, oxide or amorphous carbon.

Because photoresist reacts to light and heat, it is stored in light-tight bottles at the specified temperature, often refrigerated, and used before its expiration date. A cold bottle must warm to room temperature before opening, or condensed moisture will change its performance, and the liquid is filtered through very fine filters just before coating. Lithography areas are lit with yellow light that lacks the short wavelengths resists respond to. Formulations balance resolution, sensitivity, line-edge roughness and etch resistance, which cannot all be maximized at once.

faq.q: What is the difference between positive and negative photoresist?
faq.a: In a positive resist the exposed areas become soluble and are removed by the developer, so the pattern matches the opaque parts of the mask. In a negative resist the exposed areas remain and the unexposed areas dissolve, reversing the image.

faq.q: What is a chemically amplified resist?
faq.a: It is a resist in which exposure generates acid from a photoacid generator, and that acid catalyzes many solubility-changing reactions during a post-exposure bake. One photon's effect is multiplied, giving the high sensitivity needed for KrF, ArF and EUV lithography.

faq.q: How is photoresist removed after etching or implantation?
faq.a: It is usually removed by ashing, in which an oxygen plasma or similar oxidizes the organic resist into CO2 and water vapor, followed by a wet clean to remove residues.

EUV露光.desc: Lithography using extreme ultraviolet light with a wavelength of 13.5 nm. It uses reflective optics and a vacuum environment.

about.h: Why EUV needs mirrors and vacuum
about.p: Light at 13.5 nm is absorbed by almost every material, including air and the glass used for lenses, so an EUV scanner cannot use refractive optics or a transmissive photomask. Instead it relies on multilayer mirrors built from roughly 40 alternating molybdenum/silicon pairs with a period of about 7 nm, which reflect by constructive interference. Each mirror returns only about 65–70% of the light, and with around ten mirrors in the path only a small fraction of the source power reaches the wafer. The whole optical path therefore runs in vacuum, and the source must be extremely bright.

about.h: How the 13.5 nm light is made
about.p: Production EUV sources use laser-produced plasma (LPP). Tin droplets roughly 30 µm across are fired at around 50,000 per second; a pre-pulse laser flattens each droplet, and a high-power CO2 laser then heats it into a plasma of hundreds of thousands of degrees that emits strongly near 13.5 nm. A multilayer collector mirror gathers the emission, while hydrogen gas keeps scattered tin from coating the collector. Reaching stable source power above about 250 W was the milestone that made high-volume manufacturing practical.

An EUV mask is a mirror rather than a stencil. A low-thermal-expansion glass substrate carries the Mo/Si multilayer, and a patterned absorber, typically tantalum-based, sits on top. Light arrives about 6° off normal and the unabsorbed regions reflect into the projection optics, usually with 4x demagnification. Because the multilayer itself forms the reflecting surface, a buried defect in the stack can print, so blank defectivity is a major cost and yield issue. The oblique illumination also introduces shadowing effects that optical proximity correction (OPC) must account for.

An EUV photon carries about 92 eV versus about 6.4 eV for ArF at 193 nm, so the same dose delivers roughly 14 times fewer photons. With only hundreds to thousands of photons per small feature, Poisson shot noise of about √N causes line-edge roughness, bridges and missing contacts; raising dose helps but cuts throughput. Metal-oxide resists containing tin or hafnium absorb more strongly to ease this. Sub-nanometer mirror roughness scatters light into dark regions as flare, and resist outgassing can deposit carbon on mirrors, so tools use hydrogen cleaning and resists are screened for outgassing.

faq.q: Why does EUV lithography use 13.5 nm instead of an even shorter wavelength?
faq.a: 13.5 nm is where Mo/Si multilayer mirrors reach their best practical reflectivity and where tin plasma emits strongly, so a usable source and optics exist there. Shorter wavelengths would need new mirror materials and sources with acceptable efficiency.

faq.q: What is the difference between EUV and DUV lithography?
faq.a: DUV (deep ultraviolet) lithography, such as ArF at 193 nm, uses transmissive lenses and masks and can run in air or with water immersion. EUV uses 13.5 nm light with all-reflective optics, a reflective mask and a vacuum path, allowing fine patterns in a single exposure that DUV would need multiple patterning to reach.

faq.q: Why is EUV lithography so prone to random defects?
faq.a: Each EUV photon carries much more energy, so far fewer photons make up a given dose and their count fluctuates statistically. These stochastic fluctuations produce roughness, bridging and missing contacts that cannot be removed by better optics alone.

開口数(NA).desc: A value that expresses the range of angles of light a lens can collect. A larger NA gives higher resolution.

about.p: Numerical aperture is defined as NA = n·sinθ, where θ is the half-angle of the cone of light a lens accepts or focuses and n is the refractive index of the medium between lens and image. In air n is about 1, so NA must stay below 1, and practical dry lithography lenses stop somewhat short of that. Filling the gap with a higher-index liquid raises NA beyond 1 at the same angle. NA is a property of the optical system as a whole, distinct from wavelength and from the process factor k1.

about.h: Why larger NA resolves finer features
about.p: A fine periodic pattern diffracts light into orders at angles that grow as the pitch shrinks; an image forms only if the lens captures at least two of them. A larger NA captures steeper orders, so finer pitches survive. This gives the Rayleigh relation R = k1·λ/NA used in lithography and the diffraction limit of about 0.61λ/NA in microscopy, around 200 nm for visible light. Optical discs follow the same scaling: the focused spot shrinks with shorter wavelength and higher NA, which is how Blu-ray stores more than DVD.

Lithography has pushed NA from about 0.3 to 1.35. ArF immersion fills the roughly 1 mm gap between final lens and wafer with ultrapure water, whose index is about 1.44 at 193 nm, allowing NA up to 1.35; with k1 near 0.27 that resolves about 39 nm. EUV at 13.5 nm uses mirror optics, with NA 0.33 in standard scanners and 0.55 in High-NA tools, improving resolution about 1.7 times. High-NA EUV uses different demagnification in the two directions, which halves the exposure field.

about.h: The price: depth of focus and polarization
about.p: Depth of focus follows DOF = k2·λ/NA², so it shrinks with the square of NA, to around 100 nm at the leading edge. Wafer flatness, topography and resist thickness must then be tightly controlled, one reason CMP planarization matters, and scanners measure wafer height for every shot to adjust focus. At high NA, light also arrives at steep angles, about 70° in water at NA 1.35, where TM-polarized beams interfere weakly and lose contrast. Immersion tools therefore use illumination polarized TE relative to the line orientation.

faq.q: Can numerical aperture be greater than 1?
faq.a: Yes, if the space between lens and image is filled with a medium of index above 1. Water immersion at 193 nm allows NA up to about 1.35, whereas a lens working in air is limited to below 1.

faq.q: How does numerical aperture affect depth of focus?
faq.a: Depth of focus scales as λ/NA², so raising NA shrinks it quickly. Doubling NA cuts depth of focus to about a quarter, which tightens flatness and focus-control requirements.

faq.q: What numerical aperture do EUV scanners use?
faq.a: Standard EUV scanners use NA 0.33, and High-NA EUV tools use NA 0.55, which improves resolution about 1.7 times at the same 13.5 nm wavelength.

異方性エッチング.desc: Etching that proceeds only in a particular direction (mainly vertically). Needed to pattern fine features.

about.p: Anisotropy compares lateral and vertical etch rates and is often expressed as A = 1 − (lateral rate / vertical rate): A = 1 is perfectly vertical, A = 0 is isotropic. In practice engineers quote the taper angle, the sidewall angle from the surface, with values near 90° meaning highly anisotropic. Anisotropic etching transfers the mask dimension into the film with almost no undercut, enabling features tens of nanometers wide and several micrometers deep. An isotropic etch would widen each opening by about the etch depth on each side.

An RF-driven wafer electrode charges to a negative DC self-bias, tens to hundreds of volts, because mobile electrons reach it more easily than ions. Positive ions accelerate across the sheath nearly perpendicular to the wafer, especially at low pressure where collisions are rare. Ion bombardment strongly enhances chemical etching where it lands, so feature bottoms etch much faster than sidewalls. Polymer or oxide-like passivation on the sidewalls blocks lateral attack while ions clear it from the bottom. Deep silicon etching often alternates an SF6 etch step with a C4F8 passivation step, the Bosch process, leaving small scallops on the walls.

Too much passivation narrows the bottom and tapers the profile; too little lets radicals and scattered ions bow the sidewalls outward. Ions reflecting off sloped walls or deflected by charging can cause microtrenching at the bottom corners. Etch rate also tends to fall as aspect ratio increases. Taper is chosen per application: features to be filled later often benefit from about 85° for void-free filling, while gates and fins are made nearly vertical to keep top and bottom dimensions equal.

The term also describes orientation-dependent wet etching of single-crystal silicon. Alkaline solutions such as KOH or TMAH etch the (111) planes far more slowly than (100) planes, so on a (100) wafer they form V-grooves and pits with sidewalls at about 54.7° to the surface. This crystallographic anisotropy is widely used in MEMS for cavities and membranes, but it is not the ion-driven vertical anisotropy used for patterning fine circuit features.

faq.q: What is the difference between anisotropic and isotropic etching?
faq.a: Anisotropic etching proceeds mainly in one direction, usually straight down, so the pattern keeps the mask's width. Isotropic etching proceeds equally in all directions and undercuts the mask, as most wet etches do.

faq.q: Can wet etching be anisotropic?
faq.a: Yes, in a crystallographic sense: KOH or TMAH etch silicon much more slowly along (111) planes, producing sloped facets at about 54.7° on (100) wafers. For vertical sidewalls in fine patterns, plasma dry etching is required.

faq.q: What is the Bosch process?
faq.a: It is a deep reactive ion etching method for silicon that alternates short SF6 etch steps with C4F8 passivation steps. It can etch very deep vertical trenches and through-silicon vias, leaving characteristic scalloped sidewalls.

選択比.desc: In etching, the ratio of the etch rate of the target film to that of the mask or underlying film. Higher selectivity means less damage to the underlayer.

about.h: Calculating selectivity and the mask budget
about.p: Selectivity is computed separately for each film that must survive: selectivity to the mask and selectivity to the underlying layer are usually quoted as two different numbers. If oxide etches at 100 nm/min while the resist mask erodes at 20 nm/min, selectivity to the mask is 100 ÷ 20 = 5, so removing 500 nm of oxide consumes 100 nm of resist. After allowing for overetch and for faster erosion at mask edges, the mask should be at least about 150–200 nm thick. When resist cannot provide that margin, a hard mask such as oxide, nitride or a carbon film is used instead.

Etch rate and film thickness vary across the wafer, so when the endpoint is detected some film remains, especially along step sidewalls. An overetch, often 20–50% of the main etch time, clears it, but meanwhile the underlying layer is exposed. Gate etching shows why this matters: polysilicon over a gate dielectric only a few nanometres thick needs selectivity above 100. The usual recipe is a fast main etch that sets the profile, then a switch to gentler, highly selective conditions, typically Cl2/HBr chemistry that forms volatile SiCl4 and SiBr4 while barely attacking oxide.

Selective etching usually exploits a reaction that proceeds on one material and stalls on another. In oxide etching, carbon-rich fluorocarbons such as C4F8 or C4F6 deposit polymer on every surface; oxygen released from the oxide consumes the polymer so oxide keeps etching, while on nitride or silicon the polymer remains and etching stops, which enables self-aligned contacts. Adding oxygen to the gas burns off polymer and lowers selectivity. Wet and gas-phase examples include hot phosphoric acid for nitride over oxide, XeF2 for silicon with selectivity above 1000, and SiGe removal for nanosheet release.

Selectivity and anisotropy often pull against each other. Wet etching easily achieves high selectivity but proceeds isotropically, undercutting the mask by about the film thickness. Dry etching gains directionality from ion bombardment, yet energetic ions also sputter masks and underlayers, so raising ion energy tends to lower selectivity. Process engineers balance gas chemistry, ion energy and passivation to get both. Selectivity is also distinct from uniformity, which describes etch-rate variation across the wafer, and the same concept applies to CMP, where ceria slurries polish oxide tens to over a hundred times faster than nitride.

faq.q: How is etch selectivity calculated?
faq.a: Divide the etch rate of the film being removed by the etch rate of the film that should remain, such as the mask or underlayer. For example, 100 nm/min of oxide against 20 nm/min of resist gives a selectivity of 5.

faq.q: What is the difference between selectivity and anisotropy?
faq.a: Selectivity compares etch rates of different materials, while anisotropy compares vertical and lateral etch rates within the same material. An etch can be highly selective but isotropic, as many wet etches are.

faq.q: Why does adding oxygen to a fluorocarbon etch reduce selectivity?
faq.a: Oxygen burns off the carbon-containing polymer that protects nitride, silicon and resist, and it frees more fluorine radicals. Etching then proceeds on those materials too, and resist erodes faster.

CMP.desc: Chemical mechanical polishing. Planarizes the wafer surface by combining the chemical action of a slurry with mechanical polishing by a pad.

about.h: How chemical mechanical polishing removes material
about.p: In chemical mechanical polishing (CMP), a head holds the wafer face-down against a porous polyurethane pad on a rotating platen roughly 70 to 80 cm across while slurry flows between them. The slurry chemistry converts the film surface into a softer layer, such as an oxidized metal or hydrated oxide, and abrasive particles tens to over a hundred nanometers in size, together with the pad, wipe it away. Removal follows Preston's equation: rate = k × pressure × relative velocity. Raised features carry more local pressure and polish faster, which is why the surface flattens.

about.h: Where CMP is used in a chip flow
about.p: Advanced logic uses dozens of CMP steps. Shallow trench isolation (STI) oxide is polished with ceria slurry down to a silicon nitride stop, with oxide-to-nitride selectivity of tens to over 100. Tungsten plugs need an oxidizer such as hydrogen peroxide to soften the metal. Copper wiring cannot be dry-etched because copper halides are not volatile, so it is made by damascene: copper fills trenches and CMP removes the excess in stages, bulk copper first, then the Ta/TaN barrier. Global flatness also keeps each level within a lithographic depth of focus of about 100 nm.

CMP results depend on layout. Dishing is the dish-shaped recess that forms in wide metal lines and pads, where the soft metal at the center is polished below the surrounding dielectric; it deepens with width and raises line resistance. Erosion is the thinning of both metal and dielectric across dense arrays of narrow lines. Because dense regions polish more slowly than sparse ones, designers cap line widths, slot wide lines and insert electrically inactive dummy fill so that pattern density, and therefore post-CMP thickness, stays uniform.

Endpoint detection watches platen motor torque or the optical reflectance seen through a window in the platen, which change when the underlying film appears; eddy-current sensors track metal thickness. A diamond conditioner continuously dresses the pad to stop glazing, and multi-zone heads with about 5 to 10 pressure zones plus a retaining ring tune removal from center to edge. Scratches come mostly from agglomerated slurry particles, so slurry is filtered. Afterwards wafers move, still wet, to brush scrubbing and chemical cleaning so dried particles cannot bond to the surface.

faq.q: What does CMP stand for in semiconductor manufacturing?
faq.a: CMP stands for chemical mechanical polishing, also called chemical mechanical planarization. It flattens the wafer surface using a slurry that chemically softens the film and a pad and abrasive particles that mechanically remove it.

faq.q: What is the difference between dishing and erosion in CMP?
faq.a: Dishing is the recess that forms at the center of a single wide metal line or pad because the metal polishes faster than the dielectric around it. Erosion is the overall loss of both metal and dielectric thickness across a dense array of fine lines.

faq.q: Why is copper wiring made with CMP instead of etching?
faq.a: Copper does not form volatile compounds with the halogen gases used in plasma etching, so it cannot be patterned cleanly by dry etching. Instead, trenches are etched in the dielectric, filled with copper, and CMP removes the copper outside the trenches.

RCA洗浄.desc: A cleaning method that removes particles and organics with SC-1 (ammonia and hydrogen peroxide) and metal contamination with SC-2 (hydrochloric acid and hydrogen peroxide).

ダマシン法.desc: A method of forming interconnects by etching trenches in an insulating film, filling them with metal, and removing the excess metal by CMP. Used for copper wiring.

about.h: Why copper needs a damascene flow
about.p: Aluminum interconnects were patterned subtractively: deposit a metal film, then dry-etch it through a resist mask. Copper does not form volatile halides at practical etch temperatures, so it cannot be plasma-etched the same way. The damascene process reverses the order. The pattern is etched into the insulating film first, copper fills the openings, and chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) removes the excess, leaving metal only where the trenches were. The name comes from the inlay craft associated with Damascus, where gold or silver was set into grooves cut in metal.

A typical copper damascene sequence is: deposit the interlayer dielectric, often a low-k film; pattern and etch trenches, and for dual damascene also vias; sputter a barrier such as Ta/TaN to stop copper diffusing into the dielectric, followed by a copper seed layer a few to tens of nm thick; electroplate copper to fill the features; anneal to grow the copper grains; then polish away overburden copper and barrier by CMP. A dielectric cap is deposited on top to seal the copper before the next level is built.

In single damascene, vias and lines are formed in separate cycles, each with its own fill and CMP. Dual damascene etches both the via holes and the line trenches into the dielectric and fills them in one plating and one CMP step, saving process steps and removing an interface between via and line. Bottom-up fill during electroplating is essential for both: the plating bath contains a suppressor, an accelerator and a leveler that make copper grow faster at the feature bottom so no voids or seams remain.

CMP removes copper and dielectric at rates that depend on pattern density, so wide lines can dish and dense arrays can erode, thinning the wiring. Layout rules require minimum and maximum metal density, and dummy fill shapes are added to even it out. As line widths shrink, the barrier, which conducts poorly, occupies a larger share of the cross-section, and electron scattering at surfaces and grain boundaries raises copper resistivity, so narrow lines get disproportionately more resistive. Electromigration reliability also depends strongly on the quality of the cap interface.

faq.q: Why is copper wiring made with the damascene process instead of etching?
faq.a: Copper does not form volatile etch products at practical temperatures, so it cannot be patterned by plasma etching like aluminum. Etching the dielectric, filling with copper and polishing off the excess avoids etching copper at all.

faq.q: What is the difference between single and dual damascene?
faq.a: Single damascene forms vias and lines in separate fill and CMP cycles, while dual damascene etches both into the dielectric and fills them with copper in a single plating and CMP step.

faq.q: What is the barrier layer for in copper damascene?
faq.a: A thin barrier such as Ta/TaN keeps copper from diffusing into the dielectric and silicon, where it would cause leakage and device failure, and it also helps adhesion.

Low-k材料.desc: An interlayer dielectric with a low dielectric constant. It lowers the capacitance between wires, reducing signal delay and power consumption.

ワイヤボンディング.desc: A method of connecting the chip's bond pads to a lead frame or substrate with thin wires of gold, copper or similar metals.

about.p: In thermosonic ball bonding, the wire passes through a fine ceramic tube called a capillary. An electric spark melts the wire tip into a ball about twice the wire diameter, which is pressed onto the chip's bond pad with heat (roughly 150–200 °C), force and ultrasonic vibration to form the first bond. The capillary then draws a loop to the lead frame or substrate, where it presses the wire flat into a stitch, the second bond, and tears it off ready for the next ball. Because a ball has no orientation, wires can run in any direction.

Bonding wires are typically 15–50 µm in diameter, thinner than a human hair, to match pads only tens of micrometers across. Gold was the traditional choice, but copper has largely displaced it on cost and also conducts electricity and heat better. Copper oxidizes and is harder, so balls are formed under nitrogen–hydrogen gas, palladium-coated wire is common, and parameters are tuned to avoid damaging pads. Power devices use thick aluminum wire of about 100–500 µm, flat ribbons or copper clips, usually joined by wedge bonding, which presses the wire flat from the side.

Bond pads are usually aluminum about 1 µm thick, even on chips with copper interconnects, because aluminum's thin native oxide protects it and it bonds reliably. Excess force or ultrasound, or a hard copper wire, can crack the dielectric or silicon beneath the pad, a defect called cratering, which is a particular concern over mechanically weak low-k films. Probe marks left by wafer test must not spoil the bonding area. Over long high-temperature service, gold–aluminum intermetallics grow at the ball bond and can form voids if the joint is poorly controlled.

Wire bonding remains the most widely used chip interconnect by unit volume because the equipment is inexpensive and routing is flexible. Its limits are that connections sit only around the die edge and each wire adds resistance and inductance, a rule of thumb being about 1 nH per millimeter. Flip-chip places bumps across the whole die face for more I/O and shorter paths. Stacked packages for NAND flash and DRAM still wire-bond staircase-offset dies, sometimes more than 16, while very high bandwidth stacks use TSVs or hybrid bonding.

faq.q: Why is copper wire replacing gold wire in wire bonding?
faq.a: Copper is far cheaper than gold and has better electrical and thermal conductivity. Its drawbacks, easier oxidation and greater hardness, are handled with forming gas during ball formation, palladium-coated wire and carefully tuned bonding conditions.

faq.q: What is the difference between ball bonding and wedge bonding?
faq.a: Ball bonding melts the wire tip into a ball and bonds it with heat, force and ultrasound, so the wire can leave in any direction; it is used with gold and copper wire. Wedge bonding presses the side of the wire flat with a wedge tool, fixes the wire direction, and is common with aluminum wire and ribbons.

faq.q: Which end of the wire is bonded to the chip?
faq.a: Normally the ball (first bond) goes on the chip pad because it is compact, and the stitch (second bond) goes on the lead or substrate. The order is sometimes reversed to achieve very low loops in stacked-die packages.

フリップチップ.desc: A mounting method in which the chip is placed face down and connected directly to the substrate with bumps. Short connections make it suitable for high pin counts.

BGA.desc: Ball grid array. A high-pin-count package with solder balls arranged in a grid on its underside.

about.p: A ball grid array places the die on a substrate, usually a multilayer organic laminate, connected by wire bonds or flip-chip bumps, then covers it with mold compound or a lid. The substrate's wiring fans signals out to an array of solder balls across the whole underside, typically at a pitch of about 0.4–1 mm. Using the full area rather than just the perimeter gives far more terminals than a QFP of the same size, with shorter, lower-inductance paths. During reflow, surface tension of the molten balls helps pull the package into alignment with its board pads.

In high-pin-count BGAs, many balls carry power and ground rather than signals, and more than half is not unusual. High-performance chips can draw over 100 A, and spreading that current across many parallel balls lowers resistance and inductance, limiting IR drop and supply noise. Balls under the die can also conduct heat into the board. The dense array has a cost on the board side: escaping signals from inner rows requires multilayer printed circuit boards with vias between pads, and fine-pitch arrays may need finer board features.

Because the joints are hidden under the package, they cannot be inspected visually. X-ray imaging reveals bridges, missing balls and voids, and X-ray CT reconstructs a three-dimensional view that separates overlapping structures. Reliability concerns differ by use. Temperature cycling fatigues joints because package and board expand at different rates. In phones, drop shock can crack joints or the brittle intermetallic layer at the pad, so board-level drop tests are emphasized, and underfill is often added to reinforce the joints.

An LGA uses flat lands in the same grid instead of balls, so it can sit in a socket with spring pins, as with many PC processors, or be soldered with paste printed on the board. QFP and SOP use gull-wing leads at the edges, easy to inspect but limited in pin count, and QFN has exposed pads under its edges with a central thermal pad. A CSP shrinks the package to no more than about 1.2 times the die area, often with BGA-style balls. Inside advanced packages, microbumps at tens of micrometres and hybrid bonding go far finer than BGA balls.

faq.q: What is the difference between BGA and LGA?
faq.a: A BGA has solder balls on its underside, while an LGA has flat lands in the same grid. LGAs are often used with sockets that press spring contacts onto the lands, allowing replacement, and give a lower mounted height.

faq.q: How are BGA solder joints inspected?
faq.a: Since the joints are hidden under the package, they are inspected with X-ray imaging, and X-ray CT when a 3D view is needed to find voids, bridges or cracks.

faq.q: What is the typical ball pitch of a BGA?
faq.a: Package-to-board BGAs typically use pitches of about 0.4–1 mm. Finer connections inside packages use microbumps with pitches of tens of micrometres.

バーンイン.desc: A test that operates products under stress such as high temperature and high voltage to remove units prone to early failure before shipment.

about.p: Some chips pass every electrical test at time zero yet contain latent defects: a thin spot in a gate oxide, a marginal via, a particle bridging two lines, or contamination. Under normal use these weak parts fail early, producing the high, falling failure rate of the infant-mortality period at the start of the bathtub curve. Burn-in deliberately accelerates those failures in the factory so the weak units can be identified and removed, leaving a shipped population whose failure rate is already in the low, nearly constant random-failure period.

Parts are loaded onto burn-in boards inside ovens and operated for hours to tens of hours at around 125 °C with supply voltage set above nominal. Temperature accelerates thermally activated failure mechanisms roughly following the Arrhenius relation, and elevated voltage stresses dielectrics, so a short burn-in emulates a much longer period of field use. In static burn-in the device is only biased, while dynamic burn-in toggles internal nodes with test patterns so that more of the circuit is stressed. Conditions are chosen so that good parts lose only a small fraction of their wear-out lifetime.

about.h: Where it fits in the test flow
about.p: A typical flow is wafer test, assembly, final test and shipment. Burn-in is usually inserted around final test, followed by a post-burn-in electrical test that catches the units that failed under stress. Wafer-level burn-in, done before dicing, is used when bare known-good dies are needed for multi-chip packages. Because burn-in costs oven time, boards and floor space, it is applied mainly to high-reliability products such as automotive and server parts, while other products may rely on shorter elevated-voltage stress tests and statistical reliability data.

about.h: Not to be confused with display burn-in
about.p: In displays, burn-in means something different: permanent image retention when a static image is shown for a long time. OLED pixels emit their own light and age with accumulated current, so pixels that stay bright, such as a status bar, dim relative to their neighbors and leave a ghost image. Inorganic micro-LED displays are promoted partly because they do not suffer this effect. Semiconductor burn-in is a deliberate screening test, while display burn-in is an unwanted aging artifact.

faq.q: Why is burn-in done at high temperature and voltage?
faq.a: Most early-failure mechanisms, such as defective oxides and weak interconnects, are accelerated by heat and electric field. Stressing at around 125 °C and above-nominal voltage makes latent defects fail within hours instead of months in the field.

faq.q: Does burn-in shorten the life of good chips?
faq.a: It consumes a small part of their life, but the stress level and duration are chosen so that wear-out still begins well after the intended service life. The benefit of removing infant-mortality failures outweighs this small loss.

faq.q: What is the bathtub curve?
faq.a: It is a plot of failure rate versus time with three periods: a high, decreasing early-failure rate, a low and nearly constant random-failure rate, and a rising wear-out rate. Burn-in is used to get past the first period before shipment.

DFT(テスト容易化設計).desc: A design approach that builds test features such as scan chains and BIST into the circuit in advance.

about.p: Manufacturing test looks for physical defects, usually modeled as faults such as a node stuck at 0 or stuck at 1. Detecting a stuck-at-0 fault requires driving that node to 1 from the chip's inputs (controllability) and then propagating the resulting difference to an output where the tester can see it (observability). Deep inside a large sequential design, many nodes are almost impossible to reach from the pins, so test patterns become enormous and coverage stays poor. Design for testability (DFT) adds structures that raise both properties so faults can be detected with far fewer patterns.

Scan design replaces each flip-flop with a scan flip-flop that has a multiplexer at its input. In test mode a scan-enable signal links the flip-flops into long shift registers called scan chains. The tester shifts a pattern in, switches to functional mode for one or a few capture clocks so the combinational logic responds, then shifts the captured values out while shifting the next pattern in. Because every flip-flop is now directly settable and readable, testing the sequential circuit reduces to testing combinational logic, and automatic test pattern generation (ATPG) tools can reach high fault coverage.

Built-in self-test (BIST) moves pattern generation onto the chip. Memory BIST runs march algorithms that write and read address sequences to find stuck, coupling and address-decoder faults in embedded SRAM, and its results can drive redundancy repair. Logic BIST uses a linear feedback shift register (LFSR) to generate pseudo-random patterns and compacts responses into a signature in a multiple-input signature register (MISR). BIST also allows testing in the field, for example at power-up. Boundary scan, standardized as IEEE 1149.1 (JTAG), places scan cells at the I/O pins to test board-level connections.

DFT is not free. Scan multiplexers add area and a little delay to every flip-flop, extra routing is needed for scan chains, and shifting patterns can toggle far more nodes than normal operation, so test power and IR drop must be checked. Test time on expensive automatic test equipment drives cost, which is why on-chip test compression is widely used. DFT should not be confused with design for manufacturability (DFM), which shapes layouts, for example with redundant vias and relaxed spacing, so that chips yield well in the first place.

faq.q: What does DFT stand for in chip design?
faq.a: In chip design and test, DFT means design for testability: adding scan chains, built-in self-test and similar structures so manufactured chips can be tested efficiently. The same letters also stand for the discrete Fourier transform in signal processing and density functional theory in materials simulation.

faq.q: What is a scan chain?
faq.a: A scan chain is a set of flip-flops connected as a shift register in test mode, so the tester can load any internal state and read out the state after a capture clock. It makes internal logic controllable and observable through a few pins.

faq.q: What is the difference between scan testing and BIST?
faq.a: Scan testing relies on external test equipment to supply patterns through scan chains and compare results. BIST generates patterns and checks responses with on-chip circuits, so it needs little tester support and can also run in the field.

歩留まり.desc: The proportion of good products to the total produced. A key factor in semiconductor manufacturing cost.

about.p: Semiconductor yield is usually tracked as a chain of stages. Line yield is the fraction of wafers that survive the fab without being scrapped. Die yield, measured at wafer probe test, is the fraction of dies on a wafer that work electrically. Assembly and final-test yields cover packaging and the last screening. Overall yield is roughly the product of these numbers, so a few percent lost at each stage compounds. Because the cost of processing a wafer is nearly fixed, the number of good dies per wafer directly sets the cost of each sellable chip.

Random defects such as particles land on the wafer more or less independently of the circuit layout. A simple Poisson model gives die yield Y = exp(−A·D0), where A is die area and D0 is defect density. With D0 = 0.1 cm⁻², a 1 cm² die yields about 90 percent, but a 4 cm² die only about 67 percent. This is why large SoCs are expensive and why splitting a design into smaller dies that are tested before packaging is attractive. Real fabs use refined models that account for defect clustering, but the trend is the same.

In scaled chips a particle only tens of nanometres across, comparable to wire spacing, can short or open a circuit, and trace metal or organic contamination raises leakage or shifts threshold voltage. Process non-uniformity causes losses that cluster in regions, often at the wafer edge: uneven etch rate, CMP thickness that varies with pattern density, or slip dislocations from thermal stress. Engineers separate random defects from systematic ones, such as layout-sensitive patterns, because the cures differ: cleaner processing for the first, design and process tuning for the second.

Fabs clean wafers before and after many steps, monitor defect counts with inspection tools, and record every wafer's laser-scribed ID so that failures can be traced to a specific tool or step. Wafer maps that combine wafer ID with die location reveal spatial signatures pointing to the cause. Design for manufacturability (DFM) helps too, for example dummy fill that evens out pattern density for CMP. Memories add redundancy: DRAMs carry spare rows and columns, and faulty addresses are rerouted to them through fuses or antifuses, even after packaging with post-package repair.

faq.q: How do you calculate die yield from defect density?
faq.a: The simplest estimate is the Poisson model Y = exp(−A·D0), with A the die area and D0 the defect density per unit area. More realistic models, such as negative-binomial ones, account for defects that cluster and predict somewhat higher yield for large dies.

faq.q: Is sputter yield the same as manufacturing yield?
faq.a: No. Sputter yield is a physics term for the number of target atoms ejected per incident ion during sputtering, typically about 0.5 to 3 for argon ions at a few hundred eV, and has nothing to do with the fraction of good chips.

faq.q: Why does yield matter so much for chip cost?
faq.a: Processing a wafer costs roughly the same whether its dies work or not, so the cost of each good chip is the wafer cost divided by the number of good dies. Lower yield therefore raises unit cost directly.

バスタブ曲線.desc: A curve showing how the failure rate changes over time. It consists of the early-failure, random-failure and wear-out periods and is shaped like a bathtub.

エレクトロマイグレーション.desc: The movement of metal atoms in interconnects caused by electric current. It creates voids and hillocks that lead to open or short circuits.

about.h: The electron wind and where damage forms
about.p: Conduction electrons scatter off metal ions and transfer momentum, pushing atoms in the direction of electron flow, which is opposite to conventional current. Atoms travel mostly along fast diffusion paths: grain boundaries in aluminum and the top interface between copper and its dielectric cap in copper. Damage appears where this atomic flux is interrupted, such as at a via bottom blocked by the barrier metal. Atoms leave the upstream side without replacement and a void forms, raising resistance or opening the line, while atoms pile up downstream as hillocks that can crack the dielectric and short to a neighboring line.

Black's equation, MTTF = A·J⁻ⁿ·exp(Ea/kT), says median lifetime falls with current density J, with n typically about 2, and falls exponentially with temperature. Reliability tests therefore stress lines at high current density and temperatures around 300 °C, then extrapolate to use conditions. Failure times follow a lognormal distribution, and because a chip holds hundreds of millions of wires, the design target is the time when a tiny fraction, such as 0.1 ppm, has failed. This sets per-wire current-density limits on the order of MA/cm².

about.h: Materials and structures that resist it
about.p: Adding about 0.5% copper to aluminum puts copper at grain boundaries and slows aluminum transport by an order of magnitude or more. Copper wiring, with resistivity about 1.7 µΩ·cm versus about 2.7 µΩ·cm for aluminum and a higher melting point, improved electromigration resistance further. Because copper moves mainly along its top surface, the dielectric cap (SiCN or SiN) and selective metal caps such as cobalt govern lifetime. A bamboo grain structure helps aluminum greatly but is not enough for copper. In short lines the Blech effect applies: back-stress stops net transport when current density times length is below a critical value.

Designers add redundant vias, widen metal around vias, and run electromigration analysis together with IR-drop analysis at sign-off. Self-heating in FinFET and SOI devices raises nearby wire temperature and speeds failure. In flip-chip solder bumps, current crowding at the trace-to-bump corner nucleates voids, one reason copper pillars are favored. Electromigration should not be confused with stress migration, where voids form from thermal stress without current, or with ion migration, where moisture lets metal ions grow dendrites between biased electrodes on boards.

faq.q: What is the difference between electromigration and stress migration?
faq.a: Electromigration is driven by current, as electrons push metal atoms along the wire. Stress migration forms voids without any current, as atoms move to relieve tensile stress left by thermal mismatch, and it is worst around 150–250 °C.

faq.q: Why does copper resist electromigration better than aluminum?
faq.a: Copper has a higher melting point, so its atoms are less mobile at operating temperatures, giving an order of magnitude or more improvement in lifetime. Its lower resistivity also means less heating for the same current.

faq.q: What is the Blech effect?
faq.a: In short wires, atoms pushed toward one end build up a stress gradient that drives a backflow. When the product of current density and line length is below a critical value, this backflow cancels the electron wind and the line does not degrade.

論理合成.desc: The design step that converts a circuit described in RTL into a netlist made of gates from a cell library.

about.p: Synthesis takes three inputs: RTL in a hardware description language, a cell library describing each gate's function, timing, area and power, and constraints such as clock periods and I/O delays, usually in SDC format. The tool first translates the RTL into generic logic, inferring registers, multiplexers and arithmetic operators. It then optimizes the Boolean logic independently of technology, maps it onto library cells, and finally sizes, buffers and restructures paths to meet the constraints. The output is a gate-level netlist plus timing, area and power reports.

Synthesis turns code into circuits, not instructions, so every block runs concurrently. An always @(posedge clk) block becomes edge-triggered flip-flops. A combinational block that does not assign an output on every branch, such as an if without else, forces the tool to infer a latch to hold the old value. Synthesis ignores sensitivity lists, so an incomplete list makes simulation disagree with the gates; @(*) avoids this. Delays such as #10 and testbench tasks such as $display are simulation-only and are ignored.

The same RTL can yield very different netlists. A tight clock pushes the tool toward larger, faster cells, low-threshold-voltage cells and parallel structures, such as a carry-lookahead adder in place of a ripple-carry one, increasing area and leakage; a relaxed clock lets it minimize area. False paths and multicycle paths tell the tool where not to spend effort. Wrong constraints are dangerous: a design can pass every tool check yet fail in silicon. Because wire delays are only estimated before layout, physically aware synthesis uses placement information to improve correlation.

A typical flow runs specification, RTL design, logic synthesis, place and route, parasitic extraction, and signoff timing analysis before tape-out. High-level synthesis (HLS) sits above it, generating RTL from C or C++ by scheduling operations into clock cycles; logic synthesis then turns that RTL into gates. Formal equivalence checking proves the netlist implements the same logic as the RTL without simulation. Scan insertion for testing is commonly done during or right after synthesis. For FPGAs, synthesis maps logic onto lookup tables and flip-flops rather than standard cells.

faq.q: What is the difference between logic synthesis and high-level synthesis?
faq.a: High-level synthesis converts C or C++ algorithm descriptions into RTL, deciding which clock cycle each operation runs in. Logic synthesis takes RTL and converts it into a gate-level netlist of library cells.

faq.q: Why does synthesis create an unintended latch?
faq.a: If a combinational block leaves an output unassigned on some path, the output must remember its previous value, and a latch is the only way to do that. Assigning a default value or covering every case removes it.

faq.q: What are the inputs and outputs of logic synthesis?
faq.a: Inputs are the RTL, a cell library and timing constraints (typically SDC). The output is a gate-level netlist with reports on timing, area and power.

STA(静的タイミング解析).desc: A method that calculates the delay of every path in a circuit without test patterns and checks that timing constraints are met.

about.p: Static timing analysis breaks a synchronous design into timing paths, mainly from one flip-flop to the next. For each path it adds cell delays, interpolated from characterized library tables indexed by input transition time and output load, and wire delays, giving the data arrival time. It compares this with the required time set by the clock edge and the capturing flip-flop's setup or hold requirement. Slack is required minus arrival; negative slack is a violation. No test vectors are needed, so every path is covered, but logical correctness must still be verified by simulation.

about.h: Constraints tell STA what to check
about.p: The tool needs timing constraints, typically in SDC format: clock periods and waveforms, input and output delays, and exceptions. A false path excludes a connection that can never be exercised, such as one blocked by mutually exclusive select signals. A multicycle path gives a path N cycles for setup, and normally a hold multicycle of N − 1 to move the hold check back to its usual edge. Wrong constraints are dangerous: a chip can pass every tool check yet fail in silicon. Reports summarize results as worst negative slack (WNS) and total negative slack (TNS).

Delays change with process, voltage and temperature (PVT), so analysis is repeated at multiple corners. Setup is usually worst at the slow corner with slow transistors and low voltage; hold is worst at the fast corner. In advanced processes temperature inversion, where low-voltage circuits slow down as they get colder, adds corners. Within one die, on-chip variation (OCV) derating makes the data and launch clock paths slower and the capture clock faster for setup checks. Common path pessimism removal (CRPR) then credits back the impossible slow-and-fast treatment of clock buffers shared by both paths.

A setup violation means a path is too slow: remedies include reducing logic levels, upsizing cells or using faster low-threshold cells, and placing cells closer to shorten wires, or, as a last resort, lowering the clock frequency. A hold violation means a path is too fast, and since the check does not involve the clock period, it is fixed by inserting delay buffers. Graph-based analysis takes the worst transition at every node and can be pessimistic, so path-based analysis (PBA) recomputes failing paths with their real transitions to avoid unnecessary fixes.

faq.q: What is the difference between static timing analysis and timing simulation?
faq.a: STA computes worst-case delays for every path from the circuit structure without input vectors, so its coverage is exhaustive and fast. Timing simulation applies specific vectors and checks behavior, so it only covers the paths those vectors exercise but also verifies function.

faq.q: What is slack in STA?
faq.a: Slack is the required time minus the arrival time for a path. Positive slack means the constraint is met with margin, and negative slack means a violation that must be fixed.

faq.q: What are WNS and TNS in timing reports?
faq.a: WNS (worst negative slack) is the slack of the single worst path, and TNS (total negative slack) is the sum of negative slacks over all violating endpoints. A small WNS with a large TNS means many paths fail by a little.

FOUP.desc: A sealed container for transporting and storing 300 mm wafers.

about.p: A FOUP (front opening unified pod) is a sealed plastic container holding up to 25 wafers of 300 mm diameter in slots, with a front door designed to be opened by equipment. The idea is a minienvironment: wafers are exposed only inside the FOUP and inside tools, so the extreme cleanliness is needed in those small volumes rather than across the whole fab. Dimensions, the door mechanism and mounting features are standardized, so a FOUP fits any vendor's tool. A related front-opening shipping box (FOSB) is used to ship wafers between companies.

A 300 mm wafer 775 µm thick weighs about 128 g (π × (15 cm)^2 × 0.0775 cm × 2.33 g/cm^3), against about 53 g for a 200 mm wafer. A loaded FOUP totals around 8 kg, too heavy and too valuable to carry by hand all day without drop and particle risk. Fabs therefore use an automated material handling system (AMHS) whose core is overhead hoist transport (OHT): vehicles running on ceiling rails lift FOUPs and lower them onto tool load ports, freeing floor space. Large fabs run hundreds of vehicles or more.

At each tool, the FOUP sits on a load port within the EFEM (equipment front end module). The load port unlatches and removes the door, and a robot moves wafers between FOUP and process chamber, all inside a space kept clean by a fan filter unit (FFU). Wafers therefore never meet room air between steps. When processing ends, wafers return to the FOUP, the door closes, and the OHT carries the pod to the next tool or to a stocker.

about.h: Nitrogen purge and the SMIF predecessor
about.p: Air sealed in a FOUP still contains oxygen and moisture, which can oxidize wafer surfaces and deposit molecular contamination while lots wait between steps. Purging FOUPs with nitrogen lowers both and also prevents gases outgassing from freshly etched wafers from building up and contaminating the others, a concern that grows in advanced processes. In the 200 mm era the SMIF (standard mechanical interface) pod served the same minienvironment purpose: a sealed pod around a separate cassette that opened downward into the tool. The FOUP merged cassette and pod into one front-opening box.

faq.q: What does FOUP stand for?
faq.a: Front opening unified pod: a sealed, front-opening container that carries and stores up to 25 wafers of 300 mm diameter between tools.

faq.q: How heavy is a FOUP full of wafers?
faq.a: About 8 kg with 25 wafers of 300 mm, each wafer being roughly 128 g, which is why fabs move FOUPs with overhead hoist transport.

faq.q: What is the difference between a FOUP and a SMIF pod?
faq.a: A SMIF pod, used mainly with 200 mm wafers, encloses a separate cassette and opens from the bottom. A FOUP integrates the cassette into the pod and opens from the front.

SDS(安全データシート).desc: A document describing the hazards of a chemical, how to handle it, first-aid measures and more.

ファウンドリ.desc: A company or business model that specializes in manufacturing semiconductors designed by other companies.

about.p: A foundry manufactures wafers from circuit layouts supplied by its customers, who own the designs and sell the finished chips. The customer submits layout data, photomasks are made from it, and the foundry runs the wafers through front-end and back-end-of-line processing, measures test structures in a wafer acceptance test (WAT) to confirm parameters such as threshold voltage and sheet resistance, and ships the wafers. Probe testing, dicing and packaging may be done by the foundry or by an outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) company. A pure-play foundry sells no chips of its own, so it never competes with its customers.

Designers cannot target a process without knowing its rules, so the foundry supplies a process design kit (PDK). It contains the design rules, SPICE models for transistors and passive devices including variation models, rule decks for design rule checking (DRC) and layout versus schematic (LVS), parasitic extraction data, and layouts of basic devices. Standard-cell libraries, memory compilers and interface IP may come from the foundry or third parties. The PDK is the contract: a design that passes its checks is expected to be manufacturable and to behave as the models predict.

A leading-edge fab costs so much that few companies can fill one with their own products, and a foundry spreads that cost across many customers. The same idea applies to prototyping. A multi-project wafer (MPW), or shuttle, places designs from several customers on one mask set and wafer run, so they share mask and processing costs, which for advanced-node mask sets alone can reach tens of millions of dollars. Each participant receives only a small number of chips, enough for evaluation but not production, which makes MPWs popular with universities and startups.

These four business models divide the industry's work. A fabless company designs and sells chips but owns no fab and relies on foundries. An integrated device manufacturer (IDM) both designs and manufactures its own products, and some IDMs also offer foundry services. A foundry manufactures for others, and an OSAT packages and tests. The pure-play foundry model was established in 1987, and today leading-edge logic manufacturing is heavily concentrated in Taiwan, which is why governments elsewhere treat foundry capacity as a supply-chain risk.

faq.q: What is the difference between a foundry and a fabless company?
faq.a: A fabless company designs and sells chips without owning manufacturing plants, while a foundry owns fabs and manufactures chips designed by other companies. The two models depend on each other.

faq.q: What is a pure-play foundry?
faq.a: A pure-play foundry only manufactures chips for customers and sells no chip products of its own. This avoids competing with the companies whose designs it builds, which helps earn their trust.

faq.q: What does a foundry provide to chip designers?
faq.a: Mainly a process design kit (PDK) with design rules, device models, verification rule decks and basic device layouts, often together with cell libraries and IP. Designers use it to make layouts the foundry can manufacture.

ファブレス.desc: A company model that owns no fabrication plant and focuses on designing and selling semiconductors.

about.h: How a fabless company builds chips
about.p: A fabless company owns no wafer fabrication plant. It specifies the product, writes and verifies the register-transfer-level (RTL) design, and completes physical design using the foundry's process design kit (PDK), commercial electronic design automation (EDA) tools and often licensed IP blocks. The finished layout is taped out to a foundry, which manufactures the wafers; an outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) company, or increasingly the foundry, packages and tests the chips. The fabless company then sells the product, so its value lies in architecture, circuit design, software and customer relationships rather than in manufacturing.

A leading-edge fab requires enormous investment and keeps getting more expensive each generation, and one company's products often cannot keep such a fab fully loaded. Consolidating manufacturing at specialized foundries lets many customers share the equipment and keep utilization high, while design companies avoid the capital burden. This lowered the barrier to entry, so even young companies can bring leading-edge chips to market. Typical fabless products include smartphone systems-on-chip (SoCs), GPUs, communication and networking chips. Some integrated device manufacturers moved toward this model by selling or closing fabs.

An integrated device manufacturer (IDM) designs, fabricates, packages and sells its own chips. Having design and process teams in one company makes it easier to co-optimize the two, which matters in memory, power and analog devices where the manufacturing technology itself differentiates the product. Fab-lite companies sit in between: they keep fabs for mature processes and specialty technologies where they have unique strengths, while outsourcing leading-edge products to foundries. The model is common among microcontroller, analog and power semiconductor makers that want to limit capital spending without losing manufacturing know-how.

Without their own fabs, fabless companies depend on foundry capacity, pricing and schedules, and during shortages they compete with other customers for wafer starts. They design within the foundry's rules and device options, with limited ability to customize the process, although large customers work closely with foundries on design-technology co-optimization. Concentration of advanced foundry capacity in a few locations also concentrates supply risk. In exchange they gain flexibility to choose processes per product and can put capital into engineering rather than plants.

faq.q: What does fabless mean in the semiconductor industry?
faq.a: Fabless means a company has no fab, or wafer manufacturing plant, of its own. It designs and sells chips and outsources manufacturing to foundries and packaging and test to OSATs.

faq.q: What is the difference between fabless and IDM?
faq.a: A fabless company only designs and sells chips, relying on outside manufacturers. An IDM, or integrated device manufacturer, does design, manufacturing and sales in-house.

faq.q: What is a fab-lite company?
faq.a: A fab-lite company keeps some fabs for mature or specialty processes while outsourcing its most advanced products to foundries. It is a middle path between fabless and a full IDM.

チップレット.desc: A small chip made for a specific function. Several chiplets are connected inside one package to build a larger system.

TSV(シリコン貫通電極).desc: An electrode that passes through the silicon substrate. It connects stacked chips vertically over a short distance.

about.p: A through-silicon via (TSV) starts as a deep hole etched into the silicon, typically by deep reactive ion etching using the Bosch process, which alternates SF6 etching with C4F8 sidewall passivation to reach aspect ratios around 10. The sidewalls are lined with an insulating oxide, a diffusion barrier and a copper seed layer, and the hole is filled with copper by electroplating. Excess copper is removed by CMP. Finally the wafer is ground from the back, while temporarily bonded to a glass or silicon carrier, until the via tips are exposed. Void-free filling of the deep hole is the hardest step.

TSV diameters range from a few micrometers to over ten micrometers, and the silicon they pass through is thinned to tens of micrometers; HBM DRAM dies, for example, are thinned to around 30 µm so that 8 to 16 of them fit within a fixed stack height. Because the path through the die is so short, a TSV has far less resistance and capacitance than a wire bond loop, and thousands of them can be placed under one die. That density of short vertical links is what makes wide, low-energy interfaces like HBM possible.

Copper expands with temperature about six times as much as silicon (roughly 17 versus 2.6 ppm/K). After the hot steps of fabrication, the mismatch leaves residual stress in the silicon around each TSV, and stress changes carrier mobility, so nearby transistors drift in drive current. Designers therefore reserve a keep-out zone of several micrometers around every TSV in which no sensitive devices are placed. Copper can also expand upward out of the via during annealing, which must be controlled so it does not damage the wiring above.

Wire bonding connects stacked dies around their edges with long loops and is limited to the perimeter. TSVs connect through the die body, which is why they serve 3D DRAM stacks, silicon interposers and logic-on-memory stacks. Monolithic (sequential) 3D integration goes further: it builds a second transistor layer directly on the first and links them with vias only tens of nanometers wide, more than ten thousand times denser than TSV die stacking, but upper-tier processing must stay below about 500 °C.

faq.q: What does TSV stand for in semiconductors?
faq.a: TSV stands for through-silicon via, a copper-filled (or other metal-filled) hole that runs through the thickness of a silicon die or interposer to connect its front and back electrically. It is the vertical wiring used in stacked memory such as HBM and in silicon interposers.

faq.q: Why do TSVs need a keep-out zone?
faq.a: Copper and silicon have very different thermal expansion coefficients, so the silicon around a TSV ends up mechanically stressed after processing. That stress shifts the mobility and current of nearby transistors, so sensitive devices are kept several micrometers away.

faq.q: What is the difference between a TSV and a wire bond?
faq.a: A wire bond is a thin wire looped from a pad on the die edge to the package, while a TSV passes straight through the silicon. TSVs are far shorter and can be placed across the whole die area, giving many more connections with lower resistance and capacitance.

HBM.desc: High Bandwidth Memory. Multiple DRAM dies stacked with TSVs, achieving very high bandwidth through an extremely wide bus.

about.p: High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) gets its performance from an extremely wide interface rather than very fast pins. Through the HBM3 generation each stack has a 1,024-bit data bus, compared with 64 bits for a typical DDR module; HBM4 widens this to 2,048 bits. At 6.4 Gb/s per pin, an HBM3 stack delivers about 819 GB/s, and a processor with several stacks reaches several TB/s. Running many pins at a moderate rate also keeps energy per bit lower than pushing fewer pins to the high per-pin speeds of graphics memory.

A stack consists of 8, 12 or 16 DRAM dies on a base, or logic, die, all connected vertically by through-silicon vias (TSVs) and microbumps. The base die handles signaling to the processor and contains test and repair circuitry. Because the standard fixes the stack height, adding dies means thinning each to around 30 µm and shrinking the bond layers; dies are typically joined by thermocompression bonding, with hybrid bonding emerging. Every die must be a known good die, since eight dies that are each 99% good give only about 92% good stacks.

about.h: Why HBM sits on an interposer
about.p: Several stacks of 1,024 lines each add up to thousands of signals, far more than an organic package substrate with wiring tens of micrometers wide can route. HBM is therefore placed beside the processor on a silicon interposer whose wiring is 1 µm or finer, giving connections only millimeters long. This side-by-side arrangement is called 2.5D packaging, while the DRAM stack itself is 3D. AI packages need interposers larger than one lithography field of about 26 × 33 mm, so the interposer wiring is stitched across adjacent exposure fields.

GDDR, the other memory used with GPUs, takes the opposite approach: individual chips on the circuit board around the processor, each with a narrow interface running above 20 Gb/s per pin. It is cheaper and simpler to assemble but delivers less bandwidth per watt. DDR serves CPU main memory with the largest capacity and lowest cost per bit. HBM costs more and needs advanced packaging, but it is the main answer to the memory wall in AI accelerators, whose large models must stream weights from memory for every computation.

faq.q: What does HBM stand for?
faq.a: In memory, HBM stands for High Bandwidth Memory, a JEDEC-standard stacked DRAM. In ESD testing the same letters mean the human body model, an unrelated test that simulates discharge from a charged person through 100 pF and 1.5 kΩ.

faq.q: What is the difference between HBM and GDDR?
faq.a: HBM stacks DRAM dies and connects them to the processor through a very wide bus on a silicon interposer, while GDDR uses separate chips on the board with narrow but very fast interfaces. HBM gives higher bandwidth and better energy per bit at higher cost.

faq.q: Why is HBM placed so close to the GPU?
faq.a: Each HBM stack needs over a thousand data connections, which can only be routed with the fine wiring of a silicon interposer over a few millimeters. Short, dense connections are what allow the very high bandwidth at moderate per-pin speed.

サンプリング定理.desc: The theorem stating that a signal can be reconstructed if it is sampled at a frequency higher than twice its highest frequency component. Also called the Nyquist-Shannon theorem.

FinFET.desc: A 3D transistor whose channel stands up like a fin and is surrounded by the gate on three sides. It suppresses short-channel effects well.

about.h: Why the gate wraps the fin
about.p: In a planar MOSFET the gate controls the channel only from above, and at short gate lengths the drain field reaches under it, causing leakage and threshold shifts known as short-channel effects. A FinFET stands the silicon up as a narrow fin and wraps the gate over both sidewalls and the top, so the gate reaches the whole fin from three sides. The fin must be thin enough for the two sidewall gates to control its center, roughly half to equal the gate length or less, about 5 to 7 nm in advanced nodes. Even thinner fins suffer from quantum confinement, surface scattering and variability.

Current flows along the gated perimeter, so the effective channel width of one fin is twice the fin height plus the fin width. A fin 50 nm tall and 6 nm wide gives 2 × 50 + 6 = 106 nm, more than three times the width a planar device gets from a 30 nm fin pitch. Because height and width are fixed by the process, designers change drive strength only by changing the number of fins. This width quantization makes fine current ratios in analog circuits and transistor-strength ratios in SRAM cells harder to tune than with planar devices.

about.h: How fins are built and tuned
about.p: Fins are etched into silicon and separated by shallow trench isolation, with flowable CVD often used to fill the narrow gaps between them. Process steps must work on three-dimensional surfaces, which favors conformal techniques such as radical oxidation and plasma doping. Raised source and drain regions are grown epitaxially on the fins to lower resistance, using SiGe for pMOS and phosphorus-doped silicon for nMOS, which also strains the channel. On a standard (100) wafer, the fin sidewalls are (110) planes, which favor hole mobility and penalize electrons, narrowing the usual gap between nMOS and pMOS.

about.h: From planar to FinFET to GAA
about.p: The FinFET concept was published in 1999 by Chenming Hu and colleagues at UC Berkeley. Intel brought it into volume production at its 22 nm generation in 2012 under the name Tri-Gate, and other foundries followed at the 16/14 nm generation, ending the planar era for leading-edge logic. Its successor is the gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet transistor, which stacks thin horizontal silicon sheets, each surrounded by the gate on all four sides. GAA gives stronger electrostatic control and lets designers set sheet width continuously, removing the fin quantization constraint.

faq.q: What is the difference between a FinFET and a planar MOSFET?
faq.a: A planar MOSFET's gate sits only on top of a flat channel, while a FinFET's gate wraps three sides of a vertical fin. The stronger gate control suppresses short-channel leakage and the fin height adds current-carrying width without adding footprint.

faq.q: How do you calculate the effective width of a FinFET?
faq.a: For one fin, the effective width is twice the fin height plus the fin width, because the gate covers both sidewalls and the top. Total width is that value multiplied by the number of fins.

faq.q: What is the difference between FinFET and GAA?
faq.a: A FinFET gate covers three sides of a vertical fin, whereas a gate-all-around transistor surrounds stacked horizontal nanosheets on all sides. GAA offers better electrostatic control and continuously adjustable channel width instead of whole-fin steps.

High-k/メタルゲート.desc: The combination of a high-dielectric-constant gate insulator and a metal gate electrode. It keeps gate capacitance high while suppressing gate leakage.

MEMS.desc: Micro-electro-mechanical systems. Devices that integrate tiny mechanical structures and electronic circuits using semiconductor microfabrication.

about.p: MEMS (micro-electro-mechanical systems) borrow IC fabrication but add steps that free parts to move. Surface micromachining stacks a sacrificial film such as SiO2 under a structural film such as LPCVD polysilicon, then etches the sacrificial layer away to leave beams suspended a few µm above the substrate. Bulk micromachining carves the wafer itself, using KOH etching, which stops on (111) planes at about 54.7°, or deep RIE (the Bosch process) for vertical trenches with aspect ratios above 20. SOI wafers, anodic bonding and wafer-level vacuum sealing complete many devices.

Most MEMS sensors turn motion into a capacitance change. In an accelerometer a spring-suspended proof mass shifts by nanometers or less, changing comb-electrode capacitance by under a femtofarad. A gyroscope vibrates a mass at several to tens of kHz and senses the Coriolis displacement caused by rotation, usually in vacuum to raise Q. Resonant frequency is f = (1/2π)√(k/m), so stiffer springs raise bandwidth but lower sensitivity. Electrostatic actuators produce force proportional to V²/d², and parallel plates snap together (pull-in) after travelling about one third of the gap.

With structures from micrometers to millimeters, surface forces dominate over mass. Capillary forces during release drying, van der Waals forces and humidity can pin parts to the substrate, called stiction, prevented by vapor-phase HF release, supercritical drying, hydrophobic coatings and dimples. Gas trapped in narrow gaps causes squeeze-film damping, which scales inversely with the cube of the gap and is useful in accelerometers but harmful in resonators. Thermomechanical (Brownian) noise grows as the proof mass shrinks, limiting the resolution of very small sensors.

A smartphone contains several MEMS devices: accelerometers, gyroscopes, pressure sensors precise enough to resolve a change of one building floor, and microphones.
