Cars use MEMS accelerometers to trigger airbags and gyroscopes for stability control. Other examples include inkjet print heads, scanning mirrors for LiDAR and projection, silicon oscillators replacing quartz, RF switches, uncooled infrared microbolometers, ultrasonic transducers and MEMS probe cards for wafer test. MEMS are a typical More than Moore technology, often built on 200 mm or smaller wafers with mature equipment.

faq.q: What does MEMS stand for?
faq.a: MEMS stands for micro-electro-mechanical systems: tiny mechanical structures such as springs, membranes and mirrors built with semiconductor microfabrication and combined with electronics. Even smaller nanometer-scale mechanical devices are called NEMS.

faq.q: What is stiction in MEMS?
faq.a: Stiction is the permanent sticking of a movable MEMS part to the substrate or another surface, caused by capillary, electrostatic or van der Waals forces. It is fought with liquid-free release methods, anti-stiction coatings and small contact bumps.

faq.q: How does a MEMS accelerometer measure acceleration?
faq.a: A proof mass on springs lags behind when the package accelerates, changing its gap to fixed electrodes. The resulting capacitance change is converted to an acceleration reading, and at rest the sensor reads about 1 g because of gravity.

エピタキシャル成長.desc: A technique for growing a single-crystal thin film on a single-crystal substrate with the same crystal orientation as the substrate.

about.h: How epitaxy copies the substrate crystal
about.p: In epitaxial growth, atoms arriving at a clean single-crystal surface settle onto lattice sites that continue the substrate's arrangement, extending the crystal upward. The surface must be clean: a native oxide about 1 nm thick or carbon contamination seeds defects such as stacking faults, so silicon wafers are typically baked in hydrogen near 1100 °C to evaporate the oxide as SiO. Growing the same material as the substrate is homoepitaxy; growing a different one, such as SiGe on silicon or GaN on sapphire or SiC, is heteroepitaxy, which must manage lattice and thermal-expansion mismatch.

about.h: Silicon epitaxy chemistry and growth regimes
about.p: Silicon epitaxy by chemical vapor deposition (CVD) uses trichlorosilane, dichlorosilane or silane diluted in a large hydrogen flow, as in SiHCl3 + H2 → Si + 3HCl. Hydrogen carries the precursor, keeps the surface reduced and removes chlorine as HCl; chlorinated chemistries suppress nucleation on oxide, enabling selective growth on exposed silicon only. At lower temperatures the surface reaction limits growth, so the rate follows an Arrhenius dependence and temperature uniformity sets thickness uniformity. At higher temperatures gas transport limits growth and flow uniformity dominates. On 300 mm wafers, lamp-heated single-wafer reactors hold variation to about ±1–2%.

Adding phosphine, arsine or diborane to the gas stream dopes the layer in situ, avoiding implant damage and activation anneals. Because doping changes layer by layer, epitaxy can create transitions within a few nanometers, buried heavily doped layers and even profiles that are lighter at the surface, which thermal diffusion cannot do. A competing effect is autodoping: dopant evaporating from a heavily doped substrate, including its back side and edges, is reincorporated through the gas phase. Sealing the backside with oxide or polysilicon, purging before growth and growing at reduced pressure, which speeds gas diffusion, suppress it.

Epitaxial layers have fewer defects than Czochralski (CZ) wafers and doping independent of the substrate, so they form lightly doped drift layers in power devices and substrates for CMOS image sensors. In FinFETs, raised source/drain crystals of boron-doped SiGe (pMOS) and phosphorus-doped silicon (nMOS), reaching around 10^21 cm^-3, lower resistance and strain the channel, and must grow at about 600–700 °C or lower to respect the thermal budget. SiC epitaxy uses substrates about 4° off-axis so step-flow growth preserves the 4H polytype, and LEDs and lasers depend on epitaxial multilayer stacks.

faq.q: What is the difference between homoepitaxy and heteroepitaxy?
faq.a: Homoepitaxy grows a layer of the same material as the substrate, such as silicon on silicon. Heteroepitaxy grows a different material, such as SiGe on silicon or GaN on sapphire, and must cope with mismatched lattice constants and thermal expansion.

faq.q: What is selective epitaxial growth?
faq.a: Selective epitaxy deposits crystal only on exposed semiconductor surfaces and not on surrounding oxide or nitride. Chlorine-containing chemistries help by suppressing nucleation on the dielectric, and the technique is used for raised source/drain regions.

faq.q: Why use epitaxial wafers instead of ordinary polished wafers?
faq.a: An epitaxial layer has fewer crystal defects than bulk CZ silicon and its doping can be chosen independently of the substrate, for example a lightly doped layer on a heavily doped wafer for power devices.

超純水.desc: Water from which ions, particles and organic matter have been removed to the extreme. Used in large amounts for wafer cleaning, with purity controlled by resistivity and other measures.

about.p: Ultrapure water (UPW) is produced in stages, each targeting a different contaminant. After pretreatment, reverse osmosis removes most dissolved salts, organics and particles. Ion-exchange resins then strip the remaining ions, ultraviolet oxidation breaks down residual organic molecules so they can be removed, and membrane degassing lowers dissolved oxygen. Ultrafiltration near the point of use catches the finest particles. The finished water is kept circulating through the distribution loop rather than standing in pipes, because stagnant water picks up contamination from surfaces and allows bacteria to grow.

Purity is tracked mainly by resistivity, because fewer dissolved ions means lower conductivity. Pure water still contains H+ and OH− from its own dissociation, which sets a theoretical limit of about 18.2 MΩ·cm at 25 °C; semiconductor UPW is kept very close to it, and readings are temperature-compensated to 25 °C. Resistivity is blind to uncharged contaminants, so total organic carbon (TOC), particles, dissolved oxygen and silica are monitored separately at parts-per-billion levels, particles are counted with liquid particle counters, and metals are held at parts-per-trillion levels.

about.h: Where it is used in a fab
about.p: The largest use is rinsing wafers after chemical cleans, and cleaning recurs before and after deposition, etching, implantation, CMP and ashing, on the order of 200 times or more for an advanced chip. UPW also dilutes process chemicals and carries dissolved ozone for room-temperature organic removal. In ArF immersion lithography, a roughly 1 mm film of UPW between the final lens and the wafer, with a refractive index of about 1.44 at 193 nm, lets the numerical aperture reach about 1.35. Any metal it carries would shorten carrier lifetime and degrade gate oxides.

A large fab can consume tens of thousands of tonnes of UPW per day, so water is a design constraint rather than a commodity. Relatively clean rinse water is reclaimed, treated and returned as UPW feed or cooling water to raise the recovery rate, and water availability influences site selection in dry regions. Producing UPW also takes considerable electricity for pumps, membranes and UV lamps, so the UPW plant sits alongside cleanroom air handling and exhaust treatment among the utility systems that dominate a fab's energy use.

faq.q: What is the resistivity of ultrapure water?
faq.a: Close to 18.2 MΩ·cm at 25 °C, which is the theoretical maximum set by water's own dissociation into H+ and OH− ions.

faq.q: Is ultrapure water the same as deionized water?
faq.a: Deionized water has had its ions removed and may be fairly pure, but semiconductor UPW goes further, also removing organics, particles, dissolved gases and silica to parts-per-billion or lower levels.

faq.q: Why can't ordinary pure water be used to rinse wafers?
faq.a: Traces of metals, ions, particles or organics left on the wafer would create leakage, lifetime loss and defects, so rinse water must be cleaner than the surface it is meant to clean.

SIMS(二次イオン質量分析法).desc: A method that sputters a sample with primary ions and mass-analyzes the secondary ions to measure impurity depth profiles with high sensitivity.

about.h: How SIMS measures a depth profile
about.p: Secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) bombards the sample with a focused primary ion beam, typically cesium or oxygen, which sputters away atoms layer by layer. A small fraction of the sputtered atoms leave as ions, and these secondary ions are separated by mass in a magnetic-sector, quadrupole or time-of-flight analyzer. Recording selected masses while the crater deepens gives intensity versus sputter time. Measuring the final crater depth, for example with a stylus profiler, converts time to depth, and reference samples with known implanted doses convert intensity to concentration.

about.h: Sensitivity, the matrix effect and depth resolution
about.p: SIMS is among the most sensitive routine techniques, reaching around parts per billion for favorable elements, far beyond EDX at about 0.1 wt%. The choice of primary beam matters: oxygen enhances positive-ion yields of electropositive elements such as boron, while cesium enhances negative-ion yields of electronegative ones. Ion yields depend strongly on the surrounding material, the matrix effect, so quantification requires standards in the same matrix and profiles near interfaces need care. Depth resolution is limited by ion-beam mixing and crater roughness, so ultra-shallow junctions use low-energy primary beams.

about.h: SIMS vs. spreading resistance and other methods
about.p: SIMS counts all atoms of an element, whether or not they sit on lattice sites and contribute carriers. Spreading resistance profiling (SRP) bevels the sample at a shallow angle and steps probes along the bevel to measure resistance, giving the electrically active carrier concentration versus depth. Comparing the two profiles reveals how much of an implant was activated by annealing. SIMS is destructive because it consumes the measured area, in contrast to non-destructive methods such as X-ray reflectometry for film thickness or scatterometry for dimensions.

SIMS is the standard check for ion-implantation profiles and doses, dopant diffusion after anneals, junction depth, and dopant segregation at interfaces. It also detects contaminants and light elements such as hydrogen, carbon, oxygen and nitrogen in films and at interfaces, which most other techniques cannot quantify at low levels. The depth-profiling mode described here is often called dynamic SIMS; a low-dose variant, often with time-of-flight analyzers, probes only the outermost monolayers for surface contamination and organic residues.

faq.q: Is SIMS a destructive technique?
faq.a: Yes. The primary ion beam sputters away the material being analyzed, leaving a crater, so the measured area cannot be used as product.

faq.q: What is the difference between SIMS and SRP?
faq.a: SIMS measures the total atomic concentration of a dopant regardless of whether it is electrically active. SRP measures the concentration of active carriers, so comparing the two shows the activation fraction.

faq.q: Why does SIMS use cesium or oxygen primary beams?
faq.a: Oxygen raises the yield of positive secondary ions and cesium raises the yield of negative ones, so the beam is chosen to maximize sensitivity for the element of interest, for example oxygen for boron.

CD-SEM.desc: A scanning electron microscope for measuring pattern line widths (critical dimensions). Used for dimensional control after lithography and etching.

フェルミ準位.desc: The energy at which the probability of an electron occupying a state is exactly one half. It lies closer to the conduction band in n-type material and closer to the valence band in p-type.

about.h: What the Fermi level means physically
about.p: The Fermi-Dirac function f(E) = 1/(1 + exp((E − EF)/kT)) gives the probability that a state at energy E holds an electron, and it equals exactly 1/2 at E = EF. A few kT above EF (kT is about 0.026 eV at room temperature) occupation falls off almost exponentially, which is why electron density is n = Nc·exp(−(Ec − EF)/kT) and hole density is p = Nv·exp(−(EF − Ev)/kT). EF is the electrochemical potential of the electrons, so it can sit in the band gap even though no allowed states exist there.

about.h: How doping and temperature move it
about.p: In intrinsic silicon the Fermi level lies about 0.01 eV below midgap, because the conduction band has a larger effective density of states than the valence band. Donors push EF toward the conduction band following Ec − EF ≈ kT·ln(Nc/ND), about 60 mV per tenfold increase in ND; acceptors push it toward the valence band. Above roughly 10¹⁸–10¹⁹ cm⁻³ it enters a band and the material becomes degenerate. Raising temperature increases the intrinsic carrier density and pulls EF back toward midgap, one reason MOSFET threshold voltage falls by about 1–2 mV/°C.

about.h: Fermi level alignment in junctions and MOS
about.p: In thermal equilibrium the Fermi level is flat across any structure, so when two materials with different Fermi levels are joined, charge flows until they line up. The resulting band bending gives the built-in potential of a PN junction and, in a MOS structure, the flat-band voltage set by the metal-semiconductor work-function difference. The work function is the energy from EF to the vacuum level and changes with doping, whereas the electron affinity, measured from the conduction band edge (about 4.05 eV for silicon), does not. An applied voltage V separates the Fermi levels of the two sides by qV.

Under illumination or current injection, electrons and holes are no longer described by one Fermi level. Separate quasi-Fermi levels, EFn and EFp, are used, with n = ni·exp((EFn − Ei)/kT) and p = ni·exp((Ei − EFp)/kT). Their separation sets np = ni²·exp((EFn − EFp)/kT), and in a forward-biased diode or an illuminated solar cell it corresponds to the terminal voltage. Current density is proportional to the gradient of each quasi-Fermi level, so a flat quasi-Fermi level means no net current for that carrier.

faq.q: Why can the Fermi level lie in the band gap where there are no states?
faq.a: The Fermi level is a statistical parameter, the electrochemical potential of electrons, not an occupied state. It only fixes the occupation probability of the states that do exist in the bands above and below it.

faq.q: What is the difference between the Fermi level and the work function?
faq.a: The Fermi level is an energy position, while the work function is the energy needed to move an electron from the Fermi level to the vacuum level. In a semiconductor, doping moves the Fermi level and therefore changes the work function.

faq.q: What is a degenerate semiconductor?
faq.a: It is a semiconductor doped so heavily, roughly above 10¹⁸–10¹⁹ cm⁻³ in silicon, that the Fermi level moves into the conduction or valence band. It then behaves almost like a metal, and simple relations such as np = ni² no longer hold accurately.

順方向バイアス.desc: Applying a positive voltage to the p side and a negative voltage to the n side. The barrier drops and current flows readily. The opposite is reverse bias, under which almost no current flows.

about.p: At equilibrium, a PN junction has a built-in potential barrier, and the diffusion current of majority carriers trying to cross it exactly cancels the drift current pushed back by the junction field, so net current is zero. Forward bias, making the p side positive, opposes the built-in potential and lowers the barrier. Holes from the p side and electrons from the n side then diffuse across in large numbers, becoming injected minority carriers that recombine as they spread. Diffusion now outweighs drift, and current rises exponentially as I ≈ Is(exp(qV/nkT) − 1).

At room temperature kT/q is about 26 mV, so an ideal diode (ideality factor n = 1) needs about 60 mV more forward voltage for each tenfold increase in current, or n × 60 mV in general; the slope of a semilog I-V plot gives n. Because the rise is exponential, a silicon diode seems to switch on at about 0.6–0.7 V at typical small-signal currents, though there is no sharp threshold. At constant current, the forward voltage of a silicon junction falls by roughly 2 mV per °C, a property used for temperature sensing.

Reverse bias raises the barrier and widens the depletion region, leaving only a tiny current of thermally generated minority carriers until breakdown. The dominant capacitance differs as well. Under reverse bias it is the depletion (junction) capacitance. Under forward bias, injected minority carriers stored near the junction create a diffusion capacitance, roughly Cd ≈ τI/(nkT/q), that grows with current and can reach several nanofarads. That stored charge must be removed before a diode or transistor can turn off, which limits switching speed.

A bipolar transistor in the active region has a forward-biased base-emitter junction; in saturation the base-collector junction is forward biased too, giving VCE of only about 0.1–0.2 V but slow turn-off because of stored charge. LEDs emit light when forward-injected carriers recombine radiatively. A forward-biased PIN diode floods its intrinsic layer with carriers, lowering its resistance (conductivity modulation), which makes it useful as an RF switch. Silicon optical modulators that inject carriers under forward bias are efficient but limited by nanosecond carrier lifetimes, so high-speed designs use reverse-biased depletion instead.

faq.q: How do you forward bias a diode?
faq.a: Connect the p side (anode) to the more positive potential and the n side (cathode) to the more negative one, so the applied voltage lowers the junction barrier.

faq.q: Why does current increase exponentially under forward bias?
faq.a: The number of carriers with enough energy to cross the barrier follows a Boltzmann distribution, so lowering the barrier by V multiplies the injected current by about exp(qV/kT).

faq.q: What is the difference between diffusion capacitance and junction capacitance?
faq.a: Junction capacitance comes from the depletion region and dominates under reverse bias. Diffusion capacitance comes from minority carriers stored under forward bias and grows roughly in proportion to current.

内蔵電位.desc: The potential difference across the depletion layer of a PN junction even with no external voltage applied. About 0.6 to 0.8 V in silicon, it forms the barrier that stops further carrier diffusion.

about.p: Before contact, the Fermi level of n-type silicon sits near the conduction band and that of p-type silicon near the valence band. When the two are joined, electrons diffuse from the n side into the p side and holes the other way, leaving behind fixed ionized donors (positive) and acceptors (negative). This depletion-region charge creates an electric field that pushes carriers back, and equilibrium is reached when drift exactly cancels diffusion and the Fermi levels line up. The resulting band bending, divided by the electron charge q, is the built-in potential Vbi.

For a nondegenerate junction, Vbi = (kT/q)·ln(NA·ND / ni²), where NA and ND are the acceptor and donor concentrations and ni is the intrinsic carrier concentration. With kT/q of about 26 mV at room temperature, each tenfold increase in doping adds only about 60 mV, so silicon junctions typically fall between about 0.6 and 0.9 V; NA = ND = 10¹⁷ cm⁻³ gives roughly 0.83 V. Wider-band-gap materials have much smaller ni and hence larger Vbi. Because both Fermi levels stay inside the gap, Vbi stays below the band gap in volts unless both sides are degenerately doped.

Forward bias, with the p side positive, opposes the built-in potential and lowers the barrier to Vbi − V, so injected current rises exponentially. Reverse bias adds to it, and for a one-sided abrupt junction the depletion width is W = √(2ε(Vbi + V)/qN), where N is the lighter doping. The field peaks at the metallurgical junction, and the area under the triangular field profile equals Vbi + V. Since junction capacitance is εA/W, a plot of 1/C² versus reverse voltage is a straight line whose slope gives N and whose voltage intercept gives Vbi.

about.h: Why a voltmeter cannot read it
about.p: Connecting a voltmeter across an unbiased diode reads zero, because the metal–semiconductor contacts at each terminal have their own contact potentials that exactly cancel Vbi around the loop; otherwise an equilibrium device could deliver power. Vbi also differs from the diode forward voltage of roughly 0.6–0.7 V quoted for silicon, which is the bias at which current becomes appreciable and depends on current level and temperature. The same Fermi-level alignment that produces Vbi in a PN junction produces the flat-band voltage in a MOS structure and the barrier in a Schottky contact.

faq.q: Can you measure a PN junction's built-in potential with a voltmeter?
faq.a: No. The contact potentials at the metal leads cancel it, so an unbiased diode reads zero. Vbi is usually inferred from capacitance–voltage measurements instead.

faq.q: How does doping affect the built-in potential?
faq.a: Higher doping on either side raises Vbi, but only logarithmically: a tenfold doping increase adds about 60 mV at room temperature.

faq.q: Is built-in potential the same as the diode forward voltage?
faq.a: No. They are related, but the forward voltage is the applied bias needed for a practical current and is usually somewhat lower than Vbi, varying with current and temperature.

なだれ降伏.desc: A phenomenon in which carriers accelerated by a strong reverse field strike atoms and create new carriers, which multiply in a chain reaction so that a large current flows.

about.p: Under strong reverse bias, electrons and holes crossing the depletion region gain kinetic energy from the field between collisions. When a carrier gains enough energy, a collision with the lattice can break a bond and create a new electron-hole pair, a process called impact ionization. The new carriers are accelerated in turn and can ionize further atoms, so each carrier entering the region produces many. The rate of ionization rises very steeply with field, and in silicon electrons ionize more readily than holes. Breakdown is reached when the multiplication factor grows without bound and current rises sharply at nearly constant voltage.

In a reverse-biased abrupt junction, the field is zero at the depletion edges and peaks at the metallurgical junction, forming a triangle whose area equals Vbi + V. Avalanche begins roughly when the peak reaches the critical field, about 3×10⁵ V/cm in silicon. For a one-sided junction this gives VBR ≈ εEc²/(2qN), so lighter doping on the low-doped side yields higher breakdown voltage. Silicon carbide's critical field is about ten times higher, allowing a much thinner drift layer for the same rating. At junction edges and corners, curvature concentrates the field, so guard rings and field plates are used.

about.h: Temperature dependence and the Zener mechanism
about.p: As temperature rises, stronger lattice vibrations scatter carriers more often, so they need a higher field to gain ionizing energy and the avalanche breakdown voltage increases. This positive temperature coefficient helps spread current evenly, because a hotter spot breaks down later. Zener, or tunneling, breakdown in heavily doped junctions behaves the opposite way, since the bandgap shrinks with temperature and tunneling becomes easier. In silicon diodes, tunneling dominates below about 5 V and avalanche above, so the sign of the temperature coefficient tells you which mechanism is at work.

about.h: When avalanche is useful, and when it destroys
about.p: Avalanche breakdown is not inherently destructive: if current and energy are limited, the junction recovers fully, as in Zener regulators above about 5 V. Avalanche photodiodes bias just below breakdown so each photo-generated carrier is multiplied, giving internal gain, and single-photon avalanche diodes bias above breakdown so one photon triggers a detectable pulse. Power MOSFETs are rated for the avalanche energy they can absorb when switching inductive loads. Damage occurs when the dissipated energy overheats the device or current crowds into a local hot spot.

faq.q: Is avalanche breakdown destructive?
faq.a: Not by itself. A junction in avalanche recovers completely as long as the current and energy are limited; damage comes from excessive power dissipation and local overheating.

faq.q: What is the difference between avalanche breakdown and Zener breakdown?
faq.a: Avalanche breakdown multiplies carriers through impact ionization in moderately doped junctions and has a positive temperature coefficient. Zener breakdown is quantum tunneling across a very thin depletion layer in heavily doped junctions, has a negative temperature coefficient and dominates below about 5 V in silicon.

faq.q: Why does avalanche breakdown voltage increase with temperature?
faq.a: Higher temperature increases lattice scattering, so carriers lose energy more often and need a stronger field to reach the energy required for impact ionization.

能動領域.desc: The state with the base-emitter junction forward-biased and the base-collector junction reverse-biased. A collector current proportional to the base current flows, and it is used for amplification.

アーリー効果.desc: A phenomenon in which raising the collector voltage widens the base-collector depletion layer, narrowing the effective base width and slightly increasing collector current.

about.p: In a bipolar junction transistor (BJT) in the active region, the collector-base junction is reverse biased, and its depletion layer extends partly into the base. Raising the collector voltage widens that depletion layer and shrinks the neutral base width. Collector current is set by minority carriers diffusing across the base, and with a uniformly doped base it is inversely proportional to the neutral base width, so a narrower base gives a steeper carrier gradient and slightly more current. Fewer carriers also recombine in the shorter base, so current gain rises slightly as well.

On the output characteristics, collector current versus collector-emitter voltage, the active-region lines are nearly horizontal but slope slightly upward. Extended backward, they meet near one point on the voltage axis, at -VA, where VA is the Early voltage. A common model is IC = IS exp(VBE/VT)(1 + VCE/VA), which gives an output resistance ro = VA/IC. The maximum voltage gain of a single transistor, gm·ro, equals VA/VT, so a VA of 100 V allows about 4,000 at room temperature. Early voltages of tens to around a hundred volts are common for small-signal npn transistors.

Finite output resistance limits amplifier gain and makes current sources imperfect. In a simple current mirror, the reference transistor is diode-connected and sits at about 0.7 V, while the output transistor may have a much larger collector-emitter voltage; the Early effect then makes the copied current larger by roughly the voltage difference divided by VA. Cascode and Wilson mirrors hold the critical transistor's collector voltage nearly constant, raising output resistance by a factor on the order of the transistor's current gain. In SPICE, the Gummel-Poon model represents the effect with the forward Early voltage parameter VAF.

MOSFETs show a closely analogous effect: increasing the drain voltage shortens the effective channel, so drain current rises in saturation. It is called channel-length modulation and is modeled with a parameter lambda, which plays the role of 1/VA. In both devices, finite output resistance limits intrinsic gain. Device designers raise the Early voltage with heavier base doping, which keeps the depletion layer from intruding into the base, but that lowers current gain. At the extreme, the collector depletion layer reaches the emitter, causing punch-through and loss of transistor action.

faq.q: What is the Early voltage of a transistor?
faq.a: It is the voltage magnitude at which the extended active-region output curves of a BJT intersect the voltage axis, written VA. A larger Early voltage means a flatter curve and higher output resistance, ro = VA/IC.

faq.q: How does the Early effect limit amplifier gain?
faq.a: It gives the transistor a finite output resistance, so the maximum gain of a single stage is gm·ro = VA/VT. For VA around 100 V this is a few thousand, and any load resistance in parallel lowers it further.

faq.q: Is the Early effect the same as channel-length modulation?
faq.a: They are analogous rather than identical. The Early effect narrows the neutral base of a BJT, while channel-length modulation shortens a MOSFET's channel, but both raise output current with output voltage and create finite output resistance.

エミッタ接地回路.desc: An amplifier circuit in which the emitter is the common terminal for input and output. It provides both current gain and voltage gain and is the most widely used configuration.

HBT(ヘテロ接合バイポーラトランジスタ).desc: A bipolar transistor using materials with different band gaps for the emitter and base. Types include SiGe and GaAs-based devices, used in high-frequency amplifiers.

about.p: In an ordinary homojunction bipolar transistor, emitter efficiency requires the emitter to be much more heavily doped than the base, otherwise too many holes flow back from base into emitter. That forces a lightly doped base, which has high resistance and must not be made too thin. In a heterojunction bipolar transistor (HBT), the emitter has a wider band gap than the base, and the band offset blocks hole back-injection by an exponential factor. The base can then be heavily doped and very thin, lowering base resistance and transit time and raising the transition frequency fT and maximum oscillation frequency fmax.

A silicon-germanium (SiGe) HBT keeps a silicon emitter and collector but grows a SiGe base, tens of nanometres thick and doped with boron during low-temperature epitaxy. Grading germanium from near zero at the emitter side to about 20 to 30% at the collector side narrows the band gap progressively, creating a built-in field that speeds electrons across the base. A small amount of carbon limits boron diffusion so the base stays thin. Because it is built on silicon, a SiGe HBT can be integrated with CMOS in BiCMOS processes, with fT reaching hundreds of GHz.

Compound-semiconductor HBTs use emitters such as InGaP or AlGaAs on a GaAs base, or layer stacks on indium phosphide (InP). GaAs HBTs combine good breakdown voltage, high current density and a semi-insulating substrate, which suits them to the power amplifiers in mobile handsets. InP HBTs reach the highest frequencies and are used in very high-speed optical-communication circuits and millimetre-wave research. All are built from epitaxial layer stacks, so base thickness, and thus speed, is set by growth control rather than lithography.

HBT current flows vertically through layers whose thickness is defined by epitaxy, giving high transconductance and current density from a modest footprint. Turn-on voltage is set by band gap, so devices across a wafer match well, and low-frequency 1/f noise is lower than in field-effect transistors, which helps oscillator phase noise. High-electron-mobility transistors (HEMTs) conduct laterally in a two-dimensional electron gas and typically win on noise figure for low-noise receivers. Silicon CMOS wins on integration density and cost but gives lower breakdown voltage at high frequency.

faq.q: Why is SiGe used in the base of an HBT?
faq.a: SiGe has a narrower band gap than silicon, so the Si emitter to SiGe base heterojunction suppresses hole back-injection and allows a heavily doped, thin base. Grading the germanium content also adds an accelerating field, raising speed while staying compatible with silicon processing.

faq.q: What is the difference between an HBT and a conventional BJT?
faq.a: A conventional BJT uses the same material throughout, so emitter efficiency relies on doping ratios. An HBT uses a wider-gap emitter, decoupling emitter efficiency from base doping and enabling much higher frequency operation.

faq.q: Where are GaAs HBTs used?
faq.a: Mainly in RF power amplifiers for mobile phones and other wireless equipment, where their power density, breakdown voltage and efficiency at gigahertz frequencies are valuable.

反転層.desc: A layer formed at the semiconductor surface by the gate voltage, where carriers of the type opposite to the substrate gather. It becomes the MOSFET's channel.

about.p: Consider an n-channel MOS structure on a p-type substrate. A negative gate voltage pulls holes to the surface (accumulation). A small positive voltage pushes holes away and leaves a depletion region of ionized acceptors. At larger positive voltage the bands bend so far that electrons, the minority carriers, gather at the surface. Strong inversion is conventionally defined as the point where the surface potential reaches twice the bulk Fermi potential, so the surface electron density equals the bulk hole density. The gate voltage at that point is the threshold voltage.

about.h: The inversion layer as the MOSFET channel
about.p: In a MOSFET the inversion layer connects the heavily doped source and drain, which supply its carriers almost instantly. Its sheet charge is roughly Cox·(VGS − Vth), so drain current grows with gate overdrive. An nMOS forms an electron inversion layer and conducts when VGS exceeds a positive Vth; a pMOS forms a hole inversion layer in an n-well and has a negative Vth, for example −0.4 V. Electrons have higher mobility than holes, so an nMOS of the same size drives more current.

In a MOS capacitor without source and drain, inversion electrons must be generated thermally, which is slow. In a high-frequency C-V measurement, typically at 1 MHz, the inversion charge cannot follow the signal, so capacitance stays at its minimum: Cox in series with the depletion capacitance at maximum depletion width. In a low-frequency or quasi-static measurement the inversion layer responds and capacitance returns to Cox. The ratio of minimum to maximum capacitance gives the substrate doping.

The inversion layer is only a few nanometers thick and the strong interface field confines carriers in a narrow potential well. Quantum mechanics places the peak of the electron distribution about 1 nm inside the silicon rather than at the interface. This centroid offset adds roughly 0.3–0.4 nm of equivalent SiO2 thickness, lowering gate capacitance and drive current. Together with polysilicon gate depletion, it makes the electrical thickness (CET) larger than the physical equivalent oxide thickness (EOT), which matters more as EOT shrinks.

faq.q: What is the difference between depletion and inversion in a MOS structure?
faq.a: In depletion the gate has pushed majority carriers away, leaving fixed ionized dopants but few mobile carriers. In inversion the bending is strong enough that minority carriers gather at the surface in large numbers, forming a conductive layer of the opposite type.

faq.q: Is the inversion layer the same as the channel?
faq.a: In an enhancement-mode MOSFET, yes: the inversion layer formed under the gate is the conducting channel between source and drain. Below threshold it is too weak to carry significant current.

faq.q: Why does high-frequency C-V stay at minimum in inversion?
faq.a: Without a source and drain, inversion carriers come only from slow thermal generation, which cannot follow a signal around 1 MHz. Only the depletion edge responds, so the measured capacitance stays at its minimum.

短チャネル効果.desc: Phenomena in which, as gate length shrinks, the drain's electric field lowers the threshold voltage and increases off-state leakage current.

サブスレッショルドスイング.desc: The gate voltage needed to change drain current tenfold below threshold. Its theoretical lower limit at room temperature is about 60 mV per decade; the smaller it is, the sharper the on/off switching.

about.h: Where 60 mV per decade comes from
about.p: Below threshold, a MOSFET's drain current is carried by carriers diffusing over the source-channel barrier, and their number follows a Boltzmann distribution, so current rises by a factor of e for every kT/q of surface-potential change. Tenfold needs kT/q × ln 10, about 26 mV × 2.3 ≈ 60 mV at 300 K. The gate does not control surface potential perfectly: it acts through a capacitive divider of gate-oxide capacitance Cox and depletion capacitance Cd, giving S = (kT/q)·ln 10·(1 + Cd/Cox). Only with Cd = 0 does S reach about 60 mV/dec at room temperature, and the limit scales with absolute temperature.

Subthreshold swing ties off-state leakage to threshold voltage. A transistor at zero gate voltage sits roughly Vth/S decades below the current at threshold, so every 60 mV reduction in threshold voltage raises off-current about tenfold even in an ideal device. To keep leakage acceptable, threshold voltage cannot keep falling, and to keep on-current high, supply voltage must stay well above threshold. This is a fundamental reason supply voltages have stopped scaling with transistor dimensions, and why a steeper swing is so valuable.

Ideal long-channel devices approach 60 mV/dec at room temperature. In short-channel planar transistors, the source and drain depletion regions take over part of the channel control, degrading swing to roughly 80–100 mV/dec along with threshold roll-off, drain-induced barrier lowering (DIBL) and higher leakage. FinFETs, which wrap the gate around the channel on three sides, restored about 65–70 mV/dec. Swing describes the slope of log ID versus VGS, while DIBL describes how threshold shifts with drain voltage; both worsen when the gate loses electrostatic control.

Any transistor that turns on by thermionic emission over a barrier cannot switch more steeply than about 60 mV/dec at room temperature. Two research directions try to escape that. Tunnel FETs (TFETs) conduct by band-to-band tunneling between source and channel, so the source's thermal tail does not set the slope. Negative-capacitance FETs add a ferroelectric layer whose negative capacitance internally amplifies the gate voltage. Both have shown steep slopes in research, but low on-current and other practical issues remain unsolved for mainstream logic.

faq.q: Why is the subthreshold swing limited to 60 mV/decade?
faq.a: Subthreshold current follows the Boltzmann distribution of carriers over a barrier, so one decade of current requires at least (kT/q)·ln 10, about 60 mV at room temperature, of surface-potential change.

faq.q: How do you measure subthreshold swing?
faq.a: Plot drain current on a log scale against gate voltage below threshold and take the inverse slope, in millivolts of gate voltage per decade of current.

faq.q: Does subthreshold swing depend on temperature?
faq.a: Yes, the thermal limit is proportional to absolute temperature: about 60 mV/dec at 300 K, larger when hot and smaller at cryogenic temperatures.

ド・モルガンの定理.desc: The rules for transforming logic expressions: NOT (A AND B) equals (NOT A) OR (NOT B), and NOT (A OR B) equals (NOT A) AND (NOT B).

真理値表.desc: A table listing the output for every combination of inputs. It is used to describe the behavior of logic circuits.

組み合わせ回路.desc: A logic circuit whose output depends only on its current inputs. Examples include adders, multiplexers and decoders.

順序回路.desc: A logic circuit that stores state in flip-flops and the like, so its output depends on both inputs and past state. Examples include counters and registers.

負帰還.desc: Returning part of the output to the input with opposite polarity. Gain drops, but it becomes stable, and distortion and bandwidth improve.

about.p: An amplifier with open-loop gain A has a fraction β of its output fed back and subtracted from the input. The closed-loop gain becomes A/(1 + Aβ), and when the loop gain Aβ is much larger than 1 this reduces to about 1/β. Gain is then set by passive parts, such as a resistor ratio, rather than by transistor or op-amp gain, which drifts with temperature, supply voltage and process. The amplifier itself only sees the small error left after subtraction, which is why the two inputs of an op-amp with feedback sit at almost the same voltage (the virtual short).

about.h: What you get in exchange for gain
about.p: The factor (1 + loop gain) is the exchange rate. Gain drops by that factor, and in return sensitivity to changes in A, nonlinear distortion and, when the output voltage is sampled, output impedance all shrink by roughly the same factor. Bandwidth widens: for an amplifier dominated by a single pole, the gain-bandwidth product stays nearly constant, so lowering the closed-loop gain extends the bandwidth in proportion. Depending on whether the feedback is mixed in series or in shunt at the input, input impedance is raised or lowered by the same factor.

Feedback is negative only as long as the loop does not add too much phase shift. If the phase lag around the loop reaches 180 degrees at a frequency where loop gain is still 1 or more, subtraction turns into addition and the circuit oscillates. Designers therefore check phase margin, usually aiming for 45 to 60 degrees or more. Positive feedback is used on purpose where snap action is wanted: comparators with hysteresis, Schmitt triggers, latches and oscillators. Because those circuits do not settle in a linear state, the virtual-short assumption does not apply to them.

Op-amp amplifiers, filters and voltage regulators all rely on an overall feedback loop. Local feedback is just as common: in a discrete bipolar stage, an emitter resistor raises the emitter voltage when collector current increases, which lowers VBE and pulls the current back, stabilizing the bias point against temperature and hFE spread. A bypass capacitor across that resistor removes the feedback at signal frequencies to restore AC gain. Source degeneration in MOSFET stages and phase-locked loops use the same principle.

faq.q: Why does negative feedback reduce amplifier gain?
faq.a: Part of the output is subtracted from the input, so the amplifier only amplifies a small error signal. The closed-loop gain becomes A/(1 + Aβ), which approaches 1/β when the loop gain is large.

faq.q: Can negative feedback make an amplifier oscillate?
faq.a: Yes. If the phase lag around the loop reaches 180 degrees while the loop gain is still at least 1, the feedback becomes positive and the circuit oscillates; adequate phase margin prevents this.

faq.q: What is loop gain in a feedback amplifier?
faq.a: Loop gain is the product Aβ, the gain a signal experiences going once around the feedback loop. The larger it is, the more closely the closed-loop gain approaches 1/β and the more distortion and drift are suppressed.

ボルテージフォロワ.desc: A unity-gain op-amp circuit with the output tied directly to the inverting input. With high input impedance and low output impedance, it is used as a buffer.

about.p: The op-amp output is wired straight to the inverting input and the signal drives the non-inverting input, so the whole output is fed back (feedback fraction 1). With open-loop gain A, the output is Vin × A/(1 + A), within about 1/A of the input, and in phase with it. It is the non-inverting amplifier with gain 1 + R2/R1 taken to its limit: R2 shorted and R1 removed. No resistors are needed, and the gain cannot drop below 1 in this family.

about.h: Why a gain of one is useful
about.p: The follower converts impedance. Its input draws almost no current, while its output can supply current with a low output impedance that the feedback lowers further. Consider a divider of two 10 kΩ resistors across 10 V: unloaded it gives 5 V, but a 10 kΩ load in parallel with the lower resistor pulls the node down to about 3.3 V. Placing a follower between divider and load keeps the node at 5 V. The same idea buffers high-impedance sensors, reference voltages and ADC inputs whose sampling capacitors would otherwise disturb the source.

The follower has the deepest possible feedback, so the loop gain equals the full open-loop gain and the loop crosses unity at the op-amp's highest frequency, where phase margin is smallest. Some op-amps are only stable at higher closed-loop gains; check that the datasheet says unity-gain stable. A capacitive load adds phase lag and can cause ringing, which a small series resistor at the output usually cures. Because the input voltage is also the common-mode voltage, it must stay within the common-mode input range; a 0 V to (V+ − 1.5 V) part on 5 V cannot follow a 4 V signal.

Discrete buffers such as the emitter follower (common-collector stage) and source follower also give near-unity gain with high input and low output impedance, but their output sits a base-emitter or gate-source voltage away from the input, the gain is slightly below 1, and linearity is limited. The op-amp follower removes that offset because the feedback loop forces the output to match the input, leaving only the op-amp's small input offset voltage as error.

faq.q: Why use a voltage follower if its gain is only 1?
faq.a: It isolates a high-impedance source from a load. The source sees almost no load current, while the op-amp supplies whatever current the load needs, so the voltage is passed on unchanged.

faq.q: Why does my op-amp voltage follower oscillate?
faq.a: Unity gain is the most demanding condition for stability, so an op-amp that is not unity-gain stable, or a capacitive load on the output, can leave too little phase margin. Choose a unity-gain-stable part or add a small isolation resistor in series with the output.

faq.q: What is the difference between a voltage follower and a non-inverting amplifier?
faq.a: A voltage follower is a non-inverting amplifier with the feedback resistor replaced by a wire and the ground resistor removed, giving a gain of exactly 1. A non-inverting amplifier with resistors has gain 1 + R2/R1.

カットオフ周波数.desc: The frequency at which the output of a filter or amplifier falls 3 dB (to about 0.707 times) below the passband. For an RC circuit it is 1/(2πRC).

差動増幅回路.desc: A circuit that amplifies the difference between two inputs while rejecting components common to both, such as noise. It is used as the input stage of op-amps.

エイリアシング.desc: A phenomenon in which components above half the sampling frequency falsely appear as lower-frequency components. It is prevented with a low-pass filter before A/D conversion.

about.p: Sampling at rate fs records only one value every 1/fs seconds, and a sinusoid at frequency f produces the same samples as a suitably phased sinusoid at |f − n·fs| for any integer n. Any component above the Nyquist frequency fs/2 therefore folds back and masquerades as a lower frequency: a 10 kHz tone sampled at 12 kHz appears at 2 kHz. Once sampled, the false tone is indistinguishable from a genuine 2 kHz signal and cannot be removed. The wagon wheel that seems to turn backward on film is the same effect in time.

The sampling theorem requires fs to exceed twice the highest frequency present, so content up to 20 kHz needs more than 40 kHz. Because real filters cannot cut off instantly, systems add a transition band; audio CDs sample at 44.1 kHz, leaving 20–22.05 kHz for the filter to roll off. The anti-aliasing filter is a low-pass placed before the ADC. A Butterworth response is maximally flat in the passband, Chebyshev trades ripple for steepness, and Bessel preserves waveform shape. Oversampling widens the gap so a simple RC filter suffices, with sharp digital filtering and decimation done afterward.

Aliasing is sometimes deliberate. A band-limited signal centered at a high frequency can be sampled at more than twice its bandwidth, rather than twice its highest frequency, so that it folds down to a lower frequency. This is undersampling, or bandpass sampling: a 70 MHz signal with 10 MHz bandwidth sampled at 56 MS/s appears at 14 MHz, replacing an analog mixer. The ADC's sample-and-hold must still have enough input bandwidth for 70 MHz, and the sampling clock's jitter must be low enough for that input frequency, which is demanding.

about.h: Noise folding and other kinds of aliasing
about.p: Aliasing affects noise as well as tones: wideband noise above the Nyquist frequency folds into the baseband and raises the noise floor, which is one reason anti-aliasing filtering matters even when no interfering signal is expected. In images, undersampled fine detail produces moiré patterns, the spatial version of the same effect. In software, the word means something unrelated: pointer aliasing, where two pointers may refer to the same memory, prevents compilers from keeping a value in a register across stores, and C's restrict qualifier promises that no such overlap exists.

faq.q: How do you calculate the alias frequency?
faq.a: Find the integer multiple of the sampling rate nearest the input frequency and take the absolute difference, |f − n·fs|. For example, 10 kHz sampled at 12 kHz aliases to |10 − 12| = 2 kHz.

faq.q: What is the Nyquist frequency?
faq.a: It is half the sampling rate, the highest frequency that can be represented without aliasing. Components above it fold back into the band below it.

faq.q: Can aliasing be removed after sampling with a digital filter?
faq.a: No. Once a component has folded onto a lower frequency, it occupies the same frequency as legitimate signal, so it must be filtered out in the analog domain before sampling.

量子化誤差.desc: The error that arises when rounding a continuous analog value to a digital value with a finite number of bits. At most half of one LSB.

逐次比較型ADC.desc: An ADC that uses an internal DAC and comparator to determine one bit at a time, starting from the most significant. It balances speed, accuracy and power well.

ΔΣ型ADC.desc: An ADC that oversamples at a high rate, pushes quantization noise to high frequencies and then filters it out. Used in high-resolution applications such as audio and measurement.

1T1Cセル.desc: The DRAM memory cell that stores one bit with one transistor and one capacitor. The presence or absence of charge on the capacitor represents 0 or 1.

ビット線.desc: The wire used to read and write data in memory cells. In DRAM, the small change in bit-line potential caused by a cell's charge is amplified by a sense amplifier.

about.h: What happens on a DRAM bit line during a read
about.p: Before a read, the bit line is precharged to VDD/2. When the word line turns on a cell's access transistor, the cell capacitor Cs (about 10 fF) shares its charge with the much larger bit-line capacitance Cb, several to about ten times Cs. The bit line therefore moves only about (VDD/2)·Cs/(Cs + Cb), typically tens to about a hundred millivolts, up for a stored 1 and down for a 0. A sense amplifier, a cross-coupled latch, amplifies this small difference with positive feedback and simultaneously writes the full level back, because the read destroyed the cell's original charge.

The signal depends on the transfer ratio Cs/(Cs + Cb), and every cell attached to the bit line adds capacitance. A long bit line serving many cells would dilute the signal below what the sense amplifier can resolve reliably, so arrays are divided into segments with a limited number of cells per bit line, each served by its own sense amplifiers. This trades area for signal margin. Precharging back to VDD/2 after a row is closed takes time, specified as tRP, which adds to the latency of switching rows.

A sense amplifier compares two bit lines, one connected to the selected cell and one used as reference. In the folded architecture the pair runs side by side in the same array, so noise couples onto both lines equally and cancels; however, each word line can contact cells on only one line of the pair, which makes the cell 8F², where F is the minimum feature size. In the open architecture the pair lies in separate arrays. It is more sensitive to noise but permits a 6F² cell, and it is the mainstream arrangement today.

about.h: Bit lines in SRAM and flash
about.p: Other memories use bit lines differently. An SRAM column has a complementary bit-line pair precharged to VDD; the selected cell discharges one side slightly, and the sense amplifier fires at a difference of tens to about a hundred millivolts. Writing pulls one bit line low, and at low voltage a negative bit-line assist drives it slightly below ground. In NOR flash each cell connects in parallel to the bit line for fast random reads, while NAND flash connects only the end of a series string of cells to it.

faq.q: What is the difference between a word line and a bit line?
faq.a: A word line runs along a row and drives the gates of the access transistors, selecting which cells are connected. A bit line runs along a column and carries data between the selected cell and the sense amplifier or write driver.

faq.q: Why is the DRAM bit line precharged to VDD/2?
faq.a: Starting midway lets the bit line move up for a stored 1 and down for a stored 0 by similar amounts, so the sense amplifier can compare it against a reference line held at VDD/2.

faq.q: Why is a DRAM read destructive?
faq.a: Connecting the small cell capacitor to the much larger bit-line capacitance redistributes its charge, so the cell no longer holds its original voltage. The sense amplifier restores the data by writing the amplified level back into the cell.

ワード線.desc: The wire connected to the gates of memory-cell transistors that selects the row to read or write.

about.p: A memory array is a grid. Word lines run along the rows and connect to the gates of the cells' access transistors, while bit lines run along the columns and carry data between cells and sense amplifiers or write drivers. A row decoder selects one word line from the address, and its driver raises that line, connecting every cell in the row to its bit line at once. The word line therefore chooses which cells take part, and the bit lines carry the information. Because a word line is a long, heavily loaded wire, its RC delay limits how large an array segment can be.

Activating a DRAM word line turns on thousands of cell transistors, dumping an entire row of several kilobytes onto the sense amplifiers. The access transistor is an nMOS, so if its gate rose only to the supply, the capacitor could charge only to the supply minus the threshold voltage. Word lines are therefore driven to a boosted voltage VPP, about 2.5–3 V, generated by an on-chip charge pump. Modern cells bury the word line in a silicon trench, lengthening the effective channel to keep leakage near femtoamperes so charge survives the refresh interval of 64 ms or more.

In a six-transistor SRAM cell, the word line drives the gates of the two access transistors that connect the cross-coupled latch to a complementary bit-line pair. A read begins by precharging both bit lines, typically to the supply. When the word line rises, the side storing 0 slowly discharges its bit line, and the sense amplifier fires once a difference of tens to about a hundred millivolts develops, without waiting for a full swing. The word line is then lowered and the bit lines are precharged again for the next access.

In NAND flash, the word line is the control gate shared by a row of cells. All cells on one word line form the unit of reading and programming: one page for SLC, and several logical pages for multilevel cells, three for TLC. Programming applies a high voltage to the selected word line while unselected word lines in the string receive a lower pass voltage. In 3D NAND the word lines become stacked conductive layers, often tungsten, and the array edge is etched into a staircase so that each layer can be contacted.

faq.q: What is the difference between a word line and a bit line?
faq.a: The word line selects a row by switching on the access transistors of every cell in it. The bit lines carry data to and from those cells, running perpendicular to the word lines.

faq.q: Why is the DRAM word line driven above the supply voltage?
faq.a: The nMOS access transistor drops a threshold voltage, so a gate at the supply could only charge the capacitor partway. A boosted VPP lets the cell store a full-level 1 and preserves read margin.

faq.q: How does a NAND flash page relate to a word line?
faq.a: A page corresponds to the cells sharing one word line; in multilevel cells each word line holds one page per stored bit, so a TLC word line holds three pages.

6T SRAMセル.desc: The SRAM memory cell made of two cross-coupled inverters (four transistors) and two access transistors.

about.h: How six transistors hold a bit
about.p: A 6T SRAM cell is a latch of two cross-coupled CMOS inverters, each built from a PMOS pull-up and an NMOS pull-down, so four transistors in all. Each inverter's output drives the other's input, and this positive feedback holds one storage node high and the other low indefinitely while power is applied, with no refresh. Two NMOS access transistors, gated by the word line, connect the two storage nodes to a complementary pair of bit lines, BL and BL-bar. The cell is static but not free: its transistors still leak continuously.

For a read, both bit lines are precharged high and the word line is raised; the node storing 0 pulls its bit line down slightly, and a sense amplifier detects the small difference. Current flowing in through the access transistor lifts that 0 node, so the pull-down must be stronger than the access transistor, a cell ratio of about 1.5 to 2.5, or the cell can flip. For a write, one bit line is driven low and the access transistor must overpower the pull-up PMOS holding the node high, so the pull-up is kept weakest of the three.

A 6T SRAM cell occupies roughly 120 to 150 F², where F is the minimum feature size, while a one-transistor, one-capacitor DRAM cell is about 6 F², so SRAM is around 20 times less dense and costs far more per bit. In return it needs no capacitor or special process, is built alongside logic transistors and can be accessed in about a nanosecond, against tens of nanoseconds for DRAM. That is why on-chip caches and register files use SRAM, while main memory uses DRAM.

Because read stability and writability pull the transistor sizes in opposite directions, random variation in threshold voltage makes some cells fail as supply voltage drops, which sets a minimum operating voltage for large arrays. An 8T cell adds a two-transistor read port whose bit line only senses a storage node through a transistor gate, so reads cannot disturb the stored value. Read and write paths can then be optimized separately and can operate at the same time, improving low-voltage operation at the cost of a larger cell.

faq.q: Why does an SRAM cell have six transistors?
faq.a: Four transistors form two cross-coupled inverters that hold the bit through positive feedback, and two access transistors connect the cell to the bit lines when the word line is selected. This gives a stable, refresh-free storage element built only from logic transistors.

faq.q: Does SRAM need refresh like DRAM?
faq.a: No. The cross-coupled inverters actively restore the stored levels as long as power is supplied, so SRAM needs no refresh, although the data is lost when power is removed.

faq.q: What is the cell ratio in a 6T SRAM?
faq.a: It is the strength of the pull-down transistor relative to the access transistor, typically about 1.5 to 2.5. A high enough ratio keeps the 0 node from rising past the switching threshold during a read, preventing read upset.

不揮発性メモリ.desc: Memory that retains stored data when power is removed, such as flash memory and MRAM. DRAM and SRAM are volatile.

NOR型フラッシュメモリ.desc: Flash memory with cells connected in parallel. Random reads are fast, and it is used to store programs for microcontrollers and the like.

ウェアレベリング.desc: A technique that spreads writes so rewrites do not concentrate on particular flash blocks, extending the memory's life.

PCM(相変化メモリ).desc: Nonvolatile memory that stores information by the difference between the crystalline (low-resistance) and amorphous (high-resistance) states of a chalcogenide material.

about.h: How set, reset and read work
about.p: A PCM cell is written with current pulses that Joule-heat a small volume of chalcogenide, typically GST (Ge2Sb2Te5). Reset uses a large, short pulse, tens to hundreds of nanoseconds, that melts the material above roughly 600 °C; quenching within nanoseconds freezes the disordered atoms into the high-resistance amorphous phase. Set uses a smaller, longer pulse that holds the material between its crystallization temperature (about 150 °C for GST) and the melting point until it crystallizes into the low-resistance phase. Reading applies a small bias that senses resistance without heating the cell enough to change it.

Because the crystalline and amorphous resistances differ by two to three orders of magnitude, PCM can store more than one bit per cell. Pulse amplitude and duration set the size of the amorphous region, producing intermediate resistance levels. The catch is resistance drift: the amorphous phase slowly relaxes, so its resistance rises roughly as a power of time (R ∝ t^ν, with ν around 0.1). Two-level storage tolerates this, but closely spaced levels can blur together, so multi-level PCM relies on write-and-verify programming, reference cells read alongside the data, and low-drift materials.

about.h: Scaling limits: reset current and thermal disturb
about.p: The reset current is PCM's main power cost, so cell designs shrink the volume that must melt. The mushroom cell, for example, forces current through a narrow heater electrode so only a small dome of GST is heated. Tight pitch brings a second problem, thermal disturb: when cells are only tens of nanometres apart, heat from a reset can partially crystallize an amorphous neighbour. Thermally insulating dielectrics around each cell help. Retention is also temperature-limited, since GST crystallizes near 150 °C, which is why Ge-rich compositions are used for automotive and other high-temperature applications.

PCM sits between NAND flash and DRAM. Its endurance of about 10^6 to 10^9 cycles beats NAND's thousands to tens of thousands but falls short of MRAM (above 10^10) and DRAM, which is effectively unlimited. Unlike MRAM, which stores data in the magnetization of a magnetic tunnel junction, and ReRAM, which forms and breaks a conductive filament in an oxide, PCM changes the atomic structure of a whole volume. In dense cross-point arrays each PCM element is paired with an ovonic threshold switch (OTS) selector that blocks sneak currents through unselected cells.

faq.q: What is the difference between PCM and ReRAM?
faq.a: Both store data as a resistance state, but PCM switches a chalcogenide between crystalline and amorphous phases using heat, while ReRAM moves ions in a metal oxide to form or rupture a narrow conductive filament. PCM therefore needs relatively large write currents to melt the material.

faq.q: Why is PCM set slower than reset?
faq.a: Reset only needs to melt the material and quench it within nanoseconds, while set must hold the material below its melting point long enough for atoms to arrange into a crystal, typically tens to hundreds of nanoseconds. Crystallization time is therefore what limits PCM write speed.

faq.q: What does GST stand for in phase-change memory?
faq.a: GST refers to germanium-antimony-tellurium chalcogenide alloys, most commonly Ge2Sb2Te5. It crystallizes quickly yet keeps a stable amorphous phase at room temperature, and the same family of materials was used in rewritable optical discs.

ReRAM(抵抗変化メモリ).desc: Nonvolatile memory that applies voltage to form and break conductive paths in an oxide or similar material, storing information as differences in resistance.

about.p: A resistive RAM (ReRAM) cell is a metal-insulator-metal stack, typically a few nanometers of hafnium, tantalum or titanium oxide between electrodes. Fresh cells are highly resistive, so a one-time forming step applies a higher voltage that moves oxygen ions and leaves a conductive filament of oxygen vacancies. After that, normal operation only ruptures and reconnects the thin tip of the filament: reset produces the high-resistance state and set restores the low-resistance state, typically differing by ten times or more. The state persists without power, so the memory is nonvolatile.

Most practical ReRAM is bipolar: set and reset use opposite voltage polarities, with the field shuttling oxygen ions to connect or break the filament. Unipolar devices use one polarity and break the filament mainly by Joule heating, which is harder to control. Conductive-bridge RAM (CBRAM) is a related type in which silver or copper ions from an active electrode migrate through a solid electrolyte to build a metallic bridge, offering low voltage and low write energy. All of these store data as resistance, unlike flash, which stores trapped charge.

ReRAM cells are small and built from materials already used in CMOS, and they can be placed in the interconnect layers above the transistors with only a few extra process steps. That makes them attractive as embedded nonvolatile memory in microcontrollers at nodes where embedded flash, with its floating gates, becomes hard to integrate. Endurance of roughly 10^6 to 10^9 cycles beats NAND flash but falls short of DRAM. The main weakness is variability: random filament shapes spread resistance from cell to cell and write to write, which narrows read margins and makes multilevel storage difficult.

Cells are usually paired with an access transistor (1T1R), which also limits current during set so the filament does not grow too strong. Dense crosspoint arrays without transistors are possible, but current leaking through unselected cells (sneak paths) then requires a nonlinear selector device at each crossing. To tighten resistance distributions, controllers use write-verify, repeatedly pulsing and reading until the cell lands in its target window. Because resistance can be tuned in steps, ReRAM is also studied for analog in-memory computing of neural-network weights.

faq.q: How does ReRAM store data?
faq.a: By forming or breaking a nanoscale conductive filament, usually made of oxygen vacancies, in a thin oxide; the resulting low or high resistance represents the stored bit and remains without power.

faq.q: What is the forming step in ReRAM?
faq.a: A one-time application of higher-than-normal voltage that creates the initial conductive filament in a fresh, highly resistive cell, after which lower voltages switch it.

faq.q: What is the difference between ReRAM and PCM?
faq.a: Both store data as resistance, but ReRAM switches by moving ions to form or break a filament, while phase-change memory (PCM) switches a material between crystalline and amorphous phases by heating.

FeRAM(強誘電体メモリ).desc: Nonvolatile memory that stores information in the polarization direction of a ferroelectric. Writes are fast and low-power, and it is used in IC cards and the like.

about.h: How the cell stores a bit
about.p: A ferroelectric has a spontaneous electric polarization that can be flipped by an applied field and stays in place when the field is removed. Plotting polarization against field gives a hysteresis loop; the polarization left at zero field is the remanent polarization (Pr), and the field needed to flip it is the coercive field (Ec). FeRAM stores a 1 or 0 in the sign of that polarization, usually in a one-transistor, one-capacitor (1T1C) cell resembling DRAM but with a ferroelectric capacitor. The "Fe" stands for ferroelectric, not iron.

In capacitor-type FeRAM, a read pulses the cell toward a known polarization and senses the charge released onto the bit line. A cell whose polarization flips delivers noticeably more charge than one that does not, and a sense amplifier distinguishes the two. Because the read flips cells storing the opposite state, the data must be written back afterward, much as in DRAM. Every read therefore counts as a switching cycle. Unlike DRAM, though, the information lives in polarization rather than stored charge, so no refresh is needed and data survives power loss.

Writing simply flips polarization at a few volts, so FeRAM writes in tens of nanoseconds with little energy and endures about 10^12 cycles or more, far beyond flash. That suits contactless smart cards powered by harvested radio energy, meters and medical devices that log data frequently and must survive sudden power loss, and radiation-exposed equipment, since polarization is not easily upset by ionizing radiation. Its weakness is density: ferroelectric capacitors in traditional lead zirconate titanate (PZT) scale poorly, keeping capacities in the few-megabit range.

Around 2011, doped hafnium oxide was reported to become ferroelectric in a specific orthorhombic phase at about 10 nm thickness. Because HfO2 is already a standard high-k dielectric deposited by atomic layer deposition (ALD), this revived interest in embedding ferroelectric memory with advanced logic. The same films enable the ferroelectric FET (FeFET), where polarization shifts the transistor threshold voltage, and the ferroelectric tunnel junction (FTJ), where polarization changes tunneling resistance. Both read without flipping the polarization, avoiding the destructive read of capacitor FeRAM.

faq.q: Does FeRAM contain iron?
faq.a: No. Fe stands for ferroelectric, a name borrowed from ferromagnetism because both show hysteresis; common materials are PZT, SBT and doped hafnium oxide.

faq.q: Why is FeRAM read destructive?
faq.a: Reading works by driving the cell toward one polarization and detecting whether it switches, which erases the original state of switched cells, so the data must be rewritten.

faq.q: What is the difference between FeRAM and MRAM?
faq.a: FeRAM stores bits as the electric polarization direction of a ferroelectric capacitor, while MRAM stores them as the magnetization direction of a magnetic tunnel junction and reads the resulting resistance.

磁気トンネル接合(MTJ).desc: A structure with a thin insulating film between two magnetic layers. Resistance is low when the layers' magnetizations are parallel and high when antiparallel. It is the storage element of MRAM.

about.p: A magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ) sandwiches an insulating tunnel barrier, typically MgO about 1 nm thick, between two ferromagnetic layers such as CoFeB. One layer, the reference or pinned layer, has its magnetization fixed by an antiferromagnet or a synthetic antiferromagnet so that write currents and stray fields cannot move it. The other, the free or storage layer, can be switched between two directions. Production MTJs are stacks of more than ten films, many of which exist only to stabilize the reference layer.

Electrons cross the barrier by quantum tunneling, and in a ferromagnet majority-spin and minority-spin electrons have different numbers of available states. When the two layers are parallel, majority states on both sides match and tunneling is easy, giving low resistance. When antiparallel, majority electrons must enter minority states, so resistance is high. The tunnel magnetoresistance (TMR) ratio, (R_AP − R_P)/R_P, measures the contrast: 2 kΩ versus 5 kΩ gives 150%. Laboratory MgO junctions exceed 600% at room temperature, but production cells are around 100 to 200%, so the two states differ only two- to threefold.

In spin-transfer torque (STT) MRAM, write current flows through the junction; electrons spin-polarized by the reference layer transfer angular momentum to the free layer and flip it, with current direction selecting 0 or 1. Write current scales with cell area, which made STT the mainstream approach. Reads use the same path, so read current must stay well below the switching current to avoid read disturb. Spin-orbit torque (SOT) MRAM drives write current through a heavy-metal line such as tungsten or platinum under the free layer, separating read and write paths and allowing sub-nanosecond writes in a larger three-terminal cell.

The energy barrier holding the free layer is roughly magnetic anisotropy times volume, so it shrinks as cells shrink. Its ratio to thermal energy kT, the thermal stability factor Δ, must be about 60 or more for ten-year retention; a larger Δ also demands more write current, which sets the scaling trade-off. Perpendicular magnetic anisotropy materials help. MTJs are built between interconnect layers in the back end of line (BEOL), so they must survive about 400 °C, and the magnetic films are patterned with ion-beam etching to avoid metal redeposition on the sidewalls.

faq.q: What is the TMR ratio of a magnetic tunnel junction?
faq.a: The tunnel magnetoresistance ratio is (R_antiparallel − R_parallel) divided by R_parallel. Production MRAM junctions typically show about 100 to 200%, meaning the high-resistance state is two to three times the low one.

faq.q: What is the difference between an MTJ and a GMR spin valve?
faq.a: Both use two magnetic layers whose relative alignment sets the resistance, but a giant magnetoresistance (GMR) spin valve uses a thin metallic spacer such as copper, while an MTJ uses an insulating tunnel barrier. The tunnel barrier gives a much larger resistance change, which is why MRAM uses MTJs.

faq.q: Is MTJ-based memory volatile?
faq.a: No. The bit is stored as the direction of the free layer's magnetization, which persists without power, so MRAM built from MTJs is non-volatile as long as the thermal stability factor is high enough.

パイプライン処理.desc: A method that splits instruction processing into stages such as fetch, decode and execute, and processes several instructions at once, each offset by a stage.

about.p: A pipeline splits instruction processing into stages separated by registers, like an assembly line. The classic five-stage RISC pipeline uses instruction fetch, decode and register read, execute, memory access and write-back. While one instruction executes, the next is being decoded and a third fetched, so ideally one instruction completes every clock and throughput approaches five times that of an unpipelined design. The latency of an individual instruction does not shrink and actually grows slightly, because every instruction now passes through all the pipeline registers.

The clock period must cover the slowest stage plus register overhead: clock-to-Q delay, setup time and clock skew. If logic cannot be divided evenly, the longest stage sets the frequency and the others idle for part of each cycle. Deeper pipelines shorten each stage, but the fixed register overhead becomes a larger fraction of the period, and the penalty for mispredicted branches grows because more partially processed instructions must be discarded. Beyond a point, adding stages lowers performance and raises power, which is why pipeline depth is a balanced design choice.

about.h: Hazards and how they are handled
about.p: Three kinds of hazard interrupt the ideal flow. Structural hazards arise when two instructions need the same resource in the same cycle. Data hazards arise when an instruction needs a result that has not yet been written; forwarding, or bypassing, routes results directly from later stages, though a load followed immediately by its use still typically costs a stall cycle in the classic pipeline. Control hazards come from branches, whose outcome is known only several stages after fetch; branch prediction guesses the path and flushes the wrong instructions when it misses.

RISC instruction sets, with uniform instruction lengths and load/store architectures, were designed to pipeline cleanly; x86 processors reach similar behavior by splitting complex instructions into simple micro-operations. The same idea applies to any synchronous datapath: inserting registers to split a long critical path raises the maximum clock frequency at the cost of latency, and high-level synthesis tools expose this as a pipelining option. Software pipelining is the compiler counterpart, overlapping different loop iterations so loads, computation and stores proceed in parallel, with prologue and epilogue code around the loop.

faq.q: Does pipelining reduce the latency of an instruction?
faq.a: No. Pipelining increases throughput by overlapping instructions, but each instruction still passes through every stage and usually takes slightly longer because of register overhead.

faq.q: What are the three types of pipeline hazards?
faq.a: Structural hazards from resource conflicts, data hazards from dependences on results not yet available, and control hazards from branches. Typical remedies are duplicated resources, forwarding and branch prediction.

faq.q: Why not make the pipeline as deep as possible?
faq.a: Register overhead stays fixed while stage logic shrinks, so gains diminish, and branch mispredictions waste more work in a deeper pipeline. Power and design complexity also increase.

ノイマン型アーキテクチャ.desc: A computer organization that keeps programs and data in the same main memory and fetches and executes instructions in sequence.

命令セットアーキテクチャ(ISA).desc: The processor specification as seen by software, including the instructions and registers it supports. Examples include x86, Arm and RISC-V.

about.p: An instruction set architecture (ISA) is the contract between software and processor hardware. It defines the instructions and their bit encodings, the registers visible to programs, the data types and addressing modes, how memory accesses are ordered, the privilege levels, and how interrupts and exceptions behave. Everything the ISA defines is architectural state that machine code can observe and rely on. An assembler translates assembly mnemonics almost one-to-one into these encodings, which is why each ISA has its own assembly language.

The microarchitecture is how a particular processor implements the ISA: pipeline depth, cache sizes, branch predictors, the number of instructions issued per cycle. One ISA can be implemented by tiny low-power cores and large out-of-order cores that run the same machine code at very different speeds. In the performance equation, execution time = instruction count × cycles per instruction (CPI) × cycle time, the ISA and compiler mainly set the instruction count, the microarchitecture the CPI, and circuits and process technology the cycle time. Spectre-type attacks exploit the boundary: misspeculated architectural state is rolled back, but cache contents are not.

ISA details have lasting hardware consequences. RISC-V base instructions are a fixed 32 bits (16-bit forms only with the compressed C extension), so instruction boundaries are obvious, while x86 instructions range from 1 to 15 bytes and must be partly decoded to find where the next one starts, making wide decoders complex. x86 branches test flags set by an earlier compare; RISC-V compares two registers within the branch, leaving no implicit flag state to track. The MIPS branch delay slot showed the risk of encoding one pipeline's quirks into an ISA that outlives it.

RISC-V is an open ISA whose specification anyone may implement without license fees. It combines a small base integer set (RV32I or RV64I, about 40 instructions) with optional extensions: M for multiply and divide, A for atomics, F and D for floating point, C for compressed instructions, V for vectors, plus custom instructions. Leaving out an extension saves area but costs speed: without M, the compiler turns a C multiplication into a call to a library routine that multiplies with shifts and adds.
