Arm and x86 are proprietary and licensed or implemented by their owners.

faq.q: What is the difference between an ISA and a microarchitecture?
faq.a: The ISA is the specification software sees: instructions, registers and behavior. The microarchitecture is a specific hardware design that implements that specification, so two processors with different microarchitectures can run the same programs if they share an ISA.

faq.q: Are x86, Arm and RISC-V instruction set architectures?
faq.a: Yes. They are three different ISAs, so machine code compiled for one cannot run directly on another, even though each is implemented by many different processor designs.

faq.q: What is the difference between an ISA and an ABI?
faq.a: The ISA defines what the processor executes, while the ABI is a software convention on top of it covering calling conventions, data type sizes and system calls. One ISA can have several ABIs, for example for different operating systems.

分岐予測.desc: A technique that predicts the outcome of conditional branches before they execute, so later instructions can proceed without stalling the pipeline. A misprediction forces the work to be redone.

about.p: A pipelined CPU fetches new instructions every cycle, but whether a conditional branch is taken, and where it goes, is not known until it executes several stages later. Waiting would leave the pipeline idle, and roughly one instruction in five is a branch. Branch prediction instead guesses the outcome at fetch time and continues speculatively down the predicted path. If the guess is right, no time is lost; if wrong, the speculative instructions are flushed without affecting architectural state and fetch restarts on the correct path, costing a dozen to about twenty cycles in a deep pipeline.

Static schemes use fixed rules, such as predicting backward branches (loops) taken and forward branches not taken. Dynamic predictors learn from history: a table of 2-bit saturating counters, indexed by branch address, needs two wrong outcomes in a row to flip its prediction, so a loop exit causes only one miss. Better predictors combine the address with a global history of recent outcomes to capture correlations between branches. Predicting direction is only half the job; a branch target buffer (BTB) supplies the target address, and a return address stack predicts function returns.

The impact can be estimated as added cycles per instruction (CPI): branch frequency × misprediction rate × penalty. With 20% branches, 95% accuracy and a 20-cycle penalty, that is 0.2 × 0.05 × 20 = 0.2 extra CPI, a large share of a modern core's budget. This is why accuracy improvements of a percent or two matter. For branches that depend on random data and cannot be predicted, compilers and programmers sometimes use branchless code such as conditional moves, trading a little extra work for a guaranteed absence of flushes.

Mispredicted instructions are discarded architecturally, but they can still leave traces in microarchitectural state such as caches. Spectre-class attacks train the predictor so a victim speculatively reads secret data and leaks it through cache timing. Defenses include speculation barriers after sensitive bounds checks (such as x86 lfence), masking array indices, retpoline sequences for indirect branches and microcode controls on predictors. Each restriction costs performance, so they are applied selectively. Older ISAs such as MIPS used branch delay slots instead of prediction, a rule that became a burden for later designs.

faq.q: What happens when a branch is mispredicted?
faq.a: The CPU discards the instructions it fetched and executed speculatively down the wrong path and restarts from the correct target, losing roughly 10 to 20 cycles in a typical deep pipeline.

faq.q: How accurate is branch prediction in modern CPUs?
faq.a: High-performance predictors typically exceed 95% accuracy on ordinary code, although branches that depend on random data can be much harder to predict.

faq.q: What is the difference between branch prediction and speculative execution?
faq.a: Branch prediction is the guess about which way a branch goes; speculative execution is actually running instructions along that guessed path before the guess is confirmed.

パワーMOSFET.desc: A MOSFET built to handle large currents and voltages. It switches quickly and is widely used in power supply circuits and the like.

about.h: How it differs from a logic MOSFET
about.p: Most discrete power MOSFETs are vertical devices: source and gate are on top, the drain is the back of the chip, and current flows through the channel and then down through a lightly doped n-type drift region. That drift region holds the blocking voltage, and a higher voltage rating needs a thicker, more lightly doped drift layer, which raises on-resistance. Many small cells are connected in parallel to carry large current. The p-type body, tied to the source, forms a PN junction with the drift region, creating a built-in body diode that conducts from source to drain.

When fully on, the device behaves as a resistor, RDS(on), so conduction loss is I²R: 10 A through 10 mΩ dissipates 1 W, and doubling the current quadruples it. In silicon, RDS(on) rises with temperature as carrier mobility falls, typically to about 1.5–2 times the 25 °C value at 125 °C, so loss must be estimated from the datasheet's normalized RDS(on)-versus-temperature curve. This positive temperature coefficient helps paralleled devices share current, since a hotter device conducts less.

Turning the device on means charging its gate capacitances. During the transition, the drain voltage swings and the gate drive current is consumed charging the gate-drain (Miller) capacitance Cgd, so the gate voltage stalls on the Miller plateau. Most switching loss occurs in this interval, whose length is roughly the gate-drain charge Qgd divided by gate current, so low-Qgd devices and strong gate drivers switch faster. The gate oxide is thin, so gate-source voltage is typically rated around ±20 V.

about.h: Body diode, avalanche and safe operating area
about.p: In bridges the body diode can carry freewheeling current, but in silicon its slow reverse recovery causes loss, so designs add fast external diodes or use synchronous rectification. Interrupting an inductive load releases energy ½LI², driving the drain into avalanche breakdown; avalanche ruggedness, tested by unclamped inductive switching (UIS), matters for relay, solenoid and automotive drivers without clamps. The safe operating area (SOA) chart bounds allowed voltage-current combinations; most are drawn for a 25 °C case and single pulses, so they must be derated, especially for linear-mode uses such as inrush limiting.

faq.q: How do you calculate power MOSFET conduction loss?
faq.a: Use P = I²·RDS(on), with RDS(on) taken at the expected junction temperature rather than the 25 °C datasheet headline value, since it can be 1.5–2 times higher when hot.

faq.q: What is the body diode in a power MOSFET?
faq.a: It is the parasitic PN junction between the source-connected p body and the n drift region, which conducts from source to drain. It can act as a freewheeling diode but has slow reverse recovery in silicon devices.

faq.q: What is the Miller plateau?
faq.a: The flat portion of the gate-voltage waveform during switching, when gate current goes into charging the gate-drain capacitance while the drain voltage transitions.

オン抵抗.desc: The resistance of the current path when a power device is on. The smaller it is, the lower the conduction loss.

about.p: A power MOSFET's on-resistance, RDS(on), is a series chain: the inversion channel, the JFET region between cells in planar designs, the lightly doped drift layer that holds off voltage, the substrate, and finally contacts, bond wires and package. Low-voltage devices are dominated by channel, substrate and package; devices rated at hundreds of volts by the drift layer. The channel part falls as gate voltage rises, so datasheets quote RDS(on) at a stated gate drive and temperature. Technologies are compared by specific on-resistance, resistance times active area.

While on, the switch dissipates P = I²R: 10 A through 10 mΩ gives 1 W, and doubling the current quadruples the loss. RDS(on) rises with temperature because carrier mobility falls; roughly 1.5 times the room-temperature value at 100 °C is a common rule of thumb, so thermal estimates should use hot values. This positive coefficient makes paralleling easy, since a hotter device carries less current. Near threshold, at low gate drive, the coefficient turns negative, so linear-mode operation or slow switching can still cause current crowding.

Blocking more voltage needs a thicker, more lightly doped drift layer, which is more resistive. For silicon unipolar devices the ideal specific on-resistance scales with about the 2.5th power of breakdown voltage, so doubling the rating raises it about 5.7 times: the silicon limit. Trench gates pack more channel width per area and remove the JFET resistance. Superjunction MOSFETs use alternating p and n pillars that deplete sideways, bringing 600 V-class devices well below the limit. SiC and GaN tolerate a much higher critical field, allowing thinner, more heavily doped drift regions.

A conducting MOSFET operates in its linear region, where current is nearly proportional to VDS, so it behaves like a resistor. Bipolar transistors and IGBTs instead show an on-state voltage: a saturated BJT drops about 0.1–0.3 V, and an IGBT has a junction-related knee before its resistive slope. At low voltage, a small RDS(on) usually beats a fixed knee, so MOSFETs dominate. At several hundred volts and high current, the IGBT's conductivity modulation keeps the drop low where a silicon MOSFET's drift resistance would soar.

faq.q: Why does MOSFET on-resistance increase with temperature?
faq.a: Higher temperature increases lattice scattering, which lowers carrier mobility in both the channel and the drift layer. As a rough guide, RDS(on) at 100 °C is about 1.5 times the room-temperature value.

faq.q: How do you calculate MOSFET conduction loss from RDS(on)?
faq.a: Use P = I²·RDS(on) with the RMS current through the device and the on-resistance at the expected junction temperature. In a switching converter, the RMS current already accounts for the duty cycle.

faq.q: Why do high-voltage MOSFETs have higher on-resistance?
faq.a: A higher rating needs a thicker, more lightly doped drift layer, and for silicon the ideal on-resistance grows with about the 2.5th power of breakdown voltage. Superjunction structures and SiC or GaN devices are used to get around this.

スイッチング損失.desc: Loss that occurs while a power device switches between on and off, when voltage and current are present at the same time. It grows with switching frequency.

CMOSイメージセンサー.desc: An image sensor made with a CMOS process that has an amplifier in each pixel. It is low-power, can integrate peripheral circuits, and dominates smartphone cameras and more.

about.h: From photon to voltage in a 4T pixel
about.p: Each pixel's photodiode absorbs light and collects electrons in proportion to the exposure; quantum efficiency for visible light is typically about 50–80%. In the common four-transistor (4T) pixel, a transfer transistor moves this charge to a small node called the floating diffusion (FD), a source-follower amplifier buffers the FD voltage onto a column line, a select transistor connects the row, and a reset transistor clears the FD. Conversion gain is q/C_FD, about 160 µV per electron for a 1 fF node. Neighboring pixels often share the FD and readout transistors to save area.

Interface states at the silicon/oxide surface generate dark current. The pinned photodiode buries the n-type collection region under a heavily doped p+ surface layer, which fills those states with holes and suppresses that current. The buried region also fully depletes, so charge transfer is complete, avoiding image lag. Readout uses correlated double sampling (CDS): the FD is sampled right after reset and again after transfer, and the difference removes kTC reset noise and amplifier offset, bringing read noise down to a few electrons or less. Column-parallel ADCs then digitize the signal on chip.

In a front-side illuminated (FSI) sensor, light must pass through gaps between metal wiring layers before reaching the photodiode, losing intensity and angle tolerance. A back-side illuminated (BSI) sensor thins the wafer to a few micrometers and receives light from the side opposite the wiring, which keeps sensitivity high for pixels around 1 µm and became standard in smartphone cameras. Stacked sensors go further, bonding the pixel wafer to a separate logic wafer that carries ADCs and image processing. Epitaxial silicon substrates are used for low-defect pixel regions.

A charge-coupled device (CCD) shifts charge packets across the chip to a single output amplifier, which needs several clock voltages and more power. A CMOS image sensor amplifies in each pixel and reads rows through column circuits, so it runs at lower power, reads out faster, and integrates timing, ADCs and processing on the same die. Row-by-row readout causes rolling-shutter distortion of fast motion, which global-shutter pixels avoid with in-pixel storage. Dual-conversion-gain pixels switch extra FD capacitance to cover both dim and bright scenes.

faq.q: What is the difference between a CMOS image sensor and a CCD?
faq.a: A CCD moves charge across the chip to one shared output amplifier, while a CMOS image sensor converts charge to voltage inside each pixel and reads it out row by row. CMOS sensors use less power and integrate ADCs and logic, which is why they dominate phones and most cameras.

faq.q: What does BSI mean in an image sensor?
faq.a: BSI stands for back-side illumination: the wafer is thinned and light enters from the back, so it reaches the photodiodes without passing through the metal wiring layers, improving sensitivity for small pixels.

faq.q: What is correlated double sampling in a CMOS image sensor?
faq.a: It reads the floating diffusion once after reset and once after charge transfer, then subtracts the two. Reset (kTC) noise and amplifier offsets appear in both samples and cancel, leaving the true signal.

量子効率.desc: The fraction of incident photons converted into signal electrons. The higher it is, the better the sensitivity.

about.p: External quantum efficiency (EQE) counts electrons collected per incident photon. It is the product of three factors: the fraction of light not reflected at the surface, the fraction absorbed in the active material, and the fraction of generated carriers collected before they recombine. Internal quantum efficiency (IQE) leaves out the reflection and counts per absorbed photon. For light-emitting diodes the direction reverses: EQE is photons emitted per injected electron, the product of IQE and light-extraction efficiency. Datasheets that say QE usually mean EQE at a stated wavelength.

Silicon absorbs blue light within a fraction of a micrometre of the surface, red light over several micrometres and near-infrared over tens of micrometres, and becomes transparent beyond about 1.1 µm, where photon energy falls below its band gap. Blue carriers generated near the surface are easily lost to surface recombination, while long wavelengths pass through a thin photodiode unabsorbed. Visible quantum efficiency of CMOS image sensors is typically about 50 to 80%, raised by back-side illumination, anti-reflection coatings and microlenses, and some cooled scientific sensors exceed 90%.

Responsivity R, in amperes per watt, links QE to the current a photodiode produces: R = ηqλ/hc, or about η × λ[µm]/1.24. Longer wavelengths carry less energy per photon, so one watt contains more photons and gives more current at the same η. At 1.55 µm an 80% efficient detector gives about 1.0 A/W, and even a perfect one cannot exceed about 1.25 A/W. Silicon cannot absorb this wavelength, so telecom receivers use InGaAs or germanium absorbers.

about.h: Why it matters for low-light imaging
about.p: Photon arrival is random, so even a perfect detector has shot noise equal to the square root of the signal. A sensor with lower QE loses photons before noise is added, and its shot-noise-limited signal-to-noise ratio scales with the square root of QE, so halving QE is like halving exposure time. Avalanche or electron-multiplying detectors can produce more than one output electron per photon, but that is gain applied after detection; QE itself remains at most 100% in ordinary photodiodes.

faq.q: What is the difference between internal and external quantum efficiency?
faq.a: External quantum efficiency counts collected electrons per incident photon, including reflection losses. Internal quantum efficiency counts per absorbed photon, isolating the material and collection efficiency.

faq.q: How do you convert quantum efficiency to responsivity?
faq.a: Use R ≈ η × λ / 1.24, with λ in micrometres and R in A/W. For example, 80% quantum efficiency at 1.55 µm gives about 1.0 A/W.

faq.q: Can quantum efficiency exceed 100 percent?
faq.a: Not in an ordinary photodiode without gain, since at visible and infrared wavelengths each photon generates at most one collected electron-hole pair. Devices with avalanche multiplication give more output current, but that is counted as gain separate from quantum efficiency.

裏面照射型(BSI).desc: An image sensor structure in which light enters from the back of the substrate, where there is no wiring. Light is not blocked by wiring, so sensitivity stays high even with small pixels.

about.p: In a front-side illuminated (FSI) CMOS image sensor, light enters from the side where transistors and wiring are built, passing through the microlens, color filter and several metal layers before reaching the photodiode. The metal blocks and reflects part of the light, and the tall optical stack loses rays arriving at oblique angles. In a backside-illuminated (BSI) sensor the wafer is flipped after front-side processing, bonded to a support wafer, and its original substrate thinned to a few µm, so light enters from the back and reaches the photodiode without crossing any wiring.

about.h: Why BSI matters for small pixels
about.p: As pixels shrink toward about 1 µm, the openings between metal lines in an FSI pixel become a small fraction of the pixel area and the stack becomes tall relative to pixel width, so sensitivity and angular response drop sharply. BSI keeps nearly the whole pixel area open to light and shortens the optical path from microlens to silicon. It also frees the wiring from optical constraints, allowing more metal layers. These advantages made BSI the standard structure for smartphone camera sensors.

Thinning must leave a uniform silicon layer a few µm thick across the wafer. The new back surface must be passivated, because defects there generate dark current; films with fixed negative charge are commonly used to accumulate holes at that surface. Thin silicon also makes optical and electrical crosstalk between neighboring pixels more likely, which deep trench isolation between pixels reduces. Red and near-infrared light has an absorption length of several µm or more in silicon, so very thin layers lose some long-wavelength response.

Because a BSI sensor already needs a bonded support wafer, that wafer can carry useful circuitry instead of being blank silicon. Stacked image sensors bond the pixel wafer to a logic wafer containing readout, analog-to-digital conversion and image processing, each made in a process suited to its function. This allows smaller chips or more processing per pixel area, and it builds directly on the wafer bonding and thinning techniques developed for BSI.

faq.q: What is the difference between BSI and FSI image sensors?
faq.a: In FSI, light passes through the wiring layers before reaching the photodiode; in BSI, the wafer is flipped and thinned so light enters from the back, where there is no wiring. BSI therefore collects more light, especially in small pixels.

faq.q: Why must the wafer be thinned in a BSI sensor?
faq.a: Light enters from the back, so it must reach the photodiodes near the front side before being absorbed. Thinning the silicon to a few µm puts the photodiodes within the light's absorption depth.

faq.q: Do BSI sensors have any disadvantages?
faq.a: They need extra steps such as wafer bonding, thinning and backside passivation, and the thin silicon increases crosstalk risk and reduces long-wavelength response. Deep trench isolation and careful surface treatment address these.

グローバルシャッター.desc: An electronic shutter method that exposes all pixels at the same time. Unlike a rolling shutter, which reads row by row, it does not distort images of moving objects.

HEMT(高電子移動度トランジスタ).desc: A transistor that uses the high-mobility two-dimensional electron gas formed at a heterojunction interface as its channel. It is used in high-frequency and high-power applications.

about.p: A HEMT is grown epitaxially as a heterojunction between a wide-band-gap barrier, such as AlGaAs or AlGaN, and a narrower-gap channel material, such as GaAs or GaN. The conduction-band offset creates a thin triangular potential well on the channel side, where electrons are confined in a sheet only a few nanometers thick: the two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG). A Schottky metal gate on the barrier modulates the sheet density, so the device is a field-effect transistor whose channel lies at a buried, nearly perfect crystal interface rather than at an oxide surface as in a MOSFET.

In GaAs-based HEMTs the electrons come from donors placed in the barrier, often behind an undoped spacer, so the ionized donors are separated from the undoped channel where electrons travel. This modulation doping sharply reduces impurity scattering, giving higher mobility and lower noise than a doped channel; mobility rises further on cooling as phonon scattering falls. In AlGaN/GaN no doping is needed at all: the difference in spontaneous and piezoelectric polarization induces a sheet density of about 10¹³ cm⁻², with room-temperature mobility around 2000 cm²/V·s.

GaAs HEMTs, including pseudomorphic versions with an InGaAs channel, are the classic low-noise amplifiers in satellite receivers and radio telescopes. GaN HEMTs trade some noise performance for power: GaN's wide band gap gives a breakdown field roughly ten times that of silicon, its electron saturation velocity is about 2.5×10⁷ cm/s, and the dense 2DEG supplies high current. Together these give several times the power density of GaAs, so GaN HEMTs serve base-station, radar and satellite power amplifiers and, increasingly, fast power-conversion switches.

Because the 2DEG exists with zero gate bias, a basic HEMT is normally on (depletion mode) and needs a negative gate voltage to turn off. Power circuits prefer normally-off devices for fail-safe behavior. Common fixes are a p-type GaN layer under the gate that depletes the 2DEG beneath it, a recessed gate that thins the barrier, or a cascode in which a low-voltage silicon MOSFET in series switches the HEMT off by pulling its source above its grounded gate, at the cost of an extra die and its parasitics.

faq.q: What is the difference between a HEMT and a MOSFET?
faq.a: A MOSFET's channel is an inversion layer at the silicon/oxide interface, while a HEMT's channel is a two-dimensional electron gas at an epitaxial heterojunction with little impurity or roughness scattering. HEMTs therefore reach higher electron mobility and suit high-frequency, low-noise and high-power RF work.

faq.q: Why are GaN HEMTs normally on?
faq.a: Polarization at the AlGaN/GaN interface creates the 2DEG without any gate voltage, so the channel conducts at 0 V. Normally-off operation needs a p-GaN gate, a recessed gate or a cascode with a silicon MOSFET.

faq.q: What does 2DEG mean in a HEMT?
faq.a: 2DEG stands for two-dimensional electron gas, a sheet of electrons confined in a quantum well at a heterojunction so they can move freely only in the plane of the interface. It forms the HEMT's channel.

III-V族化合物半導体.desc: Semiconductors made of group III elements (Ga, In, Al, etc.) and group V elements (As, P, N, etc.), such as GaAs, InP and GaN.

ワイドバンドギャップ半導体.desc: Semiconductors with a larger band gap than silicon, such as SiC and GaN. Their high breakdown field makes them strong for high-voltage, high-temperature operation.

GAA(ゲートオールアラウンド).desc: A transistor structure in which the gate surrounds the channel on all sides. It controls current better than FinFET and is used in the generations after FinFET.

about.h: Why wrap the gate all the way around
about.p: Short-channel effects arise when the drain's electric field reaches into the channel and competes with the gate. The scale length λ estimates how far that influence extends; gate lengths of about 5–10 λ keep it small, and every additional gated surface shrinks λ. A planar MOSFET gates one face, a FinFET three, and a gate-all-around (GAA) transistor surrounds each channel completely. This strongest electrostatic control suppresses punch-through and leakage at shorter gate lengths, and like FinFETs, GAA devices use nearly undoped channels with threshold voltage set by the gate work function.

Production GAA devices use nanosheets: silicon plates about 5 nm thick and roughly 15–50 nm wide, typically three stacked vertically about 10 nm apart, each wrapped by gate dielectric and metal. A nanosheet resembles a FinFET fin laid on its side and stacked. A FinFET's width can only change in whole fins, but sheet width can be drawn continuously in layout, using wide sheets for high-performance cells and narrow ones for low power and SRAM. More sheets add current per footprint but complicate processing and add parasitic capacitance.

Fabrication starts with an epitaxial stack of alternating Si and SiGe layers, the SiGe containing about 25–30% germanium. The stack is patterned into fins and a dummy gate is formed. The ends of the SiGe layers are recessed and filled with a dielectric inner spacer, which reduces gate-to-source/drain capacitance and prevents shorts. After source/drain epitaxy, the dummy gate is removed and the SiGe is etched away with high selectivity, leaving the silicon sheets suspended. ALD then fills the gaps with high-k dielectric and metal gate.

Samsung announced volume production of GAA at its 3 nm node in 2022 under the name MBCFET; TSMC adopted nanosheets at its 2 nm node and Intel at 18A as RibbonFET, making GAA the successor to the FinFET. Researchers are pursuing further steps: the forksheet, which places nMOS and pMOS sheets on either side of a thin dielectric wall; the CFET, which stacks nMOS over pMOS; and two-dimensional channel materials such as MoS2 that remain semiconducting at a single layer about 0.65 nm thick.

faq.q: What is the difference between GAA and FinFET?
faq.a: A FinFET's gate covers three sides of a vertical fin, while a GAA transistor's gate surrounds stacked horizontal sheets or wires on all sides. GAA gives stronger gate control and allows the channel width to be set continuously instead of in whole fins.

faq.q: What is a nanosheet transistor?
faq.a: It is a GAA transistor whose channels are thin horizontal silicon sheets, about 5 nm thick and tens of nanometers wide, stacked about three high with the gate filling the spaces between and around them.

faq.q: Why is SiGe used when making GAA transistors?
faq.a: SiGe layers grown between the silicon channel layers act as sacrificial spacers. They can be etched away selectively later, opening gaps so the gate dielectric and metal can wrap around each silicon sheet.

ナノシート.desc: A GAA transistor structure that stacks several thin, plate-like silicon channels vertically, each surrounded by the gate. Current can be tuned by the sheet width.

about.p: A nanosheet transistor stacks typically about three horizontal silicon channels, each around 5 nm thick and from about 15 to 50 nm wide, spaced about 10 nm apart vertically. The gate dielectric and metal fill every gap, so the gate surrounds each sheet on all four sides, which is why it is called gate-all-around (GAA). It resembles a FinFET fin turned on its side and stacked. The effective channel width is the perimeter of each sheet summed over the stack, so a wider sheet carries proportionally more current.

Fabrication begins with an epitaxial stack of alternating Si and SiGe layers, the SiGe containing about 25 to 30 percent germanium. The stack is patterned like a fin and a dummy gate is formed. The ends of the SiGe layers are recessed and filled with a dielectric such as nitride, forming inner spacers that reduce gate-to-source/drain capacitance and prevent shorts. After source/drain epitaxy and removal of the dummy gate, the SiGe is etched away with high selectivity, leaving the Si sheets suspended, and ALD fills the gaps with high-k dielectric and metal gate.

In a FinFET, fin height and width are fixed by the process, so drive strength can change only by the number of fins, a constraint called width quantization. Nanosheet width can be set continuously in layout: wide sheets for high-performance logic, narrow ones for low-power cells and SRAM, which allows finer tuning of drive current and capacitance. Gating the channel from all sides also gives stronger electrostatic control and better resistance to short-channel effects, delivering more current in the same footprint. Samsung's 3 nm generation in 2022 was the first announced volume production.

Adding sheets raises current per footprint, but taller stacks make source/drain epitaxy and gate fill harder, and lower sheets see more parasitic resistance and capacitance, so about three sheets is a common compromise. At thicknesses near 5 nm, quantum confinement widens the effective band gap and shifts threshold voltage; because the shift scales inversely with thickness squared, one atomic layer of variation can move it by tens of millivolts. The thermal budget is tight too: later steps run at about 600 to 700 °C or below to avoid Si/SiGe intermixing.

faq.q: What is the difference between a nanosheet and a nanowire transistor?
faq.a: Both are gate-all-around devices. A nanowire has a narrow cross-section with width close to its thickness, while a nanosheet is much wider than it is thick, carrying more current per stacked channel and allowing width to be tuned in layout.

faq.q: What is an inner spacer in a nanosheet transistor?
faq.a: It is a dielectric plug formed between the gate and the source/drain in the gaps between sheets, made by recessing the SiGe layer ends and refilling with an insulator such as nitride. It cuts parasitic capacitance and prevents gate-to-source/drain shorts.

faq.q: Why replace FinFETs with nanosheets?
faq.a: As gate lengths shrink, a gate on three sides of a fin no longer controls the channel well enough. Wrapping the gate around each sheet improves electrostatic control, and adjustable sheet width removes the fin-count quantization of FinFET design.

CFET(相補型FET).desc: A structure that stacks nMOS and pMOS transistors vertically. It is under development because it could greatly shrink the area of CMOS circuits.

about.h: How a CFET stacks the CMOS pair
about.p: In conventional CMOS, every logic gate places an nMOS and a pMOS transistor side by side, so a standard cell must hold both footprints plus the spacing between them. A complementary FET (CFET) builds one device directly on top of the other, typically an nMOS nanosheet stack above or below a pMOS nanosheet stack, with a shared gate running vertically through both. Because the two transistors of an inverter share the same input and output, folding them into one vertical stack can implement the same function in close to half the area.

about.h: Why CFET is hard to manufacture
about.p: The upper and lower tiers need different gate work-function metals and different source/drain epitaxy, such as boron-doped SiGe for the p device and phosphorus-doped silicon for the n device, all formed inside one tall structure. Two broad routes are studied: monolithic integration, where both tiers are patterned in one continuous sequence, and sequential integration, where the top tier is built on a layer bonded above the finished bottom tier. In both cases thermal budget, alignment between tiers and isolating the two tiers electrically are major difficulties.

A gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet transistor wraps the gate fully around stacked horizontal sheets, but n and p devices still sit side by side, typically tens of nanometers apart. A forksheet FET inserts a dielectric wall roughly ten-odd nanometers thick between n and p sheets so they can sit much closer, at the cost of the gate wrapping each sheet on only three sides. CFET removes the lateral n-to-p spacing altogether by moving one device above the other, which is why it is usually described as the step after GAA and forksheet.

Once transistors are stacked, the hard part is reaching them. Contacts to the lower device must pass beside the upper one without shorting to it, and both tiers need power and signal connections in a cell that has shrunk. This is why CFET is often discussed together with backside power delivery, which can feed the bottom tier from below while front-side wiring handles signals. Development targets practical use in the 2030s, and the routing scheme matters as much to that outcome as the transistor itself.

faq.q: What does CFET stand for?
faq.a: CFET stands for complementary field-effect transistor. It refers to a structure in which the nMOS and pMOS transistors of a CMOS circuit are stacked vertically instead of being placed side by side.

faq.q: What is the difference between CFET and GAA?
faq.a: A GAA nanosheet transistor describes how the gate surrounds the channel, while n and p devices still sit next to each other. A CFET keeps nanosheet-style channels but stacks the n and p devices on top of each other to shrink the cell footprint.

faq.q: Why can a CFET nearly halve cell area?
faq.a: In a CMOS gate the nMOS and pMOS share inputs and outputs, so most of the area goes to placing two devices and the gap between them side by side. Stacking one over the other removes that lateral duplication, leaving roughly one device footprint per n-p pair.

加速度センサー.desc: A sensor that detects acceleration from the movement of a small spring-supported mass. It is used for detecting smartphone orientation, in airbags and elsewhere.

about.h: How a MEMS accelerometer senses motion
about.p: A MEMS accelerometer suspends a small proof mass on silicon springs. When the package accelerates, inertia makes the mass lag behind, deflecting the springs until spring force balances the inertial force. In capacitive designs, interdigitated comb electrodes on the mass and the frame change their gaps as it moves, and the capacitance change, often below a femtofarad for nanometer-scale displacement, is read by a sensitive charge amplifier. Differential electrodes, with one gap closing as the opposite one opens, double the signal and cancel common-mode drift. Capacitive sensing is low power and temperature-stable, which is why it dominates consumer parts.

The spring–mass system resonates at f = (1/2π)√(k/m), and below resonance the static deflection is roughly the acceleration divided by (2πf)². A stiffer spring or lighter mass raises the resonant frequency, extending usable bandwidth and shock tolerance but shrinking the deflection per g, which lowers sensitivity. Designers therefore pick a resonance, typically a few kHz, that balances these needs. Full-scale range is a separate digital trade-off: with a 16-bit output, ±2 g gives about 0.06 mg per least significant bit (LSB), while ±16 g gives about 0.5 mg per LSB.

about.h: Gravity is always in the reading
about.p: An accelerometer measures the force needed to accelerate its proof mass along with the package, so at rest on a table it reports about 1 g (9.8 m/s²) directed upward, and in free fall it reads nearly zero. That gravity component is useful: phones compute tilt and screen orientation from it, pedometers detect steps from its periodic variations, and laptops once used the free-fall signature to park hard-disk heads. When only motion matters, the gravity vector must be estimated and subtracted, often with help from a gyroscope.

about.h: Accelerometer vs. gyroscope and typical uses
about.p: An accelerometer senses linear acceleration plus gravity, whereas a MEMS gyroscope senses rotation rate, typically through the Coriolis force on a vibrating mass. Combined with a magnetometer that measures Earth's field for heading, the three form an inertial measurement unit for navigation and orientation. Airbag systems were an early mass market: the accelerometer detects a crash deceleration of tens of g, and the controller decides within a few tens of milliseconds whether to deploy. Wearables also use accelerometer data to cancel motion artifacts in optical heart-rate sensing.

faq.q: Why does an accelerometer show 1 g when the phone is lying still?
faq.a: The sensor cannot distinguish gravity from acceleration, and resisting gravity looks to the proof mass exactly like accelerating upward at 9.8 m/s². In free fall the reading drops to about zero.

faq.q: Should I choose a ±2 g or ±16 g accelerometer range?
faq.a: Pick the narrowest range that will not saturate: ±2 g gives finer resolution for tilt and step counting, while ±16 g is needed for impacts, drops and sports motion. Most digital parts let you change the range in a register.

faq.q: What is the difference between an accelerometer and a gyroscope?
faq.a: An accelerometer measures linear acceleration including gravity, while a gyroscope measures angular velocity. Orientation tracking usually fuses both because each covers the other's weaknesses.

ジャイロスコープ.desc: A sensor that detects rotation rate (angular velocity). MEMS versions use the Coriolis force acting on a vibrating structure.

犠牲層エッチング.desc: A typical MEMS fabrication method that etches away a temporary layer (the sacrificial layer) beneath a structure, freeing beams or membranes so they can move.

静電容量検出.desc: A method that detects displacement, pressure and the like from changes in capacitance between movable and fixed electrodes. It is widely used in MEMS sensors.

FZ法(フローティングゾーン法).desc: A method that melts a zone of a polysilicon rod and moves that molten zone along to form a single crystal. With no crucible, oxygen content is low, suiting high-resistivity wafers.

ウエハのノッチ.desc: A small cut in a wafer's edge that indicates its crystal orientation. Used on 200 mm and larger wafers; smaller wafers used an orientation flat (a straight edge) instead.

結晶方位.desc: The direction of crystal planes and axes, expressed with Miller indices such as (100). The (100) surface is standard for silicon wafers used for MOSFETs.

about.p: Crystal planes and directions are named with Miller indices. Parentheses, as in (100), denote a specific plane; braces, as in {111}, denote the family of equivalent planes; square brackets, as in [110], a specific direction; and angle brackets, as in <110>, the family of equivalent directions. In a cubic crystal such as silicon, the direction [hkl] is perpendicular to the plane (hkl). A wafer is described by its surface plane, so a (100) wafer has the (100) plane as its top surface, with in-plane directions marked by a notch or flat.

Most CMOS wafers are (100). That surface has a lower density of available bonds per unit area than (111), giving an interface-state density at the Si/SiO2 interface roughly one tenth as large, which stabilizes threshold voltage and improves MOS behavior. Electron mobility in the inversion layer is also highest on (100). The (111) orientation, which oxidizes faster, was once common for bipolar devices. Hole mobility, by contrast, is higher on (110) surfaces, one reason channel orientation is a design variable in advanced transistors with vertical sidewalls.

Larger wafers carry a small V-shaped notch on the edge marking a reference direction such as <110>, so tools can align patterns to the crystal; wafers of 150 mm and below used a straight orientation flat instead. Silicon cleaves most easily along {111} planes, which need the least energy to break. On a (100) wafer, fractures tend to run along {110} planes perpendicular to the surface, giving straight cracks at right angles that reveal the in-plane orientation and are used for cross-section samples.

Many processes run at different rates on different planes. Thermal oxidation is faster on (111) than on (100), by up to about 1.5 times for thin oxides, which matters in FinFETs whose tops and sidewalls expose different planes; ISSG (in-situ steam generation) and radical oxidation are used because their growth depends less on orientation. Anisotropic wet etchants such as KOH attack {111} planes very slowly, so on a (100) wafer they produce V-grooves and pits bounded by {111} sidewalls at about 54.7° to the surface, a staple of MEMS fabrication.

faq.q: Why are most silicon wafers (100) oriented?
faq.a: The (100) surface gives a much lower interface-state density at the gate oxide interface than (111) and high electron mobility, which yields stable, well-behaved MOSFETs.

faq.q: What does the notch on a silicon wafer indicate?
faq.a: It marks a reference crystal direction, typically <110>, so lithography and other tools can align patterns to the crystal. Smaller wafers used a flat ground on the edge for the same purpose.

faq.q: What is the difference between (100) and {100}?
faq.a: (100) names one specific plane, while {100} names the whole family of planes equivalent to it by crystal symmetry. Square and angle brackets do the same for directions.

ゲッタリング.desc: A technique that collects and traps metal impurities in a wafer at locations away from the surface where devices are built, using oxygen precipitates and the like.

about.p: Transition metals such as iron, copper and nickel form deep energy levels near midgap in silicon. These act as recombination and generation centers, shortening carrier lifetime, raising junction leakage and dark current in image sensors, and degrading gate oxides; surface concentrations around 10^10 atoms/cm² can already matter. Many of these metals diffuse quickly at process temperatures and become less soluble on cooling, so they tend to precipitate wherever they find a sink. Gettering provides deliberate sinks away from the device region so the metals end up there instead of near transistors.

about.h: Intrinsic gettering and the denuded zone
about.p: Czochralski (CZ) silicon absorbs oxygen from its quartz crucible, typically about 10^17 to 10^18 cm⁻³, mostly at interstitial sites and measured by infrared absorption near 1107 cm⁻¹. A high-temperature anneal above about 1100 °C drives oxygen out of the surface, creating a precipitate-free denuded zone (DZ) tens of micrometers deep. Lower-temperature anneals then nucleate and grow oxygen precipitates, called bulk microdefects (BMDs), at around 10^8 to 10^10 cm⁻³ in the interior. Their strain fields and associated dislocations capture metals, while devices sit in the clean surface layer.

Extrinsic gettering adds sinks from outside the crystal. Mechanical damage on the wafer back or a deposited polysilicon backside layer provides grain boundaries and defects that collect metals. Heavily doped regions also attract certain metals, which is one benefit of p/p+ epitaxial wafers, where a lightly doped epitaxial layer sits on a heavily doped p+ substrate. Historically, phosphosilicate glass (PSG) gettering of sodium ions was crucial in stabilizing early MOS threshold voltages. Trace nitrogen doping of CZ crystals, around 10^13 to 10^15 cm⁻³, strengthens precipitation for intrinsic gettering.

Gettering is a second line of defense, not a substitute for contamination control. Cleaning keeps surface metals below roughly 10^9 to 10^10 atoms/cm², and chemicals and ultrapure water are controlled at parts-per-trillion levels. Gettering only works if metals can diffuse to the sinks during the thermal steps the wafer actually sees, and if precipitate density is high enough without intruding into the active layer. Oxygen content therefore has to be specified carefully: too little gives weak gettering, too much creates near-surface defects and thermal donors.

faq.q: What is the difference between intrinsic and extrinsic gettering?
faq.a: Intrinsic gettering uses oxygen precipitates grown inside the wafer bulk as sinks, while extrinsic gettering adds sinks from outside, such as backside damage, a polysilicon backside film or heavily doped layers.

faq.q: What is a denuded zone in a silicon wafer?
faq.a: A near-surface layer, typically tens of micrometers deep, from which oxygen has been out-diffused by high-temperature annealing so that no oxygen precipitates form where devices are built.

faq.q: Which metals does gettering target?
faq.a: Mainly fast-diffusing transition metals such as iron, copper and nickel, which create deep levels that increase leakage and reduce carrier lifetime.

ヘテロエピタキシー.desc: Growing a single-crystal film of a material different from the substrate, such as SiGe on silicon or GaN on sapphire. Growth of the same material is homoepitaxy.

格子不整合.desc: A difference in the atomic spacing (lattice constant) between a grown film and its substrate. A large mismatch causes strain and defects such as dislocations.

選択エピタキシャル成長.desc: A method that grows crystal only where silicon is exposed, not on areas covered by insulating film. It is used for SiGe in transistor sources and drains and elsewhere.

MOCVD(有機金属気相成長).desc: A method that grows crystals using metal-organic compounds and source gases such as ammonia. It is widely used to grow compound semiconductors such as GaN and GaAs.

about.p: Metal-organic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD), also called MOVPE (metal-organic vapor phase epitaxy), carries group-III metal-organic precursors such as trimethylgallium (TMGa), trimethylaluminum and trimethylindium to a heated substrate together with group-V hydride sources such as ammonia, arsine or phosphine. The molecules decompose at the hot surface and the atoms arrange themselves epitaxially, following the substrate's crystal structure. Metal-organics are held in temperature-controlled bubblers through which hydrogen or nitrogen flows, so bubbler temperature and carrier flow set the delivery rate. Switching gases changes composition at the nanometer scale, enabling quantum wells and heterostructures.

Substrate temperature, reactor pressure, growth rate and the V/III ratio, the molar ratio of group-V to group-III precursor, define the process. GaN growth uses V/III ratios of hundreds to thousands, because ammonia cracks inefficiently and nitrogen tends to desorb from the surface at high temperature. The ratio influences surface smoothness, the balance of lateral versus vertical growth, carbon incorporation from the methyl groups and point-defect levels. Production reactors hold dozens of wafers per run, which, together with uniformity and composition control, makes MOCVD the workhorse for compound-semiconductor devices.

Magnesium is the acceptor for p-type GaN, but layers grown by MOCVD come out highly resistive. Hydrogen from ammonia and the carrier gas bonds to Mg, forming Mg–H complexes that passivate the acceptors. In 1989 Hiroshi Amano and colleagues activated p-type conduction using low-energy electron-beam irradiation, and in 1992 Shuji Nakamura and colleagues showed that annealing at about 700 °C in nitrogen drives the hydrogen out, a method suited to mass production. This understanding opened the way to practical blue LEDs and laser diodes.

about.h: MOCVD vs. MBE, LPE and HVPE
about.p: Molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) evaporates sources into ultra-high vacuum around 10⁻⁸ Pa, with shutters and in-situ reflection high-energy electron diffraction (RHEED) for atomic-layer control, but at about 1 µm per hour it suits research, high-performance HEMTs and quantum devices. Liquid-phase epitaxy (LPE) grows near equilibrium from a metal solution, giving excellent crystals but poor thin-layer control. Hydride vapor phase epitaxy (HVPE) grows GaN tens of times faster, for thick layers and freestanding substrates. MOCVD sits between: thin, abrupt layers with high throughput, though pyrophoric metal-organics and toxic hydrides require careful handling.

faq.q: What is the difference between MOCVD and MBE?
faq.a: MOCVD grows crystals from chemical precursors flowing over a heated substrate and offers high throughput for production. MBE uses atomic or molecular beams in ultra-high vacuum, giving atomic-layer control and in-situ monitoring but slower growth.

faq.q: Why is the V/III ratio so high in GaN MOCVD?
faq.a: Ammonia decomposes inefficiently and nitrogen easily leaves the GaN surface at growth temperature, so a large excess of ammonia is needed to keep the surface nitrogen-rich and stoichiometric.

faq.q: Why are MOCVD precursors like trimethylgallium hazardous?
faq.a: Trimethylgallium and similar metal-organics ignite spontaneously in air and react violently with water. The hydride gases used alongside them, such as arsine and phosphine, are also highly toxic.

ドライ酸化.desc: Thermal oxidation with dry oxygen. Growth is slow, but it produces dense, high-quality oxide, used for gate oxides and the like.

about.p: In dry oxidation, silicon wafers are heated in a furnace, typically somewhere between 800 and 1200 °C, in pure oxygen, and the reaction Si + O2 → SiO2 forms silicon dioxide. The reaction takes place at the silicon/oxide interface, not at the surface: oxygen molecules must diffuse through the oxide already grown to reach the silicon. The oxide therefore grows downward into the wafer as well as upward, consuming silicon equal to about 44% of the final oxide thickness. Because the original surface is consumed, the interface moves into fresh, clean silicon, which is one reason thermal oxide interfaces are of such high quality.

The Deal-Grove model describes thermal oxidation with two rate constants. While the oxide is thin, oxygen crosses it easily and the interface reaction limits growth, so thickness increases linearly with time at the rate B/A. As the film thickens, diffusion through it becomes the bottleneck, and thickness grows with the square root of time with the parabolic constant B. The crossover occurs near a thickness of A/2, tens of nanometers to about 100 nm for dry oxidation. Below a few tens of nanometers, dry oxidation runs faster than the model predicts, so thin gate oxides are set by empirical calibration.

Wet oxidation uses steam instead of oxygen, Si + 2H2O → SiO2 + 2H2. Water dissolves in SiO2 several hundred times more readily than O2, so wet oxidation grows oxide several to ten times faster: at 1000 °C for an hour, roughly 70 nm dry versus about 400 nm wet. Some of the hydrogen remains in wet oxide, leaving it slightly less dense. Dry oxide is denser, has fewer interface states and allows precise thickness control, while wet oxide is chosen for thick isolation and masking layers where speed matters more than perfection.

The slow, controllable growth made dry oxidation the standard method for MOS gate oxides for decades, and it remains common for thin, high-quality layers such as pad oxides beneath silicon nitride and tunnel or interface layers. Small amounts of chlorine-containing gas are sometimes added to getter mobile ions such as sodium and to improve oxide quality. Growth rate also depends on crystal orientation, with (111) silicon oxidizing faster than (100). At advanced nodes, high-k dielectrics have replaced pure SiO2 gate oxides, but a thin silicon oxide interface layer still sits beneath them.

faq.q: What is the difference between dry and wet oxidation?
faq.a: Dry oxidation uses oxygen gas and grows a dense, high-quality oxide slowly, while wet oxidation uses steam and grows oxide several to ten times faster with slightly lower density. Dry oxide suits thin gate-quality layers; wet oxide suits thick isolation and masking films.

faq.q: What is the chemical reaction in dry oxidation?
faq.a: Silicon reacts with oxygen to form silicon dioxide: Si + O2 → SiO2. The reaction occurs at the silicon/oxide interface after oxygen diffuses through the existing oxide.

faq.q: Why is dry oxide used for gate oxides?
faq.a: Its slow growth allows precise control of very thin films, and the resulting oxide is dense with a low density of interface states. These properties give stable threshold voltages and reliable gate dielectrics.

ウェット酸化.desc: Thermal oxidation in an atmosphere containing water vapor. It grows faster than dry oxidation and is used to make thick oxides.

LOCOS.desc: A method that isolates devices by thickly oxidizing only areas not covered by nitride. It forms a beak-like encroachment at the edges (the bird's beak) and has been replaced by STI.

about.p: LOCOS (local oxidation of silicon) starts with a thin pad oxide, followed by a silicon nitride film that is patterned to cover the future active areas. The wafer is then oxidized, usually in steam at high temperature. Nitride blocks oxygen and water, so only the exposed silicon grows a thick field oxide, typically hundreds of nanometers. Because oxidation consumes silicon, part of that oxide sits below the original surface. Finally the nitride is stripped in hot phosphoric acid (around 160 °C) and the pad oxide is removed, leaving islands of bare silicon surrounded by field oxide.

about.h: Bird's beak and other side effects
about.p: Oxidant diffuses sideways through the pad oxide under the nitride edge, so oxide wedges in beneath the mask and lifts its edge. This bird's beak can extend roughly half the field-oxide thickness on each side, shrinking the usable active width and setting a floor on isolation pitch. The pad oxide cannot simply be removed to stop it, because it protects silicon from the nitride's stress. LOCOS also leaves a surface step that complicates later lithography, and the Kooi effect (white ribbon) can nitride the silicon at the mask edge; a sacrificial oxidation and strip is used to remove that nitride before the gate oxide is grown.

about.h: Why the field oxide is thick
about.p: Any wire running over the isolation region acts like a gate, with the field oxide as its dielectric and neighboring diffusions as source and drain. Making the field oxide hundreds of nanometers thick, more than 100 times a typical gate oxide, pushes the threshold voltage of this parasitic field transistor well above the supply voltage so it never turns on. A channel-stop implant under the field oxide is often added to raise that threshold further.

Shallow trench isolation (STI) etches trenches about 200–300 nm deep, fills them with CVD oxide and planarizes by chemical mechanical polishing (CMP), using nitride as the polish stop. The result is flat and has no lateral encroachment, so isolation can be made much narrower, and the same approach isolates FinFET fins. STI displaced LOCOS around the 0.25 µm generation. LOCOS survives in older, larger-geometry processes where its simplicity matters more than density, and variants such as poly-buffered LOCOS were developed to shorten the beak without eliminating it.

faq.q: What is the bird's beak in LOCOS?
faq.a: It is the wedge of oxide that grows laterally under the edge of the nitride mask because oxidant diffuses through the pad oxide. It can reach about half the field-oxide thickness per side and eats into the active area.

faq.q: Why was LOCOS replaced by shallow trench isolation?
faq.a: The bird's beak and the surface step prevented narrow, planar isolation as devices shrank. STI gives vertical, planarized isolation with no encroachment and became standard around the 0.25 µm generation.

faq.q: What is the Kooi effect in LOCOS?
faq.a: During steam oxidation, ammonia formed from the nitride mask can nitride the silicon surface near the mask edge, which later causes locally thin or weak gate oxide. A sacrificial oxide is grown and stripped to remove it.

熱拡散.desc: A doping method that diffuses impurity atoms into a semiconductor at high temperature. They spread from regions of high concentration to low.

about.p: At high temperature, dopant atoms in silicon hop from site to site and drift from high to low concentration, following Fick's laws. The diffusion coefficient D rises steeply with temperature in Arrhenius fashion, so process temperature, typically on the order of 900–1200 °C for classic diffusion, dominates the result, and the characteristic distance scales as the square root of D × t. The same physics continues during every later high-temperature step, which is why total thermal budget is tracked in modern processes to keep junctions from moving.

Classic diffusion used two steps. Predeposition holds the surface concentration constant, roughly at the dopant's solid solubility, and introduces a shallow layer whose profile is a complementary error function (erfc) and whose dose grows with time. Drive-in then removes the source and heats the wafer so the fixed dose spreads deeper as a Gaussian profile, with surface concentration falling. Combining the two lets surface concentration and junction depth be chosen fairly independently, although real high-concentration diffusion departs from these ideal shapes.

Dopants are supplied from gases such as phosphine or diborane, or from liquids carried by bubbling nitrogen through them. Phosphorus oxychloride (POCl3) mixed with oxygen forms a phosphorus-rich glass on the wafer from which phosphorus diffuses, and boron tribromide (BBr3) serves the same role for boron. Furnaces process hundreds of wafers per batch at low cost. Because the temperatures would destroy photoresist, the areas to be protected are masked with silicon dioxide, in which common dopants diffuse much more slowly than in silicon.

Ion implantation replaced diffusion for most IC doping because it runs near room temperature, can use resist masks, controls dose to about ±1% by counting beam current and sets depth independently through energy. It damages the lattice, however, so an anneal follows, and that anneal is itself a short diffusion step. Diffusion always yields profiles peaking at the surface, whereas in-situ doping during epitaxy can create abrupt or buried layers. Thermal diffusion survives in solar-cell emitters and deep junctions in power devices.

faq.q: What is the difference between thermal diffusion and ion implantation?
faq.a: Diffusion introduces dopants from the surface at high temperature, coupling surface concentration and depth, while implantation fires accelerated ions in at low temperature with independently controlled dose and depth. Implantation then needs an anneal to repair damage and activate the dopants.

faq.q: Why is a predeposition profile erfc and a drive-in profile Gaussian?
faq.a: Predeposition solves the diffusion equation with a fixed surface concentration, giving an erfc shape. Drive-in solves it with a fixed total dose and no further supply, giving a Gaussian that broadens with time.

faq.q: Is thermal diffusion still used?
faq.a: Yes, for crystalline-silicon solar-cell emitters using POCl3 and for deep junctions in power devices. In CMOS, dopant diffusion during anneals is still a key effect that thermal budgets must control.

ドーズ量.desc: The number of ions implanted per unit area in ion implantation, expressed in cm⁻². It is set by beam current and implant time.

投影飛程.desc: The average depth at which implanted ions come to rest. It is deeper with higher acceleration energy and with lighter ions.

チャネリング.desc: A phenomenon in which ions pass through gaps between rows of crystal atoms and penetrate deeper than expected. It is prevented by tilting the wafer during implantation and similar measures.

PECVD(プラズマCVD).desc: CVD that decomposes source gases with plasma to deposit films. It can deposit at lower temperatures than thermal CVD and is used for insulating films in interconnect steps and the like.

about.p: In plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD), RF power drives a glow discharge between a showerhead electrode and the heated wafer stage. Energetic plasma electrons break precursor molecules into reactive radicals and ions while the gas and wafer stay comparatively cool, so films grow at about 300–400 °C instead of the 600–800 °C typical of thermal CVD. That makes PECVD usable after aluminum or copper wiring is in place, when high temperatures are forbidden. The showerhead, whose many small holes spread gas evenly over the wafer, doubles as the upper electrode in most single-wafer PECVD chambers.

Silicon oxide is commonly deposited from silane with nitrous oxide (N2O) as a gentle oxidant, or from TEOS with oxygen. Silicon nitride comes from silane and ammonia, and adjusting the gas mix yields oxynitride (SiON), whose tunable refractive index suits antireflective layers for lithography. Carbon-doped oxide (SiOC) low-k dielectrics, with relative permittivity around 2.7–3.0 versus about 3.9 for SiO2, are mostly made by PECVD. PECVD nitride also serves as the final chip passivation and as a cap and diffusion barrier over copper lines.

about.h: PECVD vs. thermal CVD film quality
about.p: Low temperature has a cost. Precursors react incompletely, so PECVD films keep hydrogen as Si-H and N-H bonds: PECVD nitride may contain about 10–30% hydrogen, versus a few percent for low-pressure CVD (LPCVD) nitride, and is non-stoichiometric, often written SiNx. Such films are less dense and etch faster in wet chemicals. Conformality in narrow gaps is also generally poorer than LPCVD. Engineers therefore use thermal CVD where the thermal budget allows and reserve PECVD for steps where temperature, not film perfection, is the binding constraint.

Many PECVD tools apply a high frequency (13.56 MHz) and a low frequency (hundreds of kHz). Heavy ions can follow the slow field and bombard the growing film, densifying it and pushing it toward compressive stress. Changing the high-to-low power ratio, gas composition and temperature tunes nitride stress roughly from −3 GPa (compressive) to +1.5 GPa (tensile). This control is used for stress-liner films that strain the channel to boost transistor mobility, and for keeping wafer bow within limits in thick film stacks.

faq.q: Why can PECVD deposit at lower temperatures than thermal CVD?
faq.a: Energetic plasma electrons, rather than wafer heat, supply the energy to break precursor bonds. The wafer can therefore stay around 300–400 °C, which is safe for finished metal interconnects.

faq.q: What is the difference between PECVD and LPCVD silicon nitride?
faq.a: LPCVD nitride is deposited hot and is dense and near-stoichiometric with little hydrogen. PECVD nitride is deposited at low temperature, contains roughly 10–30% hydrogen, etches faster, and is used where the thermal budget is limited, such as passivation.

faq.q: How is film stress controlled in PECVD?
faq.a: Mainly through the ratio of low-frequency to high-frequency RF power, which sets how strongly ions bombard the film, along with gas mix and temperature. More ion bombardment generally makes the film more compressive.

ステップカバレッジ.desc: A measure of how uniformly a film covers the sidewalls and bottoms of steps and holes compared with flat areas. ALD gives excellent step coverage.

about.p: Step coverage compares film thickness on the sidewalls or bottom of a trench or hole with the thickness on the flat top surface, usually as a percentage such as bottom ÷ top. A value near 100% means the film follows the topography uniformly. The figure always depends on aspect ratio, the depth-to-width ratio of the feature, so a method that coats a shallow step well may leave the bottom of a deep contact almost bare. Poor coverage also tends to come with overhang at the opening, which can pinch off and trap a void when the feature is later filled.

about.h: Why PVD, CVD and ALD differ
about.p: In physical vapor deposition (PVD), such as sputtering or evaporation, atoms fly in nearly straight lines and barely migrate after landing, so surfaces not in line of sight from the opening are shadowed; bottom coverage in deep holes can fall below 10%. Chemical vapor deposition (CVD) delivers precursor gases that diffuse into features and react on the surface, giving much better coverage. Atomic layer deposition (ALD) alternates self-limiting surface reactions, each adding at most about one monolayer per cycle, and reaches close to 100% even in very high-aspect-ratio structures.

CVD coverage depends on which step is slower. If the surface reaction is slow (reaction-limited), gas penetrates deep into the feature before it reacts, and growth rate is nearly uniform everywhere. If gas supply is slow (supply- or transport-limited), the opening receives more precursor than the bottom, so the top thickens and may close off. Lower temperature slows the reaction and lower pressure speeds gas diffusion, so low-pressure CVD (LPCVD) at tens to hundreds of pascals is conformal. TEOS oxide and WF6-based tungsten CVD are classic examples chosen for their good coverage.

Barrier and liner layers in contacts and vias must be continuous yet thin, so their sidewall and bottom coverage directly sets reliability. Gate dielectrics and metals wrapped around FinFET or gate-all-around channels, and films lining deep 3D NAND holes, rely on ALD-level conformality. Step coverage should not be confused with gap fill: a perfectly conformal film closing a narrow trench from both sides leaves a seam, and void-free filling may need deposition–etch cycles. Sometimes poor coverage is wanted, as in lift-off, where line-of-sight evaporation keeps films on resist sidewalls discontinuous.

faq.q: Which deposition method has the best step coverage?
faq.a: ALD gives the best, typically close to 100%, because each self-limiting reaction cycle coats every exposed surface equally. CVD comes next, and line-of-sight PVD methods such as sputtering and evaporation are the worst.

faq.q: Is step coverage the same as conformality?
faq.a: They are closely related and often used interchangeably. Conformality describes how evenly a film follows topography in general, while step coverage is usually quoted as a specific thickness ratio, such as bottom-to-top or sidewall-to-top.

faq.q: Why is step coverage poor in sputtering?
faq.a: Sputtered atoms travel almost in straight lines and stick where they land, so the trench opening shadows the sidewalls and bottom. Film builds up at the top corners instead, forming overhangs.

OPC(光学近接効果補正).desc: A technique that corrects mask patterns in advance, anticipating distortion of the printed pattern caused by diffraction of light and similar effects.

about.p: When features approach the resolution limit (small k1 in R = k1·λ/NA), the projection lens passes only a few diffraction orders, so the image of a pattern is a blurred version of the mask. Line ends pull back, corners round, and the width of the same drawn line differs depending on whether its neighbours are dense or isolated. Resist and etch add their own pattern-dependent biases. Left uncorrected, these effects shift transistor gate lengths and can bridge or pinch wires, so the mask must differ from the intended wafer pattern.

Early OPC was rule-based: lookup tables added fixed biases, serifs at corners and hammerheads at line ends. Modern model-based OPC splits polygon edges into short fragments, simulates the aerial image and resist response with models calibrated on test-wafer measurements, and moves each fragment iteratively until the simulated contour matches the target, minimizing edge placement error. Sub-resolution assist features, extra lines too narrow to print, are often added beside isolated features so they behave more like dense ones and keep a wider process window.

OPC is one of the resolution enhancement techniques, alongside off-axis illumination and phase-shift masks, that have driven production k1 from about 0.6 down to roughly 0.27–0.3. Their shared aim is a wide process window, the range of dose and focus that keeps dimensions within tolerance. Source mask optimization (SMO) computes illumination shape and mask pattern together, and inverse lithography technology (ILT) derives freeform curvilinear masks from the desired image. EUV still needs OPC, including corrections for flare from mirror roughness and for mask 3D effects.

about.h: Where OPC sits in the flow
about.p: OPC is applied after tape-out, when the design layout in GDSII or OASIS format is turned into mask data. The corrected data is verified by lithography simulation to find hotspots, places likely to bridge or pinch even though design rules are met, then fractured and written onto the mask, usually with electron-beam or multi-beam writers. OPC multiplies polygon counts, so it takes large computing clusters and GPU acceleration, and it lengthens mask writing. The designer's layout is unchanged; OPC changes only what is put on the mask.

faq.q: What is the difference between rule-based and model-based OPC?
faq.a: Rule-based OPC applies fixed corrections from lookup tables according to local geometry. Model-based OPC simulates how each pattern will print and iteratively moves edge segments until the predicted contour matches the target, which handles complex layouts far better.

faq.q: What are SRAFs in OPC?
faq.a: Sub-resolution assist features are thin mask features placed near isolated patterns that are too small to print themselves. They make isolated lines image more like dense ones, widening the dose and focus window.

faq.q: Is OPC still needed with EUV lithography?
faq.a: Yes. EUV processes run at low k1 too, and they add effects such as flare from mirror roughness and mask 3D shadowing that OPC must correct.

液浸露光.desc: Exposure with the space between the lens and the wafer filled with water. It allows a numerical aperture above 1, so ArF excimer lasers can form finer patterns.

RIE(反応性イオンエッチング).desc: Dry etching that combines reactive species in a plasma with ions accelerated by an electric field. It enables vertical, anisotropic etching.

ウェットエッチング.desc: Etching that dissolves films by immersing them in chemicals. Selectivity is high and damage low, but it generally proceeds isotropically and does not suit fine patterning.

about.p: A wet etchant attacks a film by chemical reaction wherever liquid touches it, and for amorphous or polycrystalline films the rate is the same in every direction. As the etch goes down, it also goes sideways under the mask edge. Clearing a 1 µm film undercuts the mask by about 1 µm, and overetch adds more. Because the dimensional change is of the order of the film thickness, wet etching cannot define features narrower than the film is thick. MEMS (micro-electro-mechanical systems) processing exploits the same behavior to hollow out material under suspended structures.

Silicon dioxide is etched in hydrofluoric acid; buffered HF (BHF), which adds ammonium fluoride, keeps the active HF2⁻ concentration and pH stable so thermal oxide etches steadily at tens to about 100 nm per minute without lifting resist. Silicon nitride is removed in concentrated phosphoric acid near 160 °C with selectivity of tens to over 100 against oxide, which depends on the dissolved silicon in the bath. Some materials resist wet chemistry altogether: GaN, for example, is etched with chlorine-based plasmas rather than liquids.

Alkaline etchants such as potassium hydroxide (KOH) or TMAH (tetramethylammonium hydroxide) are crystallographic: the (111) planes of silicon etch roughly 100 times slower than (100) planes. On a (100) wafer, slow (111) planes emerge as sidewalls inclined at about 54.7°, forming V-grooves and pyramidal pits whose shape is fixed by the crystal rather than by time. This orientation-dependent etching produces MEMS pressure-sensor diaphragms, inkjet nozzles and the light-trapping texture on crystalline solar cells. It is anisotropic, but unlike plasma etching the direction is set by crystal planes, not by an ion beam.

about.h: Process control and where it is still used
about.p: Being thermally activated, wet etch rates often rise 1.5–2× per 10 °C, so baths are held to about ±0.5 °C and etch time is set from a known rate. Equipment is simple, batches of wafers can be processed together, selectivity is high and there is no plasma damage. Dry (plasma) etching owns fine patterning, but wet processes remain essential for blanket film removal, nitride mask stripping after LOCOS or STI, removing sacrificial nitride layers in 3D NAND stacks, native-oxide removal and wafer cleaning.

faq.q: What is the difference between wet etching and dry etching?
faq.a: Wet etching dissolves material in liquid chemicals and is usually isotropic with high selectivity and no plasma damage. Dry etching uses plasma and directional ion bombardment to cut vertical profiles, which fine patterning requires.

faq.q: How much undercut does isotropic wet etching cause?
faq.a: Roughly equal to the etched depth: a 1 µm film etched to the underlayer is undercut about 1 µm from the mask edge, plus whatever overetch adds.

faq.q: Can wet etching be anisotropic?
faq.a: Yes, for single-crystal silicon in alkaline etchants such as KOH or TMAH, which etch (111) planes far more slowly than (100) planes and produce 54.7° sidewalls on (100) wafers.

等方性エッチング.desc: Etching that proceeds at the same rate vertically and laterally. It cuts in under the mask (undercut).

スラリー.desc: The liquid used in CMP, with fine abrasive particles dispersed in chemicals. It flattens surfaces by combining chemical action with mechanical polishing.

about.h: What is in a CMP slurry
about.p: A CMP (chemical mechanical polishing) slurry is a suspension of abrasive particles, typically tens to over a hundred nanometers across, in a chemical solution. Common abrasives are silica (SiO2), ceria (CeO2) and alumina. The liquid contains pH adjusters, oxidizers for metals, corrosion inhibitors such as benzotriazole for copper, and dispersants that keep particles from clumping. Particle size, hardness, concentration and chemistry are tuned for each film, and slurry is one of the largest consumable costs in CMP.

about.h: How chemistry and abrasion work together
about.p: The chemistry converts the top of the film into a softer or more soluble layer, and the abrasive particles, pressed by the pad, wipe that layer away, exposing fresh material to react again. Tungsten CMP shows this clearly: tungsten is too hard to polish efficiently by abrasion alone, so oxidizers such as hydrogen peroxide or iron salts form a softer oxide that the particles remove. Removal rate roughly follows Preston's equation, rate = k × pressure × relative velocity, where k depends on slurry, pad and film; raised areas see higher local pressure and polish faster, which planarizes.

Oxide and interlayer dielectric polishing commonly use silica or ceria slurries. Ceria slurries can polish oxide much faster than silicon nitride, which makes nitride a natural stop layer in shallow trench isolation (STI). Copper CMP is done in stages with different slurries: a fast bulk copper step, a gentler clearing step and a barrier step that removes Ta/TaN and a little dielectric. Final polishing of bare silicon wafers uses alkaline colloidal silica, whose soft, fine particles give damage-free mirror surfaces with roughness around 0.1 nm.

Slurry particles can agglomerate into micron-sized clusters through drying, temperature swings, pH changes or shear in pumps, and these clusters scratch wafers, which can short or open copper lines and is especially harmful to fragile low-k films. Slurry is therefore circulated, temperature-controlled and passed through filters of a few micrometers just before the tool. After polishing, residual particles, metal ions and inhibitors must be removed by brush scrubbing and chemical cleans while the wafer is still wet, because dried slurry bonds firmly to the surface.

faq.q: What abrasive is used in CMP slurry?
faq.a: The most common abrasives are silica (fumed or colloidal) and ceria, with alumina used in some metal slurries; the choice depends on the film being polished and the selectivity required.

faq.q: Why is ceria slurry used for STI CMP?
faq.a: Ceria slurries can remove silicon oxide much faster than silicon nitride, so polishing effectively stops on the nitride layer that protects the active areas.

faq.q: What causes scratches in CMP?
faq.a: Most scratches come from large agglomerated slurry particles or hard debris trapped in the pad, which is why slurry is filtered and circulated and the pad is conditioned regularly.

ディッシング.desc: A CMP phenomenon in which the center of a wide metal line is over-polished into a dish-like depression.

メガソニック洗浄.desc: A cleaning method that applies ultrasound of about 1 MHz to the cleaning solution to remove fine particles from wafer surfaces.

バリアメタル.desc: A thin metal film around copper wiring that prevents copper from diffusing into insulating films or silicon, such as Ta or TaN.

about.p: Copper is an excellent conductor but diffuses readily through silicon dioxide, low-k dielectrics and silicon. In silicon it forms deep-level traps that increase junction leakage and degrade transistors; in the dielectric between wires it degrades insulation and long-term reliability. Copper lines are therefore lined on their sides and bottom with a few nanometres of barrier metal, typically a tantalum nitride and tantalum (TaN/Ta) bilayer, and capped on top with a dielectric film. The barrier also improves copper's adhesion to the dielectric and helps control the copper grain texture, which benefits electromigration resistance.

about.h: Where it fits in the damascene process
about.p: Copper is hard to pattern by dry etching, so copper wiring uses the damascene approach. Trenches and vias are etched into the dielectric, the barrier metal and a thin copper seed layer are deposited, and the openings are filled by copper electroplating. Chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) then removes the excess. Because copper and barrier need different conditions, CMP is split into stages: a fast step removing bulk copper, a gentler copper clearing step, and a final barrier step that removes the barrier and a little dielectric, each with its own slurry.

Barrier metals are far more resistive than copper, and a layer of about 2–3 nm cannot be thinned much without losing its blocking ability. In wide lines this hardly matters, but in a 20 nm via the barrier occupies a large share of the cross-section, leaving less room for copper. The barrier at the via bottom also sits directly in series with the current path. Via and line resistance therefore rise sharply with scaling. Responses include thinner, more conformal barriers deposited by atomic layer deposition (ALD), removing the barrier from the via bottom, and alternative metals needing little or no barrier.

about.h: Barrier metal in contacts and older wiring
about.p: Barrier layers are not unique to copper. In aluminum wiring, a titanium nitride (TiN) barrier kept aluminum and silicon from interdiffusing and spiking through shallow junctions. In tungsten contacts, a Ti/TiN stack lines the hole: titanium reduces contact resistance by reacting with silicon to form a silicide, and TiN acts as an adhesion and protective layer during tungsten deposition from tungsten hexafluoride. The common thread is a thin refractory metal or metal nitride that separates two materials that must touch electrically but must not mix.

faq.q: Why is TaN/Ta used as a barrier for copper?
