faq.a: Tantalum and tantalum nitride block copper diffusion even when only a few nanometres thick, adhere well to dielectrics, and provide a good surface for copper seed deposition. TaN is placed against the dielectric and Ta against the copper in a typical bilayer.

faq.q: What happens if copper diffuses into silicon?
faq.a: Copper forms deep-level traps in silicon that increase leakage current and degrade transistor characteristics. In interconnect dielectrics it can also lead to leakage and insulation breakdown between wires.

faq.q: Why does barrier metal increase via resistance at small dimensions?
faq.a: The barrier is much more resistive than copper and cannot be thinned in proportion to the via, so it takes a larger share of a small via's cross-section and sits in series at the via bottom.

多層配線.desc: A structure that stacks many wiring layers separated by insulating films and connects them vertically with vias. Leading-edge ICs have more than ten layers.

RC遅延.desc: Signal delay determined by the product of wire resistance (R) and capacitance (C). It grows as scaling makes wires thinner, limiting performance.

about.p: A wire has resistance R = ρL/(W × T), set by resistivity, length, width and thickness, and capacitance to neighboring wires and to layers above and below. A signal must charge that capacitance through that resistance. Because both are spread along the line, the 50% delay of a distributed RC wire is roughly 0.4 RC, versus about 0.7 RC for a single lumped resistor and capacitor. As an example, a 1 mm wire with a 100 nm × 100 nm cross-section and ρ = 2 µΩ·cm has about 2 kΩ; with roughly 0.2 pF per mm, RC is around 400 ps.

about.h: Why delay grows with length squared
about.p: Both R and C scale with length, so their product, and hence delay, scales with length squared: doubling an unbuffered wire roughly quadruples its delay. Breaking a long wire into segments driven by repeaters (buffers) turns this into a roughly linear dependence on length, because each segment is short and the repeater delays add rather than multiply. The price is area and power, which is significant on large chips with very many repeaters, so long nets are also routed on thick upper metal levels with lower resistance per unit length.

Shrinking width and thickness raises resistance per unit length, while capacitance per unit length stays roughly constant because spacing shrinks too, so local wires get slower even as transistors get faster. At narrow widths copper's effective resistivity also rises above its bulk value of about 1.7 µΩ·cm due to electron scattering at surfaces and grain boundaries, and barrier and liner layers occupy a growing share of the cross-section. Making wires taller lowers R but enlarges the facing sidewall area and raises coupling capacitance, so aspect ratios around 2 are a compromise.

Resistance was cut by replacing aluminum with copper interconnect. Capacitance is cut with low-k interlayer dielectrics: carbon-doped oxide (SiOC) at about 2.7 to 3.0 and porous films at about 2.2 to 2.5, compared with about 3.9 for SiO2, although these softer films complicate CMP and packaging. Design measures include repeater insertion, a wiring hierarchy with thin local levels and thick global levels, and wider spacing on critical nets. Lower capacitance also cuts switching power and crosstalk, not only delay.

faq.q: Why does wire delay increase with the square of length?
faq.a: A wire's resistance and its capacitance both grow in proportion to its length, and the delay depends on their product. Doubling the length therefore roughly quadruples the RC delay unless repeaters are inserted.

faq.q: How do low-k dielectrics reduce RC delay?
faq.a: Capacitance between wires is proportional to the dielectric constant of the insulator between them. Replacing SiO2 (about 3.9) with materials of about 2.2 to 3.0 lowers C and therefore the RC product.

faq.q: Why are repeaters inserted on long wires?
faq.a: Repeaters split a long wire into short segments, each with a small RC, so total delay grows roughly linearly with length instead of quadratically. They cost area and power, so they are placed only where needed.

特殊材料ガス.desc: High-purity gases with toxic or flammable properties used in semiconductor manufacturing, such as silane, arsine and phosphine. They are supplied under strict control.

about.h: What counts as a specialty gas
about.p: Fabs use two broad classes of gas. Bulk gases such as nitrogen, oxygen, argon and hydrogen are consumed in large volumes and are piped from on-site plants or bulk tanks. Specialty gases are used in smaller amounts for specific process steps and usually arrive in cylinders. They include deposition sources such as silane, dichlorosilane, ammonia and tungsten hexafluoride; dopant gases such as arsine, phosphine and diborane, often diluted in hydrogen or nitrogen; etch gases such as fluorocarbons, chlorine, hydrogen bromide and sulfur hexafluoride; and chamber-cleaning gases such as nitrogen trifluoride (NF3).

Many specialty gases combine several hazards. Silane is pyrophoric: it can ignite spontaneously on contact with air. Arsine and phosphine are highly toxic at very low concentrations. Chlorine, hydrogen chloride and hydrogen bromide are corrosive, especially with moisture, and attack both people and gas lines. Others are flammable, oxidizing or asphyxiating, and several fluorinated gases such as NF3, SF6 and perfluorocarbons are potent greenhouse gases. Each gas therefore has its own handling rules, detectors and emergency response.

Purity is written as a count of nines: 6N means 99.9999%, leaving at most 1 ppm of total impurities, and 5N5 means 99.9995%. Moisture and oxygen are especially harmful because they corrode lines and degrade films. Cylinders sit in continuously exhausted gas cabinets with leak detectors that trigger alarms and automatic shutoff valves. Gas reaches tools through clean, electropolished stainless-steel lines, often double-walled for toxic gases, and lines are purged before and after every cylinder change by trained staff following written procedures.

Only part of the gas reacts in the chamber, so exhaust carries unreacted specialty gases and hazardous byproducts. Point-of-use abatement units beside each tool treat it by combustion, thermal or plasma decomposition, adsorption or water scrubbing before it joins the fab's central exhaust. Treating pyrophoric gases early also prevents duct fires, and removing byproducts that turn into solids, such as silica powder from silane, prevents clogging downstream.

faq.q: What is the difference between bulk gases and specialty gases in a fab?
faq.a: Bulk gases such as nitrogen, oxygen, argon and hydrogen are used in large volumes and piped in, while specialty gases such as silane, arsine and NF3 are used in small amounts for specific steps, usually from cylinders, and are often toxic, flammable or corrosive.

faq.q: What does 6N purity mean for a gas?
faq.a: 6N means six nines, 99.9999% purity, so total impurities are 1 ppm or less. A value such as 99.9995% is written 5N5.

faq.q: Why is silane dangerous?
faq.a: Silane is pyrophoric, meaning it can ignite spontaneously when it meets air, so leaks can start fires without any ignition source. It is handled in exhausted cabinets with leak detection and automatic shutoff.

TMAH.desc: Tetramethylammonium hydroxide, a metal-ion-free organic alkali used as a photoresist developer. Care is needed because it can cause poisoning through skin absorption.

about.h: What TMAH is and why fabs use it
about.p: TMAH (tetramethylammonium hydroxide, (CH3)4N+ OH−) is a quaternary ammonium hydroxide, a strong base that contains no metal atoms. Sodium or potassium hydroxide would also dissolve exposed photoresist, but alkali metal ions that reach the gate oxide become mobile ions that drift under electric fields and shift threshold voltages, the problem that made early MOS devices unstable. A metal-free organic alkali avoids that contamination path, which is why TMAH became the standard developer for positive photoresists in semiconductor manufacturing.

The industry-standard developer is 2.38 wt% aqueous TMAH, about 0.26 N. In a positive resist, exposure makes the irradiated regions alkali-soluble: in novolak resists for i-line the photoactive compound converts into a carboxylic acid, and in chemically amplified resists for KrF and ArF, acid-catalyzed deprotection exposes acidic groups on the polymer. These regions dissolve in TMAH while unexposed regions remain. Using one common concentration across fabs keeps dissolution rates reproducible. Negative-tone development is different: an organic solvent dissolves the unexposed areas instead.

TMAH is hazardous beyond being a caustic alkali. Tetramethylammonium ions absorbed through the skin interfere with signal transmission from nerves to muscles and can cause respiratory arrest, and fatal accidents after skin contact have been reported. Concentrated stock solutions, around 25%, are far more dangerous than the 2.38% developer, because the absorbed dose rises with concentration and contact area. Handling requires chemical-resistant gloves, face protection and aprons, and any contact calls for immediate flushing with water and prompt medical care even if the skin looks unharmed.

TMAH also etches silicon anisotropically, like KOH: (100) planes etch much faster than (111) planes, producing V-grooves and cavities bounded by sloped facets. Because it is metal-free and compatible with CMOS processing, TMAH solutions are widely used in MEMS fabrication to release structures or form membranes. The etch rate and surface smoothness depend on concentration and temperature, and the etch strongly slows on heavily boron-doped silicon, which can serve as an etch stop.

faq.q: What concentration of TMAH is used as a photoresist developer?
faq.a: The standard is 2.38 wt% TMAH in water, about 0.26 N, which gives reproducible development rates and is used by most fabs.

faq.q: Why is TMAH used instead of NaOH as a developer?
faq.a: NaOH leaves sodium ions that can migrate into gate oxide as mobile charge and shift threshold voltages. TMAH is a metal-free organic base, so it develops resist without that contamination.

faq.q: Why is TMAH so dangerous on skin?
faq.a: Besides causing alkaline burns, TMAH is absorbed through the skin and its tetramethylammonium ions block nerve-to-muscle signaling, which can cause respiratory failure, especially with concentrated solutions.

プリカーサ(前駆体).desc: A source compound that reacts to form the desired film in CVD or ALD, such as TEOS or metal-organic compounds.

about.h: How a precursor becomes a film
about.p: In chemical vapor deposition (CVD), precursor vapor flows over a heated wafer, adsorbs on the surface and decomposes or reacts with a co-reactant, leaving a solid film while volatile byproducts are pumped away. Silane (SiH4) decomposes to silicon and hydrogen, tungsten hexafluoride (WF6) is reduced to tungsten with HF as a byproduct, and TEOS breaks down to SiO2. In atomic layer deposition (ALD) the precursor chemisorbs on surface sites until they are filled, the excess is purged, and a separate reactant such as water, ozone or ammonia completes the reaction, giving about 0.1 nm per cycle.

A useful precursor must be volatile enough to deliver as vapor; liquids such as TEOS are vaporized by bubbling a carrier gas through them or by direct liquid injection. It must survive transport without decomposing in the gas phase, yet react readily at the surface. Its ligands should leave cleanly: chlorides such as HfCl4 are thermally stable around 300 °C but can leave chlorine in the film, while metal-organics such as TEMAHf react at lower temperature but can leave carbon. Safety matters too, which is why liquid TEOS is often preferred over pyrophoric silane for oxide.

At low temperature the surface reaction is slow and sets the deposition rate, which then follows the Arrhenius law and depends exponentially on temperature, so wafer temperature uniformity controls thickness uniformity. Because precursor molecules can diffuse deep into trenches before reacting, this regime gives good step coverage. At high temperature the reaction is fast and the arrival rate of precursor limits growth, so gas-flow uniformity matters and trench openings receive more film and can pinch off. Large exposed areas consume more precursor and slow deposition, an effect known as loading.

Silicon films and epitaxy use silane, dichlorosilane (SiH2Cl2) and trichlorosilane (SiHCl3), usually diluted in hydrogen that also keeps the surface reduced and carries away chlorine as HCl. Oxide uses TEOS, tungsten plugs use WF6, and titanium nitride often uses TiCl4. High-k ALD uses HfCl4 or TEMAHf with H2O or O3, and Al2O3 uses trimethylaluminum (TMA) with water inside an ALD window of about 150 to 300 °C. Dopant gases such as phosphine and diborane are added for in-situ doping, and focused ion beam tools inject precursor gases to deposit local platinum or tungsten.

faq.q: What is the difference between a precursor and a reactant in ALD?
faq.a: The precursor carries the element that ends up in the film, such as the hafnium in HfCl4 or the aluminum in trimethylaluminum. The reactant, often water, ozone or ammonia, is dosed in a separate step to convert the adsorbed precursor layer into oxide or nitride and to restore reactive surface sites for the next cycle.

faq.q: Why is TEOS often used instead of silane for silicon oxide CVD?
faq.a: TEOS is a liquid at room temperature and is not pyrophoric, so it is safer to store and handle than silane. Its surface-driven decomposition also gives more conformal oxide with better step coverage in narrow gaps.

faq.q: Is a carrier gas the same as a precursor?
faq.a: No. A carrier gas such as hydrogen, nitrogen or argon only transports and dilutes the precursor vapor and does not supply atoms to the film, although hydrogen in silicon epitaxy also acts as a reducing agent that keeps the surface clean.

NF3(三フッ化窒素).desc: A gas used for cleaning CVD chambers and the like. Its global warming potential is high, so emission reduction is required.

about.h: How NF3 cleans a CVD chamber
about.p: Chemical vapor deposition (CVD) coats not only the wafer but also the chamber walls, showerhead and heater. Left to build up, these films crack and flake, shedding particles onto wafers. Chambers are therefore cleaned periodically, at intervals set by the accumulated film thickness. NF3 is dissociated in a plasma into fluorine radicals, which react with silicon-based deposits such as silicon oxide, silicon nitride or amorphous silicon to form volatile SiF4 that the vacuum pumps carry away. The nitrogen leaves as harmless N2, and the chamber never has to be opened for a wet clean.

Older cleans fed perfluorocarbons (PFCs) such as C2F6 into the chamber and struck a plasma there. Much of the gas passed through undecomposed, and ion bombardment wore chamber parts. A remote plasma source instead dissociates NF3 in a separate cavity upstream, with over 95% efficiency, and sends mostly neutral fluorine radicals into the chamber. NF3 suits this because its nitrogen-fluorine bonds are much weaker than the carbon-fluorine bonds in PFCs, so it breaks apart readily. Higher gas utilization gives faster cleans, less wear and far less unreacted greenhouse gas in the exhaust.

NF3 is a potent, long-lived greenhouse gas: its global warming potential is about 16,000 times that of CO2 on a 100-year basis, and it persists in the atmosphere for centuries. Fabs therefore treat tool exhaust with point-of-use abatement systems that decompose residual fluorinated gases by combustion, plasma or heat, then wet-scrub the resulting hydrogen fluoride. Whatever escapes counts as a direct (Scope 1) emission in corporate greenhouse gas accounting, so abatement efficiency and gas utilization in the tool both matter for a fab's reported footprint.

Besides chamber cleaning, NF3 is a fluorine source in some etch steps and in dry pre-cleans. In SiCoNi-type processing, a remote NF3/NH3 plasma converts native oxide into an ammonium fluorosilicate salt that is then removed by gentle heating, with no liquid that could collapse tall structures. Unlike nitrogen, which is piped in bulk for purging, NF3 is a specialty gas delivered in cylinders. It is toxic and becomes a strong oxidizer at high temperature, so it is kept in ventilated gas cabinets with leak detection.

faq.q: Why is NF3 used instead of C2F6 or CF4 for chamber cleaning?
faq.a: NF3 dissociates much more completely in a plasma, especially in a remote plasma source, so it delivers more fluorine radicals per molecule and cleans faster. Less gas leaves the tool unreacted, which sharply cuts greenhouse gas emissions compared with PFC-based cleans.

faq.q: What is the global warming potential of NF3?
faq.a: About 16,000 times that of CO2 over 100 years, and it stays in the atmosphere for hundreds of years. That is why fabs abate NF3 exhaust and report emissions as Scope 1.

faq.q: Is NF3 used to etch wafers?
faq.a: Its main use is cleaning deposition chambers, but it also serves as a fluorine source in some etch processes and in dry native-oxide pre-cleans that combine NF3 and NH3 in a remote plasma.

リードフレーム.desc: A thin metal sheet combining the pad that holds the chip with the external terminals (leads). It is used in packages such as QFP.

about.p: A lead frame is stamped or etched from a thin metal sheet, roughly 0.1 to 0.25 mm thick, as a strip holding many units. Each unit has a central die pad (paddle) held by tie bars, inner leads that fan in toward the die, outer leads that become the package pins, and dam bars that keep the leads in place and stop mold resin from escaping. Rails along the strip carry indexing holes so assembly machines can position each unit precisely.

Assembly starts with die bonding, which fixes the chip to the die pad with silver paste, solder or die-attach film. Wire bonding then connects each chip pad to an inner lead with fine gold or copper wire. The strip is encapsulated in epoxy molding compound, after which trim and form cuts away the dam bars and rails and bends the outer leads into gull-wing or J shapes. In leadless packages such as QFN (quad flat no-lead), the leads stay flat on the bottom and units are separated by sawing.

Copper alloys conduct electricity and heat far better and are the usual choice, especially for power and thermally demanding parts, but their thermal expansion (about 17 ppm/K) is much larger than silicon's (about 2.6 ppm/K). Alloy 42, an iron-nickel alloy with about 42% nickel, expands only around 4 to 5 ppm/K, close to silicon, which reduces stress on large dies, but it is a poor heat conductor. Frames are plated to aid bonding and soldering, for example silver on bond areas and tin or nickel-palladium-gold on the leads.

Lead-frame packages such as SOP, QFP, QFN and TO-type power packages are cheap and robust, and a QFN's exposed die pad soldered to the board makes an efficient heat path. Their limitation is that all leads sit on the perimeter, so pin count and pitch are bounded. High-pin-count chips instead use ball grid arrays (BGAs) on organic laminate substrates with area-array connections. Reliability concerns for lead frames include mold-compound delamination from the pad or leads, typically inspected with a scanning acoustic microscope after moisture-soak reflow testing.

faq.q: What is a lead frame made of?
faq.a: Usually a copper alloy, chosen for its high electrical and thermal conductivity, or Alloy 42 (iron with about 42% nickel), chosen because its thermal expansion is close to silicon's. The frame is plated to make wire bonding and soldering reliable.

faq.q: What is the difference between a lead frame and a package substrate?
faq.a: A lead frame is a single patterned metal sheet whose leads form the external terminals around the package edge. A substrate is a multilayer wiring board that routes signals to an area array of solder balls, supporting far more connections.

faq.q: Why do QFN packages have an exposed pad on the bottom?
faq.a: The exposed pad is the lead frame's die pad. Soldering it to a copper area on the circuit board gives a short, low-resistance path for heat and ground current.

アンダーフィル.desc: Resin filled into the gap between the chip and the substrate in flip-chip assembly. It spreads out stress from thermal expansion mismatch and protects the bump joints.

about.p: Silicon expands at about 3 ppm/K, while organic package substrates expand at about 15 to 17 ppm/K. In a flip-chip assembly the solder or copper-pillar bumps are the only link between the two, so every temperature swing shears them. The mismatch displacement grows with distance from the chip center, so corner bumps are strained most and tend to fail first by fatigue cracking. Underfill bonds the chip to the substrate across the whole gap, so the pair flexes together and the strain is carried by the resin rather than concentrated in a few joints, extending thermal-cycling life many times over.

In the classic capillary process, the chip is first reflowed onto the substrate, then a low-viscosity epoxy loaded with fine silica particles is dispensed along one or two die edges. Capillary action draws it through the gap between the bumps, after which it is cured. The silica filler lowers the resin's expansion coefficient and stiffens it. Flow needs adequate standoff height, which is one reason copper pillars, which keep their height during reflow, help at fine pitch. Alternatives include no-flow underfill applied before placement, pre-applied non-conductive film for thermocompression bonding, and molded underfill formed during encapsulation.

Underfill only helps if it fills completely and stays attached. Voids left by trapped air, filler settling, or delamination at the chip or substrate interface, often driven by absorbed moisture during reflow, can leave bumps unsupported and become crack starters. A cured underfill also makes rework nearly impossible, so a faulty die usually means scrapping the package. Material choice balances flow speed, cure temperature, modulus, expansion coefficient and adhesion against package warpage.

Underfill is also applied between BGA or chip-scale packages and the circuit board in handheld products, where drop impact and board bending can crack solder joints or the brittle intermetallic layer at the pad. It should not be confused with mold compound, which encapsulates the whole package, or with thermal interface material (TIM), which fills the gap between the die back and a heat spreader to conduct heat rather than to hold joints together.

faq.q: What is underfill used for in flip-chip packages?
faq.a: It fills the gap between chip and substrate so that stress from their different thermal expansion is shared by the resin instead of concentrating on the bumps. This greatly improves solder-joint fatigue life under temperature cycling.

faq.q: Is underfill used on BGAs on circuit boards?
faq.a: Yes. Phones and other handheld devices often underfill BGA and chip-scale packages on the board to help solder joints survive drop impact and board bending.

faq.q: Can a flip chip with underfill be reworked?
faq.a: Generally not in practice. Cured underfill bonds the chip firmly to the substrate, so removing and replacing the die is very difficult, which is why assemblies are tested before underfill when possible.

プローブカード.desc: A fixture that presses many needles (probes) onto chip electrodes on the wafer to connect them electrically to a tester.

ATE(自動試験装置).desc: Equipment that applies test patterns to chips, measures their outputs and automatically judges pass or fail. Also called a tester.

about.p: Automatic test equipment (ATE) applies power and signals to a device under test (DUT), measures its responses, compares them with expected values and sorts parts into pass, fail or performance bins. A test program sequences the steps. The tester has hundreds to thousands of channels; each pin's electronics can drive logic levels with programmed timing, compare outputs against expected values at strobe times, and force voltage or current while measuring the other through a per-pin parametric measurement unit. Device power supplies provide and monitor the supply rails.

ATE is used at two main points. In wafer test, also called wafer sort, a prober steps the wafer under a probe card whose needles touch each chip's pads, which are tens of micrometers across; probe marks are inspected so they do not impair later wire bonding or bumping. Failing dies are marked so they are not packaged. In final test, a handler moves packaged parts into sockets on a load board, often at hot or cold temperatures, and sorts them by result.

A typical flow starts with continuity checks for opens and shorts, then DC parametric tests such as leakage and supply current, then functional and structural tests. For digital logic, scan patterns generated by automatic test pattern generation (ATPG) detect manufacturing faults, often at speed. Memories are exercised with algorithmic patterns or built-in self-test (BIST). Analog, mixed-signal and RF parts need instruments for linearity, noise and frequency response, so tester platforms are specialized for logic and SoC, memory, mixed-signal or RF devices.

Testers are expensive, so test cost is roughly test time multiplied by the tester's cost per second. Manufacturers cut it by testing many devices in parallel (multi-site test), trimming redundant tests and adding design-for-test (DFT) features. Scan chains, compression and BIST let a modest number of tester pins and shallow pattern memory cover large chips, and reduced-pin-count test lets cheaper testers handle more sites at once.

faq.q: What does ATE stand for in semiconductors?
faq.a: ATE stands for automatic test equipment, the tester that applies test patterns to chips, measures their outputs and judges pass or fail automatically.

faq.q: What is the difference between a prober and a handler?
faq.a: Both feed devices to the ATE. A prober positions a wafer under a probe card for wafer-level test, while a handler picks up packaged chips, places them in test sockets and sorts them after final test.

faq.q: Why does design-for-test reduce ATE cost?
faq.a: Structures such as scan chains, test compression and built-in self-test let the chip test itself or be tested through few pins, shortening test time and allowing more devices to be tested in parallel on less expensive equipment.

スキャンテスト.desc: A test method that uses scan chains, formed by linking a circuit's flip-flops in series, to set and observe internal states.

about.p: In scan design each flip-flop is replaced by a scan flip-flop with a multiplexer at its input. When a scan-enable signal is asserted, the flip-flops link into shift registers called scan chains, so a tester can shift any desired state into every flip-flop. One functional clock (capture) then lets the combinational logic compute, and the results are latched back into the flip-flops. Shifting the chain out reads these results while the next pattern shifts in. This turns the hard problem of testing deep sequential logic into testing combinational logic between controllable and observable registers.

Scan patterns are produced by automatic test pattern generation (ATPG) tools, which target fault models such as stuck-at faults, where a node is assumed fixed at 0 or 1, and transition faults, which model nodes that switch too slowly and are tested with at-speed capture clocks. The quality of a pattern set is reported as fault coverage. The cost of scan is extra area for the multiplexers and routing, a small delay added to flip-flop inputs, and the design effort of design for testability (DFT) rules such as keeping clocks and resets controllable during test.

For large chips, the number of flip-flops makes raw scan data and shift time enormous. Test compression splits the logic into many short chains fed by an on-chip decompressor and drained into an output compactor. Because most bits in a pattern are don't-cares, data volume and test time can fall by a factor of tens or more. Compaction has a weakness: an unknown value (X) from an uninitialized memory, an analog block or a clock-domain crossing corrupts the compacted signature, so X sources are avoided in design and X-masking blocks the affected scan cells.

Internal scan targets the logic inside the chip by chaining its flip-flops. Boundary scan, standardized as IEEE 1149.1 (JTAG), places scan cells at the chip's I/O pins so that board-level interconnects and solder joints can be tested and pins can be driven or observed without physical probes. The two are complementary, and the JTAG port is often reused to control internal test features. Neither replaces functional testing entirely, since scan patterns exercise structure rather than the chip's real use cases.

faq.q: What is the purpose of a scan chain?
faq.a: A scan chain links a chip's flip-flops into a shift register during test so every internal state can be set and read directly. This makes high fault coverage achievable with automatically generated patterns.

faq.q: What is the difference between scan test and JTAG boundary scan?
faq.a: Internal scan chains the core flip-flops to test the on-chip logic, while boundary scan (IEEE 1149.1) chains cells at the I/O pins to test connections between chips on a board. Both use serial shifting, but they cover different parts of the system.

faq.q: Why are unknown (X) values a problem in scan compression?
faq.a: An X entering the output compactor mixes with other bits and makes the compacted result unpredictable, so it cannot be compared with the expected value and faults may go undetected. X-masking and X-free design practices prevent this.

エリプソメトリ.desc: A measurement method that shines polarized light on a sample and determines thin-film thickness and refractive index from the change in polarization on reflection. It is nondestructive.

about.p: Ellipsometry shines polarized light onto a sample at an oblique angle, often around 65–75° for silicon, and analyzes the polarization of the reflected beam. The light is split into p-polarized (in the plane of incidence) and s-polarized (perpendicular) components, which reflect differently from a film stack. The instrument measures two quantities: Ψ, related to the ratio of their reflection amplitudes, and Δ, their phase difference, defined by tanΨ·exp(iΔ) = rp/rs. Because it measures a ratio and a phase rather than absolute intensity, it is insensitive to source fluctuations.

about.h: From Ψ and Δ to thickness and index
about.p: Ψ and Δ do not give thickness directly. The analyst builds an optical model of the stack, for example a silicon substrate, a thin interfacial layer and an oxide film, with each layer's thickness and optical constants n and k, then adjusts the unknowns until the calculated Ψ and Δ match the measurement. Spectroscopic ellipsometry measures across many wavelengths, giving enough data to fit multilayer stacks. For films only a few nanometers thick, thickness and refractive index become strongly correlated, so the index is usually fixed at a known value.

about.h: Strengths and limits in a fab
about.p: Ellipsometry is fast, non-contact and non-destructive, with thickness repeatability better than 0.1 nm, which makes it the workhorse for monitoring gate oxides, nitrides and other thin films. Its accuracy is only as good as the model: interface layers, surface roughness, absorbing films and unknown composition all complicate the fit. The beam spot is relatively large, so measurements on product wafers are made on dedicated test pads, typically in the scribe lines, rather than on dense circuit patterns.

Oxide interference colors give only a rough estimate of thickness. Spectral reflectometry measures reflected intensity versus wavelength; it is simpler and works well for thicker films, but carries less information than ellipsometry's phase data for very thin layers. X-ray reflectivity and cross-sectional TEM serve as references, the latter destructive. Ellipsometry measures film thickness and optical constants only; sheet resistance needs a four-point probe, and surface metal contamination needs a method such as TXRF.

faq.q: What does ellipsometry measure?
faq.a: It measures how reflection changes the polarization of light, expressed as the amplitude ratio Ψ and phase difference Δ. Fitting these to an optical model yields film thickness and refractive index.

faq.q: What is the difference between ellipsometry and reflectometry?
faq.a: Reflectometry measures only the intensity of reflected light, while ellipsometry also measures the phase difference between two polarizations. The extra phase information makes ellipsometry more sensitive for very thin films.

faq.q: Can ellipsometry measure films only a few nanometers thick?
faq.a: Yes, with sub-0.1 nm repeatability, which is why it is used for gate dielectrics. For such thin films, though, the refractive index is usually fixed in the model because it cannot be separated reliably from thickness.

四探針法.desc: A method that passes current through the outer two of four collinear needles and measures voltage across the inner two to find the sheet resistance of wafers and thin films.

TEM(透過電子顕微鏡).desc: A microscope that observes thinned samples by passing an electron beam through them. With atomic-level resolution, it reveals cross-sectional structures and crystal defects.

about.h: How a TEM forms an image
about.p: A transmission electron microscope (TEM) sends a high-energy electron beam through a specimen and images the electrons that emerge on the far side. Electrons accelerated to the hundreds of kilovolts typical of TEMs have wavelengths of a few picometres, so resolution is limited mainly by lens aberrations; aberration-corrected instruments resolve below 0.1 nm and show individual atomic columns. Contrast arises from thickness and composition, from diffraction by crystal planes and from phase interference, which is why dislocations, stacking faults and lattice fringes are visible.

A scanning electron microscope (SEM) scans a beam over the surface of a bulk sample and collects secondary or backscattered electrons, giving topography and contrast at nanometre scale without heavy preparation. A TEM requires a specimen thin enough, typically 100 nm or less, for electrons to pass through, but reveals internal structure at atomic resolution. Scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) combines the two ideas: a finely focused probe is scanned across a thin sample and transmitted signals are recorded point by point, which also enables spectroscopic mapping.

For semiconductor devices the standard route is focused ion beam (FIB) lift-out. A protective metal layer is deposited over the region of interest, gallium ions mill trenches on either side, and a thin slab is cut free, attached to a grid and thinned to its final thickness, usually with progressively lower beam energy to limit surface damage. Dual-beam tools combine the FIB with an SEM to watch the process. The method lets a single failing transistor or via be targeted, but the analysis is destructive, so it relies on sampled or dedicated wafers.

Two spectroscopies add composition to structure. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) detects characteristic X-rays emitted when inner-shell electrons are knocked out, identifying elements with a detection limit around 0.1 wt%. Electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) measures how much energy transmitted electrons lose; combined with STEM it maps elements and even chemical bonding states at near-atomic resolution and is especially strong for light elements. Both are used on gate dielectric stacks and interfaces, and TEM cross-sections serve as reference data for calibrating fast inline methods such as scatterometry.

faq.q: How thin does a TEM sample need to be?
faq.a: Typically about 100 nm or less so the electron beam can pass through, and thinner still for the highest-resolution imaging. In semiconductor labs such lamellae are usually cut with a focused ion beam.

faq.q: What is the difference between TEM and SEM?
faq.a: SEM images the surface of a bulk sample using electrons scattered back or emitted from it, while TEM images electrons transmitted through a thinned sample. TEM reaches atomic resolution and shows internal structure, but sample preparation is destructive and slower.

faq.q: What is the difference between EDX and EELS?
faq.a: EDX analyzes X-rays emitted by the sample and is convenient for identifying medium and heavy elements, while EELS analyzes energy lost by transmitted electrons and excels at light elements and chemical bonding information. EELS requires a thin TEM sample; EDX also works in an SEM.

キラー欠陥.desc: A defect that makes a chip fail, such as particles or pattern anomalies of a size and location that cause shorts or opens in wiring.

ポアソン歩留まりモデル.desc: A model that assumes defects are randomly distributed and expresses yield as Y = exp(−D×A), where D is defect density and A is chip area.

SPC(統計的工程管理).desc: A method of maintaining quality by monitoring process data with control charts and the like and detecting anomalies statistically.

about.p: Statistical process control separates common-cause variation, the random scatter inherent to a stable process, from special-cause variation, which signals that something has changed. Measurements such as film thickness, critical dimension, overlay or particle counts are plotted in time order on control charts with a center line and control limits, usually at plus and minus three standard deviations of the in-control process. A point beyond the limits, or a non-random pattern such as a long run on one side of the center line, triggers an out-of-control action plan: hold the lot, check the tool, find the cause.

Control limits come from the process's own past behavior, while specification limits come from design or customer requirements. A process can be statistically in control yet still produce out-of-spec parts if its spread is too wide. Capability indices connect the two: Cp compares the specification width with six standard deviations, and Cpk also accounts for how far the mean sits from the nearer limit. A Cpk of 1.33 or more is a common minimum target, and critical steps often aim higher.

SPC watches and stops; it does not correct. Advanced process control (APC) uses metrology data to adjust recipes automatically, for example extending polish time when incoming film is thick (run-to-run control). Fault detection and classification (FDC) monitors tool sensor traces such as pressure, power and flow in real time. Because sensor values are correlated, multivariate charts like Hotelling's T-squared can flag an abnormal combination even when each variable looks normal on its own chart. In practice, APC corrects drift and SPC confirms the corrected process stays stable.

With three-sigma limits, a stable, normally distributed process still puts about 0.27% of points outside the limits by chance. A fab running thousands of charts therefore sees false alarms every day, and adding pattern rules raises sensitivity at the cost of more alarms. Engineers tune chart types, sampling plans and rules per parameter, and must recompute limits after deliberate process changes. Too-loose limits hide real drift; too-tight ones cause needless lot holds and erode trust in the system.

faq.q: What is the difference between control limits and specification limits?
faq.a: Control limits are calculated from the process's own variation and show whether it is behaving consistently. Specification limits are the acceptable range set by design requirements; a stable process can still violate them if its spread is too large.

faq.q: What does a Cpk of 1.33 mean?
faq.a: It means the nearer specification limit is four standard deviations from the process mean. For a normally distributed process this corresponds to only a few dozen out-of-spec parts per million on that side.

faq.q: Is SPC the same as APC?
faq.a: No. SPC detects abnormal variation and stops the process for investigation, while APC automatically adjusts tool settings based on measurements to keep results on target.

工程能力指数(Cpk).desc: An index of how much margin a process's variation and mean offset leave relative to the specification limits. A common benchmark is 1.33 or higher.

about.p: The process capability index Cp compares the specification width with the natural process spread: Cp = (USL − LSL)/6σ, where USL and LSL are the upper and lower specification limits and σ is the process standard deviation. Cp assumes the process mean sits at the center of the specification. Cpk removes that assumption by measuring the distance from the mean to the nearer limit in units of 3σ: Cpk = min(USL − μ, μ − LSL)/3σ. When the mean is centered, Cpk equals Cp; any offset makes Cpk smaller.

about.h: A worked example and typical targets
about.p: Suppose the specification is ±6 around a target and σ = 1. Cp = 12/6 = 2. If the mean drifts 3 units from center, the nearer limit is only 3 units away, so Cpk = 3/3 = 1, even though Cp is unchanged. Cpk = 1 means the nearest limit is 3σ from the mean, about 0.135% of a normal distribution beyond it. A common minimum is Cpk ≥ 1.33, which puts the nearest limit at 4σ and leaves only a few tens of ppm beyond it. Critical parameters may require 1.67 or more.

Specification limits come from customer or design requirements and define acceptable product. Control limits on a control chart come from the process's own mean and variation and signal when something unusual has happened. A process can be in statistical control yet produce out-of-spec parts if it is too variable, or meet spec while being out of control after a sudden shift. Cp and Cpk link the two worlds, and they are meaningful only when the process is stable; computing Cpk from unstable data predicts nothing about future output.

The ppm interpretations assume a roughly normal distribution, which does not always hold for quantities such as particle counts or leakage current. For one-sided specifications, only the relevant half is used, for example (USL − μ)/3σ when only an upper limit exists. Many quality systems distinguish Cpk, computed from short-term within-subgroup variation, from Ppk, computed from the overall long-term standard deviation; Ppk is usually lower. In fabs these indices are tracked for parameters such as critical dimension, film thickness, overlay and electrical test results.

faq.q: What is the difference between Cp and Cpk?
faq.a: Cp compares specification width with the 6σ process spread and assumes a centered mean. Cpk uses the distance from the actual mean to the nearer specification limit, so it also penalizes an off-center process.

faq.q: What Cpk value is considered good?
faq.a: A Cpk of 1.33 or higher, meaning the nearest specification limit is at least 4σ from the mean, is a widely used minimum; 1.67 or higher is often required for critical characteristics.

faq.q: Can Cpk be higher than Cp?
faq.a: No. Cpk equals Cp when the mean is exactly centered and is smaller whenever the mean is offset toward either limit.

TDDB(経時絶縁破壊).desc: A phenomenon in which an insulating film under sustained voltage eventually breaks down even below its breakdown voltage. It is used to evaluate the lifetime of gate oxides and the like.

about.p: Time-dependent dielectric breakdown (TDDB) is a wear-out failure. A field too weak to break an insulator immediately still drives carriers through it, and over time these create defects (traps) in the film. The defects accumulate at random positions until a chain of them bridges the two electrodes, at which point current runs away and the film breaks down. A thinner film needs fewer defects to complete such a path, and it also sees a higher field at a given voltage, so scaling makes TDDB harder to manage. Breakdown shorts the gate to the channel and destroys the transistor.

High-quality thermal SiO2 breaks down instantly at about 10 MV/cm, so a 10 nm film fails near 10 V and a 2 nm film at only a few volts. To survive the usual ten-year life target, devices are designed to run at a few MV/cm or less. In very thin gate oxides, tunneling leakage may become the limiting issue before breakdown does. Between interconnects, about 0.7 V across a spacing of ten-odd nanometers already produces fields of hundreds of kV/cm, enough to matter over years.

At use conditions TDDB takes years, so test structures are stressed at elevated voltage and temperature until they fail in hours to weeks. Times-to-failure are fitted statistically, commonly with a Weibull distribution, and extrapolated to the use field. The E model (lifetime ∝ exp(−γE)) and the 1/E model (lifetime ∝ exp(G/E)) can differ by orders of magnitude after a long extrapolation; the E model predicts shorter low-field lives and is often chosen as the conservative option. Power-law voltage models have also been proposed for ultrathin films, and which fits best depends on the dielectric and field range.

about.h: Gate TDDB vs. BEOL TDDB and other mechanisms
about.p: Gate TDDB concerns the transistor gate dielectric. BEOL (back-end-of-line) TDDB concerns the insulator between neighboring wires, and grows more important as spacing shrinks: low-k films are less robust than oxide, copper ions can migrate into the dielectric, and post-CMP interfaces are often weak, while via misalignment locally narrows spacing. TDDB differs from ESD (electrostatic discharge) damage, which is instantaneous overstress, from NBTI (negative-bias temperature instability), which shifts threshold voltage rather than breaking the film, and from electromigration, which is atom transport in metal lines.

faq.q: What is the difference between TDDB and dielectric breakdown voltage?
faq.a: Breakdown voltage describes immediate failure when the field exceeds the insulator's strength, about 10 MV/cm for good SiO2. TDDB is failure after a long time at a lower field, caused by gradual defect build-up.

faq.q: Why are TDDB tests done at higher voltage than operating voltage?
faq.a: At operating voltage failures would take years. Higher voltage and temperature make them happen in hours to weeks, and a voltage-acceleration model extrapolates the result back to use conditions.

faq.q: What is the E model vs. 1/E model in TDDB?
faq.a: They are two ways of extrapolating lifetime versus field: exponential in E or exponential in 1/E. At low fields the E model predicts much shorter lifetimes, so it is usually treated as the conservative choice.

NBTI.desc: A degradation phenomenon in which the magnitude of a pMOS threshold voltage gradually increases under negative gate voltage at high temperature.

about.h: How NBTI damages a pMOS transistor
about.p: NBTI (negative bias temperature instability) occurs when a pMOS gate is held negative relative to its channel, so the channel is inverted with holes, at elevated temperature. Holes at the Si/SiO2 interface help break Si–H bonds left from hydrogen passivation, creating interface traps, while positive charge also builds up in the gate dielectric. Both effects make the threshold voltage more negative, so its magnitude grows, and drive current and transconductance fall. No drain current is needed: a pMOS simply sitting with its gate low and its source at VDD is under NBTI stress.

NBTI shift grows over time roughly as a power law with a small exponent, so most of the change appears early and then continues slowly over years of operation. When the stress is removed, part of the shift recovers, starting within microseconds, as some trapped charge escapes. This makes measurement tricky, because a slow measurement after stress underestimates the damage, and it explains why AC stress, where the gate toggles, degrades a device less than constant DC stress. Nitrogen added to gate oxides to block boron penetration is known to make NBTI worse.

PBTI (positive bias temperature instability) is the nMOS counterpart: positive gate bias and heat trap electrons at defects in high-k layers such as HfO2, raising the nMOS threshold. It was minor with SiO2 gates but became significant after high-k/metal gate adoption. Hot carrier injection (HCI) is different in kind: it needs current flow and a strong lateral field near the drain, where energetic carriers damage the interface or get injected into the dielectric. NBTI, by contrast, is driven by the vertical gate field and temperature alone.

Because NBTI slowly raises pMOS threshold voltage, logic paths get slower over the product lifetime. Designers use aging-aware timing libraries and add guardband so that a chip still meets its frequency target after years at worst-case voltage and temperature. Circuits that hold a pMOS in a static on-state are most exposed, such as SRAM cells storing the same value for long periods, where shifted pull-up devices degrade read stability and noise margin. Reliability engineers characterize NBTI with accelerated stress at higher voltage and temperature and extrapolate to use conditions.

faq.q: What does NBTI stand for?
faq.a: NBTI stands for negative bias temperature instability, a wear-out mechanism in which a pMOS transistor under negative gate bias and high temperature gradually develops a larger threshold voltage magnitude.

faq.q: What is the difference between NBTI and hot carrier injection?
faq.a: NBTI is caused by the vertical gate field and temperature and occurs even with no current flowing, mainly in pMOS. Hot carrier injection requires current and a strong lateral field near the drain, where high-energy carriers damage the gate dielectric or interface.

faq.q: Does NBTI damage recover?
faq.a: Partly. When the negative gate bias is removed, some of the threshold shift relaxes quickly, but a permanent component remains and accumulates over the lifetime of the device.

MTTF(平均故障時間).desc: The average time until a non-repairable product fails. It is used as an indicator of product lifetime.

about.p: Mean time to failure (MTTF) is the expected time until a non-repairable item fails, mathematically the integral of the reliability function R(t). In the random-failure period the failure rate λ is roughly constant, time to failure follows an exponential distribution, R(t) = exp(−λt), and MTTF = 1/λ. A part with λ = 1×10⁻⁵ per hour therefore has an MTTF of 10⁵ hours, about 11 years. At t equal to MTTF only exp(−1), about 37%, of parts are still working, so the mean is far from a guaranteed life.

Semiconductor failure rates are usually quoted in FIT, one failure per 10⁹ device-hours. Converting, 100 FIT corresponds to an MTTF of 10⁷ hours, roughly 1,140 years for a single part. Such a number is meaningful only across populations: one million parts at 100 FIT running for 10,000 hours are expected to produce 10⁶ × 10⁴ × 100 / 10⁹ = 1,000 failures. When λt is small, λt itself is a good approximation of the probability that a given part fails within time t.

The failure rate over a product's life is often drawn as a bathtub curve: early infant-mortality failures, a long flat period of random failures, then rising wear-out failures. An MTTF computed from the flat-period rate says nothing about when wear-out begins and can exceed the actual useful life by orders of magnitude. For wear-out mechanisms, engineers instead fit distributions such as lognormal or Weibull to stress-test data and quote a median or percentile time to failure under stated conditions.

Interconnect lifetime under electromigration is modelled by Black's equation, MTTF = A·J⁻ⁿ·exp(Ea/kT), where J is current density, n is about 2, Ea is an activation energy and T is absolute temperature. Higher current density and higher temperature both shorten life, the latter exponentially. Tests are therefore accelerated at elevated current and temperature, around 300 °C for example, and extrapolated to use conditions, and design rules cap current density per wire on the order of MA/cm². MTTF here describes component life, unlike the fault tolerant time interval in functional safety.

faq.q: How do you calculate MTTF from a failure rate?
faq.a: If the failure rate λ is constant, MTTF = 1/λ. For example, 1×10⁻⁵ failures per hour gives 10⁵ hours, and a rate given in FIT converts as MTTF = 10⁹ / FIT hours.

faq.q: What percentage of parts have failed when they reach their MTTF?
faq.a: Under a constant failure rate, about 63%, because reliability at t = MTTF is exp(−1) ≈ 37%. MTTF is an average, not a minimum life.

faq.q: What is the difference between MTTF and MTBF?
faq.a: MTTF applies to items that are discarded when they fail, while MTBF applies to repairable systems and measures time between successive failures. MTTR, mean time to repair, describes how long restoration takes.

RTL(レジスタ転送レベル).desc: A design abstraction that describes circuits by how data moves and is processed between registers. It is written in Verilog or VHDL and serves as the input to logic synthesis.

about.p: An RTL model divides a synchronous circuit into two kinds of things: registers, which capture new values on a clock edge, and the combinational logic that computes those values from current register contents and inputs. Writing at this level means stating, cycle by cycle, what each register will hold next, without choosing specific gates. In Verilog this appears as clocked always blocks with nonblocking assignments for flip-flops and separate combinational blocks or assign statements. All blocks describe hardware that operates concurrently, which is the biggest mental shift for programmers coming from sequential software.

RTL sits between algorithm-level descriptions and the gate-level netlist. Above it, high-level synthesis (HLS) can generate RTL from C or C++ by scheduling operations into clock cycles. Below it, logic synthesis maps RTL onto flip-flops and gates from a standard-cell library, optimizing against timing, area and power constraints, and place and route then produces the layout. Some intent is deliberately kept outside the RTL: the Unified Power Format (UPF, IEEE 1801) describes power domains, shutoff, isolation and level shifters in separate files so the power architecture can change without editing the RTL.

Only part of an HDL maps to hardware. Delay statements such as #10 advance simulation time but are ignored by synthesis, because real delay comes from gates and wires. System tasks like $display, file I/O and the case-equality operator === are testbench tools. Classic coding pitfalls change the hardware itself: a combinational block that does not assign an output on every path infers an unintended latch, and mixing blocking and nonblocking assignments carelessly can make simulation disagree with the synthesized circuit. Good RTL style keeps simulation and hardware behavior identical.

Most verification effort happens at RTL, where simulation is fast enough for millions of cycles. Progress is measured by code coverage, which tracks executed lines and branches, and functional coverage, which tracks specified scenarios; full code coverage alone does not prove every specified combination was tested. Some bugs are invisible to RTL simulation. Clock-domain-crossing (CDC) tools catch missing synchronizers, because simulated flip-flops never go metastable. Formal equivalence checking confirms the netlist matches the RTL, and gate-level simulation with SDF delay data exposes reset, unknown-value and timing problems.

faq.q: What is the difference between RTL and a gate-level netlist?
faq.a: RTL describes registers and the logic between them in a hardware description language without choosing specific gates, while a gate-level netlist is the synthesized result, a list of actual library cells and their connections.

faq.q: Is RTL the same as Verilog?
faq.a: No. RTL is an abstraction level; Verilog, SystemVerilog and VHDL are languages that can express RTL as well as testbenches and lower-level gate descriptions.

faq.q: Why does my RTL simulate correctly but fail after synthesis?
faq.a: Common causes are simulation-only constructs such as delays, inferred latches from incomplete assignments, incomplete sensitivity lists and blocking/nonblocking assignment misuse, which make simulated behavior differ from the generated gates.

配置配線.desc: The design step that arranges cells on the chip (placement) from the netlist produced by logic synthesis and determines the wiring between them (routing).

about.h: Where place and route sits in the flow
about.p: Logic synthesis turns RTL into a gate-level netlist, but that netlist has no geometry. Place and route (P&R) converts it into a physical layout. It starts with floorplanning, which sets the die size, the positions of large blocks such as memories, the I/O locations and the backbone of the power grid. Standard cells are then placed in rows, the clock tree is synthesized (clock tree synthesis, CTS) to deliver the clock with controlled skew, and finally the signal nets are routed on the metal layers. The output goes on to extraction, timing sign-off and physical verification.

Placement positions thousands to millions of cells to minimize total wire length while avoiding congestion, regions where more wires are needed than routing tracks exist. It is timing-driven: cells on critical paths are pulled together, and tools insert buffers or resize gates as they go. A final legalization step snaps every cell onto the standard-cell rows without overlap. Decisions made at floorplanning, such as placing blocks that exchange heavy traffic next to each other, set the limits of what placement can achieve and are expensive to change later.

Routing usually proceeds in two stages. Global routing divides the chip into a coarse grid and assigns each net a path through regions, estimating congestion. Detailed routing then assigns real tracks and vias on each metal layer while obeying the design rules for width and spacing. Layers typically alternate preferred directions, horizontal on one and vertical on the next, to keep routing regular. Lower layers are thin and dense for local connections, while thick upper layers carry long global signals, clocks and power with lower resistance.

After routing, parasitic extraction computes each wire's resistance and capacitance from its geometry and its overlap and spacing with neighbors. These values feed static timing analysis, power analysis and crosstalk checks. In scaled technologies wire delay is a large share of path delay, so a design that met timing after synthesis can fail after routing. Fixes such as buffer insertion, cell resizing and rerouting are iterated until timing closes, and design rule checking (DRC) and layout-versus-schematic (LVS) verification confirm the layout before tape-out.

faq.q: What is the difference between placement and routing?
faq.a: Placement decides where each cell sits on the die, while routing creates the metal wires and vias that connect the placed cells according to the netlist. Placement quality largely determines how easy routing will be.

faq.q: What comes before and after place and route?
faq.a: Logic synthesis comes before it and supplies the gate-level netlist. After it come parasitic extraction, static timing analysis and physical verification such as DRC and LVS before the layout is released for manufacturing.

faq.q: Why is floorplanning so important in place and route?
faq.a: Floorplanning fixes the die size, block positions, I/O placement and power grid, which constrain everything that follows. A poor floorplan causes congestion and long wires that later steps cannot fully repair.

DRC(デザインルールチェック).desc: Verification that checks whether a layout follows the geometric rules required for manufacturing, such as line widths and spacings.

about.p: A DRC (design rule check) tool scans the polygons of every layout layer and flags geometry that the fab cannot reliably build. Typical rules cover minimum width and spacing, enclosure of a via or contact by the metal above and below, extension of one layer past another, minimum area, and minimum and maximum pattern density so that CMP polishes evenly. Antenna rules, which limit how much metal can connect to a gate during processing, are usually run in the same flow. Each rule traces back to a limit of lithography, etching, CMP or reliability.

At mature nodes a few hundred simple width and spacing rules were enough. Advanced processes have thousands, many of them context dependent: required spacing can depend on the width of neighbouring lines and how far they run in parallel, line ends need extra clearance, and multiple patterning adds coloring rules that govern which shapes may share a mask. The rules are delivered by the foundry as a rule deck within the PDK (process design kit) and executed by physical verification tools, because manual checking of billions of shapes is impossible.

These three sign-off checks are easily confused. DRC looks only at geometry and does not care what the circuit does. LVS (layout versus schematic) extracts devices and connectivity from the layout and compares them with the schematic netlist, catching opens, shorts and wrong devices. ERC (electrical rule check) looks for electrical mistakes such as floating gate inputs, shorted supplies or unconnected wells. Synthesis and place-and-route tools also report design rule violations of a different kind, such as maximum transition or capacitance limits, which are electrical constraints rather than layout geometry.

DRC runs repeatedly during physical design, on individual blocks and then on the full chip after everything is assembled, since violations often appear at block boundaries. Routers fix many errors automatically, and the rest are fixed by hand. A clean DRC and LVS result is required before mask data is released to the fab. Occasionally a violation is accepted through a formal waiver agreed with the foundry. Many processes also supply recommended rules for manufacturability, which are not mandatory but improve yield when followed.

faq.q: What is the difference between DRC and LVS?
faq.a: DRC checks that layout shapes obey manufacturing rules such as minimum width and spacing. LVS checks that the circuit extracted from the layout matches the intended schematic, so a layout can pass DRC and still fail LVS.

faq.q: What is a DRC rule deck?
faq.a: A rule deck is the foundry-supplied file that encodes a process's design rules in the language of a physical verification tool. It is part of the process design kit and is updated as the process matures.

faq.q: What happens if a chip is taped out with DRC violations?
faq.a: The foundry normally requires DRC-clean data or approved waivers. Unwaived violations risk shapes that print incorrectly, causing shorts, opens or reliability failures that reduce yield.

ISO 14644-1.desc: The international standard that defines cleanroom cleanliness classes by the number of airborne particles. The smaller the number, the cleaner.

ULPAフィルタ.desc: A high-performance air filter that captures even finer particles than a HEPA filter. It is used in the ceilings of high-cleanliness cleanrooms.

ダウンフロー.desc: A cleanroom airflow method that sends clean air in one direction from the entire ceiling to the floor, quickly carrying generated particles away under the floor.

about.p: In a downflow (vertical unidirectional flow) cleanroom, nearly the whole ceiling is covered with high-efficiency HEPA or ULPA filters, often as fan filter units. Filtered air flows straight down through the working space, passes through perforated floor panels into the underfloor plenum, and returns through side chases or return shafts to the ceiling plenum to be filtered again. Particles shed by people and tools are swept downward and out of the room before they can drift sideways or rise toward wafers.

A conventional cleanroom supplies filtered air through only part of the ceiling and relies on mixing to dilute particles, so contamination lingers and spreads. Downflow instead moves the whole room's air in parallel streamlines, so a particle generated at one spot is carried away rather than diluted. This is why the cleanest classes, roughly ISO Class 5 and better, generally require unidirectional flow, while mixed-flow rooms suit less demanding areas. The price is enormous air volume and fan energy.

Supply velocity is usually about 0.3 to 0.5 m/s. Faster flow becomes turbulent around people and equipment and stirs particles up, while slower flow can be overcome by thermal plumes rising from hot tools. At 0.4 m/s, air travels about 1,440 m per hour, so a room 3 to 4 m tall is fully replaced several hundred times per hour, compared with a few changes per hour in an ordinary office. Moving that much air is a major share of a fab's electricity use.

The floor must pass air, so it is built from perforated panels or gratings laid over a waffle slab, a thick concrete floor with a grid of holes that also gives the stiffness lithography scanners need for vibration control. Modern fabs carry wafers in sealed pods and load them through tool front ends with their own filter units, so the highest cleanliness is needed only inside these mini-environments. The surrounding bays can then use lower filter coverage, saving energy while protecting the wafer.

faq.q: What air velocity is used in a downflow cleanroom?
faq.a: Typically about 0.3 to 0.5 m/s. That is fast enough to overcome thermal updrafts but slow enough to stay smooth rather than turbulent around people and tools.

faq.q: Why do cleanrooms have perforated floors?
faq.a: The holes let the downward airflow pass into the underfloor space and return for recirculation. A solid floor would turn the flow sideways and stir particles back up into the room.

faq.q: Why do cleanrooms use so much energy?
faq.a: Unidirectional downflow replaces the room's air several hundred times per hour, so large fans run continuously, and the air must also be kept at tightly controlled temperature and humidity.

分子状汚染(AMC).desc: Gaseous contaminants in the air such as acids, alkalis and organics. Particle filters cannot remove them, so chemical filters are used.

パーフルオロカーボン.desc: Also called PFCs. Fluorinated gases such as CF4 and C2F6 used in etching and chamber cleaning. Their greenhouse effect is very large.

GHS.desc: The internationally harmonized system that communicates chemical hazards with pictograms and precautionary statements.

about.p: GHS, the Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals, was developed under the United Nations to replace the patchwork of national labeling schemes. It defines common criteria for classifying physical hazards (such as flammability, oxidizing properties, gases under pressure and corrosion of metals), health hazards (such as acute toxicity, skin corrosion and carcinogenicity) and environmental hazards (such as aquatic toxicity), and it specifies how the result is communicated on labels and safety data sheets. GHS is not itself a law; countries and regions adopt it into their own chemical regulations.

A label carries a product identifier, supplier details, one or more of nine pictograms, a signal word, hazard statements and precautionary statements. The pictograms are black symbols in red-bordered diamonds: flame, flame over circle (oxidizer), exploding bomb, gas cylinder, corrosion, skull and crossbones, exclamation mark, health hazard (a human silhouette) and environment. The signal word is Danger for the more severe categories and Warning for the less severe ones. Hazard statements describe the hazard in standard wording, while precautionary statements say how to store, handle and respond.

The safety data sheet (SDS) is the detailed companion to the label. Under GHS it has 16 sections in a fixed order, covering identification, hazards, composition, first aid, firefighting, accidental release, handling and storage, exposure controls and personal protection, physical and chemical properties, stability and reactivity, toxicology, ecology, disposal, transport, regulations and other information. The fixed layout means an engineer can find, for example, the required gloves or the first-aid measure for skin contact in the same place on any supplier's sheet.

about.h: GHS in a fab, and what it is not
about.p: Fab chemicals show the whole range of pictograms: hydrofluoric acid carries skull and corrosion symbols, concentrated hydrogen peroxide an oxidizer symbol, resist solvents a flame, and silane both flame and gas-cylinder symbols. GHS only classifies and communicates hazards; it does not restrict use. Restrictions on substances in products, such as lead in electronics under the EU RoHS directive, and reporting of chemical releases under pollutant release and transfer register (PRTR) schemes are separate regulations.

faq.q: How many GHS pictograms are there?
faq.a: There are nine GHS pictograms: flame, flame over circle, exploding bomb, gas cylinder, corrosion, skull and crossbones, exclamation mark, health hazard and environment. Some jurisdictions do not make the environment pictogram mandatory.

faq.q: What is the difference between Danger and Warning on a GHS label?
faq.a: Both are GHS signal words. Danger is used for the more severe hazard categories and Warning for the less severe ones, and a label shows only one of them.

faq.q: What is the difference between GHS and RoHS?
faq.a: GHS is a system for classifying chemical hazards and communicating them through labels and safety data sheets. RoHS is an EU directive that restricts hazardous substances such as lead and mercury in electrical and electronic equipment.

除害装置.desc: Equipment that removes hazardous substances from tool exhaust gas by combustion, adsorption, water scrubbing and the like.

RoHS指令.desc: The EU regulation restricting the use of specific hazardous substances such as lead and mercury in electrical and electronic equipment.

about.p: RoHS (Restriction of Hazardous Substances) applies to electrical and electronic equipment placed on the EU market and has applied since 2006. It originally restricted six substances: lead, mercury, cadmium, hexavalent chromium and two brominated flame retardants, PBB and PBDE. Four phthalate plasticizers were added later. The maximum concentration is 0.1 wt% for most substances and 0.01 wt% for cadmium. The 2011 recast, often called RoHS 2, tied compliance to CE marking and broadened the range of covered products.

Limits apply to each homogeneous material, meaning a material that cannot be mechanically separated into different materials, not to the weight of the whole product. A lead's tin plating, a solder joint, the mold compound and the die-attach material are each judged separately. A tiny amount of lead concentrated in one solder joint can therefore violate the rule even if it is a negligible fraction of the device. Suppliers document compliance through material declarations and test reports, often using X-ray fluorescence screening.

Banning lead pushed the industry from tin-lead solder to tin-silver-copper (SAC) alloys such as SAC305, which melt around 217 to 220 °C instead of 183 °C. Reflow peaks rose to about 260 °C, increasing package stress and moisture-induced cracking, so moisture sensitivity ratings and package materials had to be requalified. Pure tin lead finishes replaced tin-lead plating, which brought tin whisker growth back as a reliability concern to be managed.

Where no practical substitute exists, time-limited exemptions apply, for example high-lead solders used for die attach in some power packages and lead in certain glass and ceramic components. These exemptions are reviewed periodically. RoHS is often confused with REACH: REACH regulates chemicals themselves, requiring registration of substances made or imported at one tonne or more per year and disclosure of substances of very high concern above 0.1 wt% in articles, whereas RoHS bans specific substances in finished electrical equipment. Similar laws exist outside the EU.

faq.q: Which substances are restricted under RoHS?
faq.a: Lead, mercury, cadmium, hexavalent chromium, PBB and PBDE flame retardants, and four phthalates. Most are limited to 0.1 wt% in any homogeneous material, and cadmium to 0.01 wt%.

faq.q: Does RoHS ban all lead in electronics?
faq.a: No. It limits lead to 0.1 wt% per homogeneous material, but listed exemptions still allow lead in some applications, such as certain high-lead die-attach solders and glass in components, where alternatives are not yet practical.

faq.q: What is the difference between RoHS and REACH?
faq.a: RoHS restricts a short list of hazardous substances inside electrical and electronic products. REACH is a broad EU chemicals regulation covering registration, evaluation, authorisation and restriction of substances across all industries.

IDM(垂直統合型デバイスメーカー).desc: A semiconductor company that does everything in-house, from design through front-end and back-end manufacturing to sales.

about.p: An IDM (integrated device manufacturer) owns the whole chain: circuit design, front-end wafer fabrication in its own fabs, back-end assembly and test, and selling the finished devices under its own name. This contrasts with the disaggregated model, in which a fabless company designs chips, a foundry fabricates wafers for many customers, and an OSAT (outsourced semiconductor assembly and test) company packages and tests them. Many companies sit between the extremes, so the label describes a business structure rather than a product category.

about.h: Why some products favor the IDM model
about.p: When manufacturing technology itself differentiates the product, keeping design and process teams under one roof pays off. Memory, power devices and analog chips are typical examples: cell structures, high-voltage device layouts or precision passive components are co-optimized with process steps that the company develops itself. Short feedback loops between yield analysis and design changes also speed up learning. The cost is capital: building and continuously upgrading fabs requires enormous investment, and fabs must stay highly utilized through demand cycles to remain profitable.

about.h: IDM vs. fabless, foundry and fab-lite
about.p: A fabless company owns no fabs and buys wafers from foundries, so it avoids fab capital but depends on the foundry's process and capacity. A foundry manufactures to customer designs and does not sell its own chips. A fab-lite company is a partial IDM: it keeps fabs for mature processes and products where it has unique process strengths, and outsources leading-edge products that would need the largest investments to foundries. Fab-lite is common among microcontroller, analog and power semiconductor makers seeking to limit capital burden while keeping manufacturing know-how.

An IDM can run engineering lots on its own lines and adjust the process as needed. Companies without fabs, and universities or startups, often prototype through an MPW (multi-project wafer) run, in which a foundry places designs from several customers on one mask set and shares the mask and wafer costs among them. Each participant receives only a small number of chips, which is enough for evaluation but not for volume production. These options illustrate how ownership of manufacturing shapes a company's development cycle.

faq.q: What does IDM stand for in semiconductors?
faq.a: IDM stands for integrated device manufacturer, a company that designs, fabricates, assembles, tests and sells its own chips rather than relying on foundries and outsourced assembly.

faq.q: What is the difference between an IDM and a fabless company?
faq.a: An IDM owns and runs its own wafer fabs, while a fabless company only designs chips and pays a foundry to manufacture them.

faq.q: What is a fab-lite company?
faq.a: A fab-lite company is a partial IDM that keeps some fabs, usually for mature or specialized processes, while outsourcing products that need leading-edge processes to foundries.

OSAT.desc: A company that provides back-end services such as semiconductor assembly and testing under contract.

about.p: An OSAT (outsourced semiconductor assembly and test) company performs the back-end steps that turn finished wafers into tested, shippable chips. Typical services include wafer probing, backgrinding to thin the wafer, dicing, die attach, wire bonding or flip-chip bumping, molding, marking, and final electrical test. The front end, building transistors and interconnect on the wafer, is done by an integrated device manufacturer (IDM) or a foundry; the OSAT receives the processed wafers and returns packaged, tested parts to the chip company.

about.h: Place in the industry's division of labor
about.p: The modern supply chain splits work among fabless design companies, foundries for wafer fabrication, and OSATs for packaging and test. A fabless company may never own a factory: it sends designs to a foundry and has the resulting wafers assembled and tested by an OSAT. IDMs often keep some back-end work in house but outsource part of it for capacity or cost. Back-end work is more labor- and floor-space-intensive than wafer fabrication, and major OSAT sites are concentrated in Taiwan, China and Southeast Asia.

As scaling slows, more performance comes from packaging: flip-chip bumps, copper pillars, fan-out wafer-level packaging, silicon interposers and chiplets stacked or placed side by side. These steps use wafer-level processes such as lithography, plating and redistribution layers, so OSATs have invested in fab-like equipment, while foundries have started offering their own advanced packaging. The simple split of front end at the foundry and back end at the OSAT therefore no longer holds for the most advanced products.

faq.q: What does OSAT stand for?
faq.a: OSAT stands for outsourced semiconductor assembly and test. It refers to companies that package and test chips under contract for other semiconductor companies.

faq.q: What is the difference between an OSAT and a foundry?
faq.a: A foundry manufactures the wafers, building transistors and wiring in the front-end process. An OSAT takes finished wafers and does the back-end work of cutting, packaging and testing the chips.

faq.q: Do fabless companies need OSATs?
faq.a: Usually yes. A fabless company owns no fabrication or assembly lines, so it relies on a foundry for wafers and on an OSAT, or a foundry offering packaging, for assembly and test.

ムーアの法則.desc: The empirical rule that the number of transistors on an integrated circuit doubles about every two years. It has served as a target for semiconductor scaling.

about.p: In 1965 Gordon Moore noted that the number of components on the most cost-effective integrated circuit was doubling about every year, and in 1975 he revised the pace to about every two years. It is an empirical observation about technology and economics, not a law of physics. The frequently quoted 18-month figure is not Moore's own and usually refers to performance rather than transistor count. Because the whole industry planned equipment, materials and design tools around this cadence, it worked partly as a self-fulfilling target.

Moore's law concerns how many transistors fit on a chip. Dennard scaling, described in 1974, explained why shrinking was so beneficial: if dimensions and supply voltage scale down by the same factor, power density stays constant while circuits get faster. Around the mid-2000s supply and threshold voltages stopped scaling, because the subthreshold swing of about 60 mV per decade at room temperature makes leakage explode at low thresholds.
