Clock frequencies plateaued and designers turned to multiple cores and power management, while transistor counts kept rising.

Keeping pace required repeated reinvention. Lithography moved to shorter wavelengths, immersion optics, multiple patterning and extreme ultraviolet (EUV). Transistors gained strained silicon, high-k dielectrics with metal gates, then FinFETs and gate-all-around nanosheets to keep the channel under gate control. Layout tricks such as fewer tracks per standard cell, together with 3D stacking and chiplets, add density beyond pure shrinking. Modern node names such as 5 nm or 3 nm are generation labels and no longer equal any physical gate length.

about.h: Cost per transistor and the slowdown
about.p: The underlying goal of scaling is better PPA, meaning performance, power and area, plus lower cost per transistor. For decades each node delivered all of these. Today, rising fab, mask and lithography costs and the added process steps of multiple patterning have slowed the fall in cost per transistor, and the doubling interval has stretched. The industry still advances density, but gains increasingly come from packaging, specialization and design rather than from shrinking alone.

faq.q: Is Moore's law a law of physics?
faq.a: No. It is an empirical observation and industry roadmap target describing how transistor counts have grown, roughly doubling every two years, driven by engineering and economics.

faq.q: Is Moore's law dead?
faq.a: Transistor density is still increasing, but more slowly and at higher cost per wafer, and the old link to lower cost per transistor and higher clock speed has weakened. Much of the progress now comes from new device structures, 3D integration and chiplets.

faq.q: What is the difference between Moore's law and Dennard scaling?
faq.a: Moore's law describes the growth in transistor count per chip. Dennard scaling described how shrinking transistors along with voltage kept power density constant, and it broke down when voltage stopped scaling.

ハイブリッドボンディング.desc: A technique that directly bonds copper electrodes and dielectric surfaces without bumps, providing huge numbers of connections at extremely fine pitch.

about.p: Each surface is planarized by chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) so that copper pads sit a few nanometres below the surrounding dielectric. The surfaces are cleaned and activated with plasma, aligned and pressed together, and the dielectrics bond near room temperature. A subsequent anneal strengthens that bond, while thermal expansion pushes the recessed copper pads into contact, where atomic diffusion joins them. The result is simultaneous dielectric-to-dielectric and copper-to-copper bonding with no solder, no bumps and no underfill, which is why it is called hybrid.

Solder microbumps, bonded for example by thermocompression, need space so molten solder does not bridge neighbours, which keeps their pitch at tens of micrometres, around 20 µm at best. Hybrid bonding goes below 10 µm and down to a few micrometres. Because connection count scales inversely with the square of pitch, shrinking from 40 µm to 4 µm gives 100 times more connections per area. The joints are also very short, cutting parasitic capacitance and inductance, which raises bandwidth and lowers energy per bit transferred between dies.

Wafer-to-wafer (W2W) bonding joins whole wafers at once, giving high throughput and the best alignment, but it pairs good dies with bad ones and requires identical die sizes, so stacked yield is the product of both wafers' yields. Chip-to-wafer (C2W) bonding places tested, singulated known-good dies onto a target wafer, improving stacked yield and allowing different die sizes, at the cost of slower placement. Both demand sub-nanometre roughness and extreme cleanliness: a single particle of about 100 nm can leave an unbonded void millimetres across.

Stacked CMOS image sensors, which bond a pixel wafer to a logic wafer, were the first major commercial use. Processors now stack a cache SRAM die directly on the compute die, adding several times the cache capacity without enlarging the processor, and hybrid bonding is being extended to HBM memory stacks. It also connects photonic and electronic chips with minimal parasitics. These are 3D packages, stacking dies vertically, as opposed to 2.5D packages that place dies side by side on an interposer; the two are often combined in one product.

faq.q: What is the difference between hybrid bonding and microbumps?
faq.a: Microbumps join dies with small solder bumps at pitches of tens of micrometres. Hybrid bonding directly fuses copper pads and surrounding dielectric without solder, reaching pitches below 10 µm and far higher connection density.

faq.q: What pitch can hybrid bonding achieve?
faq.a: Production hybrid bonding works below 10 µm pitch, down to a few micrometres, compared with roughly 20 µm or more for solder microbumps.

faq.q: What is the difference between wafer-to-wafer and chip-to-wafer bonding?
faq.a: Wafer-to-wafer bonds entire wafers at once for speed and alignment accuracy but cannot exclude bad dies. Chip-to-wafer places only known-good dies, improving yield and allowing different die sizes, but is slower.

シリコンインターポーザ.desc: A silicon intermediate substrate that holds chips side by side and connects them densely with fine wiring. It is used to connect GPUs and HBM, among other things.

about.p: A silicon interposer is a slab of silicon processed with the same copper damascene wiring used for chip interconnect, giving lines and spaces of about 1 µm or finer in several metal layers. It is usually passive, containing wiring but no transistors. Chips such as a processor and memory stacks are attached face down with dense microbumps, and through-silicon vias (TSVs) carry power, ground and external signals down through the interposer to larger bumps on an ordinary package substrate. This arrangement, chips side by side on a shared silicon base, is called 2.5D packaging.

about.h: Why GPUs and HBM need it
about.p: High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) reaches its bandwidth through width rather than per-pin speed: each stack has a 1,024-bit data bus through the HBM3 generation. HBM3 at 6.4 Gb/s per pin gives about 819 GB/s per stack, and several stacks around a GPU add up to several TB/s. That requires thousands of signal wires only millimeters long, far more than an organic package substrate with lines tens of micrometers wide can route. The interposer's fine wiring makes the connection possible, and short wires also keep energy per bit low.

An interposer must be larger than all the dies it carries, so large AI packages need interposers several times the area of a single lithography exposure field, built by stitching exposures together; this adds cost and yield risk. Alternatives trade density for cost. Silicon bridges embed small pieces of silicon in the package substrate only under die-to-die edges, as in Intel's EMIB. Organic redistribution-layer (RDL) interposers use polymer dielectric and copper, are cheaper and easier to make large, and better match the substrate's thermal expansion, but offer coarser wiring.

In 2.5D integration, dies sit side by side on an interposer and communicate laterally; in 3D integration, dies are stacked vertically and connected through TSVs or hybrid bonding. 2.5D keeps every die exposed for cooling and lets dies from different process nodes be mixed easily, while 3D gives the shortest connections and smallest footprint but concentrates heat. The two are often combined: HBM itself is a 3D stack of DRAM dies, and those stacks are placed in 2.5D fashion next to the processor on an interposer, as in TSMC's CoWoS (chip on wafer on substrate).

faq.q: What is a silicon interposer used for?
faq.a: It carries several chips side by side and connects them with micrometer-scale wiring, most notably linking a GPU or AI accelerator to multiple HBM stacks with thousands of short wires.

faq.q: What is the difference between 2.5D and 3D packaging?
faq.a: 2.5D places dies side by side on an interposer or bridge, while 3D stacks dies directly on top of each other using TSVs or hybrid bonding.

faq.q: Why not use an organic substrate instead of a silicon interposer?
faq.a: Standard organic substrates have lines tens of micrometers wide and cannot route thousands of HBM signals in the available area; organic RDL interposers and silicon bridges are cheaper alternatives with somewhat lower density.

有効質量.desc: An apparent mass used to treat electrons and holes in a crystal as if they were free particles responding to external forces. It is set by the curvature of the band; a smaller effective mass tends to give higher mobility.

about.p: An electron in a crystal moves through the periodic potential of the atoms, so its response to an applied force differs from that of a free electron. Band theory absorbs this into the energy–wavevector relation E(k). Near a band edge E is roughly parabolic, E ≈ ħ²k²/2m*, and the effective mass is defined by the curvature, m* = ħ² / (d²E/dk²). A sharply curved band gives a light carrier and a flat band a heavy one. The electron's actual rest mass does not change; m* is simply the parameter that makes Newton's law F = m*a work inside the crystal.

Mobility is roughly μ = qτ/m*, where τ is the mean time between scattering events, so lighter carriers accelerate more between collisions. In lightly doped silicon at room temperature, electron mobility is about 1400 cm²/V·s and hole mobility about 450 cm²/V·s, mainly because holes are heavier. This is why a CMOS pMOS is commonly drawn 2–3 times wider than its nMOS partner to match drive current. GaAs electrons, with m* of about 0.067 times the free-electron mass, reach about 8500 cm²/V·s, which suits high-frequency amplifiers.

Near the top of the valence band the curvature is negative, so an electron there would have negative effective mass; treating the missing electron as a hole with positive charge and positive mass restores intuitive behavior, and the sign of the Hall voltage confirms it. Effective mass can also depend on direction. Silicon's conduction band has six equivalent valleys, each with a heavy longitudinal mass of roughly 0.9–1.0 m0 and a light transverse mass of about 0.19 m0. In GaAs, a strong field can push electrons into the higher, heavier L valley, the transferred-electron effect behind the Gunn diode.

Because effective mass comes from band structure, changing the lattice changes it. Tensile strain in silicon, for example from a thin layer grown on relaxed SiGe, splits the six conduction valleys so electrons crowd into those offering the light transverse mass in the transport direction, while intervalley scattering drops; electron mobility can rise by roughly 1.5–2 times. For pMOS, compressive strain from embedded SiGe source/drain regions lightens the holes. SiGe and germanium channels are pursued because their hole effective mass is intrinsically lower than silicon's.

faq.q: Is effective mass the real mass of an electron?
faq.a: No. The electron's rest mass is unchanged; effective mass is a parameter derived from band curvature that lets you use F = ma for a carrier inside the crystal's periodic potential.

faq.q: Why do holes have lower mobility than electrons in silicon?
faq.a: Holes in silicon have a larger effective mass than conduction-band electrons, so the same field accelerates them less between scattering events. The result is roughly a threefold mobility gap at room temperature.

faq.q: Can effective mass be negative?
faq.a: Yes, near the top of a band the curvature is negative, so an electron there would have negative effective mass. Physicists describe those states with holes of positive mass and positive charge instead.

縮退半導体.desc: A semiconductor doped so heavily that the Fermi level lies inside the conduction or valence band. It behaves almost like a metal and is used in tunnel diodes and low-resistance contacts.

間接遷移型.desc: A band structure in which the bottom of the conduction band and the top of the valence band occur at different momenta. Transitions need a phonon, so light emission is inefficient. Silicon and germanium are typical examples.

SRH再結合(ショックレー・リード・ホール再結合).desc: Recombination of electrons and holes through deep levels (traps) in the band gap. It mainly determines minority-carrier lifetime in silicon and is accelerated by metal contamination and crystal defects.

オージェ再結合.desc: Recombination in which the released energy is given to another carrier instead of being emitted as light. It becomes significant at high carrier densities and affects lifetime in heavily doped layers and efficiency loss in LEDs.

擬フェルミ準位.desc: Separate Fermi levels for electrons and holes, used to describe a semiconductor driven out of equilibrium by light or current injection. The larger the split between them, the more excess carriers there are.

拡散長.desc: The average distance minority carriers diffuse before recombining, given by L = √(Dτ) from the diffusion coefficient D and lifetime τ. It strongly affects the efficiency of solar cells and photodetectors.

アインシュタインの関係式.desc: The relation D = μkT/q that links the diffusion coefficient D and mobility μ of carriers. It shows that materials with higher mobility also allow faster diffusion.

電子親和力.desc: The energy difference between the vacuum level and the bottom of the conduction band of a semiconductor. It is used to estimate band offsets at heterojunctions and barrier heights at metal contacts.

仕事関数.desc: The energy difference between the vacuum level and the Fermi level: the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from a material. It affects the threshold voltage of metal gates and the height of Schottky barriers.

about.p: The work function is measured from the Fermi level to the vacuum level, whereas the electron affinity is measured from the conduction-band edge to the vacuum level. In a metal the Fermi level lies inside a band, so the work function is a single material property, typically about 4 to 6 eV and somewhat dependent on crystal face and surface cleanliness. In a semiconductor the work function equals the electron affinity plus the gap between the conduction band and the Fermi level. Silicon's electron affinity is about 4.05 eV, so its work function ranges from about 4.05 eV (heavily n-type) to 5.17 eV (heavily p-type).

When a metal touches an n-type semiconductor, the ideal (Schottky-Mott) barrier height for electrons is the metal work function minus the semiconductor's electron affinity. A high-work-function metal on n-type silicon should therefore make a rectifying Schottky contact. In practice, interface states pin the Fermi level, so barrier heights on silicon vary much less with the metal than the simple rule predicts. Ohmic contacts are therefore made mainly by heavy doping under the contact, which thins the barrier so carriers tunnel through it.

In a MOS structure, the difference between the gate and channel work functions sets the flat-band voltage, which adds directly to the threshold voltage. Polysilicon gates gave the right values automatically: n+ poly near the conduction band for nMOS and p+ poly near the valence band for pMOS. With high-k dielectrics, metal gates replaced poly, so the metals must provide effective work functions near 4.1 eV for nMOS (aluminum-containing stacks such as TiAl) and near 5.1 eV for pMOS (TiN-based stacks). FinFETs and gate-all-around devices use lightly doped channels, so stacking thin layers to tune the effective work function is the main way to offer multiple threshold options.

The effective work function of a metal gate depends on reactions at its interfaces with the high-k film, and the roughly 1000 °C anneals used to activate source and drain can shift it unpredictably. A gate-last, or replacement metal gate, flow therefore builds the transistor around a sacrificial polysilicon gate, removes it after the hot steps, and only then deposits the high-k and work-function metals. Work function also governs thermionic and photoelectric emission, and it is measured by photoemission spectroscopy or Kelvin probe techniques.

faq.q: What is the difference between work function and electron affinity?
faq.a: Work function is the energy from the Fermi level to the vacuum level; electron affinity is the energy from the conduction-band edge to the vacuum level. In a semiconductor the electron affinity is fixed by the material, while the work function changes with doping.

faq.q: Does doping change the work function of silicon?
faq.a: Yes. Doping moves the Fermi level, so silicon's work function varies from about 4.05 eV when heavily n-type to about 5.17 eV when heavily p-type.

faq.q: Why does the gate metal work function affect threshold voltage?
faq.a: The gate-to-channel work-function difference sets the flat-band voltage, which shifts the threshold voltage one-for-one. Choosing or tuning the gate metal therefore sets the threshold without heavy channel doping.

真性キャリア密度.desc: The density of thermally generated electrons and holes in an undoped semiconductor, written ni. For silicon it is about 1×10¹⁰ cm⁻³ at room temperature and rises steeply with temperature. In equilibrium, n × p = ni².

about.p: Even in perfectly pure silicon, thermal energy occasionally lifts a valence electron across the band gap, leaving a hole behind, so electrons and holes appear in equal numbers. Their equilibrium density, the intrinsic carrier density ni, follows ni ∝ T^(3/2)·exp(−Eg/2kT). For silicon at room temperature ni is about 1×10¹⁰ cm⁻³, quoted as 1.0–1.5×10¹⁰ depending on the source, so only about one atom in 10¹² contributes a carrier. Narrower gaps give far more: germanium is about 2×10¹³ cm⁻³, while GaAs is only about 2×10⁶ cm⁻³.

In thermal equilibrium n × p = ni², whether or not the material is doped. Adding donors raises the electron density and gives holes more partners to recombine with, so holes fall in proportion. With 1×10¹⁶ cm⁻³ fully ionized donors, n ≈ 1×10¹⁶ and p = (1×10¹⁰)² / 10¹⁶ = 1×10⁴ cm⁻³. These minority carriers are a trillion times scarcer than majority carriers, yet they set junction reverse current and bipolar transistor action. The law fails away from equilibrium: under illumination or forward bias, np exceeds ni².

Because ni contains exp(−Eg/2kT), it rises steeply with temperature, roughly doubling for every 10 °C near room temperature in silicon. Minority-carrier densities rise with it, so pn-junction reverse leakage climbs rapidly when hot. The same effect makes a silicon diode's forward voltage fall about 2 mV/°C at constant current, used for on-chip temperature sensing and cancelled in bandgap references. When ni approaches the doping level, the device loses its doping-controlled behavior, one reason wide-gap SiC and GaN suit high-temperature operation.

A region is extrinsic when its doping far exceeds ni, which at room temperature happens with only tiny amounts of dopant. At diffusion temperatures, however, ni itself rises to around 10¹⁸ cm⁻³ or more, so only heavily doped regions remain extrinsic. There, the shifted Fermi level increases the population of charged point defects and the internal field pushes ionized dopants along, making diffusion coefficients concentration dependent. Arsenic profiles consequently become box-like, with flat tops and steep fronts, instead of ideal erfc or Gaussian shapes.

faq.q: What is the intrinsic carrier concentration of silicon at 300 K?
faq.a: About 1×10¹⁰ cm⁻³, with published values ranging roughly from 1.0 to 1.5×10¹⁰ cm⁻³ depending on the band-gap and effective-mass data used.

faq.q: Does n × p = ni² hold in a forward-biased diode?
faq.a: No. The relation holds only in thermal equilibrium; with forward bias V, the product near the junction rises to about ni² × exp(qV/kT) because carriers are being injected.

faq.q: Why does intrinsic carrier density increase with temperature?
faq.a: More thermal energy lets more valence electrons jump the band gap, and the dependence is exponential in −Eg/2kT. Wider band gaps make the rise far smaller at a given temperature.

ショットキーバリアダイオード.desc: A diode that uses a metal-semiconductor junction (Schottky junction). It has a low forward voltage and switches fast because there is no minority-carrier storage.

接合容量(空乏層容量).desc: Capacitance arising because the depletion layer of a PN junction acts like a parallel-plate capacitor. It decreases as reverse bias widens the depletion layer; varactor diodes use this property.

about.p: The depletion region of a pn junction contains fixed charge: ionized donors on the n side and ionized acceptors on the p side, with almost no mobile carriers in between. When the voltage across the junction changes, the edges of this region move, adding or removing charge on each side, just as charge is added to the plates of a capacitor. The small-signal capacitance per unit area is therefore C = ε/W, where W is the depletion width and ε is the permittivity of silicon, about 11.7 times that of vacuum.

For a one-sided abrupt junction, W = √(2ε(Vbi + V)/qN), where Vbi is the built-in potential, V the reverse bias and N the doping on the lightly doped side. Capacitance therefore falls roughly as 1/√(Vbi + V), so quadrupling the total voltage halves it. Circuit models write Cj = Cj0/(1 + V/Vbi)^m, with m = 1/2 for abrupt and 1/3 for linearly graded junctions. Plotting 1/C² against V gives a straight line whose slope yields N and whose intercept yields Vbi, the basis of capacitance-voltage (C-V) doping profiling.

Junction capacitance dominates under reverse bias and small forward bias. Under significant forward bias, a second effect takes over: injected minority carriers are stored near the junction, and because that stored charge changes with voltage, it behaves as diffusion capacitance, proportional to current and carrier lifetime. Diffusion capacitance can reach nanofarads at high current and limits the switching speed of diodes and bipolar transistors. The distinction matters in design: a reverse-biased junction gives a small, voltage-tunable capacitor, while a forward-biased one stores charge that must be removed before turn-off.

Varactor diodes exploit the voltage dependence to tune LC resonators in voltage-controlled oscillators and PLLs, with hyperabrupt doping profiles widening the tuning range. Photodiodes are reverse-biased partly to cut junction capacitance and speed their response, and depletion-type silicon optical modulators vary depletion width to move majority carriers, reaching tens of gigahertz. Elsewhere it is parasitic: source and drain junctions of MOSFETs load every logic node, and silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafers reduce that load by placing transistors on a buried oxide instead of a bulk junction.

faq.q: Why does junction capacitance decrease with reverse bias?
faq.a: Reverse bias widens the depletion region, and since capacitance is permittivity divided by width, a wider region gives a smaller capacitance, roughly as one over the square root of voltage for an abrupt junction.

faq.q: What is the difference between junction capacitance and diffusion capacitance?
faq.a: Junction capacitance comes from fixed charge in the depletion region and dominates under reverse bias; diffusion capacitance comes from minority carriers stored under forward bias and grows with current.

faq.q: How do you measure doping from junction capacitance?
faq.a: Measure capacitance versus reverse bias and plot 1/C² against V; for an abrupt junction the slope gives the doping of the lightly doped side and the intercept gives the built-in potential.

拡散容量.desc: Capacitance in a forward-biased PN junction caused by injected minority carriers stored in the neutral regions. It grows in proportion to forward current and limits high-speed operation.

逆回復時間.desc: The time during which reverse current keeps flowing after a conducting diode is reverse-biased, until the stored minority carriers are removed. It causes switching loss and noise.

伝導度変調.desc: A large drop in the resistance of a lightly doped layer when many minority carriers are injected into it. PIN diodes and IGBTs use it to combine high breakdown voltage with low on-state voltage.

about.p: A high-voltage device needs a thick, lightly doped layer to block voltage, and in the off state that layer contains few free carriers and is highly resistive. When the device conducts in forward bias, the heavily doped p and n regions on either side inject holes and electrons into it. At high injection their densities far exceed the background doping and stay roughly equal to preserve charge neutrality. Conductivity is proportional to carrier density times mobility, so the layer's resistance falls by orders of magnitude, and the voltage across it depends only weakly on its thickness.

about.h: Why power devices rely on it
about.p: In a unipolar device such as a power MOSFET or Schottky diode, only the doping supplies carriers in the drift layer, and the ideal specific on-resistance of silicon rises roughly with the 2.5th power of the breakdown voltage. Bipolar devices escape this limit. A PIN diode floods its i-layer with carriers, and an IGBT adds a p+ layer on the collector side of a MOSFET-like structure so that injected holes modulate the drift layer while the MOS gate controls the electron current. This keeps on-state voltage low at ratings from about 600 V to 6.5 kV.

The injected carriers do not vanish instantly when the device is told to turn off. A PIN diode conducts a reverse-recovery current while stored charge is swept out, and an IGBT shows a tail current as holes left in the drift layer recombine, because the MOS channel cannot extract them. Both add switching loss and limit the usable frequency. Carrier-lifetime control, for example by electron irradiation or heavy-metal diffusion, speeds switching but raises on-state voltage, a classic trade-off in power-device design.

Silicon MOSFETs carry only majority carriers, so they show no conductivity modulation, switch fast and dominate below a few hundred volts. Wide-band-gap SiC MOSFETs reach high voltage with a thin drift layer instead, competing with IGBTs at mid-to-high voltage. The effect is also used in PIN diodes as RF switches and attenuators: forward current lowers the i-layer resistance roughly in proportion to the current, while reverse bias leaves a high-resistance, low-capacitance layer.

faq.q: Why don't power MOSFETs have conductivity modulation?
faq.a: A MOSFET conducts only with majority carriers supplied by the drift-layer doping, and no minority carriers are injected. Its drift-layer resistance therefore stays high at high voltage ratings.

faq.q: Why does conductivity modulation slow down switching?
faq.a: The injected electrons and holes must be removed or recombine before the device can block voltage, which causes reverse-recovery current in diodes and tail current in IGBTs. This stored charge adds switching loss.

faq.q: How does an IGBT achieve low on-voltage at high voltage?
faq.a: Its p+ collector injects holes into the lightly doped drift layer, and together with electrons from the MOS channel they raise the carrier density far above the doping. This conductivity modulation lowers the drift-layer resistance.

トンネルダイオード(エサキダイオード).desc: A diode with very heavily doped p and n sides that shows negative resistance in forward bias due to tunneling. It was discovered by Leo Esaki in 1957.

理想係数.desc: The factor n in the diode equation I ∝ exp(qV/nkT). It is close to 1 when diffusion current dominates and close to 2 when recombination in the depletion layer dominates, so it indicates junction quality.

オーミック接触.desc: A metal-semiconductor contact with low resistance in both directions and a linear current-voltage relation. It is made by heavily doping the semiconductor surface so carriers can tunnel through the barrier.

飽和領域.desc: The state of a bipolar transistor in which both the base-emitter and base-collector junctions are forward-biased. The collector-emitter voltage falls to about 0.1-0.3 V, corresponding to a switch in the on state.

about.p: A bipolar transistor has four operating regions defined by its two junctions. In the active region the base-emitter junction is forward-biased and the base-collector junction reverse-biased, and IC ≈ hFE × IB. If the base current is raised until the collector circuit cannot supply hFE × IB, for example when VCC/RC is smaller, the collector voltage falls until the base-collector junction also becomes forward-biased. That is saturation. Collector current is now set by the external circuit and barely increases with more base current, and the ratio IC/IB, called the forced beta, falls below hFE.

about.h: Saturation as the on state of a switch
about.p: Because the two forward-biased junctions largely cancel, the collector-emitter voltage VCE(sat) is only about 0.1–0.3 V, close to a closed switch, and the conduction loss is about VCE(sat) × IC. Designers guarantee saturation by driving base current several times IC/hFE(min), often 2–10 times. The cost appears at turn-off: in saturation excess minority charge is stored in the base and collector, and it must be removed before the transistor can leave saturation, delaying switching. Schottky clamps or avoiding deep saturation are classic ways to speed this up.

The same word describes a very different condition in a MOSFET. A long-channel nMOSFET with VGS > Vth enters saturation when VDS ≥ VGS − Vth: the channel pinches off at the drain end, and the drain current becomes nearly independent of VDS, following ID = (1/2)μCox(W/L)(VGS − Vth)². Here the current is saturated, not the voltage. In short-channel devices velocity saturation makes current saturate at lower VDS and pushes the dependence on overdrive toward linear, so detailed compact models are used for design.

For amplifiers, the useful operating regions correspond across the two devices: MOSFET saturation plays the role of the bipolar active region, where the output current is controlled by the input and is relatively insensitive to output voltage. For switches, bipolar saturation corresponds to the MOSFET triode (linear) region, where the device behaves like a low resistance. Mixing these up is a common source of confusion. An amplifier must keep a bipolar transistor out of saturation, but must keep a MOSFET in saturation, with VDS above VGS − Vth setting the minimum output swing.

faq.q: What is VCE(sat) of a bipolar transistor?
faq.a: VCE(sat) is the collector-emitter voltage when the transistor is saturated, typically about 0.1–0.3 V for small silicon devices, rising at high current because of collector resistance. It sets the on-state voltage drop and conduction loss of a BJT switch.

faq.q: Is the saturation region of a BJT the same as that of a MOSFET?
faq.a: No. BJT saturation has both junctions forward-biased and acts like a closed switch, whereas MOSFET saturation is the pinched-off region with nearly constant drain current used for amplification. The MOSFET region analogous to BJT saturation is the triode or linear region.

faq.q: Why is a bipolar transistor slow to turn off from saturation?
faq.a: In saturation, excess minority carriers are stored in the base and collector regions. This stored charge must be removed before the collector current can fall, which adds a storage delay to turn-off.

遮断領域.desc: The state of a bipolar transistor in which both junctions are reverse-biased and almost no collector current flows. It corresponds to a switch in the off state.

about.p: A bipolar junction transistor (BJT) has four operating regions set by its two junctions. In the forward-active region the base-emitter junction is forward biased and the base-collector junction reverse biased; in saturation both are forward biased; in cutoff both are reverse biased. In practice a silicon transistor is effectively in cutoff whenever VBE is below about 0.5 V, because forward current is then negligible. Only junction leakage, on the order of nanoamperes, reaches the collector, so the collector-emitter path behaves like an open switch.

about.h: Cutoff as the off state of a switch
about.p: In switching circuits a BJT alternates between cutoff (off) and saturation (on). In cutoff almost no collector current flows, so there is no drop across the load resistor and VCE rises to nearly the supply voltage; power dissipation is close to zero. If the base is left floating, collector-base leakage flows into the base and is amplified by the current gain, so the transistor may not turn off fully, especially when hot, since leakage rises steeply with temperature. A resistor between base and emitter diverts this leakage and guarantees cutoff.

Switching speed depends on how fast the transistor crosses between regions. Turning on from cutoff requires charging the junction capacitances until VBE reaches about 0.6–0.7 V before collector current rises, a delay time. Turning off from saturation is slower, because excess minority charge stored in the base must be removed before the transistor can return to cutoff (the storage time). Circuits that keep the transistor out of deep saturation, such as Schottky-clamped transistors, shorten this turn-off delay.

For a MOSFET, the comparable off state is VGS below the threshold voltage, although subthreshold current still flows and is usually larger than BJT cutoff leakage in scaled devices. Note that the word saturation means different things for the two devices: BJT saturation is the fully on switch state, whereas MOSFET saturation corresponds to the BJT's active region. The cutoff region is also unrelated to the cutoff frequency (fT), which is the frequency at which current gain falls to one.

faq.q: What are the conditions for a BJT to be in the cutoff region?
faq.a: Both the base-emitter and base-collector junctions are reverse biased, or in practice VBE is below about 0.5 V for silicon. Collector current is then limited to leakage of around nanoamperes.

faq.q: Why put a resistor between base and emitter?
faq.a: With a floating base, collector-base leakage flows through the base-emitter junction and is amplified by the current gain, so the transistor may conduct slightly. The resistor shunts that leakage away so the transistor stays firmly in cutoff.

faq.q: Is the cutoff region related to the cutoff frequency?
faq.a: No. The cutoff region is a DC bias state where the transistor is off, while the cutoff frequency (fT) is the frequency at which the transistor's small-signal current gain drops to one.

カレントミラー回路.desc: A circuit that uses two matched transistors to copy the current flowing in one into the other (or at a fixed ratio). It is widely used for bias current sources and active loads in analog ICs.

トランジション周波数.desc: The frequency at which the common-emitter current gain falls to 1, written fT. It is a key indicator of a transistor's high-frequency performance.

エミッタフォロワ.desc: A common-collector amplifier. Its voltage gain is about 1, but its high input impedance and low output impedance make it a buffer that drives the next stage without loading the signal.

ダーリントン接続.desc: A connection that feeds the emitter current of one transistor into the base of a second. The overall current gain is roughly the product of the two, so a small base current can control a large current.

クロスオーバーひずみ.desc: Distortion in a class-B push-pull amplifier near 0 V, where neither transistor conducts during the handover between positive and negative half-cycles. Class-AB biasing with a small idle current reduces it.

ミラー効果.desc: The effect by which a capacitance between the input and output of an inverting amplifier appears (1 + gain) times larger from the input. It degrades the high-frequency response of common-emitter and common-source stages.

about.p: Consider a capacitor C connected between the input and output of an inverting amplifier with voltage gain −Av. When the input rises by v, the output falls by Av·v, so the voltage across the capacitor changes by (1 + Av)·v. The input must therefore supply (1 + Av) times the charge it would for a grounded capacitor, and the capacitor appears at the input as C(1 + Av). Seen from the output the same capacitor looks roughly like C(1 + 1/Av), close to C itself. This equivalent input capacitance is often called the Miller capacitance.

In a common-emitter stage the base-collector capacitance Cμ is multiplied this way; in a common-source stage it is the gate-drain capacitance Cgd, which includes gate-to-drain overlap capacitance. With Cμ = 2 pF and a gain of 100, the input sees about 200 pF. Together with the source resistance Rs it forms a low-pass pole near 1/(2π·Rs·C_Miller), which often sets the upper bandwidth of the stage. Higher gain therefore directly costs bandwidth, which is why high-gain inverting stages driven from high-impedance sources are slow.

The classic remedy is the cascode: a common-base (or common-gate) transistor stacked on the input device holds the input transistor's collector or drain at a nearly constant voltage. The input device then has a voltage gain of only about one, so its feedback capacitance is barely multiplied, while the overall stage keeps high gain. A common-base stage alone also avoids the problem because its base is AC-grounded. Lowering the driving source resistance raises the pole frequency, and choosing devices with small feedback capacitance helps as well.

about.h: When the Miller effect is useful
about.p: The same multiplication is exploited on purpose in op-amp frequency compensation. A small capacitor placed across a high-gain inverting stage behaves like a large one, creating a dominant pole at a low frequency so that the gain falls below unity before other poles add much phase shift. This keeps the amplifier stable even as a unity-gain follower without needing a physically large capacitor on chip. In power MOSFET switching, the Miller effect also explains the plateau in gate voltage while the drain voltage swings and Cgd is being charged.

faq.q: What is Miller capacitance?
faq.a: Miller capacitance is the enlarged input capacitance, about C(1 + |Av|), that a capacitor bridging the input and output of an inverting amplifier presents to the signal source. For transistors the bridging capacitor is usually Cμ (bipolar) or Cgd (MOSFET).

faq.q: Why does a cascode amplifier reduce the Miller effect?
faq.a: In a cascode the input transistor drives the low impedance of a common-base or common-gate device, so its own voltage gain is about one. The feedback capacitance is then multiplied only by about two instead of by the full stage gain.

faq.q: Does the Miller effect occur in non-inverting amplifiers?
faq.a: The large multiplication requires an inverting gain; with a follower whose gain is near +1, the voltage across the bridging capacitor barely changes and its effective input capacitance actually shrinks. That is why emitter and source followers have good high-frequency behavior.

チャネル長変調.desc: In a saturated MOSFET, raising the drain voltage moves the pinch-off point toward the source, shortening the effective channel and slightly increasing drain current. It makes the output resistance finite.

about.h: Why drain current keeps rising in saturation
about.p: When VDS exceeds VGS − Vth, the inversion layer vanishes at the drain end of the channel, a condition called pinch-off. Further increases in VDS are absorbed by a short depletion region between the pinch-off point and the drain, and that region widens as VDS grows. The pinch-off point therefore moves toward the source, leaving a conducting channel of effective length L − ΔL. Since drain current is inversely proportional to channel length and the voltage across the remaining channel stays near VGS − Vth, the current rises slightly instead of staying perfectly flat.

about.h: The λ model and output resistance
about.p: Channel-length modulation is usually modeled by adding a factor to the square-law equation: ID = (1/2)μCox(W/L)(VGS − Vth)²(1 + λVDS), where λ is the channel-length modulation coefficient. The slope of ID versus VDS is about λID, so the small-signal output resistance is ro ≈ 1/(λID). Because ΔL is a larger fraction of a short channel, λ is roughly inversely proportional to L, and doubling L roughly doubles ro. In short-channel devices, drain-induced barrier lowering (DIBL) adds to the output conductance as well.

about.h: Why it matters for analog design
about.p: The intrinsic gain of a single transistor is gm·ro, and with gm = 2ID/(VGS − Vth) this becomes 2/(λ(VGS − Vth)). In highly scaled transistors it is only about 10–20, which is not enough for many amplifiers. Designers respond by using longer-than-minimum channel lengths in analog blocks, stacking cascode devices to multiply output resistance, and using multiple gain stages. Channel-length modulation also degrades current mirrors: a mismatch in drain voltage between the reference and output devices produces a current error proportional to λ.

about.h: Channel-length modulation vs. the Early effect
about.p: Bipolar transistors show an analogous effect called the Early effect, or base-width modulation. A higher collector-emitter voltage widens the collector-base depletion region, narrowing the neutral base and slightly increasing collector current. Its strength is expressed by the Early voltage VA, the point where extrapolated output curves meet the voltage axis, giving ro ≈ VA/IC. For MOSFETs the equivalent quantity is 1/λ, sometimes also called an Early voltage. Both effects tilt the otherwise flat output characteristics and limit the voltage gain available from a single device.

faq.q: What is lambda (λ) in the MOSFET drain current equation?
faq.a: λ is the channel-length modulation coefficient, which describes how much saturation drain current rises per volt of VDS through the factor (1 + λVDS). Its inverse behaves like an Early voltage and sets the output resistance ro ≈ 1/(λID).

faq.q: Why do analog circuits use longer channel lengths?
faq.a: Channel-length modulation is weaker in long channels because the pinch-off shift is a smaller fraction of L. Longer devices therefore have higher output resistance and intrinsic gain, along with better matching.

faq.q: What is the difference between channel-length modulation and the Early effect?
faq.a: Both make output current rise with output voltage and give a finite output resistance. Channel-length modulation shortens the effective channel of a MOSFET, while the Early effect narrows the neutral base of a bipolar transistor.

速度飽和.desc: Under strong electric fields, carrier drift velocity stops increasing in proportion to the field and levels off at about 1×10⁷ cm/s. In short-channel MOSFETs it makes drain current smaller than the square law predicts.

about.p: At low electric field, carrier drift velocity is v = μE, so 1000 cm²/V·s at 100 V/cm gives 1×10⁵ cm/s. As the field rises, carriers gain energy faster than ordinary scattering removes it, until they lose energy mainly by emitting optical phonons. The velocity then levels off. For electrons in silicon the departure from linearity becomes noticeable above roughly 10⁴ V/cm, and the saturated velocity is about 1×10⁷ cm/s at room temperature; holes saturate at a somewhat lower velocity. A common empirical fit is v = μE/(1 + E/Ec), with critical field Ec = vsat/μ.

about.h: What it does to MOSFET current
about.p: Lateral fields in short channels are large: 1 V across 50 nm is 2×10⁵ V/cm, well beyond the critical field. A long-channel MOSFET follows the square law, ID = (1/2)μCox(W/L)(VGS − Vth)². When carriers are fully velocity saturated, the current approaches ID ≈ W·Cox·vsat·(VGS − Vth), linear in overdrive and nearly independent of channel length. Real devices sit between the two limits, which the alpha-power law captures with an exponent between 1 and 2, closer to 1 for very short channels.

In a long-channel device, current saturates when VDS reaches VGS − Vth and the channel pinches off at the drain end. In a short-channel device, carriers reach saturation velocity first, so the current saturates at a smaller VDS than VGS − Vth. Transconductance stops rising with overdrive and tends toward W·Cox·vsat, and shortening the gate gives less extra current than simple scaling predicts. Mobility degradation and parasitic source and drain resistance add further deviations, so practical design relies on compact models such as BSIM rather than the square law.

Saturation velocity is a key material figure of merit for high-frequency and power devices. GaN's electron saturation velocity, about 2.5×10⁷ cm/s, contributes to its strength in high-frequency power transistors. GaAs behaves differently: at high field, electrons transfer to a higher, heavier conduction-band valley and actually slow down, giving a region of negative differential mobility that Gunn diodes exploit to build microwave oscillators.

faq.q: What is the saturation velocity of electrons in silicon?
faq.a: About 1×10⁷ cm/s at room temperature. Drift velocity stops being proportional to field at fields above roughly 10⁴ V/cm and approaches this value.

faq.q: Why does velocity saturation make MOSFET drain current linear in gate voltage?
faq.a: Once carriers move at a fixed maximum velocity, current equals channel charge times that velocity. The channel charge is proportional to VGS − Vth, so the current becomes roughly linear rather than quadratic in overdrive.

faq.q: What is the difference between velocity saturation and pinch-off?
faq.a: Pinch-off is the long-channel mechanism in which the channel vanishes at the drain end once VDS reaches VGS − Vth. Velocity saturation is a field-driven limit on carrier speed that makes short-channel current saturate at a lower VDS.

相互コンダクタンス.desc: The ratio of the change in drain current to the change in gate voltage, written gm. It expresses a transistor's amplifying ability; amplifier gain is roughly gm times the load resistance.

DIBL.desc: Short for drain-induced barrier lowering. In short-channel MOSFETs, a higher drain voltage lowers the potential barrier at the source, reducing the threshold voltage and increasing off-state leakage.

GIDL(ゲート誘起ドレインリーク).desc: Off-state leakage caused by band-to-band tunneling in the strong field where the gate overlaps the drain. It is a concern for data retention in DRAM, among others.

about.p: Consider an off nMOS with its gate at 0 V or below and its drain at a high voltage. In the region where the gate overlaps the heavily doped drain, the large gate-to-drain voltage creates a strong vertical field that depletes the drain surface and bends the energy bands so steeply that the valence band on one side lines up with the conduction band a few nanometres away. Electrons then tunnel band to band. They are collected by the drain, while the generated holes flow to the body, so GIDL (gate-induced drain leakage) appears as drain-to-body current.

On a log-scale drain current versus gate voltage plot, ordinary subthreshold leakage keeps falling as the gate is driven further off. GIDL does the opposite: making the gate more negative for an nMOS, or raising the drain voltage, increases the gate-to-drain field, so the off-current turns upward again. The total leakage therefore has a minimum at some intermediate gate voltage. GIDL is also distinct from DIBL (drain-induced barrier lowering), which lowers the threshold voltage and increases subthreshold current rather than adding a tunneling path.

A DRAM cell must hold its charge for tens of milliseconds between refreshes, so its access transistor must leak extremely little. Charge escapes mainly through subthreshold leakage and junction leakage at the storage node, which includes GIDL. Driving the word line slightly negative when the cell is off suppresses subthreshold current but raises the gate-to-drain voltage and therefore GIDL, so the two must be balanced. Because a small tail of the leakiest cells sets the refresh period, designers ease the fields with buried-gate cell transistors and carefully shaped junction doping.

GIDL grows with the electric field at the gate edge, so the remedies reduce that field: lighter or graded doping where the drain meets the gate edge, reduced gate-to-drain overlap, a thicker dielectric at the gate corner, and limits on how far the gate is driven negative. Thin gate dielectrics make the field and the GIDL stronger. The same mechanism can also be useful; some 3D NAND designs deliberately generate holes by GIDL to raise the channel potential during erase.

faq.q: What is the difference between GIDL and DIBL?
faq.a: GIDL is a leakage current from band-to-band tunneling in the gate-drain overlap region, and it grows as the gate is driven further off. DIBL is drain voltage lowering the source barrier, which reduces the threshold voltage and increases subthreshold current.

faq.q: Why does GIDL increase with negative gate voltage?
faq.a: For an nMOS, a more negative gate raises the gate-to-drain voltage, increasing the vertical field and band bending at the drain edge. Stronger band bending makes band-to-band tunneling more likely, so leakage rises.

faq.q: Is GIDL part of subthreshold leakage?
faq.a: No. Subthreshold leakage is carrier diffusion over the source barrier, while GIDL is a tunneling current at the drain, usually grouped with junction leakage. They respond to gate voltage in opposite directions.

パンチスルー.desc: A condition in which the source and drain depletion regions merge and current flows that the gate cannot control. It occurs when the channel is too short or the substrate doping is too low.

about.h: How punch-through develops in a MOSFET
about.p: When drain voltage is applied, the drain-to-body junction is reverse biased and its depletion region spreads toward the source. Depletion width grows roughly with the square root of voltage divided by doping, so a short channel and lightly doped substrate let it reach the source-side depletion region. Once the two merge below the surface, the drain itself pulls down the potential barrier that normally holds back source carriers. Current then flows deep in the substrate, where the gate field is weak, so the transistor cannot be switched off and drain current climbs steeply with drain voltage.

about.h: Punch-through vs. DIBL and avalanche breakdown
about.p: Punch-through is the extreme case of drain-induced barrier lowering (DIBL). With moderate DIBL, the drain only partly lowers the source barrier, so threshold voltage falls as drain voltage rises and the subthreshold swing worsens. In punch-through the barrier in the subsurface region effectively disappears and gate control is lost. It is a purely electrostatic effect and needs no impact ionization, unlike avalanche breakdown, where carriers gain enough energy in a high field to generate new electron-hole pairs.

about.h: How process and structure suppress it
about.p: The usual cure is more doping exactly where the depletion regions would meet, without raising doping at the channel surface, which would increase threshold voltage and cut mobility. Halo (pocket) implants, tilted about 20–45°, place channel-type dopant under the source/drain edges. Retrograde wells use implants of hundreds of keV to MeV to put peak doping deep below the surface. Bulk FinFETs add a heavily doped punch-through stopper at the fin base, which the gate cannot control. SOI substrates and gate-all-around (GAA) structures remove the uncontrolled path altogether.

Bipolar transistors suffer a similar failure. A thin base reduces recombination and raises current gain and speed, but at high collector-base reverse voltage the collector depletion region can spread across the whole base and reach the emitter depletion region. The base potential barrier then collapses and collector current rises uncontrollably, which caps the usable breakdown voltage. Base width and base doping are therefore chosen together, trading current gain and high-frequency performance against punch-through voltage.

faq.q: What is the difference between punch-through and avalanche breakdown?
faq.a: Punch-through happens when the drain and source depletion regions merge and the source barrier collapses, which is purely electrostatic. Avalanche breakdown happens when carriers in a high field create new electron-hole pairs by impact ionization, multiplying the current.

faq.q: How do halo implants prevent punch-through?
faq.a: Halo implants add extra dopant of the substrate type locally under the edges of the source and drain. This narrows the drain depletion region near the channel ends, so it cannot reach the source, while leaving the rest of the channel lightly doped.

faq.q: Why do bulk FinFETs need a punch-through stopper?
faq.a: The gate wraps only the upper part of the fin, so the lower part near the substrate offers a leakage path the gate cannot shut off. A heavily doped layer of the opposite type at the fin base blocks this path.

フラットバンド電圧.desc: The gate voltage at which the bands at the semiconductor surface of a MOS structure are flat. It is set by the work-function difference between gate and substrate and by charges in the oxide, and is one component of the threshold voltage.

about.h: Why the bands bend at zero bias
about.p: In a MOS structure the gate and the semiconductor usually have different work functions. In equilibrium their Fermi levels must line up, so the work-function difference φms appears as a potential split between the oxide and the semiconductor surface, bending the bands even with the gate grounded. Charge in the dielectric adds to this: fixed charge near the interface, mobile ions such as sodium, trapped charge and charged interface states all induce opposite charge in the semiconductor. The flat-band voltage VFB is the gate voltage that exactly cancels these effects, leaving the surface neither accumulated nor depleted.

about.h: The formula and its role in threshold voltage
about.p: For charge Qox located at the oxide-silicon interface, VFB = φms − Qox/Cox; charge distributed inside the oxide counts less the closer it sits to the gate. Threshold voltage builds on it: for an nMOS device, Vth = VFB + 2φF + Qdep/Cox, where φF is the Fermi potential and Qdep the depletion charge at strong inversion. Any shift in VFB therefore moves Vth one for one. For an n+ polysilicon gate on p-type silicon of moderate doping, φms is roughly −0.9 V, and positive oxide charge pushes VFB further negative.

about.h: Setting it with the gate metal
about.p: In high-k/metal-gate transistors, choosing the gate work function is the main lever on VFB and thus on Vth. nMOS devices need a work function near the silicon conduction band, around 4.1 eV, and pMOS devices one near the valence band, around 5.1 eV. Stacks of thin metal layers of different composition and thickness give several threshold flavors on one chip for high-speed and low-leakage circuits.

A capacitance-voltage (C-V) sweep of a MOS capacitor moves through accumulation, depletion and inversion. Accumulation capacitance gives Cox and hence oxide thickness, and VFB is read where the curve reaches the flat-band capacitance, the series combination of Cox and the semiconductor's capacitance at flat band. Comparing measured VFB with the expected φms gives the effective oxide charge. A VFB shift after bias-temperature stress reveals mobile ion contamination, while stretch-out of the curve indicates interface traps, which makes VFB a routine process-control check.

faq.q: What determines the flat-band voltage of a MOS capacitor?
faq.a: The work-function difference between gate and semiconductor and the charges in the oxide and at the interface. For interface charge it is VFB = φms − Qox/Cox.

faq.q: Is flat-band voltage the same as threshold voltage?
faq.a: No. Flat band is the gate voltage where the surface bands are flat, while threshold is where strong inversion begins. Threshold equals VFB plus the voltage needed to bend the bands by 2φF and support the depletion charge.

faq.q: How is flat-band voltage measured?
faq.a: From a C-V measurement on a MOS capacitor: the gate voltage at which the capacitance equals the calculated flat-band capacitance is taken as VFB. Shifts in VFB reveal changes in oxide charge.

LDD構造.desc: Short for lightly doped drain. The drain is made lightly doped only at its edge next to the gate, relaxing the electric field and suppressing hot-carrier degradation.

基板バイアス効果.desc: An increase in threshold voltage when reverse bias is applied between source and substrate (body), because the depletion charge grows. Also called the substrate bias effect; it is sometimes used to tune the threshold.

about.p: In an n-channel MOSFET the gate must first support the negative charge of the depletion region under it before an inversion layer can form. When the source-to-body junction is reverse-biased (VSB greater than zero, meaning the body is negative relative to the source), the depletion region widens and holds more charge, so a larger gate voltage is needed to reach inversion. The textbook expression is Vth = Vth0 + γ(√(2φF + VSB) − √(2φF)), where the body-effect coefficient γ = √(2qεSi·NA)/Cox grows with heavier substrate doping and with thicker gate oxide.

about.h: Where the body effect shows up in circuits
about.p: In a stack of series nMOS transistors, such as a NAND gate pull-down, only the bottom device has its source at ground. The upper devices see raised source potentials, so their Vth rises and they conduct less current. In a single nMOS pass transistor with its gate at VDD, the output can only rise to about VDD − Vth, and because Vth increases as the source climbs, the final level is lower still. In a source follower, the body effect adds a back-gate transconductance gmb that pulls the voltage gain further below 1.

Analog designers often express the body effect as the ratio gmb/gm, which for bulk transistors is commonly in the range of roughly 0.1 to 0.3 depending on doping and bias. A source follower in a common p-substrate process, where the nMOS body is tied to ground, has its gain limited to about gm/(gm + gmb) even with an ideal load. Placing the transistor in its own well and tying body to source removes the effect, at the cost of extra area and well capacitance.

about.h: Body bias as a tuning knob
about.p: The same physics is used deliberately. Reverse body bias raises Vth to cut subthreshold leakage in standby, and forward body bias lowers Vth to gain speed, which also lets designers compensate for process variation after fabrication. The knob depends on the device structure. In FinFETs the thin fin is controlled almost entirely by the gate, so body biasing has little effect, whereas FD-SOI (fully depleted silicon-on-insulator) transistors with a thin buried oxide allow a wide back-bias tuning range.

faq.q: Is the body effect the same as the substrate bias effect?
faq.a: Yes. Both names describe the change in MOSFET threshold voltage caused by a voltage between source and body (substrate); reverse bias raises Vth and forward bias lowers it.

faq.q: Why does the body effect reduce the gain of a source follower?
faq.a: As the output (source) moves, the source-to-body voltage changes and shifts Vth, which acts like a second transconductance gmb opposing the signal. The gain becomes roughly gm/(gm + gmb) instead of approaching 1.

faq.q: How can the body effect be eliminated?
faq.a: Connecting each transistor's body to its own source removes VSB, but this requires the device to sit in a separate well, which costs area and is only possible for the well-type transistor in a given process.

貫通電流.desc: Current that flows from supply to ground in a CMOS gate during the brief time while the input switches and both the pMOS and nMOS are on. Also called crowbar current, it adds to power consumption.

トランスミッションゲート.desc: An analog switch made of an nMOS and a pMOS connected in parallel. The nMOS passes 0 well and the pMOS passes 1 well, so both values pass without voltage loss.

メタステーブル.desc: A state in which a flip-flop's output stays between 0 and 1 for a while when setup or hold time is violated. Asynchronous signals are passed through two flip-flops (a synchronizer) to guard against it.

about.h: Why a flip-flop can hang between 0 and 1
about.p: A flip-flop stores its state in cross-coupled inverters, which have two stable points and one unstable balance point in between. If the data input changes inside the window defined by the setup time (before the clock edge) and hold time (after it), the latch can be left near that balance point. Positive feedback then amplifies the small imbalance with a time constant τ, but the closer it starts to balance, the longer resolution takes, with no hard upper bound. The output may sit at an intermediate voltage or switch late, and the final value is unpredictable.

With an asynchronous input, metastability can only be made rare, not prevented. A two-flip-flop synchronizer gives the first stage almost one clock period to resolve before the second stage samples it. Mean time between failures is approximately MTBF = e^(t_r/τ) / (T_0 × f_clk × f_data), where t_r is the available resolution time and τ and T_0 depend on the flip-flop. Because t_r sits in an exponent, a third stage adds about one period and multiplies MTBF enormously: with τ = 20 ps, an extra 1 ns gives a factor of e^50, over 10^21.

about.h: What a synchronizer does not fix
about.p: Each synchronized bit may capture a change one cycle early or late, so a multi-bit value such as 0111 to 1000 can arrive as 1111 or 0000. Counters therefore cross in Gray code, where only one bit changes per step, as with asynchronous FIFO pointers; arbitrary data uses a handshake or an asynchronous FIFO. A short pulse from a fast domain can fall between slow-clock edges and vanish, so it must be stretched or converted to a toggle. Crossing signals should come straight from a flip-flop, because a combinational glitch can be captured as a valid value.

In a single synchronous clock domain, a setup violation means the data path is too slow, and static timing analysis finds it; slowing the clock or speeding the path fixes it. Across asynchronous clocks there is no fixed phase relationship, so violations happen eventually no matter how fast the logic is, and timing analysis cannot close them. That is why designs rely on CDC (clock domain crossing) verification, where tools find every crossing and check for a proper synchronizer, Gray-coded pointer or handshake. Such bugs are rare, so ordinary simulation seldom catches them.

faq.q: What causes metastability in a flip-flop?
faq.a: Data changing within the setup-and-hold window around the clock edge, which leaves the internal latch near its unstable balance point. It is unavoidable when the input is asynchronous to the clock.

faq.q: Why are two flip-flops used to synchronize an asynchronous signal?
faq.a: The first flip-flop may go metastable, and the second samples it a full clock period later, by which time it has almost certainly resolved. This raises MTBF exponentially but does not make failure impossible.

faq.q: Can a synchronizer be used for a multi-bit bus?
faq.a: Not bit by bit, because different bits can be captured on different cycles and produce an invalid intermediate value. Use Gray code for counters, or a handshake or asynchronous FIFO for general data.

グレイコード.desc: A code in which successive values differ in only one bit. It prevents read errors in rotary encoders and when passing counter values between different clock domains.

about.h: Converting between binary and Gray code
about.p: The usual Gray code is the reflected binary code, built by listing the n-bit sequence, appending its mirror image and prefixing 0 to the first half and 1 to the second. Conversion from binary B is a single expression: G = B XOR (B >> 1), so each Gray bit below the most significant one is the XOR of two neighboring binary bits. Converting back takes a running XOR from the most significant bit down: the top bit is copied, and each lower binary bit is the previous binary bit XOR the current Gray bit. For three bits the sequence is 000, 001, 011, 010, 110, 111, 101, 100.

about.h: Why one-bit changes matter in encoders
about.p: In plain binary, stepping from 0111 to 1000 flips four bits at once. A rotary or linear absolute encoder reads each bit from its own track, and the transitions on those tracks never line up perfectly, so a reading taken at the boundary can mix old and new bits and report a value far from either position. With Gray code only one track changes at each step, so a reading at the boundary can only be the old or the new value, both of which are correct to within one step.

An asynchronous FIFO passes data between two clock domains, and each side must see the other's read or write pointer to compute full and empty flags. Sending a binary pointer through synchronizer flip-flops is unsafe because several bits may change together and be captured at different clock edges, producing a pointer value that never existed. A Gray-coded pointer changes one bit per increment, so even if that bit is caught mid-transition, the receiving side gets either the old or the new pointer. This works only when the pointer advances by one per clock and the counter wraps at a power of two.

about.h: Gray code in flash memory and Karnaugh maps
about.p: Multi-level cell (MLC) and triple-level cell (TLC) NAND flash store two or three bits as one of four or eight threshold-voltage states. Wear and interference broaden the state distributions, and a misread almost always lands in a neighboring state. Assigning bit patterns in Gray order, such as 111, 110, 100, 101, 001, 000, 010, 011 for TLC, turns each such misread into a single-bit error that error-correcting code handles cheaply. Karnaugh maps use the same ordering on their axes so that physically adjacent cells differ by one variable and can be grouped.

faq.q: How do you convert binary to Gray code?
faq.a: XOR the binary number with itself shifted right by one bit: G = B XOR (B >> 1). The most significant bit stays the same, and every other Gray bit is the XOR of two adjacent binary bits.

faq.q: Why are FIFO pointers Gray-coded for clock domain crossing?
faq.a: A Gray-coded pointer changes only one bit per increment, so a synchronizer that samples it during a transition still yields either the old or the new value. A binary pointer can change many bits at once and be captured as a completely wrong value.

faq.q: What is the difference between Gray code and BCD?
faq.a: Gray code is an ordering of binary patterns in which successive values differ by one bit. BCD (binary-coded decimal) encodes each decimal digit separately in four bits and has no one-bit-change property.

2の補数.desc: The usual binary representation of negative integers. Inverting all bits and adding 1 negates a number. n bits cover −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1, and the same adder can be used for subtraction.

about.p: In n-bit two's complement, every bit has its usual binary weight except the most significant bit, which carries weight −2ⁿ⁻¹. In 4 bits, 1111 therefore reads as −8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = −1, and 1000 is −8. To negate a value, invert every bit and add 1: +1 (0001) becomes 1110, then 1111. Zero has a single pattern, which leaves one more negative value than positive, so the range is −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1: −128 to +127 in 8 bits and −32,768 to +32,767 in 16 bits.

Two's complement arithmetic is simply binary arithmetic modulo 2ⁿ, so one adder handles signed and unsigned numbers identically, and only the interpretation of the result differs. Subtraction A − B becomes A + (inverted B) + 1, implemented by inverting B and setting the adder's carry-in to 1. Sign-magnitude, where 1001 means −1 in 4 bits, has two zeros and needs separate add and subtract logic, and ones' complement also has two zeros and an end-around carry. Booth multipliers likewise rely on two's complement to generate negative partial products cheaply.

Signed overflow happens only when two operands of the same sign produce a result of the opposite sign, for example 0111 + 0001 = 1000 (7 + 1 giving −8) in 4 bits; adding numbers of opposite sign never overflows. Hardware detects it as the XOR of the carry into and the carry out of the most significant bit, reported as the V (overflow) flag. The C (carry) flag instead signals unsigned overflow. The asymmetric range creates corner cases: negating or taking the absolute value of the most negative number, or computing −128 × −1 in 8 bits, overflows.

Widening a two's complement value copies its sign bit into the new upper bits. A RISC-V addi immediate is a 12-bit field covering −2048 to 2047; −1 is stored as 0xFFF and sign-extends to 0xFFFFFFFF, whereas zero-filling would give 4095. An arithmetic right shift also replicates the sign bit, so 1111 1000 (−8) becomes 1111 1100 (−4); for negative odd values it rounds toward negative infinity, so −7 shifted right by one gives −4, while integer division in C truncates toward zero to −3. Offset binary, common at ADC outputs, differs from two's complement only by an inverted MSB.

faq.q: How do you find the two's complement of a negative number?
faq.a: Write the positive value in binary with the chosen number of bits, invert every bit, then add 1. For example, −5 in 8 bits is 00000101 → 11111010 → 11111011.

faq.q: How can you tell if two's complement addition overflowed?
faq.a: Overflow occurs when two positives give a negative or two negatives give a positive, which hardware detects when the carry into the MSB differs from the carry out of it. The carry-out alone indicates unsigned overflow, not signed overflow.

faq.q: Why is the range of 8-bit two's complement −128 to 127 and not symmetric?
faq.a: Zero uses one of the 256 patterns with a 0 sign bit, leaving 127 positive values, while all 128 patterns with a 1 sign bit are negative. As a result +128 cannot be represented.

カルノー図.desc: A diagram that arranges a truth table so that adjacent cells differ in one bit. Grouping neighboring 1s lets you simplify a logic expression visually.

マルチプレクサ.desc: A circuit that selects one of several inputs according to select signals and passes it to the output. The reverse, routing one input to one of several outputs, is a demultiplexer.

about.p: A 2:1 multiplexer (mux) outputs Y = S'·A + S·B: input A when the select signal S is 0 and input B when S is 1. With n select bits a mux chooses among 2ⁿ inputs, so an 8:1 mux needs three select lines. In CMOS, muxes are built from AND-OR or NAND-NAND logic, from transmission gates, or as trees of 2:1 muxes for wide inputs. A mux is also a universal logic element: tying its data inputs to the constants of a truth table makes a 2ⁿ:1 mux implement any n-input Boolean function.

Processor datapaths are full of muxes: they select ALU operands from registers or immediates, forward results through bypass paths to avoid pipeline stalls, choose the next program counter and switch shared buses. FPGA logic blocks implement arbitrary functions with lookup tables (LUTs), which are small memories read out through a mux tree. In design for testability, scan flip-flops add a mux at the data input so the flip-flops can be chained into shift registers in test mode. On boards, analog multiplexers share one ADC among several sensors, and I2C multiplexers separate devices with identical addresses.

In Verilog or VHDL, a conditional assignment, if statement or case statement usually synthesizes to a multiplexer. A long if/else-if chain implies priority, giving a series of 2:1 muxes with long delay, while a case statement on mutually exclusive values tends to become a single wide parallel mux, although modern synthesis tools often optimize either form. A common pitfall is leaving some branch without an assignment in combinational logic, which infers a latch to hold the old value instead of a pure mux.

A demultiplexer does the reverse of a multiplexer: it routes one input to one of 2ⁿ outputs chosen by the select bits. A decoder converts an n-bit code into 2ⁿ one-hot lines and is in effect a demultiplexer with its data input held at 1; decoders drive the select logic of large muxes and memory word lines. In communications, multiplexing more generally means sharing one channel among several signals by time, frequency or code.

faq.q: How many select lines does an 8-to-1 multiplexer need?
faq.a: Three, because 2³ = 8. In general a mux with 2ⁿ data inputs needs n select lines.

faq.q: What is the difference between a multiplexer and a demultiplexer?
faq.a: A multiplexer selects one of several inputs and passes it to a single output. A demultiplexer takes a single input and steers it to one of several outputs.

faq.q: How can a multiplexer implement any logic function?
faq.a: Connect the select lines to the function's input variables and tie each data input to 0 or 1 according to the truth table. The mux then outputs the correct table entry for every input combination, which is how FPGA lookup tables work.

デコーダ.desc: A circuit that activates exactly one of 2ⁿ outputs according to an n-bit input. It is used to select the row addressed in a memory. The reverse function is an encoder.

about.p: An n-to-2ⁿ decoder has one output for every possible input code. Each output is an AND of the input bits, each taken true or complemented, so it goes active for exactly one combination: output k is the minterm for code k. A 2-to-4 decoder needs four 2-input AND gates plus inverters; a 3-to-8 decoder needs eight 3-input gates. Many decoders add an enable input and use active-low outputs, and the enable lets small decoders be cascaded into larger ones. Since every minterm is available, a decoder followed by OR gates can implement any combinational function of its inputs.

An encoder does the reverse: it converts one active line out of 2ⁿ into an n-bit code. A plain encoder gives a wrong result if two inputs are active at once, so a priority encoder reports the highest-priority active input instead. A demultiplexer is a decoder whose enable carries data, routing one input signal to the output chosen by the select bits. A multiplexer can be viewed as a decoder whose outputs gate the data inputs into a common OR. Code converters such as a BCD-to-seven-segment driver are also called decoders even though their outputs are not one-hot.

Every memory array uses decoders: the row decoder turns the row address into one active word line, and the column decoder selects which bit lines connect to the sense amplifiers and I/O. Driving thousands of word lines with single wide AND gates would be slow, so large decoders use predecoding: the address is split into groups of two or three bits, each group is decoded into a few one-hot lines, and a small gate at each row combines one line from each group. Address-decoder faults are among the faults that March tests are designed to catch.

In a CPU, the instruction decoder interprets opcode fields and generates control signals; high-performance x86 cores decode variable-length instructions into simpler micro-operations and may cache them to avoid decoding again. A video decoder is a dedicated hardware block that decompresses video streams far more energy-efficiently than running the same algorithm in software on a general-purpose core. These are much larger circuits than a binary decoder, but they share the idea of translating an encoded input into the signals that act on it.

faq.q: How many outputs does a 4-bit decoder have?
faq.a: A 4-to-16 decoder has 2⁴ = 16 outputs, and exactly one of them is active for each 4-bit input code. In general an n-bit decoder has 2ⁿ outputs.

faq.q: What is the difference between a decoder and an encoder?
faq.a: A decoder converts an n-bit code into one active line out of 2ⁿ, while an encoder converts one active line out of 2ⁿ back into an n-bit code. A priority encoder handles cases where several inputs are active.

faq.q: Is a demultiplexer the same as a decoder?
faq.a: They are closely related: a decoder with an enable input becomes a demultiplexer when the enable is used as the data input. The select bits then choose which output receives the data.

シフトレジスタ.desc: A chain of flip-flops that moves data one bit to the next stage on each clock. It is used for serial-parallel conversion and as the scan chain in scan testing.

about.h: How a shift register is built
about.p: A shift register chains D flip-flops so that each output feeds the next input, and all share one clock. On every active edge each bit moves one stage along the chain. Variants are classified by how data enter and leave: serial-in serial-out acts as a delay line, serial-in parallel-out collects incoming bits into a word, parallel-in serial-out loads a word and shifts it out, and some designs also shift in both directions. In HDL the stages must be written with nonblocking assignments, as in q1 <= d; q2 <= q1;.

Serial-parallel conversion is the classic use. High-speed serial links (SerDes, serializer/deserializer) convert wide parallel buses into a few very fast serial lanes and back, reducing wire and pin count. A simple serial-in parallel-out chip such as the 74HC595 lets a microcontroller drive many LEDs from three pins. In chip testing, scan design connects a block's flip-flops into scan chains: in test mode the flip-flops form a shift register so test patterns can be shifted in, one functional clock applied, and the captured responses shifted out.

Feeding outputs back to the input turns a shift register into a counter. A ring counter recirculates a single 1 and has n states with n flip-flops. A Johnson, or twisted-ring, counter feeds back the inverted last output and cycles through 2n states, such as 000, 100, 110, 111, 011, 001 for three stages. Only one bit changes between neighboring states, so each state can be decoded with a two-input gate with little risk of glitches, and the outputs provide evenly staggered clock phases.

A linear feedback shift register (LFSR) feeds the XOR of selected outputs, called taps, back to the input. With properly chosen taps an n-bit LFSR steps through all 2ⁿ − 1 nonzero states before repeating, a maximal-length sequence that looks random. Built only from flip-flops and XOR gates, LFSRs generate test patterns and compact responses in built-in self-test (BIST), compute cyclic redundancy checks (CRC) and scramble data on communication links. Their output is fully predictable from a few bits, so they are not suitable for cryptographic randomness.

faq.q: What is a shift register used for?
faq.a: Shift registers are used for converting between serial and parallel data, building delay lines and counters, generating pseudo-random sequences as LFSRs, and forming the scan chains used to test chips.

faq.q: How many states does a Johnson counter have?
faq.a: A Johnson counter built from n flip-flops cycles through 2n states, twice as many as a ring counter with the same number of flip-flops.

faq.q: Why must a shift register in Verilog use nonblocking assignments?
faq.a: With blocking assignments each stage is updated immediately, so the next stage receives the new value in the same clock and the chain collapses to a single stage; nonblocking assignments make every stage take the value from before the edge.

全加算器.desc: A circuit that adds two bits plus a carry-in from the lower digit and outputs a sum and a carry-out. A version without carry-in is a half adder. Chaining full adders makes a multi-bit adder.

about.p: A full adder adds three one-bit inputs, A, B and a carry-in Cin, and produces a sum S and a carry-out Cout whose combined value equals the number of inputs that are 1. The sum is the parity of the inputs, S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin, and the carry is their majority, Cout = AB + BC + CA.
