The usable window is only a few volts in every case, so the spacing between states shrinks rapidly as N grows. Multi-level cells therefore need finely stepped program-and-verify sequences and several read references, making them slower, and their narrow margins tolerate less degradation. In exchange they store two to four times more data on the same cells, lowering cost per bit, which is why TLC dominates mainstream SSDs.

Each program or erase drives electrons through the tunnel oxide at fields around 10 MV/cm. Over many cycles some charge becomes trapped and new defects form, narrowing the Vt window and enabling stress-induced leakage current (SILC), which lets stored charge escape. SLC's wide gap absorbs much more of this damage before reads fail. Typical endurance is about 50,000–100,000 program/erase cycles for SLC, several thousand to 10,000 for MLC, a few thousand for TLC and roughly 1,000 for QLC. SLC also retains data better and copes with higher temperatures.

Native SLC NAND appears in industrial, automotive and embedded systems that need high endurance and retention more than capacity, and low-latency SLC devices serve some roles between DRAM and conventional NAND. More commonly, consumer TLC and QLC SSDs run part of their free space in SLC mode, often called pseudo-SLC or an SLC cache. Writes land there quickly and are later folded into denser storage during idle time. When a long transfer fills the cache, speed drops to the slower native TLC or QLC rate, which is why large copies can slow midway.

faq.q: Is SLC better than TLC?
faq.a: SLC is faster, more durable and more reliable, but it stores one third as much data per cell, so it costs much more per gigabyte. TLC is the better value for typical consumer and data-center use.

faq.q: How many write cycles does SLC NAND last?
faq.a: Typical SLC NAND is rated for roughly 50,000 to 100,000 program/erase cycles per block, an order of magnitude or more beyond TLC. Drive-level endurance also depends on wear leveling and spare area.

faq.q: What is an SLC cache in an SSD?
faq.a: It is a region of TLC or QLC flash temporarily operated with one bit per cell so incoming writes complete quickly. Data is later rewritten into the denser format, and once the cache is full, writes slow to the native speed.

TLC(トリプルレベルセル).desc: A flash format that stores three bits per cell, distinguishing eight threshold-voltage states. It lowers cost per bit but reduces endurance. Four bits per cell is QLC.

about.p: A flash cell stores data as the threshold voltage of its transistor, set by how much charge sits in the floating gate or charge-trap layer. Triple-level cell (TLC) flash programs each cell to one of eight threshold-voltage windows, encoding three bits, and reading a cell requires comparing it against seven reference voltages. The three bits are mapped to separate logical pages on the same word line, often called lower, middle and upper pages. Adjacent states are assigned Gray-coded patterns that differ in only one bit, so the common error of reading a neighboring state corrupts just one bit.

about.h: Why more bits cost endurance and speed
about.p: Squeezing eight states into the same voltage window leaves narrow gaps between them. Programming must therefore proceed in small incremental pulses, each followed by a verify read, which makes TLC writes slower than single-level cell (SLC) writes. Each program and erase also drives electrons through the tunnel oxide at high field, gradually trapping charge and broadening distributions until neighbors overlap. Typical endurance is about 100,000 cycles for SLC, several thousand to 10,000 for MLC, a few thousand for TLC and about 1,000 for QLC; data retention also suffers as gaps narrow.

Controllers hide TLC's weaknesses. An SLC cache runs part of the free space in one-bit mode so incoming writes land quickly, then migrates data to TLC blocks when the drive is idle; sustained writes that overflow the cache drop to the slower native speed. Strong error-correcting codes recover from bit errors that grow with wear, wear leveling spreads erases evenly across blocks, and spare area gives garbage collection room to work. Drive endurance is rated as total bytes written (TBW) or drive writes per day (DWPD) rather than raw cell cycles.

about.h: TLC vs. SLC, MLC and QLC
about.p: Bits per cell trade density against robustness: SLC stores one bit, MLC two, TLC three and quad-level cell (QLC) four. For the same number of cells, TLC holds three times the data of SLC, which is why it has become the mainstream choice for SSDs, usually built in 3D NAND with cells stacked in many layers. QLC pushes cost per bit lower for read-heavy, high-capacity storage, while SLC and SLC-mode operation remain in industrial and automotive parts that need maximum endurance and temperature tolerance.

faq.q: How many voltage states does TLC flash use?
faq.a: Eight threshold-voltage states, which encode three bits per cell and require seven reference levels to read.

faq.q: How many write cycles can TLC NAND endure?
faq.a: Typically a few thousand program/erase cycles, compared with roughly 100,000 for SLC and around 1,000 for QLC.

faq.q: Why does a TLC SSD slow down during long file copies?
faq.a: Writes first go to a fast SLC-mode cache; once a long transfer fills it, the drive must write directly in TLC mode, which is much slower.

NVMe.desc: An interface standard for fast access to SSDs connected over PCI Express. It processes many commands in parallel and has lower latency than SATA, which was designed for HDDs.

about.h: Why SSDs needed a new interface
about.p: SATA SSDs use AHCI, a host interface designed for hard disks: one command queue holding up to 32 commands, behind a link that tops out around 600 MB/s. Flash memory can service many requests in parallel, so this became the bottleneck. NVMe (NVM Express) is a protocol designed for non-volatile memory attached directly to PCI Express. It supports up to 64K I/O queues, each up to 64K commands deep, uses a compact command set, and lets each CPU core own its own queues, cutting software overhead and lock contention.

NVMe queues are rings in host memory. To issue a read or write, the driver places a 64-byte command in a submission queue and writes the new tail position to a doorbell register on the device. The controller fetches commands by DMA, moves the data directly to or from host memory, and writes a 16-byte entry to the paired completion queue, typically signaling the host with an MSI-X interrupt. The host then updates the completion queue's head doorbell. Host and device advance independently, so many transfers are in flight at once.

Because NVMe rides on PCIe, its bandwidth follows the link generation and lane count: about 7 GB/s for PCIe 4.0 x4 drives and over 10 GB/s with PCIe 5.0 x4. Protocol latency is a few microseconds, small compared with flash read times of tens of microseconds. NVMe drives come as compact M.2 cards, 2.5-inch U.2 drives and add-in cards. Note that M.2 is only a connector: an M.2 slot may carry SATA or PCIe, so an M.2 SSD is not necessarily NVMe. NVMe over Fabrics extends the protocol across networks.

Besides reads and writes, NVMe defines administrative commands for creating queues, identifying the controller, managing namespaces and updating firmware. The Deallocate operation, part of the Dataset Management command, is the NVMe equivalent of ATA TRIM: it tells the SSD which logical blocks no longer hold useful data, so garbage collection can erase them without copying. This reduces write amplification, which improves sustained write performance and extends flash endurance.

faq.q: What does NVMe stand for?
faq.a: NVMe stands for Non-Volatile Memory Express, also written NVM Express. It is a host interface and command protocol for accessing SSDs and other non-volatile memory over PCI Express.

faq.q: What is the difference between an NVMe SSD and a SATA SSD?
faq.a: A SATA SSD uses the AHCI protocol with a single 32-command queue and a link limited to about 600 MB/s. An NVMe SSD connects over PCIe with thousands of parallel queues, giving several to more than ten gigabytes per second and lower software latency.

faq.q: Does NVMe support TRIM?
faq.a: Yes. NVMe provides the same function through the Deallocate attribute of the Dataset Management command, which operating systems issue when files are deleted.

STT-MRAM.desc: MRAM that writes by flipping the magnetization of the MTJ's free layer using the spin-transfer torque of a spin-polarized current. It is in volume production as embedded non-volatile memory.

about.p: Each bit is a magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ): two ferromagnetic layers, typically CoFeB, separated by an MgO tunnel barrier about a nanometer thick. The reference layer's magnetization is fixed, while the free layer's can point either way. When the two are parallel, electrons tunnel easily and resistance is low; when antiparallel, resistance is higher, and the relative difference is the tunnel magnetoresistance (TMR) ratio. A cell usually pairs one access transistor with one MTJ, built in the back-end interconnect layers, and is read by comparing its resistance with a reference.

Electrons flowing from the reference layer into the free layer are spin-polarized by the reference layer, and they transfer angular momentum to the free layer, pulling its magnetization parallel. Reversing the current direction drives it antiparallel, because electrons whose spin opposes the reference layer are reflected back into the free layer, so the access transistor must pass current both ways. Earlier MRAM switched bits with magnetic fields from nearby write lines, and the needed current grew as cells shrank. With spin-transfer torque, the write current scales down roughly with junction area, which is why the approach became mainstream.

Retention depends on the energy barrier between the two magnetization states relative to thermal energy, kT. In-plane MTJs rely on an elongated cell shape for that barrier, which weakens as cells shrink. Perpendicular MTJs use the perpendicular magnetic anisotropy that arises at the CoFeB/MgO interface, so even small round cells stay thermally stable while switching at lower current. There is still a trade-off: a higher barrier gives longer retention but generally needs more write current, so devices are tuned differently for code storage and for cache-like use.

Thermal fluctuation makes switching stochastic, so a pulse of a given current and width occasionally fails to flip the bit. Raising current lowers this write error rate but stresses the thin MgO barrier toward breakdown, so designs combine current and pulse-width margins, verify-and-rewrite and error-correcting code (ECC). Reading also passes current through the junction, which exerts torque, so read current must stay well below the switching current to avoid read disturb, yet large enough for a fast, reliable sense.

faq.q: How is data read in STT-MRAM?
faq.a: A small current is passed through the MTJ and its resistance is compared with a reference: parallel magnetization gives low resistance and antiparallel gives high resistance. The read current is kept well below the write current to avoid flipping the bit.

faq.q: Why do STT-MRAM cells use perpendicular MTJs?
faq.a: Perpendicular anisotropy from the CoFeB/MgO interface keeps small, round cells thermally stable without relying on cell shape, and it allows lower switching current. In-plane cells lose stability as they shrink.

faq.q: Is STT-MRAM non-volatile?
faq.a: Yes. Data is stored as the magnetization direction of the free layer, which is retained without power, so no refresh is needed as it is in DRAM.

SOT-MRAM.desc: MRAM that flips magnetization by spin-orbit torque from a current in a heavy-metal layer. The write and read current paths are separate, giving fast, durable writes.

カルコゲナイド.desc: A compound containing group 16 elements such as sulfur, selenium or tellurium. It is used as the recording material of phase-change memory (such as GST) and in selectors (OTS) that switch on abruptly above a threshold voltage.

フォーミング.desc: An initialization step for ReRAM in which a relatively high voltage is first applied after fabrication to create the conductive filament that later switches resistance.

クロスポイント型メモリ.desc: Memory with a storage element at each intersection of row and column lines. It is very dense, but a selector is placed in series with each element to stop current sneaking through unselected cells.

ストレージクラスメモリ.desc: Non-volatile memory intended to bridge the gap in speed, capacity and cost between DRAM and NAND flash. Products based on 3D XPoint were the best-known example.

3D XPoint.desc: Cross-point non-volatile memory jointly developed by Intel and Micron. It stacked phase-change material with OTS selectors and was sold as Optane, but the business was wound down in 2022.

FeFET(強誘電体トランジスタ).desc: A transistor with a ferroelectric gate insulator. Its threshold voltage depends on the polarization direction, so a single transistor can store data non-volatilely and be read non-destructively.

TMR比.desc: In an MTJ, the difference between the resistances in the parallel and antiparallel states divided by the parallel-state resistance. The larger it is, the easier it is to tell 0 from 1; MgO barriers give large values.

インメモリコンピューティング.desc: Performing computations such as multiply-accumulate inside the memory array to cut data movement between memory and processor. Research is under way on using resistive elements and the like for AI inference.

スーパースカラ.desc: A processor design that issues and executes several instructions per clock cycle. It has multiple execution units and processes independent instructions in parallel.

about.p: A superscalar processor fetches and decodes several instructions per clock, checks which of them depend on one another, and dispatches the independent ones to multiple execution units such as integer ALUs, load/store units, floating-point units and branch units. Its throughput can therefore exceed one instruction per clock, meaning instructions per clock (IPC) above 1 or clocks per instruction (CPI) below 1. A 2 GHz core averaging a CPI of 0.5 executes 4 billion instructions per second. Recent high-performance cores are roughly 6 to 10 instructions wide.

Pipelining overlaps the stages of successive instructions and at best completes one per clock; a superscalar core effectively runs several pipelines side by side. Very long instruction word (VLIW) machines also execute several operations per cycle, but the compiler finds the parallelism and packs it into each instruction, whereas a superscalar core finds it in hardware at run time, so existing binaries benefit without recompilation. Superscalar issue can be in-order or, in most high-performance cores, combined with out-of-order execution and register renaming.

Real programs offer limited instruction-level parallelism: data dependencies, branches and cache misses stall issue slots, so branch prediction, out-of-order windows and large caches are needed to keep wide machines busy. The hardware cost also rises steeply. Dependency checks and result-forwarding paths among simultaneously issued instructions grow roughly with the square of the width, and register files need more ports. Beyond a point, each extra slot adds little IPC for considerable area, power and timing difficulty.

Issuing many instructions per cycle requires decoding many per cycle. Fixed-length instruction sets make this easy because instruction boundaries are known in advance. Variable-length sets such as x86 must first find the boundaries, then split complex instructions into simpler micro-operations; many cores keep a micro-op cache so frequently executed code can skip decoding. Superscalar execution is also distinct from multicore and SIMD, which exploit parallelism across threads and across data elements rather than among neighboring instructions.

faq.q: What is the difference between superscalar and pipelined processors?
faq.a: A pipelined processor overlaps the stages of consecutive instructions and completes at most about one per clock. A superscalar processor has multiple pipelines and execution units, so it can issue and complete several instructions per clock.

faq.q: What is IPC in a CPU?
faq.a: IPC means instructions per clock, the average number of instructions completed per cycle and the inverse of CPI. Performance is proportional to IPC times clock frequency for a given instruction count.

faq.q: Is superscalar the same as multicore?
faq.a: No. Superscalar execution runs several instructions from one thread in parallel inside a single core, while multicore puts several cores on a chip to run separate threads.

アウトオブオーダー実行.desc: Executing instructions as soon as their dependencies allow, in a different order from the program, to improve performance. Results are committed in program order through a reorder buffer.

about.p: The front end still fetches and decodes instructions in program order. Each instruction is then renamed, given an entry in the reorder buffer (ROB) and placed in an issue queue. Scheduling logic watches for instructions whose source operands are ready and sends them to free execution units, regardless of their position in the program. An instruction waiting for a slow load sits aside while later, independent instructions run. Results are held until the ROB retires instructions in their original order, so software sees exactly the behavior of a sequential machine. The window spans hundreds of instructions in high-performance cores.

Programs reuse a small set of architectural registers, which creates false dependences: a later write must not overtake an earlier read or write of the same register. Register renaming maps each new value to a fresh physical register, leaving only true data dependences, where an instruction actually needs a value computed by another. In-order commit through the ROB gives precise exceptions and lets the core execute past predicted branches, discarding wrong-path work on a misprediction. ISA details matter here; RV64I sign-extends lw results into the full register precisely so the upper bits never depend on the register's previous value.

The biggest payoff comes during cache misses. An in-order core stalls behind a missing load; an out-of-order core keeps finding independent work and can issue further loads whose misses overlap with the first. That requires a non-blocking cache, which tracks outstanding misses in miss status holding registers (MSHRs) and keeps serving hits meanwhile. The number of misses and the latency of each are unchanged, but overlapping them hides much of the cost. Together with superscalar issue, branch prediction and large caches, this raises IPC (instructions per clock), and performance scales with IPC times frequency.

about.h: Out-of-order vs. superscalar, and the cost
about.p: Superscalar describes width, issuing several instructions per cycle; out-of-order describes the order in which they execute. A core can be in-order superscalar, and recent high-performance cores combine both at roughly 6–10 instructions wide. The cost is large: dependency checking grows roughly with the square of width, and renaming tables, wakeup logic and the ROB add area and energy to every instruction. That is why efficiency cores in phone SoCs are smaller and simpler, and why GPUs spend that silicon on many simple arithmetic units for throughput instead.

faq.q: What is the difference between out-of-order execution and superscalar?
faq.a: Superscalar means issuing multiple instructions per clock; out-of-order means executing them in an order other than program order when dependences allow. The two are independent ideas that high-performance cores usually combine.

faq.q: Why do out-of-order CPUs need a reorder buffer?
faq.a: Instructions finish out of order, but the architectural state must update in program order so exceptions are precise and mispredicted work can be discarded. The reorder buffer holds results until each instruction can retire in order.

faq.q: Does out-of-order execution reduce cache misses?
faq.a: No. It hides miss latency by doing independent work, including issuing other misses in parallel, while the miss is serviced; the number of misses stays the same.

TLB(変換索引バッファ).desc: A small cache that holds recent virtual-to-physical address translations. It avoids walking the page tables in memory on every access, speeding up address translation.

about.p: On every fetch, load and store, the memory management unit (MMU) splits the virtual address into a virtual page number and a page offset; with 4 KB pages the low 12 bits are the offset and pass through untranslated. On a TLB hit, the stored physical page number is joined to the offset and permissions are checked in the same step. On a miss, a page-table walk reads the tables in memory, up to four levels for 48-bit addresses with 4 KB pages, and refills the entry. A page fault occurs only if the page-table entry is invalid or forbids the access.

TLB reach is entries times page size: 64 entries of 4 KB cover only 256 KB, while the same 64 entries holding 2 MB huge pages cover 128 MB. Because TLBs hold only tens to thousands of entries, programs with large or scattered working sets, such as databases and virtual machines, can spend a noticeable share of time walking page tables. Remedies include huge pages, a larger second-level TLB behind small first-level ones, keeping page-table entries in the data caches, and better locality.

about.h: TLB vs. page table vs. data cache
about.p: The page table is the authoritative mapping, built by the operating system per process and stored in memory; the TLB caches recently used entries from it, so it holds translations, not data. Data caches are separate but cooperate closely: many L1 caches are virtually indexed and physically tagged (VIPT), selecting the set with untranslated offset bits so the set read and TLB lookup run in parallel, then comparing the physical tag. A cache miss is handled in hardware, whereas a page fault is an exception serviced by the OS.

Processes reuse the same virtual addresses, so stale translations must not survive an address-space change. Without tags the TLB is flushed on every switch, causing a burst of misses; tagging entries with an address space identifier (ASID) lets them be reused when a process returns. Mapping the kernel into every address space means system calls need no switch. When the OS changes a mapping, it must invalidate matching entries on every core that may hold them. With nested paging and four-level tables in both guest and host, one miss can cost up to 24 memory accesses.

faq.q: What happens on a TLB miss?
faq.a: The MMU (or an OS handler on some architectures) walks the page tables in memory to find the translation, installs it in the TLB and retries the access. If the page-table entry is invalid or the access is not allowed, a page fault is raised instead and the OS takes over.

faq.q: How do you calculate TLB reach?
faq.a: Multiply the number of TLB entries by the page size. For example, 64 entries × 4 KB = 256 KB, while 64 entries × 2 MB = 128 MB, which is why huge pages reduce TLB misses.

faq.q: Is the TLB part of the CPU cache?
faq.a: It is a cache, but of address translations rather than data. It sits beside the L1 caches and is usually looked up in parallel with them, but it never holds the memory contents themselves.

SIMD.desc: Short for single instruction, multiple data: one instruction performs the same operation on several data elements at once. It speeds up image processing and AI calculations.

about.p: A SIMD (single instruction, multiple data) unit treats a wide register as a set of independent lanes. A 128-bit register holds four 32-bit values, and a 512-bit register holds sixteen; one add instruction adds all lanes in parallel. Instruction-set extensions such as x86 SSE and AVX and Arm NEON and SVE provide integer and floating-point lane operations, along with loads, shuffles and comparisons. In Flynn's taxonomy SIMD sits beside SISD, an ordinary sequential processor, and MIMD, multiple cores running independent instruction streams. Image filters, video codecs and matrix math typically speed up several-fold or more.

Compilers auto-vectorize loops that apply the same operation to each array element. The key condition is no loop-carried dependence: in a[i] = a[i-1] + b[i], each element needs the previous result, so lanes cannot run simultaneously. Data should be contiguous, and possible pointer overlap (aliasing) can make the compiler give up. A trip count unknown at compile time is not a barrier; the vector loop handles full chunks and a short remainder loop handles the rest. Media code also uses saturating arithmetic, where 8-bit signed 127 + 1 clamps to 127 instead of wrapping to −128.

An array of structures (AoS) stores each record's fields together, such as x, y, z and mass. A loop that reads only x then wastes most of each cache line and needs gather or shuffle work to fill vector lanes. A structure of arrays (SoA) keeps all x values contiguous, so every fetched line is fully used, memory traffic can drop sharply, and one vector load fills the lanes directly. The same layout lets adjacent GPU threads read adjacent addresses, which coalesces their memory accesses.

With CPU SIMD, the programmer or compiler explicitly uses fixed-width vector instructions, so code is written with the vector width in mind. GPU SIMT (single instruction, multiple threads) lets the programmer write ordinary code for one thread; the hardware groups threads, commonly 32, to run in lockstep on shared instruction issue. When threads in a group branch differently, the hardware executes each path in turn with inactive threads masked, so code still works but efficiency drops. Underneath, both rely on the same principle of amortizing one instruction over many data elements.

faq.q: What does SIMD stand for and what does it do?
faq.a: Single instruction, multiple data: one instruction operates on several data elements packed into a wide register, such as four 32-bit numbers in a 128-bit register.

faq.q: Why does my loop not auto-vectorize?
faq.a: Common reasons are a loop-carried dependence where an iteration needs the previous one's result, non-contiguous memory access, or possible pointer aliasing that the compiler cannot rule out.

faq.q: What is the difference between SIMD and SIMT?
faq.a: SIMD uses explicit fixed-width vector instructions on a CPU. SIMT, used by GPUs, runs scalar per-thread code on groups of threads in lockstep, with hardware handling branch divergence.

DMA(ダイレクトメモリアクセス).desc: A mechanism that transfers data directly between peripherals and memory without going through the CPU, so the CPU can do other work during large transfers.

about.p: In programmed I/O the CPU moves every word itself with load and store instructions. With direct memory access (DMA), the CPU instead programs a DMA controller, or the device's own DMA engine, with a source, a destination, a length and a trigger, then goes back to other work. The controller takes control of the bus, moves the data and raises a completion interrupt. In a microcontroller, for example, a timer can trigger an ADC conversion at fixed intervals and DMA can store each result into an array, waking the CPU only when the buffer is full.

Network cards and NVMe SSDs use descriptor rings: circular tables in main memory whose entries give a buffer address and length. The CPU fills free descriptors and writes once to a device register, often called a doorbell, to say how far it has written. The device reads the descriptors by DMA, performs the transfers itself and marks finished entries complete. CPU and device thus advance many transfers without waiting for each other, and lists of scattered buffers can be handled in one operation, known as scatter-gather.

DMA bypasses the CPU caches, so the two views of memory can disagree. Where hardware does not keep them coherent, the driver writes dirty cache lines back to memory before a device reads a buffer, and invalidates the cached range before the CPU reads data a device has written, so stale values are not used. The operating system may also move or swap out ordinary pages at any time, so buffers for DMA are pinned in place; pinned host memory lets a GPU transfer data without an intermediate copy and overlap transfers with computation.

Because DMA writes memory directly, a faulty or malicious device could overwrite kernel data or read encryption keys, a particular concern for devices attached through fast external ports. An IOMMU (input-output memory management unit) does for devices what the MMU does for the CPU: it translates the addresses devices use into physical addresses and blocks access outside the regions the operating system has granted. It also lets scattered physical pages appear contiguous to a device and makes it safe to assign a device directly to a virtual machine.

faq.q: What does DMA stand for?
faq.a: DMA stands for direct memory access, a mechanism that lets peripherals transfer data to and from main memory without the CPU copying each word, so the CPU can do other work during the transfer.

faq.q: What is the difference between DMA and programmed I/O?
faq.a: In programmed I/O the CPU reads or writes every data word to the device itself. With DMA the CPU only sets up the transfer and is notified when it finishes, which saves CPU time for large or frequent transfers.

faq.q: Why must the cache be invalidated after a DMA transfer into memory?
faq.a: On systems without hardware cache coherence, the CPU's cache may still hold old copies of that memory range. Invalidating it forces the CPU to read the new data the device wrote.

割り込み.desc: A CPU mechanism that temporarily suspends the current task to handle a request, for example from an external device, and then returns to the original task.

about.h: What happens when an interrupt is taken
about.p: When a device, timer or other source raises an interrupt and it is enabled, the CPU saves the address of the next instruction together with state such as the privilege mode and interrupt-enable bit in dedicated registers. It obtains a vector number for the cause, reads the handler's start address from the interrupt vector table set up by the OS, and jumps there. The handler saves the registers it uses, services the device, clears the interrupt source, restores state, and returns with a special instruction such as RISC-V mret or sret, which restores the mode and return address atomically.

Interrupts are asynchronous: a timer tick or network packet arrives regardless of which instruction is running. Exceptions such as page faults, division by zero or a deliberate system call (RISC-V ecall) are synchronous, caused by a specific instruction. Polling, in which the CPU repeatedly reads device status, is the alternative to interrupts. Interrupts are better when events are rare or the CPU should sleep, but each costs state saving and a jump, so at very high event rates, as in fast networking, batched polling can be more efficient.

An interrupt controller arbitrates simultaneous requests, often with a priority encoder, and with nesting a higher-priority interrupt can preempt a lower-priority handler, as in the Arm Cortex-M NVIC. Software can mask interrupts, but a non-maskable interrupt (NMI) is reserved for serious events such as uncorrectable memory errors or watchdog timeouts. Worst-case interrupt latency is set mostly by the longest section that runs with interrupts disabled, so operating systems split handling into a short urgent part and deferred work done later with interrupts enabled. PCI Express devices signal interrupts by memory writes (MSI) instead of dedicated wires.

Handlers should be short: no printf or waiting loops, just moving data to a buffer or setting a flag for the main loop. Variables shared with a handler must be declared volatile, or the compiler may read them only once. Read-modify-write updates like reg |= mask can lose a bit changed by a handler in between, and an 8-bit microcontroller reading a 32-bit counter can see half-updated bytes; disabling interrupts briefly fixes both. A periodic timer interrupt, for example 16 MHz divided by 16 counting to 1000 for 1 ms, provides the system tick.

faq.q: What is the difference between an interrupt and an exception?
faq.a: An interrupt is asynchronous and comes from outside the instruction stream, such as a timer or I/O device. An exception is synchronous, triggered by executing a particular instruction, such as a page fault, illegal instruction or system call.

faq.q: What is an interrupt vector table?
faq.a: It is a table, set up by the OS or firmware, that maps each interrupt or exception number to the start address of its handler. The CPU uses it to jump to the right routine for each cause.

faq.q: Why should an interrupt handler be kept short?
faq.a: While a handler runs, interrupts of the same or lower priority are usually held off and the main program is stalled, so a long handler increases latency for everything else. Heavy work is deferred to a task or main loop that runs with interrupts enabled.

キャッシュコヒーレンシ.desc: In a multicore CPU, the mechanism that keeps copies of the same address in different cores' caches consistent, for example by invalidating other copies when one core writes.

DVFS(動的電圧・周波数制御).desc: Changing operating frequency and supply voltage dynamically according to load. Since dynamic power scales with the square of voltage, lowering voltage during light loads saves a lot of power.

about.p: A CMOS chip's dynamic power is P = αCV²f, where α is switching activity, C the switched capacitance, V the supply voltage and f the clock frequency. A circuit only meets timing at a given frequency if the supply is high enough, so DVFS uses a table of valid voltage-frequency pairs, called operating points or P-states. A governor in the operating system or in on-chip power-management firmware watches load and temperature and picks a point. When speeding up, the voltage is raised first and the clock second; when slowing down, the clock drops first and the voltage follows, so the logic never runs too fast for its supply.

about.h: Why voltage is the big lever
about.p: Lowering frequency alone reduces power linearly but leaves the energy per operation, proportional to CV², unchanged, because the same work simply takes longer. Lowering voltage is what saves energy. If voltage can scale in proportion to frequency, halving both cuts dynamic power to one-eighth and energy for a fixed task to one-quarter. Even a modest 10% voltage reduction removes about 19% of dynamic power. In practice voltage cannot fall in proportion forever, so real savings are smaller than this ideal cubic picture.

Two effects bound DVFS. First, there is a minimum workable voltage: as the supply approaches the transistor threshold, speed collapses and SRAM cells become unreliable, so the bottom of the voltage range is fixed well above zero. Second, leakage power flows for as long as the circuit is powered, so running slowly for longer accumulates leakage energy. When leakage is significant it can be better to race to idle: finish the work at a high operating point, then enter a deep sleep state (C-state) or power-gate the block entirely.

DVFS runs in essentially every smartphone SoC, laptop CPU, server processor and GPU. Each voltage domain, which may be a single core or a cluster of cores, needs its own adjustable supply, usually provided by a power management IC (PMIC) or on-chip regulators that change output on command from the SoC. The same mechanism implements thermal throttling, where operating points are lowered to keep junction temperature within limits, and short boost modes, where they are raised while thermal and current headroom allow.

faq.q: Does lowering CPU frequency alone save energy?
faq.a: It lowers power but not dynamic energy per task, because each operation still costs about CV² and the work just takes longer; leakage energy can even rise. The energy savings come from the voltage reduction that a lower frequency makes possible.

faq.q: What is the difference between P-states and C-states?
faq.a: P-states are voltage-frequency operating points used while the processor is executing, which is what DVFS selects. C-states are idle states of increasing depth, from stopping the clock to removing power, used when there is no work.

faq.q: What is the difference between DVFS and clock gating?
faq.a: Clock gating stops the clock to idle logic so it stops switching, but the supply voltage and leakage remain. DVFS changes the voltage and frequency of a whole domain that is still doing work.

TDP(熱設計電力).desc: A guide to the heat a CPU or similar chip generates under a typical heavy load. Cooling systems are designed around it.

IPC.desc: Short for instructions per cycle: the number of instructions executed per clock. It expresses design efficiency; performance is roughly IPC times clock frequency. Its reciprocal is CPI.

about.p: Program run time equals instruction count times cycles per instruction (CPI) divided by clock frequency. IPC, instructions per cycle, is the reciprocal of CPI, so for a given program performance is proportional to IPC times frequency. A 3 GHz core has a cycle time of about 0.33 ns, but two 3 GHz processors can differ widely in speed because their IPC differs. IPC comparisons only make sense for the same program and instruction set, because different instruction sets need different numbers of instructions for the same work.

A simple pipeline aims for one instruction per cycle. Superscalar cores issue several independent instructions per cycle, with recent high-performance designs about 6 to 10 wide. Out-of-order execution keeps those units busy by running later independent instructions while earlier ones wait, branch prediction avoids pipeline flushes, and large caches with prefetching hide memory latency. Width cannot grow freely: dependency-checking logic grows roughly with the square of the issue width, and real programs offer limited instruction-level parallelism, so achieved IPC stays well below the peak width.

The biggest losses are stalls. A last-level cache miss that goes to DRAM can cost hundreds of cycles, a branch misprediction discards work already in a deep pipeline, and chains of dependent instructions serialize execution. An IPC far below 1 on a wide core, such as 0.3, usually means the core spends most of its time waiting on memory; restructuring data for locality, reordering loops or blocking for cache reuse typically help more than any compiler flag. Raising clock frequency does not shorten memory latency in nanoseconds, so memory-bound code sees its IPC fall as frequency rises.

Processors include a performance monitoring unit (PMU) with hardware counters for cycles, retired instructions, cache misses at each level, TLB misses and branch mispredictions. Dividing retired instructions by cycles gives IPC directly. Tools such as Linux perf read these counters while a program runs, and comparing IPC with miss and misprediction rates shows whether time is going to memory, branches or computation. Because modern CPUs constantly change frequency with load and temperature, counting cycles rather than wall-clock time gives a cleaner view of microarchitectural efficiency.

faq.q: Is a higher clock speed or a higher IPC better?
faq.a: Performance depends on their product, so neither alone decides speed. A lower-clocked core with much higher IPC can outperform a faster-clocked one on the same program.

faq.q: How do I measure the IPC of my program?
faq.a: Use hardware performance counters, for example with Linux perf, to count retired instructions and cycles; IPC is instructions divided by cycles. Cache-miss and branch-miss counts then help explain a low value.

faq.q: What does a low IPC mean?
faq.a: It means the core is idle for many cycles, most often waiting for data from memory after cache misses, or recovering from branch mispredictions and long dependency chains.

アムダールの法則.desc: The law that when only part of a program is parallelized, overall speedup is limited by the part that cannot be. For example, parallelizing 90% gives at most a 10x speedup.

about.p: Amdahl's law gives the speedup of a program whose fraction p can be parallelized across N processors as S = 1 / ((1 − p) + p/N). As N grows without limit, the p/N term vanishes and the speedup approaches 1 / (1 − p). With p = 0.9 that ceiling is 10×, and with ten processors the result is only about 5.3×, so half the hardware is effectively wasted. The serial fraction, however small it looks, ends up dominating the run time once the parallel part has been divided finely enough.

about.h: Same law, any kind of speedup
about.p: The law applies to any partial improvement, not just to adding cores. If a section taking 50% of the run time is made 4× faster, the new time is 0.5 + 0.5/4 = 0.625 of the original, an overall speedup of 1.6×, and no amount of further optimization of that section can exceed 2×. Making a part that takes 1% of the time infinitely fast gains only about 1%. This is the quantitative basis of "make the common case fast" and the reason to profile a program before optimizing it.

Amdahl's law assumes a fixed problem size, which corresponds to strong scaling: the same job is split across more processors. Gustafson's law assumes the opposite: with more processors, people solve a larger problem in the same time, for example a finer simulation grid. The parallel work grows with the problem while the serial part stays roughly constant, so the serial fraction shrinks and speedup grows almost in proportion to the processor count. This is weak scaling. Neither law is wrong; they answer different questions about how a workload is used.

about.h: Why real programs do worse than the formula
about.p: Amdahl's law already assumes the parallel part scales perfectly, so measured speedups are usually lower still. Threads wait at locks and barriers, shared data and false sharing make cache lines bounce between cores, uneven work leaves some cores idle, and many threads can saturate memory bandwidth. Communication and synchronization overhead can even grow with N, so adding cores may eventually slow a program down. The cleanest scaling comes when each thread works mostly on private data, with little communication or waiting.

faq.q: How do you calculate speedup with Amdahl's law?
faq.a: Divide 1 by the new relative run time: S = 1 / ((1 − p) + p/s), where p is the fraction of time affected and s is how much faster that part becomes (s = N for N processors). For p = 0.5 and s = 4 this gives 1 / 0.625 = 1.6×.

faq.q: What is the maximum speedup if 95% of a program is parallel?
faq.a: The limit is 1 / (1 − 0.95) = 20×, no matter how many processors are used. Reaching even close to that limit requires very large processor counts and near-perfect parallel efficiency.

faq.q: What is the difference between Amdahl's law and Gustafson's law?
faq.a: Amdahl's law fixes the problem size and shows that the serial part caps speedup. Gustafson's law lets the problem grow with the number of processors, so the serial fraction shrinks and near-linear scaled speedup becomes possible.

仮想記憶.desc: A system in which the OS and hardware map the addresses a program uses (virtual addresses) to physical memory addresses. Each program gets a large, independent address space.

GPU.desc: Short for graphics processing unit: a processor with many simple execution units that processes large amounts of data in parallel. Besides graphics, it is widely used for AI training and inference.

about.p: A GPU contains many streaming multiprocessors (SMs), each a cluster of simple execution units with its own registers and on-chip shared memory. Rather than making one thread fast with large caches and elaborate branch prediction, as a CPU core does, a GPU keeps thousands of threads in flight and switches to another group whenever one is waiting for memory. This hides latency through sheer parallelism and maximizes throughput. Threads are scheduled in fixed-size groups that issue the same instruction together in lockstep, 32 threads called a warp on NVIDIA GPUs, a model called SIMT (single instruction, multiple threads).

CPU SIMD instructions apply one operation to a vector register holding a fixed number of elements, and the programmer or compiler must code for that width. With SIMT the programmer writes ordinary code for a single thread, and the hardware groups threads into warps. Threads may take different branches, but the hardware then runs the paths one after another, wasting lanes. GPUs therefore excel when each element is processed independently with the same operation, and struggle with serial, data-dependent work such as walking a linked list.

Feeding thousands of execution units needs enormous bandwidth. Graphics boards use GDDR memory, with per-pin rates above 20 Gb/s in recent generations, placed around the GPU on short traces. AI accelerators instead place stacked HBM next to the GPU on a silicon interposer (2.5D packaging); each stack has 1,024 data lines, so several stacks deliver several TB/s. Software must cooperate: when adjacent threads read adjacent addresses, accesses coalesce into a few wide transactions, which is why a structure of arrays usually beats an array of structures.

In CUDA and similar frameworks, the CPU launches a kernel, a function that many GPU threads execute at once. One launch forms a grid of blocks, each block containing many threads that run on the same SM and can cooperate through shared memory. Each thread computes its own index to pick a data element, and the guard if (i < n) stops surplus threads in the last block from accessing memory beyond the array. Because blocks run independently, the same program scales across small and large GPUs.

faq.q: What is the difference between a CPU and a GPU?
faq.a: A CPU has a few complex cores optimized to finish individual tasks with low latency, while a GPU has many simple cores optimized for total throughput on highly parallel work. The GPU hides memory latency by switching among thousands of threads instead of relying on large caches.

faq.q: Why are GPUs used for AI?
faq.a: Neural-network training and inference consist mostly of large matrix multiplications that apply the same operations to huge arrays, which maps naturally onto thousands of parallel threads. High-bandwidth memory such as HBM keeps those units supplied with data.

faq.q: What is warp divergence?
faq.a: It happens when threads in the same warp take different branches; the hardware executes each path in turn while the other threads sit idle, reducing efficiency. Keeping branch conditions uniform within a warp avoids it.

NPU(ニューラルプロセッシングユニット).desc: A dedicated circuit for running neural-network inference quickly and at low power. It is built into the SoCs of smartphones and PCs.

about.p: Neural-network inference is dominated by matrix multiplications and convolutions, which break down into enormous numbers of multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations. An NPU packs thousands of MAC units, often arranged as a systolic array or wide matrix engine, into a small area and feeds them from on-chip SRAM buffers through dedicated data-movement engines. Separate units handle activation functions, pooling and normalization. Most mobile NPUs compute in low precision, typically 8-bit integers (INT8) or below, or 16-bit floating point.

about.h: Why it beats a CPU on efficiency
about.p: A general-purpose CPU spends much of its energy on instruction fetch and decode, branch prediction and out-of-order bookkeeping rather than arithmetic. Fetching data from external DRAM costs far more energy than a multiply, so moving data is often the real limit. An NPU removes the general-purpose machinery, keeps weights and activations in local memory so each value is reused many times, and uses narrow arithmetic, since multiplier area and energy grow steeply with bit width. The result is far higher performance per watt for AI work, at the cost of flexibility.

A GPU runs thousands of programmable threads and handles floating-point training and inference flexibly, but it draws much more power. An NPU is narrower in scope and is tuned for inference within the few-watt budget of a phone or laptop SoC. The CPU remains the fallback, so a layer the NPU cannot execute may run far slower on it and force costly data transfers. NPU throughput is quoted in TOPS (trillions of operations per second), a peak figure that depends on precision and sparsity assumptions; real speed depends on memory bandwidth and how well a model maps onto the hardware.

about.h: The software that makes it usable
about.p: An NPU is only as useful as its software stack. Models trained in floating point are quantized to INT8 or lower, either after training or with quantization-aware training, to keep accuracy. AI compilers and inference runtimes then fuse operations, choose memory layouts and tile computations to fit on-chip buffers, and generate kernels for the specific NPU. This on-device inference enables features such as photo enhancement, speech recognition and translation with low latency and without sending data to a server.

faq.q: What is the difference between an NPU and a GPU?
faq.a: A GPU is a flexible, programmable parallel processor suited to both training and inference, usually at higher power. An NPU is a specialized accelerator for low-precision neural-network inference that delivers better energy efficiency but supports fewer kinds of operations.

faq.q: What does TOPS mean for an NPU?
faq.a: TOPS means trillions of operations per second, with one multiply-accumulate usually counted as two operations. It is a peak number tied to a specific precision, so compare TOPS only at the same precision and treat it as an upper bound.

faq.q: Why do NPUs use INT8 instead of floating point?
faq.a: Narrow integer arithmetic needs much smaller, lower-energy multipliers and halves or quarters memory traffic compared with 16- or 32-bit values. Well-quantized models typically lose little accuracy for inference.

マイコン(マイクロコントローラ).desc: A small computer that integrates a CPU, memory and peripherals such as timers and ADCs on one chip. It is embedded in appliances, cars and other equipment to control them. Also called an MCU.

about.p: A microcontroller (MCU) puts a complete small computer on one die: a CPU core, embedded flash for the program, SRAM for working data, and peripherals that connect directly to the outside world. Typical peripherals include timers that generate PWM signals, a successive-approximation (SAR) ADC, general-purpose I/O pins, a watchdog timer and serial interfaces such as UART, SPI, I²C and CAN. Because the program is already stored on chip, an MCU starts running its firmware moments after power is applied, which suits control tasks that must be ready immediately.

A microprocessor or application SoC aims at computing performance: it runs a full operating system from external DRAM and storage and needs supporting chips around it. An MCU aims at cost, size, low power and predictable real-time response, running bare-metal firmware or a small real-time operating system (RTOS) from its own memory. A single car contains dozens to over a hundred MCUs, and appliances and industrial equipment use them for motor control, sensing and user interfaces. Program storage is changing too: embedded flash is hard to integrate at advanced nodes, so MRAM and ReRAM are taking its place.

MCU pins can source only small currents, so loads are driven through interface circuits. A transistor switch needs a base resistor sized from (drive voltage − 0.7 V) divided by the required base current, and power devices need a gate driver that turns a few-milliamp logic signal into amperes of gate current. Without a DAC, an analog voltage can be made by low-pass filtering PWM, giving amplitude × duty cycle. When measuring through a resistor divider, divider resistance and ADC loading must be considered, or the signal buffered.

Automotive MCUs add hardware that detects faults rather than silently misbehaving. A window watchdog resets the system if software kicks it too late or too early. SEC-DED error-correcting code (ECC) corrects single-bit memory errors and flags double-bit errors so software can enter a safe state. Clock monitors compare the main clock against an independent oscillator, and voltage monitors with their own reference detect both under- and overvoltage. Logic and memory built-in self-test (BIST) at power-up uncovers latent faults in the safety circuits themselves before driving begins.

faq.q: What is the difference between a microcontroller and a microprocessor?
faq.a: A microcontroller integrates the CPU, program memory, RAM and I/O peripherals on one chip for self-contained control tasks. A microprocessor is mainly the CPU and relies on external memory and support chips, trading cost and power for computing performance.

faq.q: What does a watchdog timer do in a microcontroller?
faq.a: It must be cleared periodically by healthy software; if a crash or hang lets it expire, it resets the MCU automatically. A window watchdog also treats clears that come too early as faults.

faq.q: How does a microcontroller output an analog voltage without a DAC?
faq.a: It generates a PWM signal and passes it through a low-pass filter, so the output averages to the supply amplitude times the duty cycle. Resolution depends on the timer count range, and ripple trades off against response speed.

SMT(同時マルチスレッディング).desc: A technique in which one CPU core processes instructions from several threads at once, making better use of its execution units. Intel calls it Hyper-Threading.

about.p: A modern out-of-order core can issue several instructions per cycle, but a single thread rarely keeps all its execution units busy because of dependencies, branch mispredictions and cache misses. Simultaneous multithreading (SMT) gives the core a separate architectural state, such as program counter and architectural registers, for each hardware thread, while the threads share execution units, caches, branch predictors and internal buffers. In the same cycle, instructions from different threads can be issued to different units. The operating system sees each hardware thread as a logical processor, typically two per core.

Because the threads compete for the same execution resources, SMT does not double performance the way a second core can. Typical gains range from about 0 to 30 percent. Workloads that stall often, such as those waiting on memory, benefit most: while one thread waits for a cache miss, the other keeps the units busy. Workloads that already saturate the floating-point units or memory bandwidth gain little, and contention in shared caches can even make individual threads slower, which matters for latency-sensitive applications.

about.h: SMT versus other kinds of multithreading
about.p: Coarse-grained multithreading switches to another thread only on a long stall such as a cache miss. Fine-grained multithreading interleaves threads cycle by cycle but issues from only one thread per cycle, an approach common in GPUs and some network processors. SMT goes further by issuing from multiple threads in the same cycle, which suits wide superscalar cores. Multicore, by contrast, duplicates the entire core. Intel brands its two-way SMT as Hyper-Threading, and some server processors support four or eight threads per core.

Two SMT threads share the L1 caches, branch predictor, execution ports and buffers at very fine granularity, so one thread can infer what the other is doing by measuring its own timing. Several side-channel vulnerabilities depend on exactly this arrangement. Systems that run untrusted code from different customers on the same hardware therefore may disable SMT or use core scheduling, which only places threads from the same trust domain on sibling logical processors. Both reduce throughput, so the decision weighs performance against isolation.

faq.q: Is Hyper-Threading the same as SMT?
faq.a: Yes. Hyper-Threading is Intel's brand name for its implementation of simultaneous multithreading, in which each physical core appears to the operating system as two logical processors.

faq.q: Does SMT double CPU performance?
faq.a: No. The two threads share one core's execution units and caches, so typical throughput gains are about 0 to 30 percent depending on the workload, far less than adding a second core.

faq.q: Why do some systems disable SMT?
faq.a: Threads on the same core share caches and execution resources closely enough for one to observe the other through timing side channels. Disabling SMT, or scheduling only mutually trusted threads together, removes that exposure at some cost in throughput.

シストリックアレイ.desc: An arrangement of many multiply-accumulate units in a grid that computes matrix products by passing data to neighboring units step by step. It is used in AI accelerators.

スーパージャンクションMOSFET.desc: A power MOSFET whose drift layer has alternating p-type and n-type pillars. It allows higher drift-layer doping without losing breakdown voltage, achieving on-resistance below the conventional silicon limit.

ボディダイオード.desc: A parasitic diode formed between source and drain by the structure of a power MOSFET. It can serve as the freewheeling diode in an inverter, but its reverse recovery needs attention.

about.h: Where the body diode comes from
about.p: A MOSFET is a four-terminal device: gate, source, drain and body. In a vertical n-channel power MOSFET, the source metal contacts both the n+ source and the p-type body, mainly so the body potential is fixed and the parasitic bipolar transistor formed by source, body and drift region cannot turn on. Shorting body to source leaves the junction between the p body and the n- drift region connected between source and drain: a diode with its anode at the source and cathode at the drain, which conducts when the drain is pulled below the source.

In inverters and motor drives, inductive load current must keep flowing when a switch turns off. During the dead time, when both switches in a half-bridge are off to prevent shoot-through, that current flows through the body diode of the opposite MOSFET, so the body diode serves as the freewheeling diode without an extra part. To reduce conduction loss, the MOSFET channel is usually turned on during reverse conduction, called synchronous rectification, so current flows through the low-resistance channel instead of the diode's forward voltage drop.

The body diode is a bipolar PN junction, so while it conducts, minority carriers are stored in the drift region. When the opposite switch turns on and reverses the voltage, that stored charge must be swept out, producing a reverse current spike that adds switching loss, stresses the switch and causes ringing and electromagnetic interference. In silicon power MOSFETs reverse recovery is relatively slow, so fast-switching designs minimize diode conduction time or add an external fast diode. SiC MOSFET body diodes store far less charge and recover much faster.

SiC brings its own issue. Because of the wide band gap, a SiC body diode has a high forward voltage, typically around 3 V or more, and forward current through it can trigger bipolar degradation: the energy released by electron-hole recombination expands basal-plane dislocations in the crystal into stacking faults, planar defects that impede conduction and raise on-voltage over time. Remedies include epitaxial buffer layers that convert basal-plane dislocations into a harmless type during growth, and integrating Schottky diodes so the body diode does not carry current.

faq.q: Does every MOSFET have a body diode?
faq.a: Any MOSFET has PN junctions between its body and source/drain, but in discrete power MOSFETs the body is tied to the source, so one of those junctions appears as a diode between source and drain. GaN HEMTs have no such PN junction and therefore no body diode, although they can still conduct in reverse through the channel.

faq.q: Can the body diode replace an external freewheeling diode?
faq.a: Often yes, especially with synchronous rectification and SiC MOSFETs. With slower silicon body diodes, fast-switching circuits may add an external fast or Schottky diode to limit reverse recovery losses.

faq.q: Why does a body diode have reverse recovery?
faq.a: It is a bipolar PN junction, so forward conduction stores minority carriers in the drift region, and that charge must be removed before the diode can block voltage, causing a brief reverse current.

ゲートドライバ.desc: A circuit that receives control signals and drives a power device's gate with the right voltage and enough current. Many include isolation or level shifting to drive high-side switches.

ノーマリーオフ.desc: The property of passing no current when the gate voltage is 0 V. It is required of power devices for safety, since current stops even if the drive circuit fails.

DC-DCコンバータ.desc: A circuit that converts one DC voltage into another. Using switches, inductors and capacitors, buck types lower the voltage and boost types raise it.

デッドタイム.desc: A short interval during which both the upper and lower switches of an inverter are off while switching between them. It prevents both from being on at once and shorting the supply.

スナバ回路.desc: A network such as a resistor and capacitor placed across a power device to suppress the voltage spikes (surges) and ringing that occur during switching.

テール電流.desc: Current that keeps flowing like a tail as an IGBT turns off, because stored minority carriers prevent it from dropping to zero immediately. It causes turn-off loss.

about.h: Why an IGBT current trails off
about.p: An insulated-gate bipolar transistor (IGBT) has a p+ collector layer that injects holes into the lightly doped n-drift region while the device conducts. These minority carriers flood the drift region and lower its resistance, an effect called conductivity modulation, which gives the IGBT its low on-state voltage. At turn-off the gate removes the MOS channel and electron supply stops almost at once, but the stored holes cannot vanish instantly. They must recombine or be swept out by the growing electric field, and the collector current decays with them, producing the tail.

The tail flows after the collector-emitter voltage has already risen to the bus voltage, so voltage times current is large during it and it adds directly to the turn-off energy (Eoff). Because this energy is paid every switching cycle, it limits silicon IGBTs to switching frequencies of roughly tens of kHz or less. The tail also grows at higher temperature, since carrier lifetime in silicon increases with temperature. Designers face a trade-off: more stored charge lowers the on-state voltage but lengthens the tail, so conduction loss and switching loss pull in opposite directions.

Lifetime control introduces recombination centers so stored carriers disappear faster; electron irradiation and hydrogen or helium implants can place these defects at chosen depths. Field-stop designs add an n-type buffer layer that lets the drift region be thinner, so less charge is stored, and a lightly injecting collector reduces how many holes enter in the first place. Unipolar devices avoid the problem entirely: silicon MOSFETs and SiC MOSFETs conduct with majority carriers only, so they show no tail current and can switch much faster.

about.h: The other meaning: differential pair tail current
about.p: In analog circuits, tail current means something unrelated: the bias current of the current source tied to the common emitters or sources of a differential pair. The input voltage difference steers this fixed current between the two transistors, so it sets the pair's transconductance, its maximum output current and the slew rate of an amplifier built on it. The output impedance of the tail current source determines how well the pair rejects common-mode signals, which shows up as the common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR).

faq.q: Why do MOSFETs have no tail current?
faq.a: A MOSFET conducts only with majority carriers through its channel, so there is no stored minority-carrier charge to remove when the gate turns it off. An IGBT relies on injected minority carriers for conductivity modulation, and removing them is what creates the tail.

faq.q: Does IGBT tail current increase with temperature?
faq.a: Yes. Carrier lifetime in silicon rises with temperature, so stored charge decays more slowly and turn-off energy is noticeably higher at elevated junction temperatures.

faq.q: What is tail current in a differential amplifier?
faq.a: It is the bias current supplied by the current source at the common node of the differential pair. The input difference splits this current between the two transistors, and its value sets gain, slew rate and output swing limits.

短絡耐量.desc: The time a power device can survive a short circuit, such as both inverter switches turning on at once, without being destroyed. Protection circuits must cut the current within this time.

ソフトスイッチング.desc: Turning a switch on or off when the voltage across it or current through it is nearly zero, as in zero-voltage switching (ZVS). It reduces switching loss and noise.

GaAs(ガリウムヒ素).desc: A III-V compound semiconductor of gallium and arsenic with a direct band gap of about 1.42 eV. Its high electron mobility makes it useful for high-frequency transistors and infrared LEDs and lasers.

about.p: Gallium arsenide is a III-V compound with the zincblende structure, in which gallium and arsenic atoms alternate on a diamond-like lattice. Its band gap of about 1.42 eV is direct, so electrons and holes recombine radiatively without needing a phonon, and the emission wavelength is about 1240/1.42 ≈ 870 nm in the near-infrared. The electron effective mass is only about 0.067 times the free-electron mass, giving an electron mobility around 8,500 cm²/(V·s), roughly six times that of silicon. The wider gap also makes its intrinsic carrier density, about 2×10⁶ cm⁻³, far below silicon's.

High electron mobility and the availability of semi-insulating substrates, which keep parasitic capacitance low, made GaAs a mainstay of RF circuits such as power amplifiers and switches in mobile phones and front ends of satellite receivers. In a GaAs HEMT, an AlGaAs/GaAs heterojunction holds a two-dimensional electron gas separated from its donors (modulation doping), so impurity scattering is low and the transistor amplifies with very little noise. At high fields GaAs electrons transfer into a heavier conduction-band valley and slow down, the effect behind Gunn-diode oscillators.

As a direct-gap material, GaAs is used in infrared LEDs for remote controls and photoelectric sensors and in lasers, including vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers (VCSELs) near 850 nm for face authentication and short-reach optical links. Alloying with aluminum raises the band gap while the lattice constant stays almost the same, so AlGaAs layers stack on GaAs without strain. Such heterostructures confine both carriers and light, the basis of semiconductor lasers. Visible emitters need wider-gap alloys such as GaAsP or AlGaInP, and blue needs GaN-based materials.

Silicon wins for large digital chips: it has an excellent native oxide for MOS gates, cheap large wafers and a mature process base. GaAs lacks a usable native oxide, its wafers are smaller and more expensive, and growing it on silicon creates antiphase boundaries and other defects. GaAs therefore occupies niches where speed, low noise or light emission matter more than integration density. Compared with GaN, GaAs has a narrower gap and lower breakdown field, so GaN has taken over the highest-power RF and power-switching roles.

faq.q: Why is GaAs faster than silicon?
faq.a: Its electrons have a much smaller effective mass, about 0.067 of the free-electron mass, so electron mobility is around 8,500 cm²/(V·s) versus about 1,400 in silicon. This lets GaAs transistors operate at higher frequencies with lower noise.

faq.q: What wavelength does GaAs emit?
faq.a: With a band gap of about 1.42 eV, GaAs emits near 870 nm, which is invisible near-infrared light. AlGaAs/GaAs VCSELs used in sensing and short optical links typically operate near 850 nm.

faq.q: Why is GaAs not used for CPUs?
faq.a: It lacks a good native oxide for MOS gates, its wafers are costlier and smaller, and its hole mobility is no better than silicon's, so dense complementary logic is impractical. Silicon CMOS offers far better integration and cost.

InP(リン化インジウム).desc: A compound semiconductor of indium and phosphorus. As a substrate for lattice-matched layers such as InGaAs, it is used for fiber-optic lasers and photodetectors and for high-speed transistors.

about.p: Indium phosphide is a III-V compound semiconductor with a zinc-blende crystal structure, a direct band gap of about 1.34 eV at room temperature and a lattice constant of about 0.587 nm. Its thermal conductivity, about 68 W/(m·K), is less than half of silicon's, so heat removal needs care in power devices. Growing large, low-defect crystals while preventing phosphorus from evaporating is difficult, so InP wafers are typically 100–150 mm in diameter, far smaller than 300 mm silicon. That keeps cost per chip high and equipment specialized.

Optical fiber has its lowest dispersion near 1.3 µm and its lowest loss, about 0.2 dB/km, near 1.55 µm. Silicon cannot emit efficiently because its band gap is indirect, and it barely absorbs beyond about 1.1 µm. Alloys grown lattice-matched on InP fill the gap: In0.53Ga0.47As, with a band gap of about 0.75 eV, absorbs out to about 1.7 µm for photodiodes, and InGaAsP compositions set the operating wavelength of lasers and modulators. Vegard's law gives the composition that matches the InP lattice, avoiding dislocations even in thick layers.

Both are direct-gap III-V substrates, but they serve different niches. GaAs lattice-matches AlGaAs and InGaP, emits at shorter near-infrared wavelengths around 850 nm used in short-reach links, and its InGaP/GaAs HBTs dominate smartphone power amplifiers. InP supports the 1.3 and 1.55 µm telecom bands and higher-speed transistors: InGaAs channels on InP reach electron mobility around 10,000 cm²/V·s for HEMTs, and InP HBTs reach transition frequencies of several hundred GHz, driving optical links beyond 100 Gb/s and millimetre-wave and terahertz circuits.

Silicon photonics builds waveguides, modulators and germanium photodetectors in CMOS-style fabs, but still needs a light source. Direct growth of InP on silicon suffers from an approximately 8% lattice mismatch, so InP is integrated in other ways. In heterogeneous integration, InP-based epitaxial layers are bonded onto an SOI wafer, the InP substrate is removed and lasers are patterned by lithography aligned to the silicon waveguides, coupling light through tapers. Alternatively, finished InP laser chips are attached separately. Because indium and phosphorus are contamination concerns, such steps are kept apart from mainstream CMOS lines.

faq.q: Why is InP used for 1550 nm lasers and detectors?
faq.a: Alloys such as InGaAsP and InGaAs grown lattice-matched on InP have band gaps that correspond to the 1.3 µm and 1.55 µm fiber windows, and they have direct gaps that emit light efficiently. Silicon cannot emit efficiently and does not absorb at these wavelengths.

faq.q: Is InP a direct bandgap semiconductor?
faq.a: Yes. InP has a direct band gap of about 1.34 eV at room temperature, so electrons and holes can recombine radiatively without needing a phonon.

faq.q: What is the difference between InP and GaAs?
faq.a: GaAs is the substrate for shorter-wavelength emitters around 850 nm and for smartphone power-amplifier HBTs, while InP supports the 1.3–1.55 µm telecom wavelengths and the fastest III-V transistors. InP wafers are generally smaller and more expensive.

Ga2O3(酸化ガリウム).desc: An oxide semiconductor with a band gap of about 4.5-4.9 eV, even wider than SiC or GaN. Its crystals can be grown from the melt, and it is being researched as a next-generation power semiconductor material.

混晶半導体.desc: A semiconductor crystal that mixes several elements, such as AlGaAs or InGaN. Changing the composition tunes the band gap and lattice constant continuously.

量子井戸.desc: A structure in which a thin layer, a few nanometers thick, with a small band gap is sandwiched between layers with a larger band gap. It confines carriers to promote recombination and is used as the active layer of LEDs and lasers.

VCSEL(垂直共振器面発光レーザー).desc: A semiconductor laser that emits light perpendicular to the substrate. It can be tested on the wafer and easily arranged in 2D arrays, so it is used in data links and as the light source for face recognition.

2次元電子ガス(2DEG).desc: A dense sheet of electrons confined at a heterojunction interface such as AlGaN/GaN. With little impurity scattering and high mobility, it serves as the channel of a HEMT.

about.p: At a heterojunction between a wide-bandgap barrier and a narrower-bandgap channel, the conduction-band offset and band bending create a roughly triangular potential well only a few nanometers wide on the channel side. Electrons trapped there have quantized energy levels for motion perpendicular to the interface but move freely along it, so they behave as a two-dimensional gas. Its density is therefore quoted per unit area, as a sheet carrier density in cm⁻², rather than per unit volume.

In AlGaAs/GaAs structures, donors are placed in the AlGaAs barrier, often behind an undoped spacer layer, and their electrons fall into the GaAs well. This modulation doping separates the electrons from the ionized donors, reducing impurity scattering and giving very high mobility, especially at low temperature. AlGaN/GaN needs no intentional doping: GaN's wurtzite crystal is polar, and the difference in spontaneous and piezoelectric polarization at the interface induces a sheet density around 10¹³ cm⁻², roughly ten times typical GaAs values, with room-temperature mobility up to about 2000 cm²/V·s.

In a high electron mobility transistor (HEMT), a gate on the barrier layer depletes or restores the 2DEG beneath it, switching the channel. High mobility gives low noise and high gain at microwave frequencies, which is why GaAs HEMTs serve satellite receivers and low-noise amplifiers. GaN's high density and breakdown field give high power density for base-station amplifiers, radar and power switching. Because the GaN 2DEG exists at zero gate bias, the basic device is normally on; normally-off parts use approaches such as a p-type GaN gate, a recessed gate or a cascode with a silicon MOSFET.

A dense, mobile 2DEG gives low sheet resistance, typically a few hundred ohms per square in AlGaN/GaN. The layers around it must not conduct or trap charge. GaN buffers are made highly resistive with carbon or iron doping so the device can be turned off at high voltage, but traps in the buffer or at the surface can capture electrons under high-voltage stress and temporarily deplete the 2DEG. This current collapse, seen as a rise in dynamic on-resistance, is reduced with surface passivation, field plates and careful buffer design.

faq.q: Why does a 2DEG have high electron mobility?
faq.a: The electrons travel in an undoped region, separated from the ionized donors or polarization charges that supply them, so they suffer little impurity scattering. A smooth heterointerface also limits roughness scattering.

faq.q: Why are GaN HEMTs normally on?
faq.a: Polarization creates the 2DEG at the AlGaN/GaN interface without any gate voltage, so the channel conducts at 0 V. A negative gate voltage is needed to deplete it unless the structure is modified for normally-off operation.

faq.q: What is the typical sheet density of a 2DEG in AlGaN/GaN?
faq.a: About 10¹³ electrons per square centimeter, which together with mobility of around 1500 to 2000 cm²/V·s gives sheet resistance of a few hundred ohms per square.

MMIC.desc: Short for monolithic microwave integrated circuit: a high-frequency IC that integrates transistors together with passive components such as inductors and capacitors on a substrate such as GaAs.

ベガード則.desc: The empirical rule that the lattice constant of an alloy varies almost linearly with composition. It is used to find the composition that lattice-matches a given substrate.

効率ドループ.desc: The drop in luminous efficiency of InGaN LEDs as current increases. Auger recombination is thought to be one cause.

ウルツ鉱型構造.desc: The hexagonal crystal structure of GaN, ZnO and others. It has polarization along certain crystal directions, which creates the 2DEG in GaN HEMTs.

CCDイメージセンサ.desc: An image sensor that shifts pixel charges along like a bucket brigade and converts them to voltage at an output stage. It offered low noise and high image quality but used more power, and CMOS sensors have replaced it in most uses.

ベイヤー配列.desc: A color filter arrangement of red, green, green and blue over each 2×2 block of pixels, with two greens because the eye is most sensitive to green. Missing colors at each pixel are interpolated from neighbors (demosaicing).

マイクロレンズ.desc: A tiny lens placed over each pixel of an image sensor. It gathers light and directs it efficiently onto the photodiode, raising sensitivity.

ローリングシャッター.desc: A readout method that exposes and reads pixel rows one after another. It is simple, but fast-moving subjects appear skewed. Exposing all pixels at once is a global shutter.

暗電流.desc: Current that flows in a photodiode even without light, caused for example by thermal generation of carriers. It rises with temperature and appears as noise in dark images.

about.p: In a reverse-biased photodiode, any electron–hole pair generated inside or near the depletion region is swept out and counted, whether light created it or not. Without light, pairs are still generated thermally, mostly through Shockley-Read-Hall (SRH) generation at deep levels in the band gap; traps near midgap from metal contamination, crystal defects and silicon/oxide interface states are the most effective. Minority carriers diffusing in from neutral regions add a further component. Because both mechanisms depend on the intrinsic carrier concentration, which grows exponentially with temperature and with decreasing band gap, dark current is strongly temperature dependent.

An image sensor pixel integrates dark current along with photocurrent, so dark signal grows with exposure time and temperature, roughly doubling every 6–8 °C in silicon. It adds an offset, and because the dark electrons arrive randomly it also adds shot noise proportional to the square root of the dark charge. Pixel-to-pixel variation in dark current is part of fixed-pattern noise, and isolated defective pixels become hot pixels in long exposures. Offset can be subtracted using optically black reference pixels or a dark frame, but the shot noise cannot, which is why astronomical cameras cool their sensors.

about.h: The pinned photodiode and other fixes
about.p: The silicon/oxide interface is rich in interface states, a major generation source. A pinned, or buried, photodiode places its n-type collection region below the surface and covers it with a heavily doped p+ layer, which fills those states with holes and greatly suppresses generation; the fully depleted n-region also allows complete charge transfer, reducing lag and reset noise.
