Clean processing and gettering reduce metallic traps, and the trench walls of deep trench isolation (DTI) between pixels must be passivated so the isolation that fights crosstalk does not itself add dark current.

about.h: Dark current vs. read noise, bias and materials
about.p: Dark current differs from read noise: read noise comes from the readout chain once per frame regardless of exposure, while dark current accumulates with time. Bias matters too; operating a photodiode at zero bias (photovoltaic mode) lowers dark current for precise weak-light measurement, whereas reverse bias speeds response at the cost of more leakage. Material choice is decisive. Germanium detectors for 1.31 and 1.55 µm telecom bands suffer higher dark current because of germanium's smaller band gap of about 0.66 eV and dislocations from the roughly 4% lattice mismatch with silicon.

faq.q: Why does dark current increase with temperature?
faq.a: Dark current comes from thermal generation of electron–hole pairs, and the intrinsic carrier concentration that drives it rises exponentially with temperature. In silicon image sensors it roughly doubles every 6–8 °C.

faq.q: How do you reduce dark current noise in a camera?
faq.a: Cool the sensor, shorten the exposure and subtract a dark frame or optically black reference to remove the offset. At the device level, pinned photodiodes and clean, well-passivated interfaces reduce the generation itself.

faq.q: Is dark current the same as leakage current?
faq.a: Dark current is the reverse leakage of a photodetector observed with no light, so it is a specific case of junction leakage. It is called dark current because it sets the detector's signal floor in darkness.

相関二重サンプリング(CDS).desc: Taking the difference between a pixel's voltage just after reset and its voltage when the signal is read. It removes reset noise and per-pixel offsets.

about.h: How CDS works in a 4T pixel
about.p: In a four-transistor CMOS pixel the floating diffusion (FD), a small capacitance node, is first reset. Opening the reset switch freezes a random kTC noise voltage on the node, plus the source-follower offset. The readout circuit samples this reset level, then the transfer gate moves photodiode charge onto the FD and the signal level is sampled. Subtracting the two samples leaves only the charge-induced change. Because the same reset event is present in both samples, its noise is correlated between them and cancels, which is where the name comes from.

about.h: What it removes and what it does not
about.p: CDS cancels anything common to both samples: reset (kTC) noise, which for a femtofarad-scale FD would otherwise be on the order of ten electrons rms; per-pixel amplifier offsets that would appear as fixed-pattern noise; and much of the slow, low-frequency 1/f noise, since the two samples are taken close together in time. It cannot remove photon shot noise, dark-current shot noise or other noise that differs between the samples. White noise from the readout chain is actually increased by about √2, because two independent noisy samples are subtracted.

True CDS requires that the reset sample be taken before the signal charge arrives on the same node. In an older three-transistor pixel the photodiode itself is the sense node, so the reset that follows a read is a new, uncorrelated event; subtracting it removes offsets but leaves reset noise. The pinned photodiode with a separate transfer gate allows complete charge transfer onto an already-sampled FD, and together with CDS this brings read noise down to a few electrons or less.

CDS originated in charge-coupled device (CCD) output stages and is now standard in CMOS image sensor column circuits. Analog CDS stores the two levels on sample-and-hold capacitors and subtracts them before conversion. Digital CDS converts both levels with the column analog-to-digital converter (ADC) and subtracts the codes; in single-slope column ADCs this is often done by counting down during the reset conversion and up during the signal conversion. Column-to-column mismatch left after CDS is handled by calibration and optically black reference pixels.

faq.q: Why is it called correlated double sampling?
faq.a: Two samples are taken of the same node, one after reset and one after the signal charge arrives, and the reset noise in both is the same random value. Because that noise is correlated between the samples, subtracting them cancels it.

faq.q: Does CDS remove fixed pattern noise?
faq.a: It removes the pixel-level part caused by amplifier offset and reset level variation. Column circuit mismatch and dark current non-uniformity need additional correction such as black-pixel references or calibration.

faq.q: Does CDS reduce shot noise?
faq.a: No. Photon shot noise and dark-current shot noise are part of the signal itself and differ between the two samples, so subtraction cannot cancel them.

埋め込みフォトダイオード(ピンドフォトダイオード).desc: A photodiode with a heavily doped p+ layer at the surface that keeps the collection region away from the interface. It suppresses dark current from interface states and allows complete charge transfer; it is standard in CMOS image sensors.

固定パターンノイズ.desc: Noise that appears in the same place every time, caused by variations between pixels or readout circuits. It is removed by correlated double sampling or calibration.

ショットノイズ.desc: Noise from statistical fluctuation in the number of photons or electrons. Its size is proportional to √N for a signal of N electrons, so it is relatively larger when light is scarce.

about.p: Light and current are made of discrete particles that arrive at random times. When events are independent, their count follows Poisson statistics: the variance equals the mean, so a signal averaging N photoelectrons fluctuates by about the square root of N. In electronic circuits the same effect appears when carriers cross a barrier independently, as in a diode junction or photodiode, giving a noise current spectral density of 2qI (the Schottky formula). It differs from thermal noise in a resistor, which arises from random thermal motion and exists even with no current.

Because noise grows as the square root of N, the shot-noise-limited signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is N divided by its square root, which is again the square root of N: 10 for 100 electrons and 100 for 10,000. Dark scenes collect few electrons, so photon noise and read noise are large relative to the signal and images look grainy. Raising ISO mainly amplifies signal and noise together and cannot reduce shot noise. Full-well capacity caps the best possible SNR of a single pixel exposure.

Since photon shot noise has variance equal to its mean in electrons, it serves as a built-in calibration source. In the photon transfer curve (PTC) method, flat-field images are captured at several light levels and the variance of the output in digital numbers is plotted against its mean. The slope gives the conversion gain between electrons and digital numbers, the low-signal floor gives read noise, and the point where variance stops rising marks full-well capacity, from which dynamic range follows.

about.h: Living with it: binning, stacking and EUV
about.p: Shot noise is a property of the light itself, so better circuits cannot remove it; only collecting more photons helps. Larger pixels, brighter lenses, multi-frame stacking in night modes and pixel binning all do this. Binning a 2×2 block quadruples the signal and roughly doubles SNR when shot noise dominates. Photon shot noise also limits extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography: each 13.5 nm photon carries about 92 eV, roughly fourteen times the energy of a 193 nm photon, so the same dose delivers far fewer photons and causes random line edge roughness and stochastic defects.

faq.q: Why is shot noise proportional to the square root of the signal?
faq.a: Randomly arriving photons or electrons follow Poisson statistics, where the variance equals the mean. The standard deviation, which is the noise, is therefore the square root of the mean count.

faq.q: What is the difference between shot noise and thermal noise?
faq.a: Shot noise comes from the discreteness of charge or photons and scales with the current or signal. Thermal noise comes from random thermal motion of carriers in a resistance and is present even when no current flows.

faq.q: Does increasing ISO reduce noise in low light?
faq.a: Not meaningfully. Higher ISO amplifies the signal and the shot noise equally. Only gathering more light, through longer exposure, a larger aperture or pixel, or averaging frames, improves the signal-to-noise ratio.

飽和電子数(フルウェル容量).desc: The maximum number of electrons one image-sensor pixel can hold. The larger it is, the brighter the scene can be before highlights clip, widening dynamic range.

about.p: During exposure, photoelectrons collect in the potential well of each pixel's photodiode, in modern CMOS sensors usually a pinned photodiode. Its capacity depends on the photodiode's area and depth, its doping profile and the voltage swing the well can accept. The readout chain can also impose a limit: charge is transferred to a floating diffusion and converted to voltage, so if that node or the output range saturates first, it sets the effective full well. Typical values range from a few thousand electrons in small smartphone pixels to tens of thousands, or about 100,000, in large-pixel cameras.

about.h: Link to dynamic range and SNR
about.p: Dynamic range is the ratio of the largest signal, the full well, to the noise floor, set mainly by read noise in electrons. A 6000-electron full well with 2 electrons of read noise gives 3000:1, about 70 dB. Full well also caps image quality in bright areas: photon shot noise equals the square root of the signal, so the best possible signal-to-noise ratio is the square root of the full well, for example 100:1 (40 dB) at 10,000 electrons.

about.h: Pixel size and conversion gain trade-offs
about.p: Shrinking pixels reduces both the light collected and the charge a pixel can hold, so small pixels clip highlights sooner and show more noise in dim scenes. Binning combines neighboring pixels to recover sensitivity when resolution is less important. Conversion gain, in microvolts per electron, poses another trade-off: high gain lowers effective read noise but lets the floating diffusion saturate at fewer electrons. Dual-conversion-gain pixels switch extra capacitance in for bright scenes, and some high-dynamic-range designs store charge that overflows the photodiode in an added capacitor.

about.h: Beyond full well, and measuring it
about.p: When light exceeds the full well, excess charge spills into neighboring pixels and bright areas spread, which is called blooming; in CCDs it can also appear as smear along the transfer direction. CMOS pixels provide an overflow path, often through the reset transistor, to drain excess charge. Full well is commonly measured with the photon transfer curve: in electrons the shot-noise variance equals the mean, so plotting variance against mean gives conversion gain from the slope, and the point where variance stops rising and collapses marks saturation.

faq.q: What is full-well capacity in an image sensor?
faq.a: It is the maximum number of photoelectrons one pixel can store before it saturates and highlights clip. Typical values range from a few thousand electrons in small pixels to around 100,000 in large ones.

faq.q: How does full-well capacity affect dynamic range?
faq.a: Dynamic range is roughly full-well capacity divided by read noise. For example, 6000 electrons with 2 electrons of read noise gives 3000:1, or about 70 dB.

faq.q: Why do smaller pixels have lower full-well capacity?
faq.a: A smaller photodiode has less area and volume in which to store charge, so it saturates at fewer electrons. It also collects less light, which reduces sensitivity.

ToF(Time of Flight).desc: Measuring distance from the time light takes to travel to an object and back. ToF sensors are used in face recognition, robotics and automotive LiDAR.

about.h: The basic relation and its timing demands
about.p: Distance equals the speed of light times the round-trip time divided by two, because the light travels out and back. A target 1 m away returns light after about 6.7 ns, and a LiDAR echo arriving after 400 ns means about 60 m; forgetting the factor of two gives 120 m. The challenge is timing precision: a 1 cm change in distance shifts the round trip by only about 67 ps. Sensors therefore either time individual pulses with very fast detectors and circuits or measure the phase of modulated light.

A direct ToF (dToF) sensor fires short laser pulses and timestamps the returning photons, typically with single-photon avalanche diodes (SPADs) and time-to-digital converters. Because a single pulse may return only a few photons among ambient-light counts, the measurement is repeated many times and the arrival times are collected in a histogram whose peak marks the target distance. This approach suits long ranges and is common in automotive and robotic LiDAR, where a scanning or flash laser builds a 3D point cloud.

An indirect ToF (iToF) sensor illuminates the scene with light modulated at tens of megahertz and measures the phase shift of the returning signal. Each pixel steers photo-generated charge into two or more storage nodes, or taps, during different phase windows, and the charge ratios give the phase. Distance follows from the phase and modulation frequency, but it wraps around: at 20 MHz the unambiguous range is 7.5 m, so several frequencies are often combined. iToF gives dense depth maps at short range, while multipath reflections and strong sunlight are its main error sources.

ToF systems use near-infrared light around 850 nm or 940 nm so the illumination is invisible; 940 nm also falls in a dip of the sunlight spectrum caused by atmospheric water absorption. Silicon absorbs these wavelengths weakly, with absorption depths of about 20 µm at 850 nm and over 50 µm at 940 nm, so thin photodiodes lose much of the light. Pixels add light-trapping surface textures and deeper collection regions. Eye-safety limits on laser power and scattering in fog or heavy rain further limit range.

faq.q: What is the difference between direct ToF and indirect ToF?
faq.a: Direct ToF times short light pulses with fast detectors such as SPADs, which suits long range. Indirect ToF measures the phase shift of continuously modulated light, giving dense, high-resolution depth at shorter range.

faq.q: How do you calculate distance from time of flight?
faq.a: Multiply the speed of light by the measured round-trip time and divide by two. For example, 400 ns gives 3×10⁸ m/s × 400 ns ÷ 2 = 60 m.

faq.q: Why do ToF sensors use 940 nm light?
faq.a: Near-infrared light is invisible, and around 940 nm sunlight is weakened by atmospheric water absorption, which reduces ambient-light interference outdoors. The drawback is that silicon absorbs 940 nm light weakly.

SPAD(単一光子アバランシェダイオード).desc: A photodetector biased above breakdown so that even a single photon triggers a large avalanche pulse. It is used for ranging, such as in LiDAR.

積層型CMOSイメージセンサ.desc: An image sensor whose pixel array and signal-processing circuitry are made on separate chips and bonded together. Each can use the most suitable process, making the chip smaller and processing faster.

インゴット.desc: A cylindrical single-crystal block grown by the CZ method or similar, before it is cut into wafers. The ends are removed and the outside is ground to a uniform diameter before slicing.

about.p: In the Czochralski (CZ) method, high-purity polysilicon is melted in a quartz crucible just above silicon's melting point of about 1414 °C. A seed crystal is dipped into the melt and slowly pulled upward while seed and crucible rotate in opposite directions, which evens out the temperature around the axis and yields a cylindrical crystal. A thin neck first lets dislocations grow out, then the diameter widens through the shoulder, or crown, into the constant-diameter body. A camera tracks the bright meniscus ring at the crystal–melt boundary, and pull rate and heater power are adjusted to hold diameter constant.

about.h: Doping and segregation along the ingot
about.p: Dopants are added to the melt: boron for p-type, phosphorus, arsenic or antimony for n-type. Most dopants have a segregation coefficient k below 1, meaning the growing crystal accepts less impurity than the melt holds, so the rejected dopant builds up in the shrinking melt and the later-grown part of the ingot is more heavily doped and lower in resistivity. Phosphorus has k of about 0.35, arsenic about 0.3 and antimony about 0.023, while boron's value of about 0.8 keeps p-type ingots fairly uniform. Only sections within the resistivity specification become product.

Only the constant-diameter body is used; the crown and the tail are cut off. The tail is deliberately tapered into a cone before the crystal leaves the melt, because abrupt separation of a full-diameter crystal causes thermal shock that creates slip dislocations, which can propagate back into the body by roughly one diameter. Pull rate also affects crystal quality, because the ratio of growth rate to temperature gradient (V/G) decides whether vacancy- or interstitial-type point defects dominate, so diameter control must not compromise it. Oxygen dissolved from the quartz crucible is incorporated as well and is measured along the ingot.

The ingot is cropped, ground to an exact diameter and given an orientation notch or, on older sizes, a flat. A multi-wire saw with hundreds of parallel wires about 0.1 mm thick then slices it into hundreds of wafers just under 1 mm thick in one run of several hours. The wafers are edge-beveled, lapped or ground for flatness, etched to remove the sawing damage layer and polished to a mirror finish before cleaning and inspection. Float-zone (FZ) growth, which uses no crucible, produces ingots with very low oxygen, favored for high-resistivity and some power devices.

faq.q: Why are silicon wafers round?
faq.a: The CZ crystal is pulled while rotating, so it grows as a cylinder and slices into round wafers. Round substrates also suit spin coating, polishing and other rotation-based processes.

faq.q: How is a silicon ingot cut into wafers?
faq.a: After grinding to diameter, the ingot is sliced with a multi-wire saw that cuts hundreds of wafers simultaneously using fine wires carrying abrasive slurry or fixed diamond. Lapping, etching and polishing then remove the saw damage.

faq.q: Why does resistivity change from the top to the bottom of an ingot?
faq.a: Most dopants segregate into the melt as the crystal grows, so the melt becomes richer in dopant over time and the bottom of the ingot ends up more heavily doped. Boron, with a segregation coefficient near 1, shows this effect least.

SOIウエハ.desc: A wafer with a thin silicon layer on a buried oxide (BOX) layer over a silicon substrate. It is made, for example, by bonding a hydrogen-implanted wafer and splitting it. Its low parasitic capacitance suits FD-SOI devices and MEMS.

シーメンス法.desc: A method that reduces trichlorosilane with hydrogen to deposit high-purity polycrystalline silicon on heated silicon rods. It is the main way to make raw silicon for semiconductors.

偏析係数.desc: The ratio of impurity concentration in the crystal to that in the melt during solidification. For most impurities it is below 1, so they concentrate in the melt and the later part of a CZ crystal has higher impurity levels.

ネッキング.desc: Growing a thin neck just after the seed at the start of CZ pulling. It lets dislocations created by thermal shock when the seed touches the melt escape, giving a dislocation-free crystal.

MCZ法(磁場印加CZ法).desc: A CZ variant that applies a magnetic field to the crucible to suppress melt convection. It makes the oxygen concentration in the crystal easier to control and is used for large-diameter crystals.

酸素析出物(BMD).desc: Tiny defects formed inside a CZ silicon wafer when its oxygen precipitates during heat treatment. Also called BMDs (bulk micro defects), they serve as gettering sites that capture metal impurities.

about.p: Czochralski (CZ) silicon is pulled from a melt held in a quartz crucible, which dissolves and releases oxygen into the crystal, giving interstitial oxygen concentrations on the order of 10¹⁸ cm⁻³. At typical device-processing temperatures this oxygen is supersaturated, so during heat treatment it clusters into silicon-oxide precipitates. Nucleation is favored at lower temperatures and growth at higher ones. Because the oxide occupies more volume than the silicon it replaces, growing precipitates emit silicon interstitials and strain the lattice, often producing punched-out dislocations or stacking faults around them. Float-zone silicon, grown without a crucible, contains little oxygen.

about.h: Intrinsic gettering and the denuded zone
about.p: Precipitates and their strained surroundings act as sinks for fast-diffusing metals such as iron, copper and nickel, which are captured in the bulk as the wafer cools instead of degrading junctions and gate oxides near the surface. This is intrinsic gettering. It works only if the top layer of tens of micrometers, where devices are built, stays free of precipitates. That denuded zone was classically formed by a high-low-high anneal: oxygen out-diffuses near the surface, then nuclei form and grow in the bulk. Rapid thermal anneals that engineer the vacancy profile are a modern alternative.

BMD density is typically controlled to about 10⁸ to 10¹⁰ cm⁻³. Too few precipitates give weak gettering; too many, or precipitates too close to the surface, cause junction leakage and can nucleate oxidation-induced stacking faults. Large precipitates also lower the wafer's resistance to slip and warpage during high-temperature steps. Modern processes have small thermal budgets, so precipitates may not nucleate on their own. Adding trace nitrogen, about 10¹³ to 10¹⁵ cm⁻³, during crystal growth promotes nucleation, shrinks vacancy-cluster voids (COPs) and strengthens the wafer, with negligible electrical effect.

Extrinsic gettering uses deliberately introduced sinks outside the device region, such as backside mechanical damage or a polysilicon film on the back, while heavily doped substrates also attract certain metals. Epitaxial wafers combine approaches: a lightly doped p-type epi layer on a p+ substrate provides a surface nearly free of precipitates and COPs, and the substrate below handles gettering while also suppressing CMOS latch-up. BMD density is commonly evaluated by preferential etching of cleaved cross-sections and counting the revealed pits, or by infrared light-scattering techniques.

faq.q: What is a BMD in a silicon wafer?
faq.a: A bulk micro defect is an oxygen precipitate, often with associated dislocations or stacking faults, that forms inside a CZ wafer during heat treatment. Controlled BMDs serve as gettering sites for metal contamination.

faq.q: What is the difference between intrinsic and extrinsic gettering?
faq.a: Intrinsic gettering uses oxygen precipitates inside the wafer bulk as sinks for metals. Extrinsic gettering uses sinks introduced from outside, such as backside damage, a backside polysilicon layer or a heavily doped substrate.

faq.q: Why must the wafer surface be free of oxygen precipitates?
faq.a: Devices are built in the top few micrometers, and precipitates or the defects around them there would cause junction leakage and oxide problems. A precipitate-free denuded zone keeps the active region clean while the bulk does the gettering.

DZ(無欠陥層).desc: A layer near the wafer surface with few defects such as oxygen precipitates, made by out-diffusing oxygen during heat treatment. Devices are built in this layer while precipitates deeper inside provide gettering.

スリップ.desc: A defect in which crystal planes shift and dislocations form under stress from temperature differences or the wafer's own weight during high-temperature processing of large wafers. It can cause problems such as overlay errors.

about.p: Silicon is brittle at room temperature but becomes much softer at the temperatures used for oxidation, diffusion and annealing. If shear stress in the wafer exceeds the critical value at that temperature, dislocations are created and glide on {111} planes, permanently shifting one part of the crystal relative to another. The stress comes from temperature differences across the wafer, for example when the edge heats or cools faster than the centre during a rapid ramp, and from the wafer's own weight concentrated at the points where it rests on a boat or support pins.

about.h: Why large wafers are more vulnerable
about.p: Gravitational stress rises with wafer diameter because a larger, heavier disk spans a greater distance between supports, and radial temperature gradients are harder to suppress across a bigger area. Slip therefore typically starts near edge contact points and appears as families of straight lines; on a (100) wafer they run along the two perpendicular ⟨110⟩ directions, where the {111} slip planes intersect the surface. X-ray topography and surface inspection are used to detect it. Rapid thermal processing, with its fast ramps, is a common place to meet slip problems.

Dislocations crossing active regions provide paths for junction leakage and act as recombination centres, especially once metal impurities collect on them, so dies cut by slip lines often fail. The plastic deformation that accompanies slip also distorts the wafer in plane and out of plane. That distortion cannot be removed by later steps, so patterns printed afterwards no longer line up with earlier layers, producing overlay errors that the scanner can only partly correct.

Process engineers limit ramp-up and ramp-down rates, design furnace boats and RTP susceptors that spread support loads and keep temperature uniform, and position support points where the combined thermal and gravitational stress is lowest. Wafer material also matters. Interstitial oxygen in Czochralski (CZ) silicon gathers on dislocations and pins them, so CZ wafers resist slip better than low-oxygen float-zone (FZ) wafers, one reason CZ is used for large-diameter IC production. Excessive oxygen precipitation, however, can make wafers more prone to warpage.

faq.q: What is slip in a silicon wafer?
faq.a: Slip is plastic deformation in which dislocations form and glide along {111} crystal planes when thermal or gravitational stress exceeds silicon's strength at high temperature. It shows up as straight slip lines, usually starting near the wafer edge or support points.

faq.q: Why are CZ wafers more resistant to slip than FZ wafers?
faq.a: CZ silicon contains interstitial oxygen from the quartz crucible, and these oxygen atoms pin dislocations so they move less easily. Low-oxygen FZ silicon lacks this pinning and slips more readily during thermal processing.

faq.q: What is the difference between slip and warp?
faq.a: Slip is a crystallographic defect, the creation and motion of dislocations along slip planes. Warp is a measure of the wafer's overall out-of-plane shape; slip can cause warpage, but warp can also come from film stress without any slip.

サーマルドナー.desc: Oxygen clusters that act as donors when CZ silicon is heated around 450°C. Because they change the wafer's resistivity, they are annihilated by a higher-temperature treatment.

モニターウエハ.desc: A wafer run through a process separately from products to check equipment or measure film thickness and particles. Also called a test wafer, it is often stripped, repolished and reused as a reclaimed wafer.

Deal-Groveモデル.desc: A model of thermal oxidation in which the oxidant diffuses through the oxide and reacts with silicon at the Si/SiO2 interface. Thickness grows linearly with time for thin oxides and with the square root of time for thick ones.

about.p: The Deal-Grove model, published in 1965, treats thermal oxidation as three steps in series: oxidant moves from the gas to the oxide surface, diffuses through the existing oxide, and reacts with silicon at the Si/SiO2 interface. In steady state the three fluxes are equal, and dividing the flux by the number of oxidant molecules incorporated per unit volume of oxide gives the growth rate. Solving this yields x² + Ax = B(t + τ), where x is oxide thickness, B is the parabolic rate constant, B/A is the linear rate constant and τ accounts for any oxide present at the start.

When the oxide is thin, oxidant crosses it easily and the interface reaction limits growth, so x ≈ (B/A)t: thickness grows linearly with time. When the oxide is thick, diffusion through it limits growth, so x² ≈ Bt and thickness grows with the square root of time; doubling the thickness then takes about four times as long. The crossover occurs near a thickness of A/2, from tens of nanometers to about 100 nm for dry oxidation depending on temperature. Both constants rise steeply with temperature and roughly in proportion to oxidant partial pressure.

Because new oxide forms at the interface, the interface is always freshly made, and silicon is consumed: about 0.44 of the final oxide thickness comes from silicon below the original surface. Wet oxidation in steam is much faster than dry oxidation in oxygen, largely because water dissolves in SiO2 at far higher concentration, which is why thick isolation or masking oxides are grown wet and at high pressure, while denser dry oxides were preferred for gates. The linear constant depends on crystal orientation, with (111) silicon oxidizing faster than (100), while the parabolic constant does not.

For dry oxidation below a few tens of nanometers, real growth is faster than the model predicts. Proposed explanations include additional oxidant transport mechanisms in very thin films and stress effects at the interface. The original model handles this by assuming an effective initial thickness, roughly 20 to 25 nm for dry oxygen, but gate oxides only a few nanometers thick still require empirical calibration. Heavy doping, chlorine additions and two-dimensional geometries such as corners, where stress slows growth, also need corrections.

faq.q: What are the linear and parabolic rate constants in the Deal-Grove model?
faq.a: B/A is the linear rate constant, governing thin oxides where the interface reaction limits growth. B is the parabolic rate constant, governing thick oxides where diffusion through the oxide limits growth.

faq.q: Why is wet oxidation faster than dry oxidation?
faq.a: Water vapor dissolves in SiO2 at a much higher concentration than oxygen, so far more oxidant reaches the interface. Both rate constants are therefore larger for wet oxidation.

faq.q: How much silicon is consumed during thermal oxidation?
faq.a: About 0.44 of the grown oxide thickness, so growing 100 nm of SiO2 consumes roughly 44 nm of silicon.

STI(シャロートレンチ分離).desc: Isolating devices by etching shallow trenches in silicon, filling them with insulator and planarizing by CMP. It has no bird's beak like LOCOS and is the standard isolation for fine-pitch ICs.

about.p: A thin pad oxide and a silicon nitride layer are deposited, then lithography and etching open trenches about 200 to 300 nm deep into the silicon. A thin liner oxide is grown, often by thermal or ISSG oxidation, to repair etch damage and round the trench corners. The trench is filled with CVD oxide and annealed to densify it. Chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) removes the excess oxide and stops on the nitride, often using ceria slurries with oxide-to-nitride selectivity of tens to over 100. Finally the nitride is stripped in hot phosphoric acid at about 160 °C.

In local oxidation of silicon (LOCOS), nitride masks the active areas while exposed silicon is thermally oxidized, but oxidant diffuses sideways under the nitride edge and grows a bird's beak that can encroach about half the oxide thickness on each side. That eats into active area, limits how close devices can be placed and leaves surface steps. STI isolates with an etched and filled trench, so the surface stays flat and isolation width is set by lithography. It replaced LOCOS around the 0.25 µm generation and is used today to isolate FinFET fins as well.

Ordinary CVD tends to pinch off at the trench opening and trap a void. From about the 0.25 µm to 65 nm generations, high-density plasma CVD filled STI by sputtering the corners while depositing; narrower trenches, down to around 10 nm, use flowable CVD or spin-on dielectrics that fill from the bottom and are then converted to oxide. Corners matter as well: a sharp top corner concentrates the gate field and creates a parasitic edge transistor, and an oxide divot from later wet cleans makes this worse, so corner rounding and recess control are tuned carefully.

The oxide in STI trenches stresses the neighboring silicon, and the amount depends on how far a transistor sits from the trench edge, so drive current can vary with active-area size and layout. Circuit models and design rules account for this. Trench etch must also avoid microtrenching at the bottom corners, which can create later filling or field concentration problems. In FinFET flows, the STI oxide is recessed after CMP to expose the upper part of each fin, and the recess depth sets the active fin height.

faq.q: What is the difference between STI and LOCOS?
faq.a: LOCOS grows thick thermal oxide in unmasked regions and suffers bird's-beak encroachment and surface steps. STI etches trenches, fills them with oxide and planarizes by CMP, giving flat surfaces and much narrower isolation.

faq.q: Why is it called shallow trench isolation?
faq.a: Its trenches are only a few hundred nanometers deep, shallow compared with the deep trench isolation, several micrometers deep, used in some bipolar, power, image sensor and older DRAM technologies.

faq.q: Why is ceria slurry used in STI CMP?
faq.a: Ceria removes silicon oxide efficiently, and with suitable additives it barely polishes silicon nitride. The high oxide-to-nitride selectivity lets polishing stop reliably on the nitride layer.

バーズビーク.desc: In LOCOS, the beak-shaped encroachment of oxide under the edge of the nitride mask. Because it wastes active area, it led to the switch to STI at finer geometries.

フォーミングガスアニール.desc: Heat treatment in a mixture of hydrogen and nitrogen (forming gas). Hydrogen terminates dangling bonds at the Si/SiO2 interface, reducing interface states.

界面準位.desc: Energy levels within the band gap at a semiconductor-insulator interface, created by broken bonds and similar defects. They trap and release carriers, causing threshold shifts, lower mobility and noise.

about.p: At the Si/SiO2 interface not every silicon atom finds an oxygen partner, leaving unsatisfied dangling bonds. These defects create allowed energy levels spread across the silicon band gap. As-oxidized interfaces typically carry about 10¹¹ to 10¹² cm⁻²eV⁻¹, and the density depends on crystal orientation, which is one reason MOSFETs are built on (100) wafers. Unlike fixed oxide charge, the charge in interface states changes with gate bias, because whether each level is filled depends on where the Fermi level sits at the surface.

Charge trapped in interface states shifts the flat-band and threshold voltages and stretches the capacitance-voltage (C-V) curve. Because the traps must be charged as the gate sweeps the surface potential, they add a capacitance that degrades subthreshold slope, so more gate voltage is needed per decade of current. Charged traps also scatter channel carriers and reduce mobility. Capture and emission of carriers produce low-frequency 1/f noise, and states near midgap act as generation centers that create leakage and dark current in image sensors.

A forming gas anneal at about 400 to 450 °C, in nitrogen with a few percent hydrogen, ties hydrogen to dangling bonds and lowers the density to around 10¹⁰ cm⁻²eV⁻¹. Those Si-H bonds can later break: hot carriers near the drain, negative bias temperature instability (NBTI) in p-channel devices and ionizing radiation all generate new interface states, causing threshold drift over the device's life. High-k gate dielectrics form poorer interfaces with silicon, so a thin SiO2 interlayer is normally kept between them.

Interface trap charge (Qit) is one of four standard MOS oxide charge types, together with fixed charge (Qf), mobile ionic charge (Qm) and oxide trapped charge (Qot). It is distinguished by its bias and frequency dependence. Common methods compare high-frequency and quasi-static C-V curves, analyze the conductance of a MOS capacitor versus frequency, or use charge pumping, which pulses a transistor's gate and measures the resulting substrate current to obtain trap density directly on small devices.

faq.q: What is the difference between interface states and fixed oxide charge?
faq.a: Fixed oxide charge sits in the oxide near the interface and does not change with bias, so it only shifts the C-V curve. Interface states exchange carriers with the silicon, so their charge varies with gate bias and they also distort the curve and degrade subthreshold slope.

faq.q: Why does forming gas anneal reduce interface traps?
faq.a: Hydrogen diffuses to the Si/SiO2 interface during the anneal and bonds to silicon dangling bonds, removing their energy levels from the band gap.

faq.q: How do interface states affect subthreshold slope?
faq.a: They add a trap capacitance in parallel with the depletion capacitance, so the gate controls the surface potential less efficiently and more millivolts are needed per decade of drain current.

RTP(急速熱処理).desc: Heating single wafers to high temperature for a few seconds, typically with lamps. It allows annealing and thin oxide growth while limiting unwanted dopant diffusion.

可動イオン.desc: Ions such as sodium and potassium that can move within the gate oxide. They drift with field and temperature and shift the threshold voltage. Because they can come from sources such as human sweat, they are tightly controlled.

about.p: Mobile ions are alkali metal ions, chiefly sodium (Na+) and potassium (K+), that can migrate through silicon dioxide because they are small and only weakly bound in the oxide network. At room temperature they move slowly, but at moderately elevated temperatures, around 200 °C, and under an electric field they drift readily across a gate oxide. Common sources are human sweat and skin, process chemicals, tools, quartzware and furnace components, which is why the semiconductor industry treats alkali metals as critical contaminants.

about.h: How mobile ions shift the threshold voltage
about.p: A charge in the gate oxide shifts the flat-band voltage, and therefore the threshold voltage, by roughly the charge divided by the oxide capacitance, weighted by how close the charge sits to the silicon. Ions near the gate electrode have little effect, but under positive gate bias positive ions drift toward the Si/SiO2 interface, where they have full effect and lower the nMOS threshold voltage. Reversing the bias pulls them back, so the shift is reversible and depends on the bias and temperature history, the signature that distinguishes mobile ions from fixed oxide charge.

The standard check is a bias-temperature stress test on a MOS capacitor. The capacitor is heated, commonly to about 200 °C or more, with a positive gate bias applied, then cooled under bias and measured with a capacitance-voltage (C–V) sweep; the procedure is repeated with negative bias. The difference in flat-band voltage between the two states gives the mobile ion charge per area. Monitor wafers processed through furnaces and other tools are tested this way to detect contamination sources early.

about.h: How the industry brought them under control
about.p: Mobile ions were the main cause of unstable MOS transistors in the 1960s, and several countermeasures made MOS technology practical. Cleanroom discipline, gloves and high-purity chemicals limit sources, and metal-free chemicals such as TMAH replace sodium hydroxide as photoresist developer. Adding a chlorine source such as HCl during thermal oxidation removes sodium as volatile chlorides or immobilizes it in the oxide. Phosphosilicate glass (PSG) layers getter sodium, and silicon nitride films act as barriers in passivation layers.

faq.q: Why is sodium contamination bad for MOS transistors?
faq.a: Sodium ions move through the gate oxide under electric fields and heat, and when they accumulate near the silicon interface their positive charge shifts the threshold voltage, making devices unstable.

faq.q: What is the difference between mobile ions and fixed oxide charge?
faq.a: Mobile ions can drift through the oxide, so the threshold shift they cause changes with bias and temperature and can be reversed. Fixed oxide charge stays near the interface and gives a constant shift.

faq.q: Why is HCl added during gate oxidation?
faq.a: Chlorine binds alkali and metal contaminants, removing them as volatile chlorides or immobilizing them in the oxide, which reduces mobile ion effects and improves oxide reliability.

ドライブイン.desc: In thermal diffusion, the high-temperature step after a fixed amount of dopant has been introduced at the surface (predeposition), which pushes the dopant deeper.

酸化増速拡散(OED).desc: Faster diffusion of boron and phosphorus during oxidation than without it, caused by silicon interstitials injected into the silicon by the oxidation.

酸窒化膜(SiON).desc: Gate oxide with nitrogen incorporated. It blocks boron penetration from the gate electrode and has a slightly higher permittivity, so it was used as the gate insulator before high-k films.

about.h: Why nitrogen was added to gate oxides
about.p: pMOS transistors with p+ polysilicon gates are doped with boron, and during the dopant activation anneal boron can diffuse through a gate oxide only about 2 nm thick into the channel, shifting the threshold voltage and degrading reliability. Nitrogen in the film strongly blocks boron diffusion. It also raises the relative permittivity from 3.9 for SiO2 to roughly 5 to 6, so for the same equivalent oxide thickness (EOT) the physical film can be thicker, and direct-tunneling leakage, which falls steeply with thickness, is reduced. Resistance to hot-carrier damage also improves.

Annealing an oxide in NO or N2O incorporates nitrogen that piles up at the Si/SiO2 interface. Plasma nitridation instead exposes the oxide to active nitrogen from a plasma at a few hundred °C, placing roughly 10 to 20% nitrogen near the top surface. That location blocks boron arriving from the gate and raises permittivity while leaving the channel interface close to pure oxide. Too much nitrogen near the channel lowers carrier mobility and can worsen negative-bias temperature instability (NBTI) in pMOS devices, so the nitrogen profile is tuned carefully.

SiON was the standard gate dielectric in the generations just before high-k. As EOT approached about 1 nm, even nitrided films leaked too much gate current, and the industry moved to hafnium-based oxides with permittivity around 20 to 25 combined with metal gates, which also removed the boron-penetration problem of polysilicon. A thin silicon oxide-based interfacial layer still sits beneath the high-k film to keep a good interface with the channel. For comparison, silicon nitride (Si3N4) has a permittivity of about 7.

Silicon oxynitride is also deposited by plasma-enhanced CVD (PECVD) from silane with nitrous oxide, sometimes with ammonia, at about 300 to 400 °C. Adjusting the gas ratio tunes the refractive index anywhere between oxide (about 1.46) and nitride (about 2.0), so SiON serves as a dielectric antireflective coating under photoresist, as well as a hard mask and passivation layer. These deposited films are much thicker and differ in composition from nitrided gate oxides.

faq.q: Why is nitrogen added to gate oxide?
faq.a: Nitrogen blocks boron diffusion from p+ polysilicon gates into the channel and raises the dielectric constant, allowing a physically thicker film with lower leakage at the same EOT. It also improves hot-carrier reliability.

faq.q: What is the dielectric constant of SiON?
faq.a: It depends on nitrogen content, but gate-quality SiON is typically about 5 to 6, between SiO2 at about 3.9 and silicon nitride at about 7.

faq.q: Why was SiON replaced by high-k dielectrics?
faq.a: At an EOT near 1 nm, SiON films became so thin that tunneling leakage was too high. Hafnium-based high-k oxides, with permittivity around 20 to 25, give the same EOT with a much thicker physical film.

過渡増速拡散(TED).desc: A temporary speed-up of boron and other dopant diffusion early in post-implant annealing, caused by excess silicon interstitials from the implant. It hinders the formation of shallow junctions.

プリアモルファス化注入(PAI).desc: Implanting germanium or similar first to make the surface amorphous, so that the following implant does not channel and a shallow junction results.

ハロー注入(ポケット注入).desc: Angled implantation of dopant of the same type as the channel near the source and drain edges. It limits the spread of the drain depletion region and suppresses short-channel effects.

レトログレードウェル.desc: A well whose doping is higher deeper below the surface, made by high-energy implantation. It suppresses punch-through and latch-up while keeping the channel doping at the surface low.

固溶度.desc: The maximum concentration of an impurity that can dissolve in a crystal at a given temperature. It sets the upper limit of electrically active dopant concentration.

スパイクアニール.desc: An anneal that ramps the wafer quickly to a high temperature and cools it again with almost no hold time. It activates dopants while limiting diffusion, for shallow junctions.

レーザーアニール.desc: Heating only the near-surface region of a wafer for an extremely short time with laser light. It achieves high activation with almost no diffusion.

ファラデーカップ.desc: A device that collects an ion beam and measures the resulting current. In ion implanters it is used to determine the implanted dose.

プラズマドーピング.desc: Implanting low-energy ions by exposing the wafer directly to a plasma containing the dopant. It delivers high doses quickly and dopes 3D structures such as fins fairly uniformly.

シャドウイング.desc: When implanting at a tilt, the effect of tall patterns such as resist casting shadows so that some areas receive no implant.

LPCVD(減圧CVD).desc: Thermal CVD performed under reduced pressure. Faster gas diffusion gives good thickness uniformity and step coverage, and many wafers can be processed at once in a vertical furnace. It is used for polysilicon and nitride films.

about.h: Why low pressure gives uniform films
about.p: Low-pressure chemical vapor deposition (LPCVD) runs thermal CVD at roughly tens to hundreds of pascals. Gas diffusivity rises as pressure falls, so reactants reach every surface quickly and the growth rate is set by the surface reaction rather than by gas transport. A surface-reaction-limited process depends mainly on temperature, and a hot-wall tube furnace holds temperature very uniform. That is why wafers can stand only a few millimetres apart, often more than a hundred per run, and still receive uniform, conformal films with good step coverage.

Polysilicon is deposited by decomposing silane (SiH4) at about 600 to 650 °C; below about 580 °C the film is amorphous. Silicon nitride comes from dichlorosilane and ammonia at about 700 to 800 °C, and oxide from TEOS decomposition at similar furnace temperatures. Polysilicon can be doped in situ by adding phosphine or diborane, which is useful for films lining deep trenches. Deposition rates are modest, typically a few to tens of nanometres per minute, which the large batch size compensates for.

Plasma-enhanced CVD (PECVD) uses a plasma to drive reactions at a few hundred degrees, which makes it usable after metallization, but its films are less dense, contain more hydrogen and etch faster. LPCVD films are dense and close to stoichiometric; LPCVD nitride holds only a few percent hydrogen compared with around 20% in PECVD nitride. Stoichiometric LPCVD nitride also has high tensile stress, so silicon-rich low-stress variants are often used in MEMS membranes. The price of LPCVD quality is its thermal budget.

Because it needs 600 to 800 °C, LPCVD belongs to the front end, before aluminum or copper wiring exists. Typical uses are polysilicon gates and resistors, nitride hard masks and spacers, pad nitride for isolation, capacitor electrodes in DRAM and floating gates or electrodes in flash, and structural layers in MEMS. Film also deposits on the furnace tube and on both sides of every wafer, so tubes need periodic cleaning and backside films sometimes must be stripped.

faq.q: What is the difference between LPCVD and PECVD?
faq.a: LPCVD uses heat alone at about 600 to 800 °C and gives dense, low-hydrogen, uniform films in large batches. PECVD uses a plasma to deposit at a few hundred degrees, enabling use over metal at the cost of film density and purity.

faq.q: Why is LPCVD deposition so uniform?
faq.a: At low pressure gas diffusion is fast, so growth is limited by the surface reaction, which depends mainly on temperature. A hot-wall furnace keeps temperature uniform across all wafers in the load.

faq.q: At what temperature is LPCVD polysilicon deposited?
faq.a: Typically about 600 to 650 °C from silane. Depositing below roughly 580 °C produces amorphous silicon, which can be crystallized by a later anneal.

TEOS.desc: Short for tetraethoxysilane, a liquid organosilicon compound widely used as the source for CVD silicon oxide. It gives oxide films with good step coverage.

電解めっき.desc: Depositing metal by passing current through a plating bath with the wafer as the cathode. It fills copper interconnect trenches, with additives making the fill proceed from the bottom up.

マグネトロンスパッタリング.desc: Sputtering with magnets behind the target that trap electrons near it and raise plasma density. It increases deposition rate and is the mainstream sputtering method today.

反応性スパッタリング.desc: Sputtering a metal target in an atmosphere containing a reactive gas such as nitrogen or oxygen to form nitride or oxide films. It is used for films such as titanium nitride (TiN).

真空蒸着.desc: Forming a film by heating a material in vacuum until it evaporates and condenses on the substrate. Electron-beam heating handles high-melting-point materials, but step coverage is poor.

HDP-CVD(高密度プラズマCVD).desc: CVD using a high-density plasma that deposits while ion sputtering trims film at the trench openings. It has been used to fill narrow trenches with insulator without voids.

静電チャック.desc: A mechanism that holds the wafer to its stage by electrostatic force. It works in vacuum and allows backside gas for temperature control; it is widely used in deposition and etch tools.

スピンコート.desc: Dispensing a liquid at the center of the wafer and spinning it at high speed so centrifugal force spreads a thin, uniform film. It is used for photoresist and spin-on dielectrics.

領域選択成膜.desc: Growing a film only in certain places by exploiting differences in the underlying materials. Because it can save lithography and etch steps, it is being researched and introduced for advanced interconnects.

ArFエキシマレーザー.desc: A laser using argon and fluorine that emits 193 nm ultraviolet light. Combined with immersion, ArF immersion lithography is a leading-edge technique alongside EUV. The 248 nm version is the KrF excimer laser.

about.h: How an ArF laser produces 193 nm light
about.p: The laser chamber holds a gas mixture of a small amount of argon and fluorine diluted in neon as a buffer gas. A fast electrical discharge excites the mixture and forms ArF molecules that are bound only in the excited state, an excimer or excited dimer. When the molecule emits a 193 nm photon it drops to a repulsive ground state and immediately falls apart, so the lower laser level is effectively always empty and population inversion is easy to achieve. The laser is pulsed, with lithography lasers running at repetition rates of several kHz.

about.h: Why lithography needs a narrow line
about.p: Few materials are transparent at 193 nm, so projection lenses are built from fused silica with some calcium fluoride elements. With so little choice of glass, chromatic aberration cannot be corrected the way it is in visible optics, and the laser output must instead be line-narrowed to a bandwidth of well under a picometer. Lithography lasers also stabilize pulse energy and wavelength from pulse to pulse, and the fluorine-based gas fill degrades over time and is periodically refreshed. Photoresists had to change as well, because phenolic KrF resists absorb too strongly at 193 nm.

Resolution follows the Rayleigh relation R = k1·λ/NA. Dry ArF scanners reach a numerical aperture (NA) of about 0.93. ArF immersion fills the gap between the final lens and the wafer with water, whose refractive index at 193 nm is about 1.44, allowing NA up to 1.35. With k1 near its practical limit, single exposures resolve roughly 38 to 40 nm half-pitch. Smaller pitches are made with multiple patterning, such as litho-etch-litho-etch or self-aligned double and quadruple patterning, which is how ArF immersion reached nodes far below its single-exposure limit.

The KrF excimer laser uses krypton and fluorine to emit 248 nm and serves less critical layers where cost matters more than resolution. EUV lithography at 13.5 nm does not use an excimer laser at all: its light comes from a tin plasma, and its optics are reflective mirrors. Even in leading-edge chips patterned with EUV for the tightest layers, many other layers are still exposed with ArF immersion, which has higher throughput and a mature infrastructure.

faq.q: What wavelength does an ArF excimer laser emit?
faq.a: It emits deep-ultraviolet light at 193 nm. The KrF excimer laser, the previous lithography generation, emits at 248 nm.

faq.q: What is the difference between dry ArF and ArF immersion lithography?
faq.a: Dry ArF has air between the lens and the wafer, limiting the numerical aperture to about 0.93. Immersion fills that gap with water, raising NA to about 1.35 so that features roughly 30 percent smaller can be resolved at the same wavelength.

faq.q: Why is it called an excimer laser?
faq.a: Excimer is short for excited dimer, a molecule such as ArF that is bound only in its excited state. Because it dissociates as soon as it emits, the lower laser level stays empty, making efficient ultraviolet lasing possible.

化学増幅型レジスト.desc: A resist in which acid generated by exposure catalyzes a chain of reactions during the post-exposure bake (PEB). It needs little exposure dose and is widely used from KrF onward, but is sensitive to basic contamination.

about.p: A chemically amplified resist (CAR) contains a polymer whose alkali-soluble groups are blocked by acid-labile protecting groups, plus a photoacid generator (PAG). Exposure produces only a small amount of acid. During the post-exposure bake (PEB), typically around 90–130 °C, each acid molecule catalytically removes protecting groups again and again, tens to hundreds of times, without being consumed. In a positive-tone CAR the deprotected regions become soluble in aqueous TMAH developer. One absorbed photon therefore drives many chemical events, which is the amplification.

about.h: Why KrF, ArF and EUV need it
about.p: Older i-line resists based on novolak and a diazonaphthoquinone sensitizer produce at most one photochemical event per absorbed photon, and novolak absorbs too strongly at deep-UV wavelengths. Excimer laser and EUV sources deliver comparatively little usable dose, so throughput depends on resist sensitivity. Chemical amplification, a concept developed at IBM in the 1980s, made practical doses possible and became standard from KrF (248 nm) onward. ArF resists use different, transparent polymer platforms, but the acid-catalyzed mechanism is the same.

Because the image is formed by acid moving during PEB, diffusion blurs the latent image and roughens line edges, so PEB temperature and time are tightly controlled and base quenchers are added to limit how far acid travels. The same sensitivity makes CARs vulnerable to airborne bases such as amines. Contaminants neutralize acid at the resist surface, leaving an insoluble skin that develops into T-shaped profiles, called T-topping, and the effect worsens with delay between exposure and PEB. Lithography tracks therefore use chemical filters to remove amines.

The trade-off is often summarized as resolution, line-edge roughness and sensitivity: improving one tends to worsen another, a tension that is especially visible in EUV. A positive CAR can also be developed in an organic solvent that dissolves the unexposed regions instead, called negative-tone development (NTD), which gives better image contrast for small contact holes and narrow trenches. Non-amplified resists, such as novolak for i-line, have no acid diffusion step and are simpler to control but need far higher doses at short wavelengths.

faq.q: What is a photoacid generator in a chemically amplified resist?
faq.a: A photoacid generator (PAG) is a compound that releases a strong acid when it absorbs exposure light; that acid then catalyzes the deprotection reaction during the post-exposure bake.

faq.q: Why is the post-exposure bake so critical for chemically amplified resists?
faq.a: The amplification reaction and acid diffusion both happen during PEB, so small changes in its temperature or time change the dose response and the printed linewidth.

faq.q: What causes T-topping in photoresist?
faq.a: T-topping occurs when airborne bases such as amines neutralize the photogenerated acid at the top of a chemically amplified resist, leaving an insoluble surface layer that overhangs the developed pattern.

ポジ型フォトレジスト.desc: A photoresist whose exposed areas dissolve and are removed during development. One whose exposed areas remain is a negative resist.

位相シフトマスク.desc: A photomask that shifts the phase of light passing through neighboring openings, using interference to improve image contrast and resolution.

マルチパターニング.desc: Forming patterns with a pitch too fine for a single exposure by splitting them across several exposures or process steps. Splitting into two is double patterning.

about.h: Why one exposure is not enough
about.p: Resolution follows R = k1·λ/NA. Argon fluoride (ArF) immersion lithography combines a 193 nm wavelength with NA 1.35, and with k1 near its practical limit of about 0.27 the finest half-pitch is roughly 39 nm, a pitch of about 80 nm. Layers in advanced logic and memory need tighter pitches than that. Multiple patterning reaches them by building the final pattern from several exposures or from process steps that multiply a relaxed pattern, so no single exposure has to resolve the final pitch.

In litho-etch-litho-etch (LELE), the layout is decomposed into two masks, often described as coloring, so that features closer than the single-exposure limit land on different masks; each is printed and etched in turn. Three masks (LELELE) extend the idea. Two catches dominate. Overlay error between exposures directly changes the spacing between neighboring features, demanding very tight alignment. And some layouts, such as three mutually close features, cannot be split into two colors, so design rules must forbid them.

about.h: SADP and SAQP: spacers set the pitch
about.p: Self-aligned double patterning (SADP) prints mandrel lines at a relaxed pitch, coats them with a conformal film, usually by atomic layer deposition (ALD), and etches it back to leave spacers on both sidewalls. Removing the mandrels leaves spacer lines at half the original pitch, with widths set by film thickness, giving excellent uniformity and no overlay between halves. Repeating the process gives self-aligned quadruple patterning (SAQP). The result is a regular grating, so additional cut or block masks remove unwanted segments, which pushes designs toward unidirectional lines.

Every extra mask, deposition and etch adds cost, cycle time and opportunities for defects, and each step contributes variation: in spacer schemes, for example, mandrel width errors make alternate spaces unequal, known as pitch walking. These costs drove adoption of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography at 13.5 nm, which returns many layers to a single exposure. At the very tightest pitches, EUV itself can again be combined with multiple patterning.

faq.q: What is the difference between LELE and SADP?
faq.a: LELE splits the layout into two masks that are exposed and etched separately, so overlay between them matters. SADP uses sidewall spacers on a single printed pattern to halve the pitch in a self-aligned way, with line width set by film thickness.

faq.q: Why is multiple patterning expensive?
faq.a: Each layer needs extra masks, lithography passes, depositions, etches and inspections, which raise cost and cycle time and add sources of variation and defects.

faq.q: Does EUV eliminate multiple patterning?
faq.a: EUV allows many layers to be printed in a single exposure, greatly reducing the need for multiple patterning. At the finest pitches, however, EUV can still be combined with double patterning.

ペリクル.desc: A thin membrane stretched a short distance above a photomask. It keeps particles off the mask surface, and particles landing on the pellicle are out of focus and do not print.

about.p: A photomask, or reticle, is imaged onto every exposure field of every wafer it prints. A single particle on its patterned surface therefore becomes a repeating defect that can kill the same die location across thousands of wafers. Masks are expensive, and cleaning them repeatedly risks damaging the pattern. The pellicle solves this by keeping particles off the patterned surface entirely, so that contamination arriving during handling, storage and exposure lands somewhere harmless.

The pellicle is a thin transparent membrane, under 1 µm thick for deep-ultraviolet tools, stretched on a frame about 6 mm from the patterned surface. The projection lens is focused on the pattern, and its depth of focus at the mask side is a tiny fraction of a millimeter. A particle on the pellicle is therefore millimeters out of focus; its image is so blurred that it only slightly dims a wide area instead of printing as a sharp defect. The membrane must transmit the exposure light with minimal loss and stay stable under prolonged irradiation.

Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) light at 13.5 nm is strongly absorbed by every material, so an EUV pellicle must be only tens of nanometers thick, made from materials such as polysilicon or carbon nanotube films, and still transmits only around 90% per pass. Because EUV masks are reflective, light crosses the pellicle twice, compounding the loss. The membrane also absorbs part of the high source power and heats up, so it must survive high temperatures while remaining mechanically intact across the full mask area.

The pellicle protects the mask, not the wafer. In ArF immersion lithography, a topcoat over the photoresist keeps immersion water from leaching resist components, and a bottom antireflective coating (BARC) under the resist controls reflections; neither has anything to do with mask contamination. A pellicle also cannot fix defects already present in the mask pattern or particles trapped under it during mounting, so masks are inspected before the pellicle is attached.

faq.q: What is a pellicle in lithography?
faq.a: A pellicle is a thin transparent membrane mounted on a frame a few millimeters above a photomask's pattern. Particles land on the membrane instead of the mask, where they are out of focus and do not print.

faq.q: Why is an EUV pellicle hard to make?
faq.a: All materials absorb EUV strongly, so the membrane must be only tens of nanometers thick yet span the whole mask, survive heating from absorbed power, and still transmit around 90% of the light on each pass.

faq.q: Does a pellicle prevent all mask defects?
faq.a: No. It only keeps new particles off the patterned surface after mounting; pattern defects, or particles trapped underneath when the pellicle is attached, still print.

フォトマスク(レチクル).desc: The master pattern used for exposure, typically a light-blocking pattern on a quartz substrate (reflective for EUV). For reduction scanners it is made four times larger than the pattern on the wafer.

about.p: Mask making starts from a mask blank: a low-defect, very flat quartz plate 6 inches square and about 6 mm thick, coated with a chromium or MoSi absorber film and resist. An electron-beam writer exposes the pattern directly into the resist. Single-beam writers can take over ten hours for a complex mask, so advanced masks with heavy optical proximity correction (OPC) or curvilinear shapes use multi-beam writers with hundreds of thousands of beamlets. After development and etching, the mask is measured, inspected for defects, repaired where possible and fitted with a pellicle.

Scanners project the mask through reduction optics, so mask features are four times larger than on the wafer, which makes them easier to write and makes small mask errors shrink on the wafer. One exposure covers a field of about 26 mm by 33 mm, roughly 858 mm², on the wafer. This reticle limit caps the size of a single die, which is why very large processors approach it and why larger systems use chiplets. Silicon interposers bigger than one field are made by stitching wiring across adjacent exposures. High-NA EUV fields are half the standard size.

A binary mask simply blocks light with chromium. An attenuated phase-shift mask uses a partially transmitting MoSi film that also shifts the light phase by 180 degrees, sharpening the image at feature edges. Because EUV light at 13.5 nm is absorbed by almost every material, EUV masks are reflective: a multilayer stack of molybdenum and silicon acts as a mirror, and a patterned absorber on top defines dark regions. EUV blanks must be nearly free of defects, since a buried flaw in the multilayer cannot be removed later.

Any defect on a mask prints in every field of every wafer exposed with it, appearing on wafer maps as a failure at the same position in each shot. A pellicle, a transparent membrane under 1 µm thick stretched on a frame about 6 mm above the patterned surface, keeps particles away from the focal plane so they are blurred and do not print. EUV pellicles must be only tens of nanometers thick, made of materials such as polysilicon or carbon nanotubes, to transmit around 90 percent of the light and survive heating.

faq.q: What is the difference between a photomask and a reticle?
faq.a: Historically a photomask carried the pattern for an entire wafer at 1:1, while a reticle carried one or a few dies for a stepper that repeats it across the wafer. Today the terms are used almost interchangeably for the master plate used in scanners.

faq.q: Why are photomask patterns four times larger than on the wafer?
faq.a: Scanners use 4x reduction projection optics. Larger features are easier to write and inspect on the mask, and errors in mask dimensions are reduced by the same factor when printed.

faq.q: What is a pellicle on a photomask?
faq.a: It is a thin transparent membrane mounted a few millimeters above the mask pattern. Particles that land on it are out of focus during exposure and therefore do not print on the wafer.

スキャナー.desc: An exposure tool that moves the mask and wafer in sync under a slit of light. It is the mainstream production lithography tool and generally projects the mask pattern at 1/4 size.

about.p: A scanner never illuminates the whole mask at once. Light passes through a slit a few millimeters wide, and the reticle and wafer stages move synchronously in opposite directions so the image sweeps across the field. Because the projection optics reduce the pattern by 4×, the reticle stage travels four times faster than the wafer stage. A standard field is about 26 mm × 33 mm, roughly 858 mm², with the long side in the scan direction. After each field the wafer steps to the next position, which is why the method is called step-and-scan.

A stepper exposes an entire field in one static flash, so its lens must be nearly perfect over the full field area. A scanner only needs a good image over a narrow slit, using the lens's best central region, and it averages lens and illumination variations along the scan direction. The trade-off is mechanical: both stages must accelerate at several m/s² and still track each other with nanometer accuracy during the scan. That capability made larger fields and better uniformity possible, and scanners replaced steppers for critical layers in high-volume manufacturing.

about.h: What happens before the light turns on
about.p: Each wafer is measured before exposure. Alignment sensors read marks from earlier layers to correct position, rotation and expansion, and a level sensor maps surface height so the image stays within the shallow depth of focus as the wafer moves. Overlay results from downstream metrology are fed back as corrections for later lots. Many scanners carry two wafer stages so one wafer is measured while another is exposed. The tool is linked to a coater/developer track, and temperatures around it are held to about ±0.1 °C to limit thermal distortion.

Deep-ultraviolet (DUV) scanners use KrF (248 nm) or ArF (193 nm) excimer lasers with refractive lenses; ArF immersion fills the gap under the lens with water to reach a numerical aperture of about 1.35. Extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) scanners use 13.5 nm light, which every material absorbs, so they rely on mirrors and reflective masks coated with molybdenum/silicon multilayers reflecting about 70%. High-NA EUV halves the exposure field. The field size sets the reticle limit on die area, one reason very large designs are split into chiplets.

faq.q: What is the difference between a scanner and a stepper?
faq.a: A stepper exposes each field in one static shot, while a scanner moves the reticle and wafer in sync under a narrow slit of light, which uses less lens area and gives larger, more uniform fields.

faq.q: What is the maximum field size of a lithography scanner?
faq.a: About 26 mm × 33 mm per exposure on standard scanners, which effectively limits the largest die that can be printed; high-NA EUV fields are half that size.

faq.q: Why does the reticle move faster than the wafer in a scanner?
faq.a: The projection lens shrinks the pattern by 4×, so the reticle must travel four times the distance, and thus four times the speed, of the wafer during each scan.

焦点深度(DOF).desc: The range of focus over which a pattern prints with acceptable quality. Raising the numerical aperture improves resolution but reduces DOF, which makes wafer planarity important.

about.p: Lithography is governed by two Rayleigh relations: resolution R = k1·λ/NA and depth of focus DOF = k2·λ/NA², where λ is the exposure wavelength, NA the numerical aperture of the projection lens, and k1 and k2 process-dependent factors. Raising NA improves resolution in proportion to NA but shrinks DOF with its square. Shortening the wavelength helps resolution while reducing DOF only linearly. Leading-edge processes are left with a DOF of roughly 100 nm, which must cover every source of height and focus error.

about.h: What uses up the focus budget
about.p: The usable DOF has to absorb wafer non-flatness within each exposure field, topography left by underlying layers, resist thickness, chucking distortion, lens field curvature and the scanner's own focus-control errors. Site flatness over a field such as 26 × 33 mm is therefore held to tens of nanometres or less. Engineers measure the process window with a focus–exposure matrix: linewidth is plotted against focus for several doses (Bossung curves), and the overlapping range that keeps linewidth and profile within specification defines the practical DOF and exposure latitude.

about.h: How fabs protect depth of focus
about.p: Chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) planarizes each interconnect level globally, removing the millimetre-to-centimetre topography that reflow or etch-back cannot, which made stacks of ten or more wiring levels practical. Scanners measure wafer height and tilt before each shot and level the wafer so the image plane follows the surface. Thinner resist films reduce the vertical range that must stay in focus. Resolution enhancement techniques such as off-axis illumination can also enlarge DOF for dense periodic patterns.

about.h: Why High-NA EUV makes DOF harder
about.p: Standard EUV scanners use NA 0.33 at a 13.5 nm wavelength, and High-NA EUV raises NA to 0.55 for about 1.7× better resolution. Because DOF scales with 1/NA², the same k2 gives roughly (0.55/0.33)² ≈ 2.8 times less depth of focus. That tightens every item in the focus budget, pushing toward thinner resists, flatter wafers and more precise focus control. High resolution and generous DOF pull in opposite directions, and much of lithography engineering is managing that conflict.

faq.q: What is the formula for depth of focus in lithography?
faq.a: The usual expression is DOF = k2·λ/NA², where λ is the wavelength, NA the numerical aperture and k2 a process factor. It shows that DOF falls with the square of NA.

faq.q: Is depth of focus the same as depth of field?
faq.a: No. Depth of field is the range of object distances that appear sharp, while depth of focus is the tolerance in the position of the image plane. In lithography the wafer sits in the image plane, so depth of focus is the relevant quantity.

faq.q: Why does a higher NA reduce depth of focus?
faq.a: A higher NA collects light over a wider cone of angles, so rays converge more steeply onto the image. A small shift away from best focus then spreads those rays more, blurring the image sooner.

オーバーレイ(重ね合わせ精度).desc: How accurately a new pattern is placed relative to the patterns made in earlier steps. Misalignment causes defects such as missed contacts, so it is controlled at the nanometer level.

about.p: Overlay is checked with dedicated targets, usually placed in the scribe lines between dies, that combine a feature printed in the previous layer with one printed in the current layer. Image-based tools find the center of each pattern and report the offset between them, while diffraction-based tools infer the shift from intensity differences in light diffracted by stacked gratings. Measurements from many sites are fitted to a wafer-level model, and the correction terms are fed back to the exposure tool so that later lots are printed closer to the ideal position.

Error accumulates from many sources: stage and reticle positioning, lens distortion, differences between the tools that exposed each layer, and distortion of the wafer itself. Film stress bows the wafer, high-temperature steps can introduce slip dislocations, and temperature matters directly: silicon expands by about 2.6 ppm/K, so a 0.1 °C change moves the edge of a 300 mm wafer by tens of nanometers. Scanners therefore measure alignment marks on every wafer and correct translation, rotation, magnification and higher-order terms, and the exposure area is held within about ±0.1 °C.

A common rule is that overlay must be held to roughly a quarter or a fifth of the minimum feature size, which means a few nanometers or less at advanced nodes. The budget is tightest in multiple patterning. In litho-etch-litho-etch (LELE) double patterning, any shift of the second exposure changes the spacing to neighboring lines directly: a 2 nm error on a 20 nm space is a 10% change in spacing, affecting wire capacitance and short risk. Spacer-based self-aligned double patterning (SADP) avoids this because line positions are set by deposition, not by a second alignment.

about.h: Overlay vs. CD, and design for misalignment
about.p: Overlay describes where a pattern lands; critical dimension (CD) describes how large it is. Both consume the same edge-placement margin, since a contact can miss its target because it is misplaced or because it is too small. Designers and process engineers buy back margin with self-aligned schemes. In a self-aligned contact (SAC), the gate is capped with silicon nitride, so a misaligned contact etch stops on the nitride instead of shorting to the gate. This lets gate-to-contact spacing shrink without demanding impossible alignment.

faq.q: What is the difference between overlay and alignment in lithography?
faq.a: Alignment is the act of measuring wafer marks and positioning the wafer before exposure; overlay is the resulting placement error between the new layer and earlier layers, measured afterwards on dedicated targets.

faq.q: How tight is overlay at advanced nodes?
faq.a: Requirements are roughly one quarter to one fifth of the smallest feature size, which works out to a few nanometers or less, and even tighter between the two exposures of LELE double patterning.

faq.q: Why does temperature affect overlay?
faq.a: Wafers, reticles and tool structures expand with temperature; for silicon at about 2.6 ppm/K, a 0.1 °C change shifts features at the edge of a 300 mm wafer by tens of nanometers, which is larger than the overlay budget.

ラインエッジラフネス(LER).desc: Nanometer-scale roughness along the edges of fine resist lines. It causes line-width variation (LWR) and leads to variation in transistor characteristics.

プロセスウィンドウ.desc: The range of exposure dose and focus over which pattern dimensions stay within tolerance. The wider it is, the more robust manufacturing is to variation.

High-NA EUV.desc: Next-generation EUV lithography that raises the projection optics' numerical aperture from 0.33 to 0.55 to improve resolution.

反射防止膜(BARC).desc: A layer coated under the resist that suppresses standing waves in the resist and dimension variation over topography caused by light reflected from the substrate.

about.h: What substrate reflection does to resist
about.p: Exposure light that passes through the photoresist reflects from the layers below, and silicon and metal films reflect strongly. The reflected wave interferes with the incoming wave and sets up standing waves, so the dose varies periodically through the resist thickness and developed sidewalls show ripples. The total energy coupled into the resist also oscillates with resist thickness, making linewidth swing periodically with small thickness changes, which is called the swing curve. Over topography, light reflected sideways from sloped edges exposes regions under the mask and causes notching.

A bottom anti-reflective coating (BARC) is a thin layer placed between the substrate and the resist. Its refractive index n, absorption coefficient k and thickness are chosen so that light entering it is absorbed and the residual reflections from its top and bottom surfaces largely cancel by destructive interference. A well-tuned BARC reduces reflectivity back into the resist to below about 1%, which flattens the swing curve and removes most standing-wave and notching effects. Because the optimum thickness depends on wavelength and the underlying stack, BARC thickness is specified for each layer.

Organic BARCs are spin-coated and baked polymers containing light-absorbing groups; they also smooth small topography and provide a good surface for resist adhesion, a role otherwise played by HMDS priming. Most do not dissolve in developer, so after lithography the BARC exposed in the resist openings is removed by a short plasma etch before the underlying film is etched, which consumes some resist. Inorganic BARCs, such as silicon oxynitride deposited by CVD, are tuned through composition and can remain in the film stack or double as a hard mask.
