about.h: BARC vs. TARC and top coat
about.p: A top anti-reflective coating (TARC) sits on top of the resist and reduces reflection at the air-resist interface, which mainly reduces the swing effect; it does not stop reflection from the substrate. A top coat in ArF immersion lithography serves a different purpose: it keeps the immersion water from leaching resist components such as the photoacid generator and keeps the surface hydrophobic for fast stage motion. A pellicle, by contrast, is a membrane that protects the photomask from particles, not part of the wafer film stack.

faq.q: What does BARC stand for in lithography?
faq.a: BARC stands for bottom anti-reflective coating, an absorbing layer coated under the photoresist to suppress reflections from the substrate during exposure.

faq.q: What is the difference between BARC and TARC?
faq.a: A BARC sits below the resist and suppresses substrate reflection, standing waves and notching, while a TARC sits on top of the resist and reduces reflection at the top surface, mainly reducing swing-curve variation.

faq.q: How is a BARC removed after lithography?
faq.a: Most organic BARCs are not removed by the developer, so the BARC in the resist openings is opened with a short plasma etch before the underlying film is etched, and the remainder is stripped with the resist.

ナノインプリントリソグラフィ.desc: Transferring patterns by pressing a mold with fine features into resist on the wafer. It can make fine patterns without expensive optics.

プラズマ.desc: A state in which a gas is ionized into a mixture of electrons, ions and radicals (reactive neutrals). It is used in many processes, including dry etching, plasma CVD and ashing.

about.h: What is inside a process plasma
about.p: Process plasmas are weakly ionized: only a small fraction of the gas molecules are ionized, while the rest are neutral molecules and radicals. An applied radio-frequency or microwave field accelerates the light electrons to energies of a few electronvolts, and their collisions break up and ionize the gas, while the heavy ions and neutrals stay relatively cool. This non-equilibrium state lets chemistry that would otherwise need hundreds of degrees run on a cool wafer. Between the glowing plasma and any surface forms a thin sheath whose electric field accelerates positive ions toward the wafer.

The two active ingredients do different jobs. Radicals are electrically neutral, chemically reactive fragments that drift in all directions and react isotropically. Ions are accelerated across the sheath and strike the wafer nearly vertically, adding physical energy and directionality. Reactive ion etching combines them to get vertical profiles, and the Bosch process for deep silicon etching takes this further by alternating SF6 etch steps with C4F8 passivation steps every few seconds; ions clear the passivation only at the bottom, giving trenches with aspect ratios above 20 and small sidewall ripples called scallops.

Plasma appears throughout the fab. Plasma CVD (PECVD) deposits films at about 300 to 400 °C instead of the 600 to 800 °C of thermal CVD, and high-density plasma CVD combines deposition with ion sputtering to fill narrow gaps. Magnetron sputtering confines electrons with magnets to sustain a dense argon plasma at about 0.1 to 1 Pa. Oxygen plasma ashing strips photoresist. Plasma nitridation and radical oxidation modify thin dielectrics at low temperature, plasma doping implants dopants at sub-keV energies, and ion implanters extract their ions from a plasma source.

Plasmas also cause problems. Charge collecting on isolated gates or resist can stress gate oxides only a few nanometres thick; in ion implantation a plasma flood gun supplies low-energy electrons to neutralize this charge. Energetic ion bombardment can damage crystals, and PECVD films usually contain hydrogen from the precursors, so their quality is below that of thermal CVD films. Plasma density and gas flow must be uniform across the wafer to keep etch and deposition rates even. Note that the plasma dispersion effect in silicon photonics refers to free carriers in a solid, not to a gas discharge.

faq.q: Why is plasma used in semiconductor manufacturing?
faq.a: Energetic electrons in a plasma create reactive radicals and ions without heating the wafer, enabling etching, deposition and surface treatment at low temperature. Ions accelerated by the sheath also make vertical, anisotropic etching possible.

faq.q: What is the difference between radicals and ions in a plasma?
faq.a: Radicals are neutral, highly reactive species that move randomly and etch isotropically, while ions carry charge, are accelerated by the sheath field and hit the wafer nearly vertically. Dry etching balances the two to control profile and selectivity.

faq.q: What is plasma damage?
faq.a: It is degradation caused by the plasma itself, mainly charge buildup that stresses thin gate oxides and lattice damage from ion bombardment. Process tuning, charge neutralization and layout rules are used to limit it.

ラジカル.desc: A neutral atom or molecule with an unpaired electron that is highly reactive chemically. Plasmas contain far more radicals than ions, and they drive chemical etching and deposition.

about.p: In a processing plasma, energetic electrons collide with feed-gas molecules. Some collisions ionize a molecule, but more of them simply break it apart into neutral fragments, because dissociation requires less energy than ionization; CF4 yields CF3 and F, and O2 yields atomic O. These fragments, with unpaired electrons, are radicals. Being uncharged, they are not pulled to the walls by the plasma sheath and survive longer than ions, so their density typically exceeds the ion density by two to three orders of magnitude or more.

Radicals arrive at the wafer from all directions and react spontaneously with suitable surfaces; fluorine radicals, for instance, convert silicon into volatile SiF4. On its own this chemistry is isotropic and highly selective. Ions are fewer, but the sheath accelerates them vertically, so they strike horizontal surfaces with tens to hundreds of electronvolts, enhancing reactions there and clearing passivation from trench bottoms. Anisotropic etching relies on this division of labour: radicals supply most of the chemistry, ions decide where it proceeds fastest, and sidewall passivation protects the vertical walls.

Some steps deliberately exclude ions. In a downstream or remote plasma, the plasma is generated away from the wafer so ions recombine before arriving and only long-lived radicals reach the surface. This gives damage-free resist ashing and isotropic cleans. Radical oxidation uses oxygen radicals to grow good-quality oxide at about 400–600 °C with little dependence on crystal orientation, which makes it suitable for FinFET fins and 3D NAND structures and for steps with tight thermal budgets.

Radical density depends on gas chemistry, pressure, RF power and how quickly radicals are consumed. Inductively coupled plasma (ICP) sources let engineers set plasma density, and with it radical and ion flux, separately from ion energy, and pulsed plasmas shift the mix of radical species. Consumption leads to loading effects: when a wafer exposes more etchable area, radicals are depleted and the etch rate falls. In deep, narrow features radicals must diffuse down the hole, so etch rate often decreases with aspect ratio.

faq.q: What is the difference between a radical and an ion in a plasma?
faq.a: A radical is an electrically neutral atom or molecule with an unpaired electron, so it is chemically reactive but not steered by electric fields. An ion carries charge and is accelerated by the sheath toward the wafer, giving directional bombardment.

faq.q: Why are there more radicals than ions in an etching plasma?
faq.a: Breaking a molecule apart takes less electron energy than ionizing it, so dissociation happens more often. Radicals also live longer because they are not drawn to the walls, so they accumulate to much higher densities than ions.

faq.q: Do radicals cause isotropic etching?
faq.a: Etching by radicals alone is isotropic because neutral radicals arrive from all directions. Directionality comes from ion bombardment combined with sidewall passivation.

ドライエッチング.desc: Removing material with plasma or gas instead of liquid chemicals. Combining ion bombardment allows anisotropic etching, which is essential for fine patterns.

about.h: What does the etching in a plasma
about.p: Etch plasmas are weakly ionized, typically about 0.01% or less, and contain electrons, positive ions, highly reactive radicals and neutral molecules. Radicals supply the chemistry and ions supply directional energy. Etching works only if the reaction product is volatile: silicon leaves as SiF4, SiCl4 or SiBr4, silicon dioxide etched with fluorocarbon gases such as CF4 or C4F8 leaves as SiF4 plus CO or CO2, and GaN etched with Cl2 and BCl3 leaves as GaCl3. Copper chlorides are not volatile at normal process temperatures, which is why copper lines are formed by damascene instead.

Ions and radicals together etch much faster than either alone; in a classic experiment, XeF2 gas plus an argon ion beam etched silicon about ten times faster than the sum of the two separately. Because ions arrive vertically, feature bottoms etch quickly while sidewalls do not. In addition, polymer from fluorocarbon gases or HBr-derived byproducts coats the sidewalls and blocks lateral attack, while ion bombardment clears it from the bottom. Too much passivation tapers the profile and too little causes bowing, so chemistry, bias and temperature are balanced.

Key figures are etch rate, uniformity, profile and selectivity; Cl2 and HBr etch polysilicon with selectivity above 100 to thin gate oxide. Endpoint is detected by optical emission spectroscopy (OES), watching emission lines that change when the film clears, such as CO at 483 nm dropping at the end of an oxide etch; interferometry helps when the open area is too small for a clear signal. Typical defects include microtrenching at feature corners and sidewall residues, which are removed by ashing and wet cleans to avoid corrosion and high contact resistance.

Wet etching dissolves films in liquid, usually isotropically, undercutting the mask by roughly the film thickness, but it is cheap, can process many wafers at once and gives high selectivity. Dry etching, including reactive ion etching (RIE) and high-density ICP etching, transfers mask patterns with little dimensional loss and is essential below a few micrometers. Fabs therefore use dry etching for patterning and wet processes for blanket film removal and cleaning. Many etch gases, especially fluorocarbons, have very high global warming potentials, so exhaust passes through abatement systems.

faq.q: What is the difference between dry etching and wet etching?
faq.a: Dry etching removes material with plasma or reactive gas and, with ion bombardment, can etch vertically for fine patterns. Wet etching uses liquid chemicals, is usually isotropic and undercuts the mask, but is simple, high-throughput and highly selective.

faq.q: Why can copper not be patterned by dry etching?
faq.a: Copper chlorides and fluorides do not evaporate below several hundred degrees Celsius, so reaction products stay on the surface instead of being pumped away. Copper wiring is therefore made by etching trenches in the dielectric, filling them with copper and polishing off the excess.

faq.q: How is the endpoint of a dry etch detected?
faq.a: Most tools monitor the plasma's optical emission at wavelengths tied to reaction products, which change sharply when the film clears and the underlayer is exposed. Laser or broadband interferometry of film thickness is used when the exposed area is small.

アッシング.desc: Removing photoresist that is no longer needed after etching or implantation by oxidizing it to ash, typically with an oxygen plasma.

about.p: Photoresist is an organic polymer of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. In an oxygen plasma, atomic oxygen radicals attack it and convert it into volatile CO, CO2 and H2O, which are pumped away; the name comes from this burning of the resist, as if to ash. Heating the wafer speeds the reaction. Many ashers are downstream (remote) designs in which the plasma is generated away from the wafer, so ions recombine before arriving and only radicals reach the surface, avoiding ion damage and charging of sensitive devices. Ashing is used after the resist has served as an etch or implant mask.

High-dose ion implantation drives hydrogen out of the resist surface and carbonizes it into a hard crust tens of nanometres thick, while the resist underneath stays soft. If the wafer is ashed hot immediately, gas released from the soft layer bursts through the crust, an effect called popping, scattering residue and particles. Post-implant strips therefore start at low temperature and ramp up, or remove the crust first with hydrogen-based plasma chemistry. The resist used for implant masking must also be thick enough to stop the ions, several times the projected range.

Oxygen plasma is a problem in copper interconnect stacks. SiOC low-k films owe their low dielectric constant to Si-CH3 (methyl) groups, and oxygen radicals strip these into Si-OH, which absorbs moisture and can raise the dielectric constant from about 3.0 to above 4. Porous films are damaged deeper because radicals penetrate through the pores. Reducing chemistries based on hydrogen replace oxygen in these steps, and silylation treatments and post-process dehydration bakes are used to repair or limit damage.

Ashing removes the organic bulk of the resist but not everything. Inorganic residues, metals introduced during implant or etch, and sidewall polymer from dry etching remain and are removed by a wet clean that follows. SPM (sulfuric acid and hydrogen peroxide, often about 4:1 at 120–150 °C), nicknamed piranha, oxidizes remaining organics. Chlorine-bearing etch residue must be removed promptly because it corrodes aluminium wiring. Ash-and-clean sequences are repeated throughout the flow, so their efficiency and gentleness affect both yield and cost.

faq.q: Why is it called ashing?
faq.a: The process burns the organic resist in an oxygen plasma, much like reducing material to ash, converting it into gases such as CO2 and H2O that are pumped away.

faq.q: What is the difference between ashing and wet resist stripping?
faq.a: Ashing removes resist dry, using plasma radicals, while wet stripping dissolves or oxidizes it with liquid chemistries such as SPM or organic strippers. In practice the two are often combined: ash first, then wet-clean the residue.

faq.q: Why are downstream ashers used?
faq.a: A downstream asher generates the plasma away from the wafer so only neutral radicals reach it. This avoids ion bombardment and charging damage to transistors and sensitive films.

終点検出.desc: Detecting the moment when the target film has been fully etched, commonly by monitoring changes in the plasma's emission spectrum.

アスペクト比.desc: The ratio of a hole's or trench's depth to its width. Higher ratios make etching and deposition harder; memory holes in 3D NAND reach several tens or more.

about.p: Aspect ratio is depth divided by width. A hole 100 nm across and 1 µm deep has an aspect ratio of 10. Memory holes in 3D NAND, about 100 nm wide and several µm deep, reach 50 to 100, and DRAM capacitor holes are also extremely tall and narrow. The same idea applies to lines: a copper interconnect's thickness-to-width ratio is often around 2. Aspect ratio should not be confused with selectivity, which is the ratio of etch rates of two materials, or with the overall shape of a die.

about.h: Why deep, narrow features are hard to etch
about.p: As aspect ratio rises, fewer reactive radicals reach the bottom because they react with or stick to the walls along the way, ions are deflected by charge built up on insulating sidewalls, and reaction products escape slowly. The etch rate therefore falls with depth, an effect called aspect-ratio-dependent etching (ARDE) or microloading, so narrow holes end up shallower than wide ones etched at the same time. Deep etches also suffer bowing, twisting and tapered bottoms, which is why high-aspect-ratio etching is one of the hardest steps in memory fabrication.

Physical vapor deposition (PVD) atoms travel in nearly straight lines, so sidewalls and bottoms of deep features are shadowed and receive little film. CVD under surface-reaction-limited conditions coats much more uniformly, and ALD can coat features with aspect ratios of several tens because each step is self-limiting. Filling a gap completely is harder than lining it: film builds up at the opening and pinches off, trapping a void. High-density plasma CVD, which sputters back the corners, and flowable CVD, which fills from the bottom, were developed for this.

Tall, thin structures can be pulled together during drying by the surface tension of liquid between them, and the force grows with aspect ratio and with narrower gaps. Low-surface-tension rinses such as IPA, hydrophobic surface treatments and supercritical CO2 drying reduce pattern collapse. In interconnects, raising aspect ratio lowers resistance but increases sidewall capacitance to neighbors, so it is balanced per metal level. In DRAM, capacitor aspect ratio is approaching practical limits, one motivation for stacking cells in 3D DRAM.

faq.q: How is aspect ratio calculated in semiconductor etching?
faq.a: Divide the depth of the hole or trench by its width or opening diameter. For example, a trench 50 nm wide and 500 nm deep has an aspect ratio of 10.

faq.q: What is ARDE in plasma etching?
faq.a: Aspect-ratio-dependent etching (ARDE) is the slowing of etch rate as features become narrower and deeper, because fewer radicals and ions reach the bottom and products escape more slowly. It makes narrow features shallower than wide ones etched at the same time.

faq.q: Why do high-aspect-ratio patterns collapse?
faq.a: When rinse liquid dries between tall, narrow structures, capillary forces from surface tension pull neighboring structures together. Higher aspect ratio and narrower spacing increase the risk.

ARDE(アスペクト比依存エッチング).desc: The slowdown of etch rate in narrower, deeper features because ions and radicals reach the bottom less easily. Also called the microloading effect.

ハードマスク.desc: A durable mask of nitride, carbon, metal or similar used when photoresist alone cannot survive the etch, for example in deep-hole etching.

about.p: Resist for fine patterns is thin, often around 100 nm, partly because tall narrow resist lines collapse. Etching consumes the mask too, and selectivity, the target etch rate divided by the mask etch rate, sets how much is lost: at 100 nm/min for oxide and 20 nm/min for the mask, selectivity is 5, so etching 500 nm of oxide consumes 100 nm of mask, and with overetch and edge erosion about 150–200 nm is needed. A hard mask, an inorganic or carbon film that resists the main etch far better, removes this limit.

about.h: How a hard mask is used
about.p: The film stack is deposited first, then lithography patterns the resist. A short etch transfers the pattern into the hard mask, the resist can be stripped, and the hard mask defines the main etch. Multilayer schemes chain this idea: in a tri-layer stack, resist patterns a thin silicon-containing antireflective layer, which in turn masks an oxygen-based etch of a thick carbon layer, because oxygen plasma removes carbon but barely attacks silicon-containing films. The thick carbon then masks the target film.

The hard mask must resist the chemistry that etches the target. Silicon nitride, oxide or oxynitride mask silicon and polysilicon etches; amorphous carbon or polysilicon masks oxide etches with fluorocarbon gases; titanium nitride has been used as a metal hard mask for trenches in low-k dielectrics. For the very deep, high-aspect-ratio holes of 3D NAND, amorphous-carbon hard masks several micrometers thick are used, so their deposition, etch and removal are major process steps. Carbon is easy to strip by oxygen ashing, while metal masks need wet removal.

Hard masks also define geometry beyond simple etch resistance. In self-aligned double or quadruple patterning, spacers deposited on mandrels and then etched back become the hard mask that sets line width. In self-aligned via schemes, the hard mask used to pattern wiring trenches is kept, or materially distinct caps are placed over lines, so a via etch stays confined within the target line's width even with a few nanometers of misalignment, avoiding shorts to neighboring lines at tight pitches.

faq.q: What is the difference between a hard mask and a photoresist mask?
faq.a: Photoresist is a light-sensitive polymer patterned directly by lithography but erodes quickly in plasma. A hard mask is a durable film such as nitride, oxide, carbon or metal that is patterned using the resist and then survives long, aggressive etches.

faq.q: Why is amorphous carbon used as a hard mask?
faq.a: Amorphous carbon etches very slowly in the fluorocarbon plasmas used for oxide and nitride, so a thick layer can last through deep etches, and it is removed easily afterward by oxygen ashing without damaging the patterned film.

faq.q: How thick should an etch mask be?
faq.a: Divide the target etch depth by the selectivity to estimate mask consumption, then add margin for overetch and corner erosion. For 500 nm of oxide at selectivity 5, about 100 nm is consumed, so roughly 150–200 nm is a safe thickness.

オーバーエッチング.desc: Continuing to etch for a set time after endpoint so the film is removed everywhere on the wafer. It is done under conditions with high selectivity to the underlying layer.

about.h: Why etching must continue past endpoint
about.p: No film is perfectly uniform. Thickness varies across the wafer, the etch rate varies from center to edge, and film deposited over steps is effectively thicker along the step sidewalls. Endpoint detection, typically by watching the plasma's optical emission change when the underlayer is exposed, signals that some areas have cleared, not all. If etching stopped there, residues and stringers along steps could short neighboring lines. Overetch continues for a set time, often about 20–50% of the main etch time, so that the film is cleared everywhere on the wafer.

about.h: Planning the time and the mask
about.p: Etch time is simply thickness divided by rate: a 500 nm film at 100 nm/min needs 5 minutes, and a 20% overetch makes it about 6 minutes. The mask is consumed throughout, so its thickness must be budgeted using selectivity, the ratio of the target film's etch rate to the mask's. With selectivity 5, etching 500 nm of oxide consumes about 100 nm of mask, so allowing for overetch and erosion at feature edges the mask should be at least about 150–200 nm thick. When photoresist cannot survive, a hard mask is used instead.

During overetch the underlying layer is exposed in the areas that cleared first and keeps being attacked, so loss there is roughly the overetch time multiplied by the underlayer etch rate. Processes therefore switch to high-selectivity conditions after endpoint. Gate etching is the classic case: a fast main etch sets the vertical profile through the gate material, then a gentler overetch with very high selectivity to the gate dielectric clears residues while barely touching the few-nanometre insulator. Punching through it would gouge the silicon underneath and ruin the transistor.

Extra etch time is not free. Once an insulating underlayer is exposed, positive charge can build up on it and deflect incoming ions sideways, undercutting the base of the pattern, a defect called notching that locally changes gate length; pulsed plasma or low-frequency bias reduces this charging. In isotropic wet etching, lateral undercut already equals roughly the film thickness at clearing and grows further during overetch. The overetch amount is therefore a compromise between complete clearing and the damage, linewidth change and underlayer loss it causes.

faq.q: Why is overetching necessary?
faq.a: Film thickness and etch rate vary across the wafer, and material on step sidewalls is effectively thicker, so some film remains when the endpoint is first detected. Overetching removes these residues everywhere.

faq.q: How much overetch is typically used?
faq.a: Overetch is often specified as a percentage of the main etch time, commonly around 20–50%, depending on film uniformity, topography and how much underlayer loss the device can tolerate.

faq.q: What is the difference between endpoint and overetch?
faq.a: Endpoint is the moment the etch tool detects that the underlayer has started to be exposed, while overetch is the additional, usually higher-selectivity etching performed after endpoint to clear the remaining film.

ICP(誘導結合プラズマ).desc: A method that generates a high-density plasma with RF current in a coil. It makes it easy to control plasma density and the energy of ions reaching the wafer independently.

about.p: An inductively coupled plasma (ICP) source drives RF current, commonly at 13.56 MHz, through a flat spiral or cylindrical coil placed outside a dielectric window of quartz or ceramic. The coil's oscillating magnetic field induces a circulating electric field inside the chamber, which accelerates electrons and keeps the gas ionized. Because power is transferred to the electrons inductively instead of through a high-voltage sheath at an electrode, the discharge reaches densities of about 10¹¹–10¹² cm⁻³ while operating at low pressures of a few pascals or less.

about.h: Separate knobs for density and ion energy
about.p: An ICP etcher uses two RF supplies. Source power to the coil sets plasma density, and therefore the flux of ions and radicals. A separate bias supply on the wafer chuck sets the DC self-bias and therefore the energy of ions striking the wafer. Engineers can etch fast with low ion energy to protect the underlayer and limit damage, or raise bias for more vertical profiles. Low pressure gives a long mean free path, so ions cross the sheath with few collisions and arrive nearly perpendicular, which supports anisotropic etching.

In a capacitively coupled plasma (CCP), RF power is applied between parallel-plate electrodes, so the same power that sustains the plasma also sets the sheath voltage; density and ion energy rise together. CCP densities are typically around 10⁹–10¹⁰ cm⁻³ with higher ion energies, and CCP tools, often with two frequencies to partly decouple the two, are widely used for oxide and nitride etching with fluorocarbon gases. ICP tools are favored for silicon, polysilicon gates, metals and compound semiconductors, where high radical flux and modest ion energy are wanted.

In fabs, ICP etchers handle shallow trench isolation, gate and fin etching, and metal lines. For GaN, chlorine-based ICP plasmas (Cl2, BCl3) etch LED and laser mesas and HEMT gate recesses at low ion energy to keep damage from degrading devices. High-density plasma CVD for gap fill also uses inductive sources. Outside processing, the same principle appears in ICP-MS, where an atmospheric-pressure argon plasma ionizes samples for trace-metal analysis, for example of droplets collected from wafer surfaces by vapor phase decomposition (VPD).

faq.q: What is the difference between ICP and CCP etching?
faq.a: ICP sustains the plasma with an inductive coil and biases the wafer with a separate RF supply, so plasma density and ion energy can be set independently and density is high. CCP drives parallel-plate electrodes, so density and ion energy are coupled and density is lower, which suits energetic dielectric etching.

faq.q: What plasma density does an ICP etcher reach?
faq.a: Typical ICP etch plasmas reach about 10¹¹–10¹² cm⁻³ at pressures of a few pascals or below, roughly one to two orders of magnitude denser than a conventional capacitively coupled plasma.

faq.q: Is the ICP in ICP-MS the same as in ICP etching?
faq.a: Both use an inductively coupled plasma, but ICP-MS runs an atmospheric-pressure argon plasma to ionize a liquid sample for mass spectrometry, while an ICP etcher runs a low-pressure reactive plasma to remove material from a wafer.

ALE(原子層エッチング).desc: Etching by alternating surface modification and removal so that each cycle removes about one atomic layer. It gives extremely precise control of etch depth.

about.p: Atomic layer etching (ALE) divides etching into separate, self-limiting half-steps. In a typical plasma ALE of silicon, chlorine is first introduced and adsorbs on the surface until it saturates, converting only the top layer into a weakly bonded chlorinated layer. After a purge, low-energy argon ions are applied with energy high enough to remove the modified layer but below the threshold for sputtering the unmodified silicon. Another purge follows and the cycle repeats. Each cycle removes a fixed amount, typically about 0.1–0.5 nm.

Because each step stops by itself, the etched depth is set by counting cycles rather than by timing a continuous etch. Removal per cycle is nearly the same in dense and isolated features, surfaces stay smooth, and the low ion energy causes little lattice damage. This makes ALE suited to steps that must stop within a few nanometers or etch films only a few atomic layers thick. The drawback is speed: gas switching and purges make each cycle slow, so ALE is usually reserved for the final, critical part of an etch.

Plasma ALE, which uses ions in the removal step, is directional and can etch the bottom of a feature without attacking its sidewalls. Thermal ALE instead uses purely chemical reactions, for example fluorinating a metal oxide surface and then removing the fluoride with a ligand-exchange precursor, so it etches isotropically. Thermal ALE is useful where a precise, uniform lateral recess is needed inside three-dimensional structures that ions cannot reach directly.

ALE is the etching counterpart of atomic layer deposition (ALD), which builds films by alternating self-limiting precursor exposures. Both trade speed for atomic-scale control and uniformity. As transistor structures move to gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheets with layers only a few nanometers thick, ALE is entering use in gate-region processing and other steps where overetch must be minimal, and it is also studied for low-damage recess etching in compound-semiconductor devices.

faq.q: What is the difference between ALE and ALD?
faq.a: Both rely on alternating self-limiting surface reactions, but ALD adds material a fraction of a nanometer per cycle while ALE removes it. They are often described as mirror-image processes.

faq.q: How much material does one ALE cycle remove?
faq.a: Typically about 0.1–0.5 nm per cycle, roughly one atomic layer or less, depending on the material and chemistry. Total depth is set by the number of cycles.

faq.q: Why is atomic layer etching not used for every etch step?
faq.a: Each cycle needs separate modification, purge and removal steps, so the net etch rate is far lower than continuous plasma etching. It is used where precision and low damage justify the lower throughput.

アンテナ効果.desc: Damage to a gate oxide when a connected conductor, such as a long wire, collects charge like an antenna during plasma processing. Design rules limit the area ratio of such wires to prevent it.

バッファードフッ酸(BHF).desc: Hydrofluoric acid buffered with ammonium fluoride. It is used for wet etching of SiO2 with a stable etch rate and little damage to resist.

シーズニング.desc: Running dummy wafers before product to stabilize the condition of an etch (or similar) chamber's walls, since wall changes alter process results.

セルフバイアス.desc: The negative DC potential that the wafer electrode naturally acquires in a capacitively coupled plasma. It accelerates positive ions toward the wafer, aiding anisotropic etching.

SC-1(APM).desc: A mixture of ammonia, hydrogen peroxide and water used first in RCA cleaning. It removes particles and organics while lightly etching the surface.

about.p: SC-1, also called APM (ammonia-peroxide mixture), is NH4OH, H2O2 and water, classically about 1:1:5 at around 70 °C. Peroxide continuously oxidizes the silicon surface to a thin oxide about 1 nm thick, while ammonia slowly dissolves that oxide at roughly 0.1–1 nm per minute. This gentle simultaneous oxidation and etching undercuts particles and lifts them off. In the alkaline solution both the silicon surface and most particles carry negative zeta potential, so detached particles are repelled rather than redeposited. The oxidizing chemistry also removes light organic contamination.

The RCA clean, published by Kern and colleagues in 1970, runs SC-1 first for particles and organics, then SC-2 (HCl, H2O2 and water) to dissolve metal contamination as chlorides, since metals tend to remain after the alkaline step. A dilute hydrofluoric acid (DHF) dip can be inserted to strip oxide, leaving a hydrogen-terminated, hydrophobic surface, and ultrapure-water rinses separate the steps. Heavier organics and resist residues are usually handled by sulfuric-peroxide mixture (SPM). Refined versions of this sequence remain the basis of front-end wafer cleaning.

The peroxide is what keeps SC-1 gentle. If its concentration is too low relative to ammonia, ammonia attacks bare silicon directly and roughens the surface, which can degrade a gate oxide grown later. Too aggressive a mix or too long a time removes more silicon or oxide than wanted. Ratios and temperature are therefore optimized, and modern fabs often use far more dilute SC-1 than the original recipe to limit material loss and roughening while still lifting particles.

SC-1 is often combined with megasonic agitation at around 1 MHz. At tens of kilohertz, collapsing cavitation bubbles deliver shocks strong enough to break fine patterns; at megahertz frequencies, fast acoustic streaming and a thin boundary layer instead dislodge particles below 0.1 µm with far less damage. The chemistry loosens and electrostatically repels particles, and the acoustic energy carries them away, which is why the pairing is so effective. Batch tanks and single-wafer spray tools both use this approach.

faq.q: What is SC-1 cleaning used for?
faq.a: Removing particles and light organic contamination from silicon wafers. It is the first step of the RCA clean and is followed by SC-2 for metals.

faq.q: What is the difference between SC-1 and SC-2?
faq.a: SC-1 is alkaline (ammonia plus peroxide) and removes particles and organics; SC-2 is acidic (hydrochloric acid plus peroxide) and removes metal contamination.

faq.q: Why does SC-1 contain hydrogen peroxide?
faq.a: Peroxide keeps the silicon covered with about 1 nm of oxide that ammonia slowly etches, so the surface is removed gently and evenly. Without enough peroxide, ammonia etches silicon directly and roughens it.

SC-2(HPM).desc: A mixture of hydrochloric acid, hydrogen peroxide and water used after SC-1 in RCA cleaning to remove metal contamination.

about.p: SC-2, Standard Clean 2, is a mixture of hydrochloric acid, hydrogen peroxide and water, also called HPM (hydrochloric acid/peroxide mixture). The classic RCA recipe uses volume ratios around 1:1:6 at about 70 to 80 °C for several minutes. It is the acidic, oxidizing companion to SC-1, the ammonia/peroxide mixture (APM). SC-2 does not measurably etch silicon or silicon dioxide, and it leaves a thin chemical oxide that makes the surface hydrophilic.

Hydrogen peroxide oxidizes metallic contaminants on the surface to ions, and the acidic chloride solution keeps them dissolved, partly as soluble chloride complexes, so they are rinsed away rather than redepositing. This targets alkali metals such as sodium and transition metals such as iron, nickel and zinc, as well as aluminum. In the alkaline SC-1 bath some of these metals, for example iron and aluminum, tend to form hydroxides that stay on or return to the wafer, which is why the acidic step follows.

The RCA clean, published by Kern and colleagues in 1970, runs SC-1 first to remove particles and organics, then SC-2 to strip metals, with ultrapure-water rinses between steps and a dilute hydrofluoric acid (HF) dip optionally inserted to remove oxide. A sulfuric acid/peroxide mixture (SPM) may precede everything when heavy organics such as resist residue are present. SC-2 is not effective for particles; particles adhere more readily in acidic solutions, so particle removal relies on SC-1 and physical action such as megasonics.

Refined versions of the sequence remain the basis of front-end cleaning, especially before gate oxidation and other high-temperature steps where metal contamination degrades oxide integrity and carrier lifetime. Fabs often use much more dilute mixtures and lower temperatures than the original recipe, which cut chemical use while still removing metals effectively, and many cleans now run in single-wafer spin processors instead of immersion baths. HCl fumes are corrosive, so baths and tools need good exhaust.

faq.q: What does SC-2 remove in wafer cleaning?
faq.a: SC-2 removes metal contamination, such as sodium, iron, nickel and aluminum, by oxidizing the metals and keeping them dissolved as ions in the acidic chloride solution. It does not remove particles effectively.

faq.q: Why is SC-2 done after SC-1?
faq.a: SC-1 removes particles and organics but can leave some metals behind as hydroxides in its alkaline solution. The acidic SC-2 step then dissolves those metals.

faq.q: What do HPM, APM and SPM stand for?
faq.a: HPM is the hydrochloric acid/hydrogen peroxide mixture (SC-2), APM is the ammonia/hydrogen peroxide mixture (SC-1), and SPM is the sulfuric acid/hydrogen peroxide mixture used to strip heavy organics.

SPM(硫酸過水).desc: A mixture of sulfuric acid and hydrogen peroxide. Its strong oxidizing power removes organics such as resist.

希フッ酸(DHF).desc: Hydrofluoric acid diluted with water. It removes native oxide from silicon and leaves a hydrophobic, hydrogen-terminated surface.

自然酸化膜.desc: A thin oxide about 1 nm thick that forms naturally when silicon is exposed to air or water. Because it raises contact resistance and disturbs epitaxial growth, it is removed right before such steps.

about.p: Native oxide is not grown on purpose. When bare silicon meets air or water, oxygen and moisture react with the surface, and the film grows quickly at first, then nearly stops at around 1 nm because further growth requires oxidants to diffuse through the oxide. The result is thin, often non-stoichiometric and can trap water and carbon. Thermal oxide, by contrast, is grown deliberately at about 800–1,200 °C to a controlled thickness, forming a dense film with a high-quality interface. That excellent thermal oxide is one reason silicon displaced germanium, which lacks a comparably good oxide.

about.h: Why it gets in the way
about.p: Even 1 nm of insulator matters at an interface that must conduct or grow crystal. Under a contact or silicide it raises contact resistance and can block the metal-silicon reaction. Before epitaxy, residual oxide or carbon prevents proper single-crystal growth and seeds defects such as stacking faults. It also degrades the uniformity of very thin gate dielectrics and the quality of direct bonding. Because a cleaned surface starts reoxidizing immediately, fabs limit the queue time between the clean and the next step, or link the two in vacuum.

The standard wet method is dilute hydrofluoric acid (DHF), typically 0.5–1% for tens of seconds, which dissolves SiO2 and leaves a hydrogen-terminated, hydrophobic surface; water beading off the wafer confirms removal. In RCA-style cleaning it complements SC-1, which removes particles and organics, and SC-2, which removes metals. Dry cleans using HF vapor or NF3/NH3-based remote plasma avoid liquids, so tall, narrow structures cannot collapse, and can be clustered with deposition chambers. Before silicon epitaxy, a hydrogen bake near 1,100 °C converts the oxide to volatile SiO, with lower-temperature alternatives where thermal budget is tight.

Native oxide is not always a nuisance. In vapor phase decomposition (VPD), HF vapor dissolves the native oxide and a scanned droplet collects surface metals for ICP-MS or TXRF analysis, reaching sensitivities around 10⁸–10⁹ atoms/cm². On aluminium bond pads, a dense native oxide a few nanometres thick protects the metal from corrosion, although probe needles and bonding must break through it. Other semiconductors are less fortunate: GaAs and germanium lack a good native oxide, which complicates their surface passivation and gate dielectrics.

faq.q: How thick is native oxide on silicon?
faq.a: Typically about 1 nm. It forms quickly in air or water and then almost stops growing at room temperature.

faq.q: How do you remove native oxide from silicon?
faq.a: Dip the wafer in dilute HF (about 0.5–1%) for tens of seconds, or use HF vapor or a remote-plasma dry clean. Before epitaxy, a high-temperature hydrogen bake can also remove it.

faq.q: What is the difference between native oxide and thermal oxide?
faq.a: Native oxide forms uncontrolled at room temperature, stops at about 1 nm and is of poor quality. Thermal oxide is grown deliberately at about 800–1,200 °C to a chosen thickness and has a dense film and a good interface.

パッドコンディショニング.desc: Abrading the surface of a CMP polishing pad with a diamond tool to restore its texture and slurry-holding ability, stabilizing the removal rate. Also called dressing.

エロージョン.desc: In CMP, excessive polishing of an entire region of dense lines, insulator included, so it ends up lower than its surroundings. Along with dishing of wide lines, it is a typical CMP defect.

プレストンの式.desc: The empirical rule that the CMP removal rate is proportional to the product of polishing pressure and the relative speed between pad and wafer.

セリア(酸化セリウム).desc: An abrasive used in CMP slurries. It reacts chemically with oxide and gives high selectivity to nitride, so it is used for STI CMP.

パターン倒壊.desc: A defect in which tall, fine patterns topple or stick together during cleaning and drying because of the surface tension of liquid left between them.

枚葉式洗浄.desc: A cleaning method that processes one wafer at a time. It minimizes cross-contamination and allows per-wafer control. Immersing many wafers in a tank at once is batch cleaning.

MBE(分子線エピタキシー).desc: Epitaxial growth in ultra-high vacuum by supplying source materials to the substrate as molecular beams. It controls thickness and composition at the atomic-layer level and is used in compound-semiconductor research and quantum structures.

オートドーピング.desc: Unintended incorporation into a growing epitaxial layer of dopant from the substrate or elsewhere via the gas phase. It is a problem when growing lightly doped layers on heavily doped substrates.

臨界膜厚.desc: The maximum thickness to which a lattice-mismatched layer can be grown while staying strained without forming dislocations. Beyond it, misfit dislocations appear.

ミスフィット転位.desc: A dislocation at the interface between crystals with different lattice constants that relieves strain. It forms when the grown layer exceeds the critical thickness.

貫通転位.desc: A dislocation that runs up through the grown layer to the surface. GaN on sapphire or silicon has high densities (about 10⁸-10⁹ cm⁻²), which degrade device performance and reliability.

積層欠陥.desc: A planar defect in which the stacking order of atomic planes is disrupted. It is a concern in epitaxial layers, thermal oxidation (OSF) and SiC crystals.

横方向エピタキシャル成長(ELO).desc: Growing crystal from mask openings and letting it spread sideways over the mask. Dislocations from below do not propagate into the overgrown regions, reducing dislocations in materials such as GaN.

超格子.desc: A periodic structure of alternating layers of different materials, each a few nanometers thick. It shows electronic properties absent in bulk crystals and is used in lasers, buffer layers and more.

SiGe(シリコンゲルマニウム).desc: An alloy of silicon and germanium with a larger lattice constant than silicon. Grown epitaxially, it is used to strain channels, as the base of HBTs and as the sacrificial layer in GAA transistors.

about.p: Silicon and germanium are both group IV elements with the diamond structure and mix in any ratio, so SiGe is a continuous alloy rather than a compound. Adding germanium enlarges the lattice constant from about 0.543 nm for silicon toward 0.566 nm for germanium, roughly 4% larger, and lowers the band gap from 1.12 eV toward 0.66 eV. SiGe also has higher hole mobility than silicon. It is grown by chemical vapor deposition using germane (GeH4) with silane or dichlorosilane, and the gas flow ratio sets the germanium content, which high-resolution X-ray diffraction can then measure together with strain.

SiGe grown on silicon is compressively strained because its larger lattice is squeezed to match the substrate, and this strain stays coherent only up to a critical thickness, roughly tens of nanometers at 20% germanium. Selective epitaxy embeds boron-doped SiGe in pMOS source and drain regions, which squeezes the channel and raises hole mobility; advanced processes also use SiGe as the pMOS channel itself. The reverse trick serves nMOS: a thin silicon layer grown on relaxed SiGe, reached through a graded buffer several micrometers thick, is stretched into tensile strain that raises electron mobility.

In a SiGe heterojunction bipolar transistor (HBT), the base is an epitaxial SiGe layer tens of nanometers thick, boron-doped during growth. Its narrower band gap blocks holes from flowing back into the emitter, so the base can be thin and heavily doped without losing injection efficiency. Grading the germanium from near 0% at the emitter side to 20 to 30% at the collector side builds in an electric field that speeds electrons across. A little carbon limits boron diffusion. Transition frequencies of hundreds of gigahertz suit SiGe BiCMOS to RF front ends, optical links and automotive radar.

Nanosheet gate-all-around (GAA) transistors start from an epitaxial stack of alternating silicon and SiGe layers, with about 25 to 30% germanium. The SiGe ends are first recessed and filled with dielectric inner spacers. After the dummy gate is removed, the remaining SiGe is etched away with high selectivity, often by remote-plasma or chemical etching, leaving suspended silicon sheets that high-k dielectric and metal gate then wrap on all sides. Because high temperature would relax strain or intermix the layers, later steps are held to a thermal budget of about 600 to 700 °C or less.

faq.q: Why is SiGe used in pMOS transistors?
faq.a: SiGe has a larger lattice constant than silicon, so SiGe embedded in the source and drain compresses the silicon channel, and compressive strain raises hole mobility. SiGe also has higher intrinsic hole mobility, so it is used as a pMOS channel material as well.

faq.q: What is a SiGe HBT?
faq.a: It is a bipolar transistor whose base is made of SiGe, whose narrower band gap than the silicon emitter forms a heterojunction. This allows a thin, heavily doped base and, with graded germanium, a built-in accelerating field, giving transition frequencies of hundreds of gigahertz.

faq.q: Is SiGe a compound semiconductor?
faq.a: No, it is an alloy of two group IV elements that mix in any proportion, not a compound of elements from different groups like GaAs. Its properties vary continuously with germanium content, and it is processed with silicon-compatible equipment.

ひずみシリコン.desc: Silicon whose band structure is modified by strain to raise carrier mobility. Tensile strain helps nMOS and compressive strain helps pMOS; it is applied with SiGe source/drain regions, nitride films and the like.

HVPE(ハイドライド気相成長).desc: Vapor-phase growth using gallium chloride, formed by reacting HCl with gallium, together with ammonia. Its very high growth rate is used to grow thick GaN crystals for free-standing substrates.

ステップフロー成長.desc: A growth mode in which the crystal extends sideways from atomic steps on a slightly off-axis substrate. In SiC it is used so the layer inherits the substrate's polytype.

4H-SiC.desc: The SiC polytype mainly used for power devices. It has a wide band gap of about 3.3 eV and relatively high electron mobility.

ビア.desc: A conductor that electrically connects the wiring layers above and below it in a multilevel interconnect. It is made by filling a hole in the insulator with metal.

コンタクト.desc: The connection between a transistor's source, drain or gate and the lowest wiring layer. It is made by filling a contact hole in the insulator with tungsten or similar metal.

シリサイド.desc: A compound of silicon and a metal, such as NiSi or TiSi2. It is formed on source, drain and gate surfaces to reduce resistance and contact resistance.

デュアルダマシン法.desc: Forming both the trench for a wire and the hole for a via in the insulator, filling them with copper together and finishing with a single CMP step. It reduces process steps.

about.h: How dual damascene builds a wiring level
about.p: A dielectric stack, usually a low-k film with thin etch-stop or cap layers, is deposited first. Lithography and etching then open two kinds of features in it: via holes that reach down to the wiring level below, and trenches shaped like the wires of the current level. A thin diffusion barrier such as TaN/Ta and a copper seed layer are sputtered, copper is electroplated to fill vias and trenches together, and chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) removes the excess copper and barrier from the top surface, leaving metal inlaid only where it was patterned.

about.h: Why copper needs a damascene process
about.p: Aluminum wiring was made by depositing a metal film and etching it into lines. Copper is difficult to pattern that way because its reaction products with common plasma etch chemistries are not volatile at normal process temperatures. Damascene processing sidesteps the problem by etching the dielectric instead and filling it with metal, much like the inlay craft of Damascus that gave the method its name. The barrier layer is essential because copper diffuses readily into silicon and dielectrics, where it degrades devices and insulation.

Single damascene builds vias and lines in separate passes, each with its own dielectric patterning, barrier and seed deposition, plating and CMP. Dual damascene patterns both features before a single metallization, saving one round each of deposition, plating and CMP per wiring level. Because the via and the line above it are one continuous piece of copper, there is no barrier interface between them, which lowers via resistance and helps electromigration reliability. Advanced chips repeat this module for each of their many copper levels.

Dual damascene comes in variants that differ in which feature is opened first: via-first etches the holes before the trenches, trench-first does the reverse, and hard-mask schemes help align vias to the trench above. At advanced nodes vias are only about 20 nm across and a chip contains billions of them, so void-free filling, uniform CMP and avoiding damage to fragile low-k dielectrics during etch and resist removal strongly affect both performance and yield. A single open via can kill a circuit.

faq.q: What is the difference between single and dual damascene?
faq.a: Single damascene forms vias and wiring lines in separate deposition, plating and CMP sequences. Dual damascene opens both in the dielectric first and fills them with copper in one sequence, saving steps and avoiding a barrier layer between via and line.

faq.q: Why is copper wiring not made by etching like aluminum?
faq.a: Copper does not form volatile etch products easily with standard plasma chemistries, so patterning a copper film by dry etching is impractical. Instead, the dielectric is patterned and filled with copper, then polished flat.

faq.q: Where does the name damascene come from?
faq.a: It comes from the traditional inlay craft associated with Damascus, in which gold or silver was set into grooves cut in a metal surface, just as copper is inlaid into grooves in the dielectric.

シード層.desc: A thin copper film deposited by sputtering or similar before copper electroplating. It provides the conductive path for the plating current.

エアギャップ.desc: Leaving part of the insulator between wires as empty space. Since air has a relative permittivity of about 1, it greatly reduces capacitance between wires.

about.h: Why air between wires lowers capacitance
about.p: The capacitance between neighboring wires is proportional to the relative permittivity (k) of the material between them. Silicon dioxide has k of about 3.9, carbon-doped low-k films reach roughly 2.5 to 3, and air or vacuum sits at about 1, lower than any solid. Replacing part of the inter-wire dielectric with an air gap therefore cuts inter-wire capacitance by about 20 to 30% in practical structures, which reduces RC delay, dynamic switching power and crosstalk between adjacent signals.

One approach finishes the copper lines first, removes the dielectric between them by etching, and then deposits a cap film with poor step coverage so that it pinches off at the top and seals a void below. Another deliberately deposits a dielectric that cannot fill narrow spaces conformally, leaving voids between closely spaced lines. Either way, the gap forms naturally only where lines are tight, which matches where capacitance matters most. Air-gap ideas are also applied to the spacers beside transistor gates to cut gate-to-contact capacitance.

A cavity weakens the wiring stack mechanically, which matters during CMP, wafer dicing and packaging stress. Air conducts heat poorly, so wires surrounded by gaps run hotter. A via landing from the level above must not punch into a gap, so layouts keep gaps away from via landing areas, sometimes with an extra mask. Moisture and process chemicals must not get trapped inside. For these reasons air gaps are typically used only on the dense, tight-pitch levels where capacitance reduction pays off most, while other levels keep solid low-k dielectric.

about.h: Intended air gaps vs. unwanted ones
about.p: Outside interconnect design, an air gap is usually a defect. In packages, delamination between mold compound and die or lead frame leaves a thin air layer that weakens the joint and can lead to cracking. Scanning acoustic microscopy (SAT) detects it non-destructively: solids and air differ so strongly in acoustic impedance that an air gap reflects nearly all of the ultrasound, making delaminations, cracks and voids stand out clearly. Unintended voids in metal or dielectric fill are similarly treated as defects.

faq.q: Why do air gaps reduce interconnect capacitance?
faq.a: Capacitance scales with the permittivity of the material between conductors, and air has a relative permittivity of about 1, lower than any solid dielectric. Replacing part of the dielectric with air lowers inter-wire capacitance, typically by about 20 to 30%.

faq.q: What is the difference between an air gap and a low-k dielectric?
faq.a: A low-k dielectric is a solid film with reduced permittivity, typically around 2.5 to 3, that fills the space between wires. An air gap leaves part of that space empty, reaching lower effective capacitance but with weaker mechanical strength and heat conduction.

faq.q: What are the disadvantages of air gaps?
faq.a: They reduce mechanical strength, worsen heat dissipation, and create a risk that vias land in the cavity. These issues limit air gaps to the densest wiring levels.

IRドロップ.desc: The drop in supply voltage reaching a circuit because current (I) flows through the resistance (R) of the power wiring. It increases delay and can cause malfunctions.

クロストーク.desc: Noise that appears on one wire when the signal on a neighboring wire changes, mainly through capacitive coupling. Wider spacing and shield wires reduce it.

about.p: Two neighboring wires form a capacitor. When the aggressor wire switches, it injects charge through the coupling capacitance Cc into the victim wire. If the victim is floating or only weakly driven, the resulting glitch is roughly the aggressor swing multiplied by Cc / (Cc + Cg), where Cg is the victim's capacitance to ground and other wires. A driven victim pulls back toward its level at a rate set by its driver resistance, so weak drivers and long parallel runs give the largest and longest glitches. A glitch that reaches a latch, clock or dynamic node can flip a stored value.

Crosstalk matters even when nothing glitches, because it alters timing. If the victim and aggressor switch in the same direction at the same time, the voltage across Cc barely changes and the coupling capacitance effectively vanishes, speeding the victim. If they switch in opposite directions, the voltage across Cc changes by twice the swing, so the capacitance effectively doubles, a Miller-factor effect, slowing the victim. Static timing analysis with signal-integrity awareness therefore uses extracted coupling capacitances and switching windows to bound the best and worst cases.

A wire's capacitance has lateral components to neighbors on the same layer, vertical components to layers above and below and to the substrate, and fringe components from fields curling around its edges. In a parallel-plate approximation C = εS/d, so halving spacing roughly doubles lateral capacitance. Advanced metal layers use tight pitch and tall wires, with thickness-to-width ratios around 2, to keep resistance down, which further enlarges facing sidewall area. Lateral coupling thus becomes the dominant share of total capacitance, and parasitic extraction with field solvers after place and route quantifies it.

The main levers are spacing, shielding and dielectric constant. Wider spacing on critical nets, power or ground shield wires between sensitive signals, and low-k dielectrics such as carbon-doped oxide (about 2.7–3.0) or porous films (about 2.2–2.5) instead of SiO2 (about 3.9) all reduce coupling. Stronger victim drivers recover faster, and avoiding long parallel runs limits the coupling length. The word is used beyond wiring: image-sensor pixels leak light and charge into neighbors, and multiplexed sample-and-hold inputs can carry residue from a previous channel.

faq.q: What are aggressor and victim nets in crosstalk analysis?
faq.a: The aggressor is the switching net that injects noise, and the victim is the neighboring net that receives it through coupling capacitance. The same net can be an aggressor in one analysis and a victim in another.

faq.q: How do you reduce crosstalk in chip layout?
faq.a: Increase spacing, insert grounded or power shield wires, shorten parallel routes, and strengthen victim drivers. Low-k dielectrics reduce coupling capacitance at the process level.

faq.q: Is on-chip crosstalk capacitive or inductive?
faq.a: On-chip crosstalk in short and medium wires is dominated by capacitive coupling. Inductive coupling becomes significant for long, fast global wires, packages and circuit boards.

パッシベーション膜.desc: A film formed as the topmost layer of a chip to protect the circuitry from moisture, contamination and mechanical damage. Silicon nitride and polyimide are typical materials.

裏面電源供給.desc: Placing the power wiring on the back of the wafer so the front-side wiring can be used for signals. It reduces voltage drop and routing congestion.

about.h: Why move power to the back
about.p: In a conventional chip, both signal and power wiring sit above the transistors in a back-end-of-line (BEOL) stack of about 15 levels. Power enters at the top through thick wires and then descends through more than ten levels of increasingly fine wires and vias to reach each transistor, losing voltage along the way (IR drop). Power rails also occupy routing tracks inside every standard cell, crowding the signal wiring. Backside power delivery separates the two networks: signals stay on the front, while power is delivered from the back of the wafer.

The front side, transistors and signal wiring, is processed first. The wafer is then bonded face-down to a carrier wafer and the original silicon is thinned from the back to hundreds of nanometers or a few micrometers. Very small vias are etched from the back to reach buried power rails or the transistors' source and drain contacts directly, and thick, low-resistance power wiring is built on the back. Announced implementations include Intel's PowerVia and TSMC's A16 process, among others.

Feeding transistors from directly below shortens the power path and lowers IR drop, freeing front-side tracks for signals, which eases routing congestion and allows smaller standard cells. The costs are extra process complexity: wafer bonding and thinning, alignment of backside features to front-side devices despite distortion from bonding, and new approaches to failure analysis. Heat removal also changes, because the active layer ends up sandwiched between bonding and wiring layers, so thermal design must be reconsidered.

about.h: Why it matters for scaling now
about.p: As transistors shrink, performance is increasingly limited by parasitics rather than the channel: source, drain and contact resistance can approach half of total on-resistance, and wiring resistance rises as pitches shrink into the 20 nm range. Gains therefore come from extrinsic improvements such as better contact materials, low-k or air-gap spacers and backside power delivery. It is often paired with gate-all-around transistors and is considered especially important for stacked CFET devices, whose lower tier is hard to reach from above.

faq.q: What is a backside power delivery network (BSPDN)?
faq.a: It is a chip wiring scheme that places the power distribution network on the back of a thinned wafer and connects it to transistors from below, leaving the front-side metal levels for signals.

faq.q: What is the difference between backside power delivery and a buried power rail?
faq.a: A buried power rail embeds the cell's power lines below the transistors instead of in the first metal level. Backside power delivery moves the whole power network to the back of the wafer and can feed buried rails or transistor contacts directly through backside vias.

faq.q: Why does backside power delivery reduce IR drop?
faq.a: Power no longer has to descend through ten or more thin front-side metal levels and vias; it arrives through short, thick backside wires, so the resistance between the supply and each transistor is much lower.

MOL(ミドル・オブ・ライン).desc: The contacts and local interconnects that link transistors (FEOL) to the multilevel wiring (BEOL). With scaling, their resistance has grown and now limits performance.

表皮効果.desc: The concentration of high-frequency current near the surface of a conductor, which raises its effective resistance. The higher the frequency, the thinner the surface layer carrying the current.

ブラックの式.desc: An empirical formula for interconnect lifetime under electromigration in terms of current density and temperature. Lifetime is inversely proportional to a power of current density and falls exponentially as temperature rises.

about.p: Black's equation is an empirical model for the median or mean time to failure of a wire under electromigration: MTTF = A·J^(−n)·exp(Ea/kT). J is the current density, n the current-density exponent (2 in Black's original form, with values between about 1 and 2 reported), Ea the activation energy of the dominant atomic diffusion path, k Boltzmann's constant, T the absolute temperature, and A a constant that captures material, geometry and microstructure. Ea is on the order of 0.5 to 1 eV, depending on the metal and on whether atoms move mainly along grain boundaries or interfaces.

about.h: Using it to extrapolate test data
about.p: Electromigration failures at use conditions would take years to appear, so test structures are stressed at elevated temperatures, around 300 °C, and high current densities, then the equation extrapolates the results. The acceleration factor is (J_test/J_use)^n multiplied by exp[(Ea/k)(1/T_use − 1/T_test)]. The sensitivity is large: with n = 2, halving current density quadruples lifetime, and with Ea near 0.9 eV, raising temperature from 105 °C to 125 °C shortens lifetime by roughly a factor of four. Fitting n and Ea requires tests at several currents and temperatures.

Electromigration happens because conduction electrons transfer momentum to metal atoms, slowly pushing them in the direction of electron flow. Where more atoms leave a region than arrive, such as at a via or grain-boundary junction, voids form and eventually open the line; where atoms pile up, hillocks can short to neighbours. In copper, transport is dominated by the top interface with the dielectric cap, so cobalt caps can extend lifetime substantially. Black's equation does not capture back-stress effects: very short lines can be immune because opposing mechanical stress halts atom flow (the Blech effect).

Foundries translate Black's equation and test data into maximum allowed current densities per metal layer, width and temperature, typically on the order of MA/cm². Power and ground lines carrying steady DC current in one direction are the most critical. Signal lines with alternating current partly recover because atoms move back and forth, so their limits are less strict. Joule heating raises the local temperature of heavily loaded wires, which feeds back through the exponential term. Sign-off flows therefore check electromigration together with IR drop on the power grid.

faq.q: What is Black's equation used for?
faq.a: It estimates interconnect lifetime under electromigration as a function of current density and temperature. Engineers use it to extrapolate accelerated test results to operating conditions and to set current-density limits for wires.

faq.q: How does temperature affect electromigration lifetime?
faq.a: Lifetime falls exponentially with temperature through the exp(Ea/kT) term. For an activation energy near 0.9 eV, a 20 °C rise around 105 to 125 °C cuts lifetime by roughly four times.

faq.q: What is the current density exponent n in Black's equation?
faq.a: It describes how strongly lifetime depends on current density; Black originally used n = 2. Measured values range roughly from 1 to 2 depending on whether void nucleation or void growth limits lifetime.

ダイシング.desc: Cutting a wafer into individual chips (dies). Besides sawing with a rotating blade, there are methods such as stealth dicing, which forms a modified layer inside the wafer with a laser.

about.p: The wafer is first mounted on adhesive dicing tape stretched across a ring frame so the dies stay in place once cut. A diamond blade tens of micrometres thick, spinning at high speed, cuts along the scribe lines (streets) while water cools it and flushes away debris. The cut removes a kerf tens of micrometres wide, so streets must allow for kerf plus edge chipping, and test structures (TEGs) placed there are destroyed. With fragile low-k dielectric stacks, a laser usually grooves the surface first so the blade does not chip or delaminate them.

Stealth dicing focuses an infrared laser, at a wavelength silicon largely transmits, inside the wafer to create a modified layer along each street; expanding the tape then cleaves the wafer along it. The surface is not cut, so the process is dry, produces almost no debris and has nearly zero kerf. It suits contamination- and vibration-sensitive MEMS, thin wafers and very small dies, where narrower streets raise dies per wafer. Laser ablation grooving is different: it removes surface material, mainly to open the top layers before blade dicing.

about.h: Where dicing sits in the flow
about.p: Dicing follows wafer test and back grinding, which thins the wafer from about 750 µm to its target, down to tens of micrometres for stacked memory. Dies are then picked from the tape for die bonding, wire bonding or flip-chip attach, and encapsulation. In dicing before grinding (DBG), partial-depth grooves are cut first and grinding separates the dies, reducing breakage of very thin chips. In wafer-level packaging, redistribution layers and solder balls are formed before singulation. Slicing an ingot into wafers is a different step, done with a multi-wire saw.

Dicing leaves damage at die edges: front-side and backside chipping, microcracks and a damaged sidewall layer. These flaws can grow under thermal cycling or handling and lower die strength, so cut quality is inspected and blade type, feed speed and cut depth are tuned to each wafer stack. Seal rings around each die help stop cracks and moisture from reaching active circuitry. In silicon photonics, edge couplers need a clean facet after singulation, while grating couplers allow optical testing on the wafer before dicing.

faq.q: What is the difference between blade dicing and stealth dicing?
faq.a: Blade dicing removes a kerf tens of micrometres wide with a spinning diamond blade and water, while stealth dicing forms a modified layer inside the wafer with an infrared laser and cleaves it by expanding the tape. Stealth dicing is dry, with almost no kerf or debris.

faq.q: Is back grinding done before or after dicing?
faq.a: Usually before: the wafer is thinned first and then diced. In dicing before grinding (DBG) the grooves are cut first and grinding completes the separation, which suits very thin chips.

faq.q: What is kerf in wafer dicing?
faq.a: Kerf is the width of material removed by the cut. With blade dicing it is tens of micrometres, which sets a minimum width for the scribe lines between dies.

ダイボンディング.desc: Attaching and fixing a diced chip at its position on a lead frame or package substrate, using adhesive, solder or sintered material.

バックグラインド.desc: Grinding the back of a wafer before dicing to thin it for packaging. Chips for stacking are thinned to a few tens of micrometers.

WLP(ウエハレベルパッケージ).desc: A package in which redistribution wiring and external terminals are formed while the chips are still in wafer form, before dicing. The result is a small package about the size of the chip.

about.h: How a wafer-level package is built
about.p: In a wafer-level package (WLP), packaging steps run on the whole wafer at once instead of on individual dies. On top of the chip's passivation, a polymer dielectric is coated, and copper redistribution layers (RDL) are plated to route signals from the fine-pitch bond pads to a coarser array of terminal positions. Under-bump metallization is formed at those positions and solder balls are attached. Only then is the wafer diced. Because every die is processed in parallel by wafer-fab-like lithography and plating, the package adds almost no area and the cost per die falls as die count per wafer rises.

In fan-in WLP the redistribution wiring and solder balls must fit inside the die outline, so the package is exactly die-sized and the number of terminals is limited by the die area and ball pitch. Fan-out WLP removes that limit: diced, known-good dies are placed on a carrier with space between them and embedded in mold compound to form a reconstituted wafer. The RDL can then extend beyond the die edge onto the mold area, allowing more I/O. Fan-out needs no laminate substrate and is thin, so it is used even for smartphone processors.

A chip-scale package (CSP) is any package no larger than about 1.2 times the die area, usually with BGA-style ball terminals underneath. Many CSPs still mount the die on a small substrate with wire bonds or flip-chip bumps. A fan-in WLP is the limiting case of a CSP: there is no separate substrate at all, and the package outline equals the die. That makes it the smallest and thinnest option, with very short connections that keep parasitic inductance low, which suits high-frequency and power-management parts.

Without a substrate in between, the silicon is soldered almost directly to the printed circuit board. Silicon and board materials expand differently with temperature, so thermal cycling strains the solder joints, and the strain grows with die size. Fan-in WLP is therefore most common for relatively small dies with modest pin counts, such as power-management chips, sensors and RF components in phones and wearables. Larger or higher-I/O dies move to fan-out WLP or to conventional flip-chip packages. The bare silicon edges also need care during handling and board assembly.

faq.q: What does WLP stand for in semiconductor packaging?
faq.a: WLP stands for wafer-level package, a package whose redistribution wiring and solder terminals are formed on the whole wafer before it is diced into individual chips.

faq.q: What is the difference between fan-in and fan-out WLP?
faq.a: Fan-in WLP keeps all terminals within the die outline, so the package is exactly die-sized but I/O count is limited. Fan-out WLP embeds dies in mold compound so wiring and balls can extend beyond the die edge.

faq.q: Is WLP the same as CSP?
faq.a: WLP is one type of chip-scale package. CSP covers any package up to roughly 1.2 times the die area, while a fan-in WLP matches the die size exactly and has no separate substrate.

CSP(チップサイズパッケージ).desc: A general term for packages shrunk to nearly the size of the chip. They are widely used in compact devices such as smartphones.

リフローはんだ付け.desc: Printing solder paste on a circuit board, placing components and heating everything in an oven to melt the solder. It is the standard method for surface mounting.

熱抵抗.desc: A measure of how hard it is for heat to flow, in °C/W. Multiplying dissipated power by thermal resistance gives the temperature rise. Junction-to-ambient thermal resistance is written θJA.

about.p: Thermal resistance treats heat flow like current in a circuit: power plays the role of current, temperature difference plays the role of voltage, and the temperature rise across a path is power multiplied by thermal resistance. Because only differences matter, °C/W and K/W are the same unit. Resistances along one path add in series, so a device on a heatsink sees junction-to-case, case-to-heatsink and heatsink-to-air terms summed. Parallel heat paths, such as heat leaving through both the package top and the board, combine like parallel resistors and lower the total.

θJA is junction-to-ambient resistance measured on a standardized test board in still air, so it depends strongly on board copper area, layer count and airflow, and is best used for comparing packages. θJC is junction-to-case resistance measured with the case held at a fixed temperature, and is the starting point when a heatsink is attached. ψJT is not a true resistance but a characterization parameter: it relates junction temperature to the measured top-of-package temperature when most heat actually flows into the board, so Tj ≈ Ttop + P × ψJT.

A transistor dissipating 0.5 W in a small TO-92 package with θJA around 200 °C/W rises about 100 °C above ambient, which can exceed a typical 150 °C junction limit on a warm day. A power device with θJC = 1.0 °C/W, 0.5 °C/W of thermal grease and a 3.0 °C/W heatsink has 4.5 °C/W in total, so 10 W of loss raises the junction 45 °C above ambient. A 50 W processor on a 0.5 K/W cooler runs about 25 °C above the surrounding air.

about.h: Steady state vs. transients, and reliability
about.p: Thermal resistance describes steady state. Real packages also store heat, so for short power pulses designers use transient thermal impedance curves, which start low and approach the steady-state value as pulse length grows. Over a product's life, thermal resistance can increase: in power modules, repeated heating and cooling cracks solder layers and lifts bond wires because silicon, aluminum and copper expand at different rates. Heat spreaders, thermal interface materials (TIMs) and better die attach keep resistance low, and lower junction temperature generally extends lifetime.

faq.q: How do you calculate junction temperature from thermal resistance?
faq.a: Add the ambient temperature to power times the junction-to-ambient thermal resistance: Tj = Ta + P × θ. For example, 2 W in a 40 °C/W package runs 80 °C above ambient.

faq.q: Can I use the datasheet θJA for my own board?
faq.a: Only as a rough guide. It is measured on a standard test board in still air, and a real board with different copper area, layer count or airflow can change it by up to around a factor of two, so verify by measurement.

faq.q: Is °C/W the same as K/W?
faq.a: Yes. Thermal resistance relates a temperature difference to power, and a difference of 1 °C equals a difference of 1 K.

ウエハテスト(プローブテスト).desc: Checking the electrical characteristics of each chip on the wafer by touching probes to its pads before dicing. It finds bad chips before assembly so they are not packaged needlessly.

about.p: A prober loads the wafer onto a chuck, aligns it optically and steps it so that the needles of a probe card land on each die's pads, which are tens of micrometres square. After first touch, the needles are pushed a little further, called overdrive, so the tips scrub through the aluminium oxide and make stable contact. Automatic test equipment (ATE) with hundreds to thousands of channels then supplies power, drives patterns and measures responses. The chuck can be heated or cooled, roughly −40 to 150 °C, and many probe cards contact several dies at once to cut test time.

Typical wafer-level tests check continuity, opens and shorts, supply and leakage currents, and logic function through scan patterns or built-in self-test, plus analog and memory blocks. Memory testing also finds failing cells whose addresses are programmed into fuses or antifuses, redirecting accesses to spare rows and columns (redundancy repair). Analog references are often trimmed the same way. Some products also write the lot number, wafer number and die coordinates into on-chip fuses, so a field return can be traced back to its manufacturing and test history.

The usual sequence is wafer test, assembly, final test and shipment, sometimes with burn-in or system-level test added. Wafer test screens out bad dies before money is spent packaging them, since defects cost more the later they are found. Final test checks the packaged part and confirms nothing was damaged in assembly; some high-speed measurements are also easier through a socket than through probe needles. In multi-die packages, wafer test must deliver known good die, because one bad die can scrap the whole assembly. Stage yields multiply: 95% process yield times 90% test yield gives about 85.5%.

Results are stored as electronic wafer maps rather than the ink dots once used to mark bad dies; die bonders read the map and pick only good, correctly graded dies. The maps are also a diagnostic tool. Failures clustered at the wafer edge point to deposition or etch uniformity, failures repeating at the same position in every exposure shot point to a reticle defect, and streaks suggest scratches. Adaptive test changes limits based on upstream data, and part average testing rejects in-spec dies that are statistical outliers, a common practice for automotive parts.

faq.q: What is the difference between wafer test and final test?
faq.a: Wafer test probes each die on the uncut wafer to screen out bad dies before packaging, while final test checks the finished, packaged part before shipment. Both use automatic test equipment, paired with a prober and a handler respectively.

faq.q: What is a probe card?
faq.a: A probe card is the interface between the tester and the wafer, carrying many fine needles or MEMS contacts laid out to match the pad positions of one or more dies. It is custom-made for each product.
