faq.q: Why test chips on the wafer before packaging?
faq.a: Packaging a defective die wastes materials and assembly cost, and in multi-die packages one bad die can ruin the whole module. Wafer test also enables memory repair, trimming and early feedback on process problems.

BIST(組み込み自己テスト).desc: Test circuitry built into the chip so that it generates test patterns and checks results by itself. It is widely used, for example, to test memories.

about.p: A BIST controller, a test pattern generator and a response analyzer are built onto the chip. In logic BIST the pattern generator is usually a linear feedback shift register (LFSR), which produces pseudo-random bits that are shifted into the scan chains. After each capture clock, the chain outputs are compacted by a multiple-input signature register (MISR) into a short signature that is compared with the value expected from a fault-free design. Any unknown value, for example from an uninitialized memory, would corrupt the signature, so such sources must be blocked during test.

Embedded memories are dense and regular, so they are tested with algorithmic patterns rather than random ones. March tests walk through all addresses in ascending and descending order, writing and reading complementary data, and detect stuck-at, transition, coupling and address-decoder faults in a number of operations proportional to the memory size. Memory BIST runs at full speed from an on-chip clock. Combined with built-in redundancy analysis, it can decide which spare rows or columns should replace failing cells, and the repair is then programmed into fuses.

about.h: Why build test into the chip
about.p: BIST reduces the need for expensive tester channels, pattern memory and test time, which makes it easier to test many chips in parallel on one tester. It also enables at-speed testing with on-chip clocks and self-testing after the chip is in a product. Automotive microcontrollers run logic and memory BIST at power-up to find latent faults, including faults in the safety mechanisms themselves, which raises the latent fault metric required by functional safety standards. The costs are added area, startup time and a small chance that a faulty circuit produces the correct signature (aliasing).

In scan testing driven by automatic test pattern generation (ATPG), software computes deterministic patterns that target specific faults, and the tester applies them, usually through on-chip compression. That reaches high coverage with relatively few patterns. Logic BIST's pseudo-random patterns need many more cycles and miss random-pattern-resistant faults unless extra test points are inserted, but they require almost nothing from outside the chip. In practice, production test commonly uses compressed ATPG for logic and memory BIST for memories, with logic BIST added where in-system self-test is needed.

faq.q: What is the difference between logic BIST and memory BIST?
faq.a: Logic BIST applies pseudo-random patterns from an LFSR through scan chains and compresses responses into a signature. Memory BIST applies deterministic algorithms such as March tests to embedded memories and can also identify cells to repair.

faq.q: Why do automotive chips run BIST at power-up?
faq.a: Faults in safety mechanisms such as ECC logic or comparators stay hidden during normal operation. Running BIST at every start finds these latent faults before driving, as functional safety standards require.

faq.q: Does BIST replace automatic test equipment?
faq.a: Not entirely. BIST reduces tester requirements and test time, but production testing still uses testers for scan patterns, parametric measurements and to start BIST and read its results.

ATPG(自動テストパターン生成).desc: Automatically generating test patterns that detect faults from a circuit's netlist. It is used together with scan design.

about.p: Automatic test pattern generation (ATPG) works from the gate-level netlist and a fault model. For each target fault it must activate the fault, driving the faulty line to the opposite of its stuck value, and propagate the difference along a sensitized path to an observable output, while finding primary-input values that justify both. Classic algorithms such as the D-algorithm and PODEM search this space. Each new pattern is fault-simulated to mark every other fault it happens to detect, and patterns are compacted, because test time and tester memory grow with pattern count.

The stuck-at model assumes a line is permanently 0 or 1, giving 2n faults for n lines. It is abstract, yet patterns that detect stuck-at faults also catch many real shorts and opens, and it remains the baseline for measuring fault coverage, the fraction of modeled faults the pattern set detects. Defects that only slow a signal are invisible to static tests, so delay fault models such as transition faults add at-speed patterns that launch a transition and capture the result one clock later. Coverage is always relative to a model, not to every possible physical defect.

Generating tests for a deep sequential circuit is very hard, because internal states can be reached only through many clock cycles. Scan design, a design-for-testability (DFT) technique, adds a multiplexer at each flip-flop input so that in test mode the flip-flops link into shift-register chains. The tester shifts a state in, applies one functional capture clock and shifts the result out. ATPG then only has to solve combinational logic between scan cells, which is what makes high coverage practical for chips with hundreds of millions of gates.

Functional verification asks whether the design is correct; ATPG assumes the design is correct and asks whether each manufactured chip matches it. Its output is test patterns, also called test vectors: input values per time step plus the expected responses, which automatic test equipment applies and compares. Other screens complement it. Part average testing (PAT) rejects chips whose measurements are statistical outliers even though they pass, a practice common for automotive parts, while automatic defect classification (ADC) belongs to wafer inspection, not to electrical test.

faq.q: What is ATPG in VLSI testing?
faq.a: It is software that automatically generates input patterns and expected outputs that detect modeled manufacturing faults, such as stuck-at faults, from a circuit's netlist.

faq.q: Why does ATPG need scan chains?
faq.a: Scan chains let the tester set and read every flip-flop directly, turning a hard sequential test problem into a combinational one that ATPG can solve efficiently with high coverage.

faq.q: What is the difference between stuck-at and transition fault models?
faq.a: Stuck-at faults model a line fixed at 0 or 1 and are found with static tests. Transition faults model a line that switches too slowly and need at-speed launch-and-capture patterns.

縮退故障.desc: The basic fault model in logic testing, which assumes a signal line is stuck at 0 or 1.

故障検出率(フォールトカバレッジ).desc: The fraction of modeled faults that a set of test patterns can detect. The higher it is, the less likely defective chips are to escape.

IDDQテスト.desc: A test that measures the supply current of a CMOS circuit at rest and flags defects such as bridging faults when it is abnormally high.

KGD(ノウングッドダイ).desc: A chip confirmed to be good before packaging. It matters when several chips go into one package, because a single bad chip ruins the whole module.

パレート図.desc: A chart that lists items such as defect types as bars in descending order of count, with a line for the cumulative share. It shows which items to tackle first.

about.h: How a Pareto chart is built
about.p: Start by tallying occurrences per category over a fixed period, for example defect types found at inspection or failure bins at wafer test. Plot the categories as bars in descending order, largest on the left, with small categories often grouped into an "other" bar at the far right. Then overlay a line showing the cumulative percentage against a second axis from 0 to 100%. The bars show which category is biggest; the line shows how many categories you must address to cover a given share of the problem.

The chart is named after the Pareto principle, the empirical observation that a few causes often account for most of the effect. In defect data it is common for the top two or three categories to make up 70–80% of the total, which tells an engineering team where limited effort pays off first. It is a tendency, not a law. A flat Pareto chart, where no category dominates, is itself informative: it suggests a broad, systemic cause rather than one dominant failure mode.

Counting alone can mislead, so bars are often weighted by impact, such as yield loss, scrap cost or the fraction of defects that actually kill a die. A frequent but harmless defect may then drop below a rarer killer defect. Engineers also stratify: the top bar is broken down into a second-level Pareto chart by tool, chamber, layer or product to narrow the cause. After a fix, a new chart over the same period length shows whether the target bar shrank and what has become the next priority.

about.h: Pareto chart vs. other quality tools
about.p: A Pareto chart is one of the classic seven basic quality-control tools, and each answers a different question. A histogram shows the distribution of a continuous measurement in ordered bins, while a Pareto chart sorts discrete categories by size. A scatter plot reveals correlation between two variables, a control chart tracks stability over time, a wafer map shows where failures occur on the wafer, and a shmoo plot shows pass/fail across supply voltage and frequency. Pareto analysis decides which problem to attack first; the others help explain it.

faq.q: What is the difference between a Pareto chart and a histogram?
faq.a: A histogram groups a continuous variable into ordered bins to show its distribution, so bar order follows the value axis. A Pareto chart plots discrete categories sorted from largest to smallest and adds a cumulative-percentage line.

faq.q: Why does a Pareto chart have a cumulative line?
faq.a: The cumulative percentage line shows how much of the total is covered by the top categories combined. It lets you read off, for example, that fixing the first three causes would address about 75% of all defects.

faq.q: What is the Pareto principle?
faq.a: It is the observation, often summarized as the 80/20 rule, that a small number of causes produce most of the effects. The exact ratio varies and should be checked with data rather than assumed.

管理図.desc: A chart that plots process measurements over time against a center line and control limits (usually ±3σ) to judge whether the process is stable. Points outside the limits or runs on one side signal problems.

about.p: A control chart plots a statistic, such as an individual measurement, a subgroup mean or a defect count, in time order against a center line at the process average. The upper and lower control limits sit three standard deviations of that plotted statistic away from the center; for subgroup means, this is the process standard deviation divided by the square root of the subgroup size. When the process is stable and roughly normal, only about 0.27% of points fall outside the limits by chance, so a point beyond them is strong evidence that something has changed.

Points inside the limits can still signal trouble when their pattern is unlikely to be random. Common rule sets, such as the Western Electric or Nelson rules, flag a long run on one side of the center line, a steady upward or downward trend, or several points clustered near one limit. Nine consecutive points on the same side of the center, for example, occur by chance less than 1% of the time in a stable process, so they suggest a shift in the mean before any product goes out of specification. Each added rule also raises the false-alarm rate.

Variables such as film thickness or line width use an X-bar and R chart, which tracks subgroup mean and range on separate panels to catch both shifts in center and changes in spread. Larger subgroups use standard deviation instead of range, and processes with one measurement per lot use an individuals and moving-range chart. Attribute data use a p chart for fraction defective, whose limits vary with sample size, an np chart for defective counts, and c or u charts for defect counts. EWMA and CUSUM charts detect small, gradual shifts faster.

Limits are first calculated in a setup phase from roughly 20 to 25 subgroups of a process believed to be stable, after removing points with known special causes; the chart is then used for ongoing monitoring. Control limits must not be confused with specification limits: a process can be stable yet produce out-of-spec parts, or be within spec while drifting out of control. Specification limits for individual parts also should not be drawn on a chart of subgroup means. Limits are recalculated after intentional process changes.

faq.q: Why are control limits set at three sigma?
faq.a: Three-sigma limits balance sensitivity against false alarms: a stable process puts only about 0.27% of points outside them by chance, while real shifts of meaningful size are detected quickly.

faq.q: When should I use a p chart instead of an X-bar R chart?
faq.a: Use a p chart when each item is classified as good or defective and you track the fraction defective. Use an X-bar and R chart when you have continuous measurements, such as thickness or dimensions, taken in subgroups.

faq.q: Can a process be in control but out of specification?
faq.a: Yes. Being in control means the process varies only randomly around a stable mean; if that spread is wider than the specification, or the mean is off target, it will still produce defects consistently.

特性要因図.desc: A diagram that organizes the causes affecting a problem (the effect) in the shape of a fish skeleton. Also called a fishbone diagram.

about.p: The problem being studied, called the effect, is written at the head on the right side, and a horizontal spine runs to it. Major bones branch off the spine for categories of causes, classically the 4Ms: man (people), machine, material and method. Many teams add measurement and environment to make 5M+E or 6M. Each major bone carries smaller bones for more specific causes, and those can branch further, so the diagram shows a hierarchy from broad category to concrete, checkable cause. It is also called an Ishikawa diagram after the quality engineer Kaoru Ishikawa.

Start by stating the effect narrowly and measurably, for example a rise in particle defects after a particular etch step rather than simply low yield. The team then brainstorms causes under each category, asking why repeatedly to move from vague items to specific ones, and avoids judging ideas while the diagram is being filled. Once the list is reasonably exhaustive, the most plausible causes are marked and each is checked against data, such as tool logs, inspection results or a designed experiment. The diagram generates hypotheses; it does not prove which cause is responsible.

Suppose wafer edge yield has dropped on one product. Under machine the team might list chamber wall flaking, a worn edge ring or a change in maintenance interval. Under material: a new photoresist lot or incoming wafer flatness. Under method: a recent recipe change or different chamber seasoning. Under measurement: a changed inspection threshold. Under man: a manual handling step done differently by shifts. Wafer maps, tool history and lot genealogy are then used to narrow the list to the cause that actually matches the failure pattern.

about.h: Place among the seven QC tools
about.p: The cause-and-effect diagram is one of the seven basic quality control tools, together with the check sheet, Pareto chart, histogram, scatter diagram, control chart and stratification (some lists use a flowchart or graph instead). The tools complement each other: a Pareto chart ranks defect types by count to pick which effect to attack, the fishbone lists candidate causes, a scatter diagram tests whether a suspected cause correlates with the result, and a histogram shows the distribution, where two peaks often mean data from two tools or materials are mixed and should be stratified.

faq.q: Why is it called a fishbone diagram?
faq.a: The effect sits at the head on the right, the main line forms the spine, and the cause categories branch off at an angle like ribs, so the finished drawing looks like a fish skeleton.

faq.q: What are the 4Ms in a cause-and-effect diagram?
faq.a: They are man (people), machine, material and method, the standard categories for the major bones. Measurement and environment are often added, giving 5M+E.

faq.q: What is the difference between a fishbone diagram and a Pareto chart?
faq.a: A Pareto chart ranks problems or defect categories by frequency to show which few matter most. A fishbone diagram takes one chosen problem and organizes its possible causes so they can be investigated.

FMEA(故障モード影響解析).desc: A method that lists the possible failure modes of a product or process, evaluates their effects and severity, and plans countermeasures in advance.

about.p: Failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) is a structured, team-based review carried out before problems occur. For each component of a design or each step of a process, the team lists the ways it could fail (failure modes), the consequences of each failure (effects), the likely causes and the controls already in place. Each mode is then scored for severity, occurrence and detection, commonly on 1-to-10 scales, where a high detection score means the failure is hard to catch. Multiplying the three gives the risk priority number (RPN), which ranks where countermeasures should go first.

A design FMEA examines a product's design, such as a chip, package or module, asking how each function could fail and what the user would experience. A process FMEA examines manufacturing steps. In a wafer fab, for example, a CMP step might fail by over-polishing, with the effect of thin copper lines and high resistance, caused by an incorrect endpoint, and detected by thickness metrology. Countermeasures can lower occurrence, for instance through automated run-to-run control, or improve detection through added inspection. After actions are taken, the scores are re-evaluated and the document is kept current.

about.h: Limits of the risk priority number
about.p: The RPN is convenient but crude. Very different risks can share the same product: a severe failure that is rare and easily detected may score the same as a trivial one that happens often. For this reason teams usually treat high-severity modes, especially those affecting safety, as requiring action regardless of RPN. Some newer guidelines, notably in the automotive industry, replace the RPN with an action-priority table that weights severity first. Scores are also subjective, so consistent rating criteria and cross-functional review matter as much as the arithmetic.

FMEA is proactive and works bottom-up from individual failure modes to their effects. Fault tree analysis (FTA) works top-down, starting from one undesired event and tracing the combinations of causes that could produce it. Pareto charts and histograms analyze defects that have already occurred, statistical process control (SPC) watches running processes for abnormalities, advanced process control (APC) actively corrects tool settings, and gage R&R checks whether a measurement system is precise enough. In semiconductor ramp-up, FMEA results often decide where those other controls are applied.

faq.q: What does FMEA stand for?
faq.a: FMEA stands for failure mode and effects analysis. It is a method for listing possible failures of a product or process, evaluating their effects and planning countermeasures before they happen.

faq.q: How is the risk priority number calculated in FMEA?
faq.a: The RPN is the product of the severity, occurrence and detection scores, each commonly rated from 1 to 10. Higher numbers indicate risks to address first, although high-severity items usually need action regardless of RPN.

faq.q: What is the difference between FMEA and FTA?
faq.a: FMEA starts from individual failure modes and works forward to their effects, covering the whole design or process. FTA starts from one specific undesired event and works backward through a logic tree of causes.

APC(先進的プロセス制御).desc: Automatically adjusting the process settings for the next lot or wafer based on earlier measurements, as in run-to-run control. It reduces variation.

about.p: Advanced process control (APC) closes a loop between metrology and the process tool. In run-to-run (R2R) control, a simple model links a recipe knob to the result, for example polish time to removed thickness in CMP. After each lot or wafer is measured, the controller updates its estimate of the tool's current behaviour, often with an exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) to filter measurement noise, and computes the setting for the next run. A heavier weight on recent data tracks drift quickly but also chases noise; a lighter weight is smoother but slower to react.

APC uses information from two directions. Feedforward control uses measurements taken before the step on the same wafer: if the incoming film is measured thick, the next CMP polish time is extended so the final thickness still hits target. Feedback control uses results measured after processing earlier wafers to correct slow changes in the tool, such as a falling removal rate as a pad or chamber ages. Lithography overlay and critical-dimension control, where exposure dose, focus and alignment offsets are adjusted lot by lot, are classic examples of combining both.

Statistical process control (SPC) watches a process with control charts and raises an alarm or stops the tool when a parameter drifts outside its limits; it detects problems but does not fix them. APC actively steers the process back toward target on every run, which shrinks variation without waiting for an excursion. The two work together: SPC limits are still applied to APC-controlled outputs, and in many fabs the APC umbrella also includes fault detection and classification (FDC), which monitors tool sensor traces in real time.

Several yield-related acronyms sit close to APC but do different jobs. Automatic defect classification (ADC) sorts review-SEM images of defects into categories such as particles or scratches. Part average testing (PAT) rejects chips whose test results are statistical outliers within their lot even though they meet specification, a technique used for automotive quality. ATPG, automatic test pattern generation, creates test vectors for logic. Only APC changes how wafers are processed; the others classify defects or screen finished chips.

faq.q: What is the difference between APC and SPC in semiconductor manufacturing?
faq.a: SPC monitors process data with control charts and flags or stops the process when it goes out of control. APC uses the same kind of measurements to adjust the recipe automatically for the next lot or wafer, actively reducing variation.

faq.q: What is run-to-run control?
faq.a: Run-to-run control is a form of APC that updates a tool's recipe between runs based on measurements of previous runs, for example adjusting CMP polish time from the measured removal of earlier wafers. It corrects slow drift without changing anything during a single run.

faq.q: What is feedforward control in APC?
faq.a: Feedforward control uses a measurement of the incoming wafer, taken at an earlier step, to choose settings for the current step. A thicker-than-normal incoming film, for example, leads to a longer polish so the final thickness stays on target.

システマティック不良.desc: A defect that occurs repeatedly at particular patterns or locations because of interactions between design and process. It is distinguished from random defects caused by chance particles.

アレニウスモデル.desc: A model in which reaction or degradation rates vary with temperature as exp(−Ea/kT). It is used to estimate lifetime at operating temperature from accelerated tests at higher temperatures.

FIT.desc: A unit of failure rate: 1 FIT is one failure per billion (10⁹) device-hours. It is used for parts with very low failure rates, such as semiconductors.

ワイブル分布.desc: A probability distribution widely used to analyze lifetime data. Its shape parameter can represent early-failure, random-failure and wear-out behavior.

ホットキャリア注入(HCI).desc: Degradation in which carriers accelerated by the strong field near the drain are injected into the gate insulator, shifting the threshold voltage and reducing drive current.

ラッチアップ.desc: A condition in which a parasitic thyristor structure in a CMOS circuit turns on and a large current keeps flowing between supply and ground. It is prevented by well-contact placement, guard rings and similar measures.

about.p: A bulk CMOS inverter places a pMOS in an n-well on a p-type substrate next to an nMOS. The p+ source of the pMOS, the n-well and the p-substrate form a vertical PNP transistor, while the n+ source of the nMOS, the p-substrate and the n-well form a lateral NPN transistor. Each one's collector drives the other's base, making a PNPN thyristor between the supply and ground. Normally it stays off because well and substrate contacts hold both bases at their rail potentials, but the resistance of the well and substrate between those contacts and the transistors leaves room for a local voltage drop.

about.h: How latch-up is triggered and sustained
about.p: If current is injected into the well or substrate, for example when an input pin is driven above the supply or below ground, by electrostatic discharge, by a radiation strike or by incorrect power sequencing, the voltage drop across the well or substrate resistance can forward-bias one parasitic base-emitter junction. That transistor's collector current then turns on the other, and if the loop gain exceeds one the pair feeds itself. A low-resistance path from supply to ground then stays on even after the trigger disappears and persists until power is removed, often overheating and destroying metal lines or junctions.

Most defenses lower the well and substrate resistances or the parasitic gains. In layout, well and substrate contacts are placed frequently, which is why standard-cell libraries include tap cells, and I/O transistors are enclosed in guard rings that collect injected carriers before they reach the core. Increasing the spacing between nMOS and pMOS also helps. In the process, retrograde wells with heavy doping deep below the surface and p/p+ epitaxial wafers with a low-resistance substrate shunt parasitic current. Silicon on insulator (SOI) removes the substrate path entirely, so SOI circuits are essentially immune.

Latch-up is an event, not gradual wear. Hot carrier injection (HCI) and bias temperature instability (NBTI in pMOS, PBTI in high-k nMOS) slowly shift threshold voltage over years, and electromigration slowly erodes metal lines, whereas latch-up can destroy a chip within moments of a single trigger. For this reason latch-up immunity is tested directly: qualification standards such as AEC-Q100 for automotive ICs include latch-up tests, which inject current into pins and apply overvoltage to supplies while checking that the supply current returns to normal afterward.

faq.q: What causes latch-up in CMOS?
faq.a: A parasitic PNPN thyristor formed by the wells and substrate turns on when injected current, for example from an input overvoltage or ESD, forward-biases one of its junctions. The two parasitic bipolar transistors then sustain each other, keeping a large current flowing from supply to ground.

faq.q: How do you recover from latch-up?
faq.a: The latched state persists until the supply voltage is removed or reduced enough to stop the current, so power must be cycled. If the current has already overheated metal or junctions, the damage is permanent.

faq.q: Why does SOI prevent latch-up?
faq.a: In silicon on insulator, each transistor sits in a thin silicon layer on a buried oxide, so there is no continuous well and substrate path to form the parasitic thyristor. Without that path, the regenerative loop cannot exist.

ESD(静電気放電).desc: A sudden discharge of static electricity from a charged person or object. Applied to an IC pin it can destroy gate oxides and other structures, so I/O pins have protection circuits.

about.p: A person or object can easily charge to thousands of volts, while a gate dielectric a few nanometres thick breaks down at around 10 MV/cm, only a few volts for a 2 nm film. An electrostatic discharge into a pin can therefore rupture gate oxides instantly, and the peak current can melt junctions or metal lines. Not every hit kills a part outright: some leave latent damage, such as increased leakage, that fails later in the field. Factories therefore use grounded wrist straps, conductive floors and work surfaces, and ionizers.

Each I/O pin has diodes to the supply and ground rails, which turn on when the pin is driven beyond the rails and steer the discharge current away from internal circuits. A power clamp between the rails, often a large transistor triggered by the fast edge of an ESD event, completes the current path. Protection must trigger above the normal operating voltage but below the level that damages the circuit it guards. Protection devices add capacitance, so high-speed I/O keeps them small. A 5 V tolerant input omits the diode to VDD so a higher input voltage does not flow into the supply.

Component ratings describe handling in ESD-controlled factories. The human body model (HBM), a 100 pF capacitor discharged through 1.5 kΩ, represents a charged person touching a pin; about 2 kV is a common target. The charged device model (CDM) represents a charged IC discharging when a pin touches metal, with events around a nanosecond or shorter, and is the main concern in automated handling. A datasheet rating such as HBM ±2 kV and CDM ±500 V does not cover finished equipment, where system-level tests like IEC 61000-4-2 apply ±8 kV contact discharges and board-level TVS diodes are needed.

The two are often tested together, as in automotive AEC-Q100 qualification, but they are different failures. ESD is a brief, high-energy transient that damages structures directly. Latch-up is a sustained high-current state in which parasitic pnp and npn transistors in CMOS form a thyristor and turn each other on, triggered by current injection or overvoltage on a pin. Once latched, current keeps flowing until power is removed and can overheat the chip. Higher temperature raises the parasitic gains and well resistance, so latch-up testing is done at maximum operating temperature.

faq.q: What is the difference between HBM and CDM ESD?
faq.a: HBM models a charged person discharging into a pin through 1.5 kΩ from 100 pF. CDM models the IC itself being charged and discharging very quickly when a pin touches metal, which is the dominant risk in automated assembly.

faq.q: Is an IC's HBM rating enough to pass system-level ESD tests?
faq.a: No. HBM and CDM ratings cover factory handling, while system-level tests such as IEC 61000-4-2 deliver much more energy. Pins exposed to the outside world normally need external protection such as TVS diodes.

faq.q: What is the difference between ESD and latch-up?
faq.a: ESD is a brief static discharge that destroys oxides or junctions directly. Latch-up is a parasitic thyristor in CMOS turning on and holding a large current until power is cycled.

ソフトエラー.desc: A temporary flip of data stored in memory or flip-flops caused by neutrons from cosmic rays, alpha particles and the like. The device is not damaged, so rewriting restores correct operation.

ネットリスト.desc: Data describing the elements (cells) of a circuit and how they are connected. It is the output of logic synthesis and the input to place-and-route and timing analysis.

about.p: A netlist lists instances, the cells or transistors in a circuit, and nets, the electrical connections between their pins, plus the ports that connect the circuit to the outside. It is pure connectivity: it says that the output pin of one NAND gate drives the inputs of two flip-flops, but nothing about where those cells sit or how the wires are drawn. A gate-level netlist references cells from a standard-cell library and is usually written as structural Verilog, while a transistor-level SPICE netlist lists individual MOSFETs, resistors and capacitors with their parameters for circuit simulation.

about.h: Where netlists appear in the design flow
about.p: Logic synthesis converts register-transfer level (RTL) code into a gate-level netlist that meets timing, area and power constraints. Place-and-route reads that netlist, then adds buffers and a synthesized clock tree, producing an updated post-layout netlist. Parasitic resistance and capacitance extracted from the layout are attached for static timing analysis. Formal equivalence checking compares the netlist against the RTL, automatic test pattern generation (ATPG) works on the netlist to target faults such as stuck-at faults, and layout-versus-schematic (LVS) checking compares a netlist extracted from the layout with the reference netlist.

RTL simulation is fast but abstract, so some bugs only appear after synthesis. Simulating the gate-level netlist exercises the actual gates and flip-flops, exposing reset and initialization problems that X-optimism hides in RTL, and cases where the synthesized logic differs from the designer's intent. When gate and wire delays from the layout are back-annotated in SDF (Standard Delay Format), timing-related problems also show up. Because gate-level simulation is far slower than RTL simulation, it is usually run on a limited set of tests.

The netlist and the layout describe the same chip in different ways. The netlist captures what is connected to what, while layout data in GDSII or OASIS format holds the polygons on each mask layer that will actually be printed on the wafer. Verification ties them together: LVS proves that the drawn shapes implement exactly the connections in the netlist, and design rule checking (DRC) separately confirms that the shapes obey manufacturing rules. Only layout data goes to mask making after tape-out.

faq.q: What is the difference between RTL and a netlist?
faq.a: RTL describes behavior as registers and the logic operations between them in a language like Verilog or VHDL. A netlist is the structural result after synthesis, listing specific library cells and the wires connecting them.

faq.q: What is a SPICE netlist?
faq.a: It is a transistor-level netlist in the input format of SPICE circuit simulators, listing devices such as MOSFETs, resistors and capacitors with their node connections and model parameters, used for analog and cell-level simulation.

faq.q: Does a netlist contain physical layout information?
faq.a: No. A netlist contains only components and connectivity. Cell positions and wire shapes live in the layout database and in GDSII or OASIS files, although parasitics extracted from the layout can be attached to the netlist for timing analysis.

スタンダードセル.desc: A pre-designed, pre-verified building block such as a logic gate or flip-flop. Cells share a common height so automatic place-and-route can line them up to build large circuits.

PDK(プロセスデザインキット).desc: The set of design data a foundry gives to designers, including design rules, device models, cell libraries and verification rule decks.

about.p: A process design kit (PDK) packages everything needed to design for one specific foundry process. It includes the design rules, which give minimum widths, spacings and enclosures for every layer; SPICE models for transistors, resistors, capacitors and diodes; rule decks that DRC (design rule check) and LVS (layout versus schematic) tools run; technology files for parasitic extraction; and layout generators, often parameterized cells, for basic devices. Digital standard-cell libraries with their timing and physical views are sometimes included and sometimes supplied separately by the foundry or a library vendor.

In a custom or analog flow, the designer draws a schematic using PDK device symbols, simulates it with the PDK's SPICE models, builds the layout from the PDK's device cells, and runs the PDK's DRC and LVS decks to verify it. Extraction with the PDK's technology data then adds wire parasitics for post-layout simulation. Digital flows use the same rule decks and extraction data at sign-off, plus cell libraries for synthesis and place and route. Because every step relies on foundry data, a design that passes PDK checks is one the foundry can manufacture.

Manufacturing varies from lot to lot, wafer to wafer and transistor to transistor, so a PDK models devices at process corners as well as typical conditions. Corners are named by the speed of NMOS and PMOS, such as TT, FF, SS, FS and SF, and are combined with voltage and temperature extremes. For random device-to-device variation, statistical models support Monte Carlo simulation, which reruns a circuit hundreds or thousands of times with randomly perturbed parameters such as threshold voltage to estimate the spread of offset, gain or timing and the resulting parametric yield.

about.h: PDK vs. cell library vs. IP
about.p: The PDK describes the process itself: its devices, rules and verification data. A standard-cell library is a set of pre-designed logic gates built with that PDK, characterized for timing and power. An IP core is a larger reusable circuit block, such as an interface or processor, that is delivered for a given process. Timing constraints, usually written in SDC format, are created by the design team for their own chip and are not part of the PDK. A PDK is tied to one process version, so moving to another node or foundry means adopting a new kit.

faq.q: What does PDK stand for?
faq.a: PDK stands for process design kit, the set of design rules, device models, verification rule decks and related data that a foundry gives designers for a specific manufacturing process.

faq.q: Is a standard-cell library part of the PDK?
faq.a: Sometimes. Some foundries ship standard cells with the PDK, but cell libraries are often delivered separately, either by the foundry or by a third-party library provider, and are built on top of the PDK.

faq.q: What are process corners in a PDK?
faq.a: Process corners are model sets representing fast and slow extremes of NMOS and PMOS devices, such as SS or FF, used with voltage and temperature extremes to check that a circuit works across manufacturing variation.

テープアウト.desc: Handing over the finished, verified layout data to manufacturing for mask making. The name comes from the days when data was delivered on magnetic tape.

SPICE.desc: A circuit simulator that calculates voltages and currents in transistor-level circuits in detail using device models. It is used for analog design and cell characterization.

about.p: SPICE (Simulation Program with Integrated Circuit Emphasis), developed at UC Berkeley in the 1970s, reads a netlist and builds circuit equations using modified nodal analysis, which applies Kirchhoff's current law at every node together with each element's current-voltage relation. Nonlinear devices are linearized and solved iteratively with the Newton-Raphson method using sparse matrix techniques. The main analyses are the DC operating point and DC sweeps, small-signal AC analysis linearized around that operating point, transient analysis by numerical integration with adaptive time steps, and noise analysis.

Results are only as good as the compact models describing each device. MOSFETs use physics-based models with hundreds of parameters, such as the BSIM family, including variants for FinFETs. Bipolar transistors use the Gummel-Poon model, which extends the Ebers-Moll model with the Early effect, high injection and charge storage. Foundries extract parameters from measured silicon and deliver them in the process design kit (PDK), along with process corners such as typical, fast and slow, and statistical models for Monte Carlo simulation of mismatch.

Analog, RF and mixed-signal blocks such as amplifiers, PLLs, data converters and regulators are designed and verified in SPICE. Standard cells are characterized with it across process, voltage and temperature to build the timing and power tables that static timing analysis and logic synthesis use. Memory bit cells, sense amplifiers and I/O circuits rely on it too, and post-layout simulation adds extracted parasitic resistance and capacitance. Because accuracy costs time, whole digital chips are verified with logic simulation and timing analysis, while faster SPICE variants trade accuracy for capacity on large circuits.

Many simulation failures come from the circuit description rather than the simulator. A node with no DC path to ground, such as one connected only through capacitors, makes the matrix singular. Ideal voltage sources in a loop, or switches with extreme resistance ratios, can prevent Newton-Raphson iteration from converging. Checking the DC operating point before transient runs, tightening time steps around fast edges and using realistic source rise times avoid most problems. A SPICE netlist describes devices and connections; it is different from a Verilog description of logic or a GDSII layout.

faq.q: What is SPICE used for in chip design?
faq.a: It simulates transistor-level circuits in detail to predict voltages, currents, timing, gain, noise and power. It is the standard tool for analog design and for characterizing standard cells.

faq.q: What is a SPICE model?
faq.a: It is a set of equations and parameters describing a device's electrical behavior, such as a BSIM model for a MOSFET. Foundries supply these models in their process design kits, often with corner and statistical variants.

faq.q: Why does my SPICE simulation fail to converge?
faq.a: Common causes are floating nodes without a DC path to ground, loops of ideal voltage sources, unrealistically sharp edges or extreme component values. Fixing the circuit description usually works better than loosening simulator tolerances.

高位合成(HLS).desc: Automatically generating RTL from an algorithm written in C, C++ or similar. It is used in developing FPGAs and accelerators.

クロックゲーティング.desc: A low-power design technique that stops the clock to idle circuit blocks, avoiding wasted switching power.

about.h: Why stopping the clock saves power
about.p: Dynamic power is roughly activity factor times capacitance times voltage squared times frequency. The clock net toggles every cycle and drives every flip-flop's clock pin through a large buffered tree, so the clock network is often one of the biggest single consumers of dynamic power. When a register's contents will not change, because its enable is inactive, clocking it wastes energy in the flip-flops and in the clock branch feeding them. Clock gating stops the clock to such registers or blocks, eliminating that switching while keeping their stored state.

Simply ANDing the clock with an enable is risky: if the enable changes while the clock is high, the gated clock can be truncated or produce a glitch. Static timing analysis checks that the enable settles before the clock rises and stays stable until it falls, which in a 2.0 ns, 50% duty cycle clock leaves only the 1.0 ns low phase. Designs therefore use integrated clock gating (ICG) cells, which contain a latch that is transparent only while the clock is low, so the enable is frozen during the high phase. ICGs also include a test-enable input so gated flip-flops are clocked during scan testing.

In register-transfer level code, a register written only when an enable is true is normally implemented with a multiplexer that feeds the old value back. Synthesis tools recognize this pattern and replace the feedback multiplexers of a group of flip-flops with one ICG, saving both power and multiplexer area. This fine-grained gating is automatic. Coarse-grained gating, controlled by a power manager or software, stops the clock to entire blocks such as an idle accelerator. Gating cells placed nearer the clock root save more power but complicate clock tree timing.

Clock gating removes dynamic power but not leakage, since the block stays powered; in exchange, state is retained and the block resumes on the very next clock edge. Power gating turns off a large switch transistor between the block and its supply, removing nearly all leakage too, but state must be saved or held in retention registers, outputs need isolation cells, and waking up takes time while the supply stabilizes. Chips combine both: clock gating for idle periods of a few cycles, power gating for long ones.

faq.q: What is the difference between clock gating and power gating?
faq.a: Clock gating stops the clock to cut dynamic power while keeping the block powered, so it resumes instantly but still leaks. Power gating cuts the supply, removing leakage as well, but requires state saving and a longer wake-up.

faq.q: Why not gate a clock with a simple AND gate?
faq.a: If the enable changes while the clock is high, the AND output can produce a shortened pulse or glitch that may clock flip-flops incorrectly. An integrated clock gating cell latches the enable during the low phase to prevent this.

faq.q: Does clock gating reduce leakage power?
faq.a: No. It only removes switching power in the gated flip-flops and clock wiring; leakage continues as long as the block is powered.

FPGA.desc: A chip whose logic configuration the user can rewrite after manufacture. It is used for prototypes, low-volume products and ASIC verification.

about.p: A field-programmable gate array (FPGA) is a grid of configurable logic blocks joined by programmable interconnect. Each logic block contains lookup tables (LUTs), small memories whose stored bits define a truth table and whose inputs drive multiplexers that select the output, so a k-input LUT can implement any function of k inputs. Flip-flops store state. Modern devices also include hard blocks such as block RAM, DSP multiply-accumulate units, clock managers, high-speed serial transceivers and sometimes processor cores. In most FPGAs the configuration lives in SRAM cells and is loaded from external flash at power-up.

Designs are written in a hardware description language such as Verilog or VHDL. Synthesis maps the logic onto LUTs, flip-flops and hard blocks, recognizing standard coding patterns: a register array written and read synchronously with the clock is inferred as block RAM, while an asynchronous read may become flip-flops or distributed memory. Place-and-route then assigns resources and wires, static timing analysis checks clock frequency, and the result is a bitstream loaded into the device. Processing blocks are often linked with standard on-chip interfaces such as AXI4-Stream.

An FPGA needs no masks or fabrication lead time and can be reprogrammed in the field, so bugs and new features can be handled after shipment. The price is overhead: the configurable routing and LUTs make the same function slower, more power-hungry and much larger in area than in an application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC), and the unit price is higher. ASICs win at high volume once their large up-front engineering and mask costs are spread across many units; FPGAs win for prototypes, low volumes and fast-changing requirements.

FPGAs appear in communications equipment, test and measurement instruments, video and signal-processing pipelines, industrial control and data-center accelerators. They are also central to verifying large SoCs: mapping the design onto FPGAs (FPGA prototyping) runs it orders of magnitude faster than software simulation, so real operating systems and applications can run before silicon exists. Hardware emulators serve the same purpose with better visibility into internal signals, while FPGA prototypes generally run faster.

faq.q: What does FPGA stand for?
faq.a: FPGA stands for field-programmable gate array: a chip whose logic and wiring can be configured by the user after manufacture, in the field, rather than fixed during fabrication.

faq.q: What is the difference between an FPGA and a microcontroller?
faq.a: A microcontroller has a fixed processor that executes software instructions one after another. An FPGA has no fixed function; its hardware itself is configured, so many operations can run in parallel every clock cycle, at the cost of a harder design flow.

faq.q: Does an FPGA keep its configuration when power is off?
faq.a: Most FPGAs store their configuration in SRAM and lose it at power-off, reloading a bitstream from an external flash memory at each power-up. Some families use on-chip flash or one-time antifuses and are non-volatile.

LVS.desc: Short for layout versus schematic: checking that the connectivity extracted from the layout matches the schematic or netlist. It is always run before tape-out, along with DRC.

about.p: Layout versus schematic (LVS) checks that the drawn layout implements exactly the intended circuit. The tool first extracts devices from the layout polygons: overlapping polysilicon and diffusion form a transistor, specific marker layers identify resistors and capacitors, and contacts and vias connect metal shapes into nets. This produces a layout netlist. It is then compared with the reference netlist from the schematic or from place and route, essentially a graph-matching problem. Besides connectivity, LVS also compares device parameters such as transistor width and length and resistor values against the reference.

The most common LVS errors are shorts, where two nets that should be separate touch, and opens, where a net is broken. A short between supply nets is especially serious. Other reports include missing or extra devices, swapped pins, transistors with wrong dimensions, and pin labels that are misplaced or misspelled, which make nets appear unconnected even if the geometry is correct. Debugging is often harder than the check itself, because a single short merges two large nets and the tool must help locate the exact polygon where they meet.

Three checks are usually run together at sign-off. Design rule checking (DRC) looks only at geometry: minimum width, spacing, enclosure, density and similar manufacturing rules, which number in the thousands in advanced processes. LVS looks at connectivity and device identity. Electrical rule checking (ERC) looks for electrically suspicious connections, such as floating inputs, outputs driven by multiple sources, shorts between different supplies and unconnected wells. A layout can be DRC-clean but fail LVS, and vice versa, so all must pass before mask data is released.

The LVS rule deck comes from the foundry's process design kit (PDK), and the same device-recognition rules underpin parasitic extraction, so a clean LVS is also a prerequisite for accurate post-layout simulation and timing. In digital flows, LVS compares the routed layout with the gate-level netlist, with standard cells treated as verified building blocks. Sign-off additionally includes static timing analysis and power-grid checks such as IR drop and electromigration. Only when all of these pass is the layout released as GDSII or OASIS data for mask making, the step called tape-out.

faq.q: What does LVS stand for?
faq.a: LVS stands for layout versus schematic, a verification step that confirms the devices and connections extracted from a chip layout match the intended schematic or netlist.

faq.q: What is the difference between DRC and LVS?
faq.a: DRC checks whether layout shapes obey the foundry's geometric manufacturing rules, while LVS checks whether the layout's devices and connectivity match the circuit netlist. Both must pass before tape-out.

faq.q: What causes an LVS short error?
faq.a: An LVS short means two nets that should be separate are electrically connected in the layout, typically through overlapping metal, a misplaced via or contact, or an incorrect label that merges net names.

ミニエンバイロメント.desc: Keeping only the small space around the wafers highly clean. Sealed carriers such as FOUPs combined with EFEMs on the tools lower the cleanliness required of the room as a whole, reducing cost.

OHT(天井走行式無人搬送車).desc: Vehicles that run along ceiling rails and automatically carry FOUPs between tools. They are the backbone of automated transport in 300 mm fabs.

FFU(ファンフィルタユニット).desc: A unit combining a fan with a high-efficiency filter. Arrays of them in the cleanroom ceiling blow clean air downward.

EFEM.desc: Short for equipment front end module: the unit at the front of a tool that opens FOUPs and transfers wafers into the tool in a clean environment. It includes load ports and a transfer robot.

about.p: An EFEM (equipment front end module) is the enclosed section at the front of a process or metrology tool. It contains load ports where FOUPs (front-opening unified pods) are docked, a mechanism that unlatches and removes the FOUP door, an atmospheric wafer-handling robot, and usually an aligner that finds the wafer notch before processing. Sensors map which FOUP slots hold wafers. A fan filter unit (FFU) on top blows HEPA- or ULPA-filtered air downward and keeps the enclosure at slight positive pressure, so room air does not leak in.

Instead of keeping an entire cleanroom at the cleanest level, modern fabs isolate wafers in small clean volumes: the sealed FOUP during transport and storage, and the EFEM during transfer into the tool. Wafers move from FOUP to tool without ever being exposed to the room, so the surrounding cleanroom can be held to a less strict class at lower cost. In the 200 mm era, SMIF pods served this role by lowering a cassette into the tool; 300 mm FOUPs open from the front and dock directly to EFEM load ports.

The EFEM operates at atmospheric pressure. For vacuum tools such as etchers and CVD systems, its robot places wafers into a load lock, which is pumped down before a vacuum robot moves them to the process chambers; finished wafers return the same way. Overhead hoist transport (OHT) vehicles deliver FOUPs to the load ports automatically. Load-port dimensions and handoff signaling follow SEMI standards, so FOUPs and transport systems from different suppliers work with many tools.

Particles are not the only concern. Moisture and oxygen can grow native oxide on exposed silicon or metal, and outgassing from just-processed wafers can contaminate others in the same FOUP. Some EFEMs therefore use a nitrogen-filled enclosure rather than filtered air, and load ports can purge FOUPs with nitrogen, limiting oxidation and cross-contamination between process steps.

faq.q: What does EFEM stand for?
faq.a: EFEM stands for equipment front end module: the front section of a semiconductor tool that opens FOUPs and transfers wafers into the tool in a clean environment.

faq.q: What is the difference between an EFEM and a load lock?
faq.a: An EFEM is an atmospheric, filtered-air enclosure with load ports and a robot that unloads FOUPs. A load lock is a small chamber that cycles between atmospheric pressure and vacuum so wafers can pass from the EFEM into a vacuum process tool.

faq.q: How is an EFEM different from an FFU?
faq.a: An FFU is a fan and filter unit that supplies clean air, used across cleanroom ceilings and on top of EFEMs. The EFEM is the complete wafer-transfer module, which includes an FFU to keep its interior clean.

HEPAフィルタ.desc: A high-efficiency air filter that captures at least 99.97% of 0.3 µm particles. Filters that capture even finer particles are ULPA filters.

局所排気装置.desc: Equipment that draws in gases and mists at their source, such as tools handling chemicals, and exhausts them. It keeps workers from inhaling hazardous substances.

about.p: Local exhaust ventilation (LEV) removes hazardous gases, vapors, mists and dusts at the point where they are released, before they reach a worker's breathing zone. A typical system consists of a hood or enclosure around the source, ducting, an air cleaner such as a scrubber where needed, a fan and a discharge stack. The key design quantity is capture velocity: the air speed at the emission point needed to pull contaminants into the hood against drafts and the motion of the release itself.

General, or dilution, ventilation mixes clean air into the whole room to lower average concentration, so a worker standing near the source can still be exposed, and large airflows are needed. Local exhaust removes contaminants before they spread, so it is more effective for toxic substances and needs much less airflow. In a cleanroom, the large recirculating airflow is designed to control particles, not chemical exposure; chemical fumes are handled by dedicated exhausts at each tool and chemical station.

about.h: Where you meet it in a fab
about.p: Wet benches draw air through slots around their chemical baths, chemical storage and dispensing cabinets are exhausted, and gas cabinets holding toxic gases such as arsine and phosphine are kept under negative pressure so any leak is swept into the exhaust. Process tools have exhaust connections for their chambers and load areas. Grinding and polishing of GaAs, which releases arsenic-containing dust, also relies on local exhaust together with protective equipment. Exhaust is usually segregated by type, such as acid, alkali and solvent, and treated before release.

A hood only protects if it actually achieves its design airflow, so systems are inspected and tested periodically, for example by measuring capture velocity or face velocity at the hood opening, and many jurisdictions require such checks by law. Exhaust pressure is monitored continuously, and tools handling hazardous chemicals are often interlocked to stop or alarm if exhaust is lost. Practical habits matter too: not blocking hood openings, keeping sashes at the correct height and working inside the capture zone.

faq.q: What is local exhaust ventilation?
faq.a: Local exhaust ventilation is a system that captures hazardous gases, vapors, mists or dust right at their source with a hood or enclosure and carries them away through ducts, so workers do not inhale them.

faq.q: What is capture velocity?
faq.a: Capture velocity is the air speed needed at the point where a contaminant is released to draw it into the exhaust hood. It is a basic design and inspection criterion for local exhaust systems.

faq.q: What is the difference between local exhaust and general ventilation?
faq.a: General ventilation dilutes contaminants throughout a room with large airflows, while local exhaust removes them at the source before they spread, giving better protection with much less air.

爆発下限界(LEL).desc: The lowest concentration in air at which a flammable gas can burn or explode. Gas detectors are often set to alarm at a percentage of this level.

酸素欠乏(酸欠).desc: A condition in which the oxygen concentration in air falls below 18%. It tends to occur where large amounts of nitrogen are used or in confined spaces, and can cause unconsciousness within a few breaths.

リスクアセスメント.desc: Identifying the hazards of tasks or chemicals, estimating the size of the risks and deciding countermeasures in order of priority.

ロックアウト・タグアウト(LOTO).desc: A procedure that isolates energy sources such as power and gas before maintenance and fits locks and tags so no one can accidentally restore them during the work.

シリコンサイクル.desc: The recurring boom-and-bust pattern of the semiconductor market driven by supply and demand. One cause is that fabs take years to build, so supply lags changes in demand.

SoC(システムオンチップ).desc: An IC that integrates the functions a system needs, such as CPU, GPU, memory controller and communications, on one chip. The heart of a smartphone is a typical example.

about.p: A typical smartphone system on chip (SoC) contains several CPU cores, a GPU, often a neural processing unit and image signal processor, on-chip SRAM caches, a memory controller with its DRAM interface, display and camera interfaces, high-speed I/O, security blocks and power management logic, and in some designs a cellular modem. Main DRAM normally stays on separate chips, often stacked on top of the SoC package. Blocks inside communicate over an on-chip interconnect; Arm's AMBA AXI family, including AXI4-Lite for register access and AXI4-Stream for data flows, is a widely used standard that lets IP from different vendors connect.

Signals that stay on one die avoid package pins, board traces and the large drivers needed to switch them, so an SoC is smaller, faster and uses less power than the same functions spread over several chips, and the board needs fewer parts. The costs are real, however. Large dies have lower yield because each defect kills more area, the die cannot exceed the lithography field of about 26 mm by 33 mm, and functions that need different processes, such as DRAM, analog or RF, are hard to build optimally on the same logic process.

about.h: Power and security inside an SoC
about.p: Because blocks differ in speed requirements and activity, an SoC is split into power domains. Each can run at its own voltage and frequency through dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) or be switched off entirely, while a small always-on domain handles wake-up. Signals crossing domains need level shifters and isolation cells. An external power management IC (PMIC) generates the many supply rails from the battery under SoC control. For security, mechanisms such as Arm TrustZone tag every bus access as secure or normal, creating a protected environment within the same chip.

An SoC puts the system on one die. A system in package (SiP) instead places several dies and passive components in one package, which makes it easy to combine chips made in different processes and to reuse existing parts, at some cost in interconnect density and power. Chiplet designs split what would be a very large SoC into several dies connected at high density in an advanced package, improving yield and allowing systems larger than one reticle field. Many companies that design SoCs are fabless and have them manufactured by foundries.

faq.q: What is the difference between an SoC and a SiP?
faq.a: An SoC integrates the system's functions on a single silicon die, while a SiP houses multiple separate dies and components in one package. SoCs give the lowest power and latency; SiPs make it easier to mix chips from different processes.

faq.q: Is a microcontroller an SoC?
faq.a: In a broad sense yes, since a microcontroller integrates a CPU, flash, SRAM and peripherals on one chip. The term SoC is usually reserved for larger application processors that run a full operating system with external DRAM.

faq.q: Why is DRAM usually not on the same die as the SoC?
faq.a: Commodity DRAM uses a specialized process optimized for dense capacitor cells, which is incompatible with a high-performance logic process. Smartphones therefore stack separate DRAM chips on or next to the SoC package instead.

ASIC(特定用途向けIC).desc: An IC designed specifically for one application or customer. It beats general-purpose chips on performance and power, but high development costs suit it to high-volume uses.

about.p: An application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) carries large one-time costs, called non-recurring engineering (NRE): architecture and logic design, verification, licensed IP blocks, physical design, and a mask set that can cost millions to tens of millions of dollars at advanced nodes, plus months of fabrication lead time. In return, the chip contains only the needed functions, so each unit is small, fast, power-efficient and cheap to make. ASICs therefore pay off when volume is high enough to spread the NRE, or when no off-the-shelf part meets the performance or power target.

Most digital ASICs follow a standard-cell flow. Engineers write register-transfer level (RTL) code in Verilog or VHDL, verify it by simulation and, for large designs, emulation or FPGA prototyping, then synthesize it into gates from the foundry's cell library, with memories mapped to memory macros. Place-and-route builds the physical layout, static timing analysis and physical verification (DRC and LVS) confirm it, and the final layout is taped out to make masks. Full-custom design is used for the most performance-critical analog or memory blocks.

An FPGA implements logic in reprogrammable fabric, with no masks or fab wait, so it suits prototypes, low volumes and changing requirements; the same function as an ASIC is faster, smaller and lower power. An application-specific standard product (ASSP) is also dedicated to one application, but is sold as a catalog part to many customers, whereas an ASIC is typically built for one product or company. General-purpose CPUs and GPUs trade efficiency for flexibility through software.

ASICs appear wherever volume or efficiency justifies custom silicon: networking switches, storage controllers, consumer electronics, automotive systems, cryptocurrency mining and AI accelerators. Many are mixed-signal. A MEMS microphone, for example, pairs its capacitive sensing element with a small readout ASIC in the same package that converts the tiny capacitance change into an electrical signal. In these sensor uses, the ASIC is often designed jointly with the sensor itself.

faq.q: What does ASIC stand for?
faq.a: ASIC stands for application-specific integrated circuit, a chip designed for one particular product or use rather than as a general-purpose part.

faq.q: What is the difference between an ASIC and an FPGA?
faq.a: An ASIC's logic is fixed in silicon at manufacture, giving the best speed, power and unit cost but high up-front cost and long lead time. An FPGA can be reconfigured after manufacture with no mask cost, but is slower, larger and more power-hungry for the same function.

faq.q: What is the difference between an ASIC and an ASSP?
faq.a: Both target a specific application, but an ASIC is usually designed for a single customer or product, while an ASSP is a standard product a chip vendor sells to many customers.

MPW(マルチプロジェクトウエハ).desc: Prototyping several customers' designs together on one wafer (one mask set). Sharing the expensive mask cost makes it popular with universities and startups.

about.p: A foundry or aggregator announces runs on a given process at scheduled dates. Each participant submits a finished layout for a die area of agreed size by the deadline. The designs are tiled together on a shared reticle, one mask set is made, and the wafers are processed as a single lot. Afterwards the wafers are diced and each participant receives its own dies, often a few dozen, sometimes packaged. Mask and wafer costs are split among the participants, usually in proportion to silicon area, which is why the scheme is also called a shuttle.

A full mask set at an advanced node can cost tens of millions of dollars, and even mature nodes cost far more than a small team can spend on a first prototype. Sharing that cost lets universities, research groups and startups fabricate real chips for a small fraction of the price. Established companies use MPWs too, for test chips that characterize new circuits, validate IP blocks or check a new process before committing to a dedicated tape-out.

An MPW serves prototyping and evaluation, not production. Each participant gets only a limited number of dies, because neighboring designs share the wafer and dicing one design out can sacrifice its neighbors. Runs follow the foundry's calendar, so a missed deadline means waiting for the next shuttle, and die size, process options and turnaround are fixed by the organizer. Wafer-level testing and yield data are also limited compared with a dedicated lot.

Once a prototype works, the design moves to its own mask set for engineering lots and then volume production. For low-volume products, a multi-layer reticle, which places several mask layers on one reticle, can cut mask cost further at the expense of scanner throughput. For digital logic alone, an FPGA can validate function without any fabrication, but analog, RF and process-specific behavior can only be confirmed on real silicon, which is what an MPW run provides.

faq.q: What does MPW stand for?
faq.a: MPW stands for multi-project wafer: a fabrication run in which designs from several customers share one mask set and one set of wafers.

faq.q: Why do startups and universities use MPW runs?
faq.a: Because mask and wafer costs are divided among all participants, an MPW lets a small team obtain real prototype chips at a fraction of the cost of a dedicated mask set.

faq.q: Can an MPW be used for volume production?
faq.a: No. Each participant receives only a limited number of dies on a fixed schedule, so MPWs are used for prototypes and test chips; production requires a dedicated mask set.

デナードスケーリング.desc: The rule that shrinking transistor dimensions and supply voltage by the same factor gives faster, denser circuits at constant power density. It broke down in the mid-2000s when voltages could no longer be lowered easily.

about.p: Dennard scaling, described by Robert Dennard and colleagues in 1974, says how to shrink a MOSFET so every quantity improves together. Divide channel length, width, oxide thickness and supply voltage by a factor k and multiply doping by k. Gate capacitance then falls by k, gate delay falls by k, and power per transistor falls by k² because both voltage and current shrink. Since each transistor also occupies 1/k² of the area, power per unit area stays constant while the chip gets faster and denser.

The rule assumes threshold voltage scales with supply voltage, but subthreshold leakage sets a floor. At room temperature the subthreshold slope cannot be steeper than about 60 mV per decade of current, because thermal voltage does not shrink with dimensions. Each step down in threshold voltage therefore multiplies off-state leakage. Gate-oxide tunneling grew as oxides approached a few nanometres. By the mid-2000s supply voltages stalled near 1 V while transistor density kept rising, so power density was no longer constant.

With voltage stuck, raising clock frequency raised power density beyond what packages could cool, so single-core frequency growth flattened and designers turned to multiple cores. Chips became power-limited rather than area-limited, which led to dark silicon: more transistors than can switch at full speed simultaneously. The industry's answers include fine-grained DVFS, power gating, specialized accelerators that perform a task with far less energy than a general-purpose core, and device innovations such as strained silicon, high-k metal gates and FinFETs that improve performance per watt.

Moore's law is an observation about integration: the number of transistors on a chip at minimum cost doubles roughly every two years. Dennard scaling is a recipe for making each of those transistors better at constant power density. The two moved together for decades, which is why each new node used to bring higher clock speeds for free. Density scaling continued after Dennard scaling ended, so Moore's law outlived it, but the extra transistors no longer came with matching power savings.

faq.q: What is the difference between Moore's law and Dennard scaling?
faq.a: Moore's law describes how many transistors fit on a chip over time. Dennard scaling describes how shrinking dimensions and voltage together keeps power density constant, and it stopped holding in the mid-2000s while density growth continued.

faq.q: Why did Dennard scaling end?
faq.a: Threshold voltage could not keep falling without an exponential rise in leakage current, because the subthreshold slope is limited by temperature, not dimensions. Supply voltage therefore stalled and power density began to rise.

faq.q: What does the end of Dennard scaling have to do with multicore processors?
faq.a: Higher clock frequencies became too power-hungry once voltage stopped scaling, so designers used the extra transistors for more cores at moderate frequency instead of one faster core.

ディスクリート半導体.desc: The category of semiconductor products that perform one function as a single device, such as diodes, individual transistors and power MOSFETs, as opposed to integrated circuits.

2.5D実装.desc: Placing several chips side by side on an intermediate substrate such as a silicon interposer and connecting them with dense, fine wiring. It is used, for example, to connect GPUs and HBM.

about.p: Each die is flipped and attached with microbumps at a pitch of a few tens of micrometres onto an interposer, an intermediate substrate that carries the chip-to-chip wiring. On a silicon interposer that wiring is made with back-end-of-line processes, with line widths around 1 µm or below. Through-silicon vias (TSVs) carry power and external signals down through the interposer to larger bumps on an organic package substrate, which in turn connects to the board through a ball grid array.

An organic substrate with lines tens of micrometres wide cannot route thousands of signals between neighbouring dies, but an interposer can. This enables very wide, short parallel links, which is exactly what high-bandwidth memory (HBM) needs: each stack has an interface 1024 bits wide in common generations, sitting a few millimetres from the processor. Short links also cost far less energy per bit than board-level connections. The same approach lets a large design be split into chiplets, improving yield and allowing each die to use the most suitable process.

Silicon interposers offer the finest wiring but are costly, and their size is tied to lithography field limits, although stitching allows interposers several times the field size. Organic interposers built from redistribution layers (RDL) of polymer dielectric and copper are cheaper, easier to make large and closer in thermal expansion to the package substrate, but their wiring is coarser. A third approach embeds small silicon bridges only under die edges where dense connections are needed, leaving the rest of the package as ordinary substrate.

In 2.5D the dies sit side by side, so each can be cooled from the top and tested before assembly. In 3D packaging, dies stack vertically and connect through TSVs or hybrid bonding, giving the shortest connections but making heat removal harder. Fan-out wafer-level packaging forms RDL directly on dies embedded in mold compound, without a separate interposer. Real products combine them: an HBM stack is itself 3D, and several stacks are placed beside a processor in a 2.5D arrangement.

faq.q: What is the difference between 2.5D and 3D packaging?
faq.a: 2.5D places dies side by side on an interposer and connects them through its fine wiring. 3D stacks dies on top of each other and connects them vertically with TSVs or hybrid bonding.

faq.q: Why does HBM need an interposer?
faq.a: HBM uses a very wide interface with roughly a thousand data signals per stack, which an ordinary organic package substrate cannot route at that density. An interposer provides the fine, short wiring needed.

faq.q: What is the difference between a silicon interposer and an organic interposer?
faq.a: A silicon interposer has the finest wiring and supports TSVs but is expensive and size-limited. An organic RDL interposer is cheaper and easier to make large, at the cost of coarser line pitch.

3D実装.desc: Stacking chips vertically and connecting them with TSVs or hybrid bonding. Shorter connections improve speed and power, but heat removal becomes a challenge.

about.p: 3D packaging stacks dies vertically and connects them through the stack instead of through package or board wiring. Through-silicon vias (TSVs) are vertical copper conductors through thinned silicon that carry signals and power from one die to the next, usually joined by microbumps. Hybrid bonding joins two dies or wafers directly, bonding copper pads to copper and the surrounding dielectric to dielectric without bumps, which allows much finer connection pitches. Dies can be bonded wafer-to-wafer, die-to-wafer or die-to-die.

about.h: Why stacking helps speed and power
about.p: Stacking puts dies only tens of micrometers apart instead of millimeters apart side by side. Shorter interconnects have lower capacitance, so signal delay and the energy spent charging wires fall. Connections can be spread across the entire die face rather than lined up at the edges, giving far more parallel links and high bandwidth. The footprint shrinks as well. Familiar examples include stacked DRAM such as HBM (high bandwidth memory), image sensors with the pixel array bonded onto a logic die, and extra cache memory stacked on a processor.

2.5D packaging places dies side by side on an intermediate substrate, typically a silicon interposer with fine wiring, and connects them laterally. 3D packaging stacks dies on top of each other. 2.5D is easier to cool because every die can contact the heat spreader, while 3D gives the shortest connections. The two are often combined: HBM is itself a 3D stack of DRAM dies on a base die, and several HBM stacks are placed beside a GPU or accelerator on an interposer in a 2.5D arrangement.

Stacking concentrates power in a small footprint, and heat from inner dies must pass through bonding layers and thinned silicon to reach the heat sink, so temperatures rise and performance and reliability suffer. Thermal floorplanning, such as putting the hottest die next to the heat sink, is essential. Yield compounds as well: one bad die can scrap a whole stack, so dies are tested before stacking to select known-good dies, which favors die-to-wafer bonding. TSVs also create mechanical stress, so nearby transistors keep out of a surrounding zone.

faq.q: What is the difference between 2.5D and 3D packaging?
faq.a: 2.5D packaging places dies side by side on an interposer and connects them laterally, while 3D packaging stacks dies vertically and connects them with TSVs or hybrid bonding.

faq.q: What is the main challenge of 3D chip stacking?
faq.a: Heat removal is the most prominent challenge, because heat from inner dies must flow through other dies and bonding layers; yield loss from a single bad die and test access are also major issues.

faq.q: What is a TSV?
faq.a: A TSV (through-silicon via) is a vertical electrical connection, usually copper, that passes through a thinned silicon die so that signals and power can travel directly to a die stacked above or below.

再配線層(RDL).desc: A wiring layer formed on a chip or wafer surface to route pads out to the positions of the external terminals. It is used in fan-out packages and interposers.

マイクロバンプ.desc: A bump far smaller than an ordinary solder ball, used to connect TSV-stacked chips or chips to an interposer. The pitch is a few tens of micrometers.

UCIe.desc: Short for Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express: an industry-standard die-to-die interface intended to let chiplets from different companies connect to each other.

CoWoS.desc: TSMC's 2.5D packaging technology, which places logic chips and HBM side by side on a silicon interposer. It is widely used for AI GPUs and similar products.

FD-SOI(完全空乏型SOI).desc: Building transistors in a very thin silicon layer on buried oxide so the channel is fully depleted. The channel can be lightly doped, and body bias can tune the threshold voltage easily.

EOT(等価酸化膜厚).desc: The thickness of SiO2 that would give the same gate capacitance as a gate insulator such as a high-k film. A physically thick film can have a small EOT, giving high capacitance while limiting tunneling current.
