about.p: Gate capacitance per unit area is ε/t, so any dielectric can be converted to the SiO2 thickness (relative permittivity 3.9) that gives the same capacitance: EOT = physical thickness × 3.9/ε. For a high-k film with ε = 20, about 5 nm of physical film gives 1 nm of EOT. A real gate stack is several layers in series, so their EOTs simply add: a thin SiO2 interfacial layer counts one-for-one, while the high-k layer on top contributes only its thickness scaled by 3.9/ε.

about.h: Why gate dielectrics moved to high-k
about.p: Shrinking a transistor requires more gate capacitance so the gate keeps control of the channel. With pure SiO2 that means a thinner film, but direct tunneling current through the oxide rises exponentially as the film thins, and below roughly 2 nm the gate leakage becomes a serious power and reliability problem. A high-k material such as hafnium oxide (HfO2, ε about 20–25) delivers the same capacitance from a physically much thicker film, so tunneling is suppressed while the EOT keeps shrinking. Silicon oxynitride (SiON, ε about 5–6) was the intermediate step, also valued for blocking boron penetration.

High-k films placed directly on silicon hurt channel mobility through interface defects, fixed charge and remote phonon scattering. A thin SiO2 or SiON interfacial layer of about 0.5–1 nm is therefore kept underneath. Because it has low permittivity, this layer contributes a large share of the total EOT, so modern stacks of about 0.8–1 nm EOT depend on making the interfacial layer as thin as possible without degrading the interface. Plasma nitridation of the oxide surface is one way to raise its permittivity without disturbing the Si/SiO2 interface.

EOT is a property of the dielectric stack alone. The capacitance-equivalent thickness (CET) extracted from a measured capacitance in inversion is larger, because the inversion-layer charge peaks about 1 nm below the interface due to quantum confinement, adding roughly 0.3–0.4 nm in SiO2 terms. With polysilicon gates, depletion inside the gate electrode adds more; metal gates remove that term, which is one reason high-k is paired with metal gates. As EOT shrinks, these fixed penalties become a growing fraction of the electrical thickness.

faq.q: What does EOT stand for in semiconductors?
faq.a: EOT stands for equivalent oxide thickness: the thickness of SiO2 that would give the same gate capacitance as the actual gate dielectric. It lets stacks made of different materials be compared on one scale.

faq.q: How do you convert a high-k film thickness to EOT?
faq.a: Multiply the physical thickness by 3.9 divided by the film's relative permittivity. For example, 3 nm of a film with ε = 22 corresponds to about 0.53 nm of EOT, to which the interfacial layer's own EOT must be added.

faq.q: What is the difference between EOT and CET?
faq.a: EOT describes only the dielectric stack, while CET is the electrical thickness inferred from measured capacitance in inversion. CET is larger because of the quantum-mechanical setback of inversion charge and, with polysilicon gates, gate depletion.

ランダムドーパントゆらぎ(RDF).desc: Threshold-voltage variation in small transistors caused by statistical variation in the number and position of dopant atoms in the channel. FinFETs and FD-SOI, which allow lightly doped channels, reduce it.

SADP(自己整合ダブルパターニング).desc: Forming spacers on the sidewalls of a core pattern, removing the core and using the spacers as the mask to make a pitch half of what lithography alone allows. Doing it twice is SAQP.

ゲートラスト(リプレースメントメタルゲート).desc: Building the transistor first with a dummy gate, then removing it after high-temperature steps such as source/drain activation and replacing it with a high-k dielectric and metal gate.

about.h: Why the gate goes in last
about.p: High-k dielectrics such as hafnium oxide (HfO2) combined with metal gates replaced SiO2 and polysilicon to cut gate leakage and eliminate poly depletion. The catch is that source/drain activation anneals, around 1000 °C, can shift the work function of the metal gate stack and degrade the high-k film, moving the threshold voltage away from its target. The gate-last, or replacement metal gate (RMG), approach avoids this by putting the sensitive gate stack in only after the hottest steps are finished.

A polysilicon dummy gate is patterned first and used to align spacers and source/drain regions, which are implanted or grown epitaxially and then activated at high temperature. An interlayer dielectric is deposited over everything, and chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) planarizes it until the tops of the dummy gates are exposed. The dummy polysilicon is etched out selectively, leaving a narrow trench between the spacers. High-k dielectric, work-function metals chosen separately for nMOS and pMOS, and a low-resistance fill metal are deposited into the trench, and a second CMP removes the excess.

In a gate-first flow the high-k and metal are deposited and patterned at the start, like a traditional polysilicon gate. It needs fewer steps, but the stack must survive the activation anneal, which makes it hard to hold the desired threshold voltages, especially for pMOS. Gate-last adds a dummy gate, an extra CMP and a difficult trench fill, but it frees the choice of work-function metals. Intel adopted gate-last at the 45 nm generation, and it has since become the mainstream approach. Variants differ in whether the high-k is deposited at the start or after dummy removal.

about.h: Gate-last in FinFET and GAA flows
about.p: Replacement gates carried over naturally to FinFETs, where the dummy removal opens space around the fin so high-k and metal can wrap its sides. In gate-all-around nanosheet flows the same opening is used to etch away the sacrificial SiGe layers between silicon sheets, after which high-k and metal fill the gaps around each sheet. The tight points are the CMP that exposes the dummies, which must stop uniformly to control gate height, and void-free filling of a trench whose width is set by the gate length.

faq.q: What is a replacement metal gate?
faq.a: A replacement metal gate is a gate built in place of a temporary polysilicon dummy gate. The dummy defines the transistor during high-temperature steps and is then removed and refilled with high-k dielectric and metal.

faq.q: What is the difference between gate-first and gate-last?
faq.a: Gate-first forms the final high-k and metal gate at the beginning, so it must survive the source/drain anneal. Gate-last forms it at the end, protecting its work function from high temperature at the cost of extra process steps.

faq.q: Why is the dummy gate made of polysilicon?
faq.a: Polysilicon is easy to deposit and pattern precisely, withstands the high-temperature anneals, and can be etched away selectively against the surrounding oxide and nitride spacers when it is time to replace it.

DTCO(設計・技術協調最適化).desc: Optimizing cell area and performance by considering circuit design and process technology together, as scaling becomes harder.

ピエゾ抵抗効果.desc: The change in a material's electrical resistivity under mechanical stress. It is especially large in silicon and is used in semiconductor pressure sensors and similar devices.

ホール素子.desc: A sensor that detects magnetic fields using the Hall effect: a magnetic field applied to a current-carrying semiconductor produces a voltage perpendicular to both. It is used, for example, to sense motor rotation.

コリオリ力.desc: An apparent force acting perpendicular to the motion of an object moving in a rotating frame. Vibratory MEMS gyroscopes detect angular rate from the displacement it causes.

ボッシュプロセス(Deep RIE).desc: A dry-etching technique that alternates short etch and sidewall-passivation steps to cut deep, vertical holes and trenches in silicon. It is used for MEMS and TSVs.

about.h: How the Bosch etch cycle works
about.p: The Bosch process is a form of deep reactive ion etching (DRIE) that switches between two plasma steps every few seconds, usually in a high-density inductively coupled plasma (ICP) reactor. In the etch step, an SF6 plasma supplies fluorine radicals that etch silicon quickly but isotropically. In the passivation step, C4F8 deposits a thin fluorocarbon polymer over every exposed surface. When etching resumes, ions accelerated toward the wafer strip the polymer from the floor of the feature much faster than from the sidewalls, so the next etch step digs down while the walls stay protected.

about.h: Scallops, aspect ratio and other limits
about.p: Because each etch step briefly etches sideways before the next passivation, the sidewalls carry small periodic ripples called scallops. Shorter cycles give smoother walls at the cost of lower etch rate. Aspect ratios above 20 are achievable, but narrow features etch more slowly than wide ones because ions and radicals reach the bottom of deep holes less easily, an effect known as aspect-ratio-dependent etching or RIE lag. On silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafers, charging at the buried oxide can also cause lateral notching at the bottom of the trench.

about.h: Bosch process vs. KOH wet etching
about.p: Bulk micromachining, which shapes the substrate itself rather than deposited films, has two main tools. Anisotropic wet etching in KOH follows crystal planes: on a (100) wafer it stops on slow-etching (111) planes, giving V-grooves and cavities with sidewalls at about 54.7°. The Bosch process is a dry etch whose profile is set by the plasma, not the crystal orientation, so it cuts vertical walls of any outline shape. That makes it the choice for dense comb drives, through-wafer holes and high-aspect-ratio trenches, whereas surface micromachining builds micrometer-thick structures from deposited films.

In MEMS, deep RIE defines the proof masses and comb fingers of accelerometers and gyroscopes, opens through-wafer holes and shapes membranes. In advanced packaging it etches the holes for through-silicon vias (TSVs), typically with aspect ratios around 10. The hole is then lined with an insulator, barrier and seed layer, filled with copper by plating, and exposed by thinning the wafer from the back. Scallops matter here: rough sidewalls make it harder to deposit a continuous liner, so TSV recipes often trade etch rate for smoother walls.

faq.q: Why does the Bosch process leave scalloped sidewalls?
faq.a: Each short SF6 etch step is partly isotropic, so it removes a little silicon sideways before the next passivation layer protects the wall. Repeating this cycle leaves a row of small ripples whose size shrinks with shorter etch steps.

faq.q: What gases are used in the Bosch process?
faq.a: SF6 is used for the silicon etch step and C4F8 for the fluorocarbon passivation step. The two are alternated every few seconds.

faq.q: What is the difference between deep RIE and KOH etching?
faq.a: KOH is a wet etch that follows crystal planes, so on (100) silicon it produces sloped walls at about 54.7°. Deep RIE is a dry plasma etch that gives vertical walls regardless of crystal orientation.

スティクション.desc: The sticking of tiny moving MEMS parts to the substrate through surface tension or surface adhesion, so they no longer move. It often happens during drying after sacrificial-layer removal.

about.p: Stiction is a consequence of scaling. Adhesive forces, such as capillary forces from liquid films, van der Waals attraction, electrostatic attraction from trapped charge and hydrogen bonding between hydrophilic surfaces, grow with contact area. The restoring force of a thin, compliant beam or membrane is comparatively weak, and the gap beneath a released MEMS structure is often only about a micrometre. Large, flat, smooth surfaces separated by such small gaps are therefore easy to pull into contact, and once they touch, adhesion can exceed the spring force that should pull them apart.

The classic case occurs at release. A sacrificial layer, often SiO2, is etched away in liquid HF and rinsed. As the rinse liquid evaporates from the narrow gap, its meniscus pulls the structure toward the substrate, and the surfaces stay stuck after drying. The cure is to avoid a liquid-gas interface. Supercritical CO2 drying passes from liquid to gas without a meniscus, vapor-phase HF removes oxide without liquid, and XeF2 gas etches silicon sacrificial layers isotropically without plasma, with selectivity above 1000 to oxide, nitride and many metals.

Stiction can also appear after a device ships. An accelerometer's proof mass may hit its stops during a shock, RF MEMS switch contacts close millions of times, and humidity or trapped charge can make a contact that once released stay stuck. Designers reduce contact area with small bumps (dimples) on the moving part, apply hydrophobic self-assembled monolayer coatings that lower surface energy, design stops with enough restoring force, and seal the device in a dry, hermetic package so moisture cannot build up capillary bridges.

Stiction is often confused with pull-in, an electrostatic instability. In a parallel-plate electrostatic actuator, once the movable electrode travels about one third of the gap, the electrostatic force grows faster than the spring force and the electrode snaps down; this happens even with perfectly clean, non-adhesive surfaces. Pull-in is reversible when the voltage is removed unless the surfaces then adhere, in which case the device has failed by stiction. Pull-in is set by voltage, gap and stiffness; stiction depends on surface forces.

faq.q: Where does the word stiction come from?
faq.a: Stiction is a blend of static friction. In MEMS it refers more broadly to any adhesion that holds a moving part against a surface so that it cannot move freely.

faq.q: How is stiction prevented in MEMS?
faq.a: During release, liquid-free or meniscus-free methods such as vapor HF, XeF2 etching and supercritical CO2 drying are used. During operation, dimples, hydrophobic anti-stiction coatings and dry hermetic packaging keep surfaces from sticking.

faq.q: Why is stiction a bigger problem for MEMS than for larger machines?
faq.a: Surface forces scale with area while inertial and restoring forces scale with volume and stiffness, so at micrometre scale surface forces dominate. In large machines the same forces are negligible compared with weight and spring forces.

陽極接合.desc: Joining silicon to sodium-containing glass by heating them together while applying a voltage. It is used, for example, to seal MEMS devices.

シラン(SiH4).desc: A gas compound of silicon and hydrogen used as the source for CVD of polysilicon, silicon oxide and silicon nitride. It ignites spontaneously in air, so it is handled under strict control.

about.p: Silane (SiH4, monosilane) decomposes on heating to deposit silicon: SiH4 → Si + 2H2. In LPCVD at about 600–650 °C it forms polysilicon for gates, resistors and MEMS layers; below about 580 °C the film is amorphous, and annealing that amorphous film near 600 °C grows larger grains than direct poly deposition. For epitaxy, silane works at roughly 600–900 °C, lower than dichlorosilane or trichlorosilane. Disilane (Si2H6) and trisilane decompose even more readily for low-temperature growth, and silane mixed with germane (GeH4) grows SiGe.

Silane also supplies silicon for dielectrics. In plasma-enhanced CVD (PECVD) at about 300–400 °C, silane with nitrous oxide (N2O) deposits silicon oxide or tunable-index oxynitride (SiON), and silane with ammonia deposits silicon nitride containing about 10–30% hydrogen, used as final passivation and as a copper cap. Higher-quality LPCVD nitride uses dichlorosilane and ammonia at 700–800 °C instead. Silane is also used to nucleate tungsten CVD before WF6 is reduced with hydrogen, and with a hydrocarbon such as propane for SiC epitaxy.

Silane is pyrophoric: it can ignite spontaneously on contact with air, burning to a white silica powder. The worse hazard is that a high-concentration leak may not ignite at once, allowing a gas cloud to accumulate and then ignite explosively. Its lower explosive limit is about 1.4% in air. Fabs therefore store cylinders in exhausted gas cabinets, deliver it through lines with leak detectors, flow-limiting devices and automatic emergency shutoff valves, and purge lines with inert gas before any maintenance.

Chlorinated sources such as dichlorosilane and trichlorosilane need higher temperatures, but the HCl they release suppresses nucleation on oxide, favoring selective epitaxy, and trichlorosilane at about 1100–1150 °C grows thick layers at several µm per minute. Silane deposits at lower temperatures without chlorine, but grows less selectively and can form particles by gas-phase reaction. For oxide, liquid TEOS is a safer alternative that gives more conformal step coverage than silane-based oxide.

faq.q: Why is silane dangerous?
faq.a: Silane is pyrophoric and can ignite spontaneously in air. A large leak may also build up before igniting, causing an explosion, so it is handled in exhausted cabinets with leak detection and automatic shutoff.

faq.q: At what temperature does silane deposit polysilicon?
faq.a: LPCVD polysilicon is typically deposited from silane at about 600–650 °C. Below roughly 580 °C the film comes out amorphous instead of polycrystalline.

faq.q: What is the difference between silane and disilane?
faq.a: Disilane (Si2H6) contains a Si–Si bond that breaks more easily than the bonds in monosilane (SiH4), so it decomposes and deposits silicon at lower temperatures, which helps keep dopant profiles sharp in low-temperature epitaxy.

ホスフィン(PH3).desc: A gas compound of phosphorus and hydrogen used to introduce n-type dopant (phosphorus) into silicon. It is extremely toxic.

about.p: Phosphine (PH3) supplies phosphorus, the most common n-type dopant for silicon. In ion implantation it is cracked and ionized in the ion source, and the mass analyzer selects P⁺ ions. In CVD and epitaxy it is flowed alongside the silicon source for in-situ doping, producing conductive polysilicon for electrodes or phosphorus-doped silicon (Si:P) source/drain regions with concentrations on the order of 10²¹ cm⁻³. It is also used to deposit phosphosilicate glass, and in compound semiconductor growth it is the phosphorus source for materials such as indium phosphide.

Only tiny amounts of dopant are needed, so pure phosphine would require flows too small for a mass flow controller to meter accurately. Diluting it to a few percent or to ppm levels in hydrogen or nitrogen lets the required dose be delivered at controllable flows. Dilution also lowers the concentration released in a leak, reducing both toxic and fire risk. For implanters, phosphine is often stored adsorbed on a porous solid in sub-atmospheric containers, which tend to draw air in rather than leak gas out if a valve or fitting fails.

Phosphine is extremely toxic, with occupational exposure limits around 0.05 ppm, and it is also flammable. Fabs therefore keep cylinders in exhausted gas cabinets, run it through double-contained lines, and install continuous leak detectors tied to emergency shutoff valves. Exhaust from process tools passes through abatement systems that burn, scrub or adsorb unreacted hydride before release. Sub-atmospheric adsorbent sources reduce the chance of a large release, but they do not change the toxicity of the gas, so detection and exhaust are still required.

Arsine (AsH3) is the other hydride n-type source; arsenic is heavier and diffuses more slowly than phosphorus, which suits shallow junctions. Phosphorus oxychloride (POCl3) is a liquid source used in furnace diffusion, where it forms phosphorus-rich glass on the wafer surface and is still common for crystalline silicon solar cell emitters. For the p-type dopant boron, diborane (B2H6) is the usual in-situ doping gas and boron trifluoride (BF3) the usual implant source gas.

faq.q: Why is phosphine so dangerous?
faq.a: It is highly toxic at very low concentrations, with exposure limits around 0.05 ppm, and it is flammable. A leak can harm people before it is noticed, so it is handled only with gas cabinets, leak detectors, automatic shutoff and exhaust abatement.

faq.q: Is phosphine an n-type or p-type dopant source?
faq.a: It is an n-type source: phosphorus has five valence electrons, one more than silicon, so each substitutional phosphorus atom donates an electron. The common p-type counterparts are diborane and boron trifluoride.

faq.q: What is the difference between phosphine and POCl3 doping?
faq.a: Phosphine is a gas used in ion implanters and for in-situ doping during CVD or epitaxy. POCl3 is a liquid source used in diffusion furnaces, where it forms a phosphorus glass on the wafer from which phosphorus diffuses into the silicon.

アルシン(AsH3).desc: A gas compound of arsenic and hydrogen used to introduce n-type dopant (arsenic) and to grow compound semiconductors such as GaAs. It is extremely toxic.

about.h: What arsine does in a fab
about.p: Arsine (AsH3) is the hydride of arsenic and the standard gas source of that element. In ion implantation, the ion source ionizes arsine to produce arsenic ions for n-type regions; arsenic is heavy and diffuses slowly in silicon, which suits shallow, heavily doped junctions. In chemical vapor deposition and epitaxy it can dope films with arsenic during growth. In compound semiconductor manufacturing it supplies the arsenic for growing GaAs, AlGaAs and InGaAs layers. Its group V partner phosphine (PH3) plays the same roles for phosphorus.

Arsine is one of the most toxic gases used in semiconductor manufacturing. Its occupational exposure limit is set at about 0.005 ppm, roughly ten times lower than phosphine's, meaning that a barely measurable leak can already exceed safe levels. Inhaled arsine attacks red blood cells, and the faint garlic-like odor is not a reliable warning. It is also flammable. Exposure limits of this kind are guideline concentrations for repeated work-day exposure and are used to decide whether local exhaust, detection and protective equipment are needed.

A conventional high-pressure cylinder can release a large amount of gas at once if a valve or line fails. For arsine and phosphine, fabs widely use sub-atmospheric containers in which the gas is adsorbed on a porous sorbent and held below atmospheric pressure. If a leak occurs, air tends to flow in rather than gas flowing out, greatly reducing the risk of a massive release, and the tool's vacuum draws the gas out during use. The gas itself is just as toxic, so detection and exhaust are still required.

Arsine sources sit in exhausted gas cabinets with continuous leak detectors, emergency shutoff valves and automatic alarms, and tool exhaust passes through abatement systems that destroy or capture the hydride before release. Arsenic also appears in solid and liquid waste: GaAs is about 52% arsenic by weight, so grinding and polishing dust, spent slurries and scrapped wafers are handled as hazardous waste, with local exhaust ventilation and protective equipment preventing worker exposure during processing.

faq.q: What is arsine used for in semiconductor manufacturing?
faq.a: Arsine supplies arsenic: as an ion-source gas for implanting n-type arsenic, as an in-situ dopant during deposition or epitaxy, and as the arsenic source for growing compound semiconductors such as GaAs and InGaAs.

faq.q: What is the difference between arsine and phosphine?
faq.a: Both are highly toxic, flammable group V hydrides used for n-type doping; arsine delivers arsenic and phosphine delivers phosphorus. Arsine's exposure limit, around 0.005 ppm, is about an order of magnitude lower than phosphine's.

faq.q: Why is arsine stored in sub-atmospheric containers?
faq.a: Holding the gas adsorbed on a sorbent below atmospheric pressure means a leak draws air in rather than pushing gas out, so a sudden large release is much less likely than with a high-pressure cylinder.

マスフローコントローラ(MFC).desc: A device in deposition and etch tools that precisely measures the mass flow of a gas and holds it at a set value.

SEM(走査電子顕微鏡).desc: A microscope that scans a finely focused electron beam over a sample and detects secondary electrons and other signals to image the surface. It resolves features of a few nanometers, far beyond optical microscopes.

about.h: How an SEM builds an image
about.p: A scanning electron microscope (SEM) has no image-forming lens in the optical sense. An electron gun, usually a field-emission source in high-end tools, produces a beam that electromagnetic lenses focus to a spot only nanometers wide, and scan coils raster it across the sample in vacuum. At each point a detector measures the electrons emitted, and that count becomes the brightness of one pixel. Magnification is simply the ratio of display size to scanned area. Because electrons at kilovolt energies have picometer-scale wavelengths, resolution is limited by spot size and beam–sample interaction rather than diffraction, reaching around 1 nm.

about.h: Secondary electrons, backscattered electrons and X-rays
about.p: Secondary electrons have low energies, conventionally below 50 eV, so only those generated within a few nanometers of the surface escape; their yield depends on local tilt and edges, giving crisp topographic images. Backscattered electrons are beam electrons deflected back with high energy, and their yield rises with atomic number, so heavier materials appear brighter, giving compositional contrast. The beam also knocks out inner-shell electrons, producing characteristic X-rays analyzed by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) to identify elements, with detection limits of about 0.1 wt%. Trace impurities need more sensitive methods such as SIMS.

Critical-dimension SEMs (CD-SEMs) measure linewidths and hole diameters top-down for process control, operating at low accelerating voltage to limit charging and beam damage to resist. Review SEMs revisit defects found by optical inspection tools and image them at high resolution, and automatic defect classification (ADC) sorts those images into categories such as particles, pattern defects and scratches. For internal structure, a wafer is cleaved or milled with a focused ion beam (FIB) and the cross-section imaged; this is destructive, so it is done on sampled or test wafers. Dual-beam FIB-SEM tools image while milling.

On insulating samples, incoming electrons cannot drain away, so charge builds up and distorts brightness and geometry. Remedies include lowering the accelerating voltage until emitted and incoming electrons roughly balance, coating the surface with a thin gold or carbon film, or imaging in low-vacuum mode, where gas ions neutralize charge. Raising the voltage usually makes charging worse. An SEM images the surface of a bulk sample from reflected and emitted signals, whereas a transmission electron microscope (TEM) sends electrons through a lamella thin enough to transmit them, reaching atomic resolution but requiring careful sample preparation.

faq.q: What is the difference between SEM and TEM?
faq.a: An SEM scans a beam across a bulk sample and detects emitted electrons, giving surface images down to about a nanometer. A TEM passes electrons through an ultra-thin slice and can resolve atomic columns, but the sample must be specially thinned.

faq.q: Why are SEM samples coated with gold or carbon?
faq.a: Insulating samples accumulate charge under the electron beam, which distorts the image. A thin conductive coating drains the charge to ground; low accelerating voltage or low-vacuum mode are alternatives when coating is unacceptable.

faq.q: What is a CD-SEM?
faq.a: A CD-SEM is an SEM specialized for automatically measuring critical dimensions, such as linewidths and hole sizes, on production wafers. It uses low beam energy to minimize charging and damage to resist patterns.

AFM(原子間力顕微鏡).desc: A microscope that traces a sharp tip over a sample and measures fine surface topography from the forces between tip and surface. It is used, for example, to evaluate surface roughness.

about.p: An atomic force microscope (AFM) carries a sharp tip at the free end of a microfabricated cantilever. As a piezoelectric scanner moves the tip and sample relative to each other in a raster, forces between tip and surface bend the cantilever. A laser beam reflected off the back of the cantilever onto a position-sensitive photodetector magnifies that bending. A feedback loop raises or lowers the tip to keep the deflection, or oscillation amplitude, constant, and the recorded height at each point builds a three-dimensional topography map with vertical resolution around 0.1 nm.

In contact mode the tip is dragged across the surface at constant deflection, which is simple but applies lateral forces that can scratch soft films or blunt the tip. In tapping mode the cantilever oscillates near its resonance and touches the surface only briefly at the bottom of each cycle; the feedback holds the oscillation amplitude constant. Tapping mode minimizes damage and is the usual choice for resists, polymers and delicate thin films, while still delivering sub-nanometer height sensitivity.

An AFM image is never the pure surface: it is the surface convolved with the tip. A tip cannot reach the bottom of a trench narrower than itself, and on steep sidewalls its flank touches first, so trenches appear shallower and narrower and lines appear wider. Sharper tips, flared tips designed for sidewall profiling, and software that estimates and removes the tip shape all reduce the error. Scanning is mechanical and slow, and fields of view are small, so AFM samples selected sites rather than whole wafers.

AFM's strengths are surface roughness after chemical mechanical polishing (CMP), thin-film surfaces and small step heights. A stylus profiler works on the same tracing principle with coarser resolution but can scan millimeters, so it suits etch depth and long-range planarity. AFM measures shape only: composition and chemical state come from XPS (X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy), and sheet resistance from a four-point probe. In advanced nodes, AFM data is often combined with optical and CD-SEM results in hybrid metrology to constrain dimensions no single tool determines well.

faq.q: What does an atomic force microscope measure?
faq.a: Surface topography, meaning height variations and roughness, with vertical resolution around 0.1 nm, from the forces between a sharp tip and the sample.

faq.q: What is the difference between contact mode and tapping mode AFM?
faq.a: Contact mode drags the tip along the surface continuously; tapping mode oscillates the cantilever so the tip touches only intermittently, greatly reducing lateral force and sample damage.

faq.q: Why does AFM make trenches look narrower than they are?
faq.a: The tip has finite size and shape, so it cannot reach into narrow trenches or follow steep walls. The image is the true profile convolved with the tip shape.

EDX(エネルギー分散型X線分光).desc: An analysis method that measures the energies of characteristic X-rays emitted under an electron beam to identify which elements are present and how much. It is used with SEM or TEM.

about.h: How characteristic X-rays are produced and counted
about.p: The primary electron beam, typically 5 to 30 keV in an SEM, knocks an inner-shell electron out of an atom. An outer-shell electron drops into the vacancy and the energy difference leaves as an X-ray photon whose energy is fixed by the element, for example about 1.74 keV for the silicon K-alpha line. A solid-state detector, today usually a silicon drift detector (SDD), turns each photon into a charge pulse proportional to its energy. A pulse-height analyzer sorts the pulses into a spectrum of counts versus energy: peak positions identify the elements, and corrected peak areas give their concentrations.

In a bulk sample the electrons scatter into a pear-shaped interaction volume that is often a micrometer or more across, so an SEM-based analysis reports the average composition of a region much larger than the beam spot. Lowering the beam energy shrinks this volume but may no longer excite the higher-energy lines of heavier elements. In a TEM or scanning TEM the specimen is a thin lamella, usually well under 100 nm thick and often cut with a focused ion beam (FIB), so the beam hardly spreads and elemental maps with nanometer-scale resolution become possible, which is essential for analyzing advanced device structures.

The detection limit is around 0.1 wt%, so EDX sees major constituents, contamination particles and film stoichiometry but not dopants at device-level concentrations. Light elements such as boron, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen emit low-energy X-rays that are easily absorbed, so their quantification is poor and boron is especially difficult. The energy resolution of an SDD is roughly 130 eV, so some lines overlap; a well-known case in chip analysis is silicon K-alpha and the tungsten M line near 1.77 keV. Insulating samples can charge up, and sensitive films can be damaged by the beam.

about.h: EDX versus SIMS and other analysis methods
about.p: EDX is quick, largely non-destructive and shows composition exactly where the microscope is looking, which makes it the first choice for identifying particles and failure sites. Secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) sputters the sample with primary ions and mass-analyzes the ejected ions, reaching ppm to ppb sensitivity and giving depth profiles, but it consumes the sample. Wavelength-dispersive spectroscopy (WDS) resolves overlapping peaks better but is slower. Spreading resistance profiling measures electrically active carriers, and infrared absorption (FTIR) measures interstitial oxygen in silicon, neither of which EDX can do.

faq.q: What is the difference between EDX and EDS?
faq.a: They are the same technique. EDX (energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy) and EDS (energy-dispersive spectroscopy) are used interchangeably, and some texts write XEDS.

faq.q: Can EDX measure dopant concentration in silicon?
faq.a: No. Typical dopant levels are far below the roughly 0.1 wt% detection limit of EDX. Use SIMS for the atomic concentration profile and electrical methods such as spreading resistance profiling for the active carrier concentration.

faq.q: Is EDX analysis destructive?
faq.a: The measurement itself usually leaves the sample intact, although the beam can charge insulators or damage sensitive films. TEM-based EDX, however, requires cutting a thin lamella, which destroys that part of the device.

XPS(X線光電子分光法).desc: An analysis method that determines the elements in the top few nanometers of a surface and their chemical bonding states from the energies of photoelectrons emitted under X-ray irradiation.

TXRF(全反射蛍光X線分析).desc: An analysis method that shines X-rays at a grazing angle so they totally reflect, then sensitively measures the fluorescent X-rays from trace metal contamination on the wafer surface.

FIB(集束イオンビーム).desc: An instrument that mills or deposits material with a finely focused ion beam. It is used for cross-sectioning tiny areas, preparing thin TEM samples and editing circuits.

XRD(X線回折).desc: An analysis method that shines X-rays on a crystal and uses the angles and intensities of the diffracted beams to determine crystal structure, lattice constant, film strain and crystal quality.

about.p: X-rays scattered by parallel planes of atoms reinforce one another only when the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths, which is Bragg's law, 2d·sinθ = nλ. Laboratory instruments commonly use copper Kα radiation with a wavelength of about 0.154 nm, comparable to atomic spacings. In a θ-2θ scan, peak positions give plane spacings d, which identify the crystal phase and lattice constant. Peak broadening reflects small crystallite size and non-uniform strain, and relative peak intensities reveal preferred orientation.

High-resolution XRD (HRXRD) uses a conditioned, nearly monochromatic beam to resolve tiny angle differences. In an epitaxial stack such as SiGe on Si, the separation between the layer peak and the substrate peak gives the lattice mismatch, from which strain and composition follow. Interference fringes around the layer peak give its thickness. A rocking curve, scanning the sample angle with the detector fixed, measures crystal perfection: near-perfect silicon gives a width of a few arcseconds, while heavily dislocated GaN on sapphire gives hundreds.

For polycrystalline thin films, grazing-incidence XRD keeps the beam near the surface to increase signal from the film rather than the substrate, and pole-figure measurements map texture, such as the preferred orientation of copper interconnect grains. Reciprocal space maps separate composition from strain relaxation in epitaxial layers. X-ray reflectivity (XRR), measured on the same instruments at very low angles, gives thickness, density and interface roughness even for amorphous films, since it relies on electron density contrast rather than crystal planes.

XRD is non-destructive, needs no vacuum or sample preparation in most cases, and averages over a spot typically millimetres across, giving good statistics but no nanometre-scale detail; transmission electron microscopy (TEM) is used for local structure. It requires crystalline order, so amorphous films show only broad humps. It is also distinct from X-ray fluorescence (XRF), which detects characteristic X-rays emitted by elements to measure composition rather than crystal structure.

faq.q: What is Bragg's law in X-ray diffraction?
faq.a: Bragg's law, 2d·sinθ = nλ, states that X-rays reflected from atomic planes spaced d apart interfere constructively at angle θ when the path difference equals a whole number of wavelengths. Measuring the diffraction angle therefore gives the plane spacing.

faq.q: What is the difference between XRD and XRF?
faq.a: XRD measures diffraction angles to determine crystal structure, lattice constants and strain. XRF measures fluorescent X-rays emitted by atoms to identify which elements are present and how much.

faq.q: What does a rocking curve FWHM tell you?
faq.a: It measures the spread of crystal plane orientations in a layer. A narrow full width at half maximum indicates few dislocations and little mosaicity, while a broad one indicates a defective crystal.

欠陥検査装置.desc: Equipment that finds particles and pattern defects on wafers, for example by detecting scattered light or by comparing images of neighboring dies.

時間的局所性.desc: The tendency to access the same data or instructions again soon after a first access, as with variables reused inside a loop. One of the reasons caches work.

空間的局所性.desc: The tendency to access addresses near one just accessed, as when reading an array in order. It is why caches fetch data a whole cache line at a time.

ダイレクトマップ方式.desc: A cache organization in which each address can be placed in exactly one location. It is simple with short hit time, but prone to conflict misses when addresses compete for the same slot.

セットアソシアティブ方式.desc: A cache organization in which data can go in any of several locations (ways) within the one set selected by the address. An n-way cache compares n tags in parallel on each access.

about.p: A cache address is divided into three fields. The low offset bits pick a byte within a line, the index bits pick one set, and the remaining high bits form the tag stored alongside the line. The number of sets equals capacity divided by line size times the number of ways. For a 32 KB cache with 64-byte lines and 32-bit addresses there are 512 lines: direct-mapped gives 512 sets, a 9-bit index and a 17-bit tag, while 4-way gives 128 sets, a 7-bit index and a 19-bit tag. Each doubling of associativity removes one index bit and adds one tag bit.

The index selects a set, and the tags of all n ways in that set are read and compared with the address tag simultaneously, so an 8-way cache needs eight comparators. Each comparison also checks a valid bit. The way whose tag matches drives a multiplexer that delivers the data; many fast L1 designs read the data of every way in parallel with the tag check and select at the end, trading power for speed. On a miss, a replacement policy such as LRU (least recently used) or a cheaper pseudo-LRU approximation chooses which way in the set to evict.

These are points on one spectrum. A direct-mapped cache is 1-way: each address has exactly one possible slot, so two hot blocks that share an index evict each other repeatedly, a conflict miss. A fully associative cache is a single set in which any line can go anywhere, removing conflict misses but requiring a comparison against every tag. Set-associative caches sit in between. Raising associativity reduces conflict misses but not compulsory or capacity misses, and returns diminish beyond about 8 ways, while comparators, multiplexer delay, hit time and power keep rising.

Level-1 caches are commonly 8 to 12 ways because hit time is critical and the cache is small. Last-level caches, where a miss costs a trip to DRAM, often use around 16 ways, since a slightly slower hit is acceptable in exchange for fewer misses. Translation lookaside buffers (TLBs) are frequently highly or fully associative because they hold few entries and a miss is expensive. When estimating hardware cost, remember that tag storage grows with associativity too, because each extra way removes an index bit and lengthens every stored tag.

faq.q: How do you calculate the number of sets in a set-associative cache?
faq.a: Divide the capacity by the line size to get the number of lines, then divide by the number of ways. A 32 KB, 4-way cache with 64-byte lines has 512 lines and therefore 128 sets.

faq.q: Does higher associativity always make a cache faster?
faq.a: No. It lowers conflict misses, but each access must compare more tags and select among more ways, which tends to lengthen hit time and raise power. The best choice balances miss rate against hit time for that cache level.

faq.q: What is the difference between a set and a way?
faq.a: A set is the group of slots that one index value selects, and a way is one slot within that set. An 8-way cache has eight ways in every set, and a block may be placed in any of them.

フルアソシアティブ方式.desc: A cache organization in which any data can be placed in any location. It has no conflict misses but must compare against every tag, so it suits small structures such as TLBs rather than large caches.

キャッシュライン.desc: The unit in which data moves between a cache and the level below, also called a cache block. Many CPUs use 64 bytes, and the low address bits give the position (offset) within the line.

about.p: Programs that touch one address usually touch its neighbors soon after, a property called spatial locality. Caches exploit it by moving data in fixed blocks, typically 64 bytes, rather than single words, and the size conveniently matches one DRAM burst: eight transfers of 8 bytes on a 64-bit DDR4 channel. Each cached line carries a tag identifying its address, a valid bit marking real data, a dirty bit in write-back caches and replacement and coherence state. An address therefore splits into tag, index and offset fields; with 64-byte lines, the lowest 6 bits are the offset.

Line size turns access patterns into miss rates. Reading an array of 4-byte integers in order misses once per 16 elements, a 6.25% miss rate, because each miss brings in the next 15 elements. Reading only every 16th element misses every time. C stores two-dimensional arrays in row-major order, so looping over the column index in the inner loop walks consecutive addresses, while swapping the loops jumps a full row per access and may evict lines before they are reused. Larger lines help sequential code but waste bandwidth and capacity when little of each line is used.

In a multicore processor, coherence protocols track ownership at line granularity. Under MESI, each line is Modified (changed and held only here, so memory is stale), Exclusive (clean and held only here), Shared (clean copies may exist elsewhere) or Invalid. A core that wants to write must first invalidate copies in other caches; a line already in M can be written repeatedly without notifying anyone. Small systems broadcast these requests, while large ones use directories that record which caches hold each line, so traffic scales with the number of cores.

Because coherence is per line, two threads writing different variables that happen to share a 64-byte line still invalidate each other's copies on every write. The line bounces between cores, results stay correct, but performance can drop sharply. Arrays of per-thread counters or flags are the classic case. The fix is to pad or align each thread's data to its own line, for example with alignment attributes in C and C++. Contrast this with true sharing, where threads really do access the same variable and communication cannot be avoided by layout.

faq.q: How big is a cache line?
faq.a: 64 bytes on most current CPUs, though some processors use 32 or 128 bytes; the size is a hardware property that software can query.

faq.q: What is the difference between a cache line and a page?
faq.a: A cache line, usually 64 bytes, is the unit moved between cache levels and memory, while a page, often 4 KB, is the unit of virtual-memory mapping managed by the OS and MMU.

faq.q: How do I avoid false sharing?
faq.a: Place data written by different threads in separate cache lines, typically by padding or aligning per-thread structures to 64 bytes.

ライトスルー方式.desc: A write policy that writes to the level below (such as main memory) at the same time as the cache. The lower level stays up to date, but write traffic is heavy, so it is paired with a write buffer.

ライトアロケート.desc: A policy that, on a write miss, first brings the line into the cache and then writes it. Usually paired with write-back; writing directly to the lower level without fetching is called no-write-allocate.

初期参照ミス.desc: A cache miss that inevitably occurs on the first access to data. A larger cache does not reduce it, but larger lines or prefetching can.

容量ミス.desc: A cache miss caused by the working set being larger than the cache. It occurs even in a fully associative cache and is reduced by a larger cache or by improving data reuse.

競合ミス.desc: A cache miss caused when several blocks compete for the same set and evict each other even though capacity remains. Higher associativity or shifting data placement reduces it.

LRU(Least Recently Used).desc: A cache replacement policy that evicts the least recently used data. It exploits temporal locality well, but exact tracking is costly with many ways, so approximations are used.

プリフェッチ.desc: Loading data into the cache before it is requested because it is likely to be needed soon. Hardware prefetchers detect access patterns, and software prefetching uses explicit instructions.

about.p: An L1 cache hit takes a few cycles, around 1 ns, while a DRAM access takes tens to about 100 ns, so a multi-GHz core can wait hundreds of cycles on a miss; this gap is called the memory wall. Compulsory misses, which occur the first time data is touched, are not reduced by more capacity or associativity because the data was never cached. Prefetching attacks this by requesting lines before the program needs them, overlapping memory latency with useful work. Larger cache lines help in a similar way by bringing in neighboring data with each miss.

A hardware prefetcher watches the stream of miss or access addresses and looks for regularity. The simplest fetches the next sequential line; stride prefetchers track the address difference between successive accesses, often per load instruction, and once a constant stride repeats they issue requests several strides ahead. Reading an int array sequentially with 64-byte lines would otherwise miss once per 16 elements, a 6.25% miss rate, and a good prefetcher hides most of those misses. Pointer chasing defeats this: in a linked list the next address is unknown until the current node arrives, so misses serialize.

Software prefetching inserts explicit prefetch instructions, either by hand or by the compiler, for patterns hardware cannot predict, such as indirect accesses through an index array. These instructions are hints that typically do not fault or change program results. The key parameter is prefetch distance: fetching too close to the use leaves latency exposed, while fetching too far ahead risks eviction before use. A common rule of thumb is to prefetch ahead by about the miss latency divided by the time per loop iteration, then tune by measurement.

Prefetching is not free. Useless prefetches consume memory bandwidth and can evict useful lines, a problem called cache pollution, which can make a program slower. Prefetchers are therefore judged on accuracy, the fraction of prefetched lines actually used; coverage, the fraction of original misses eliminated; and timeliness, whether data arrives before it is needed. Prefetching also differs from out-of-order execution, which overlaps misses only within its limited instruction window. When a data structure is hostile to prediction, reorganizing it into contiguous arrays often helps more than any prefetcher.

faq.q: What is the difference between hardware and software prefetching?
faq.a: Hardware prefetchers detect patterns like sequential or constant-stride access automatically at run time. Software prefetching relies on explicit instructions placed by the programmer or compiler, which helps with irregular but computable addresses.

faq.q: Why doesn't prefetching help linked lists much?
faq.a: Each node's address is only known after the previous node has been loaded, so there is no predictable pattern and misses cannot overlap. Storing the data contiguously or adding jump pointers is usually needed.

faq.q: Can prefetching make performance worse?
faq.a: Yes. Inaccurate or overly early prefetches waste bandwidth and evict data that was still needed, so aggressive prefetching can slow memory-bound programs.

平均メモリアクセス時間(AMAT).desc: The average time per memory access, computed as hit time + miss rate × miss penalty. A basic metric for comparing cache designs.

ミスペナルティ.desc: The extra time needed to fetch data from the next level when a cache miss occurs, determined by the lower level's access time and the line transfer time.

about.p: The miss penalty is the time to fetch the missing line from the next level of the hierarchy. It has two parts: the latency until the first data arrives and the transfer time for the rest of the line, which is line size divided by bandwidth. In a multilevel hierarchy, the L1 miss penalty is simply the average access time of L2. With a 10 ns L2 hit time, a 20% L2 local miss rate and 100 ns main memory, the L1 miss penalty is 10 + 0.2 × 100 = 30 ns, far shorter than going straight to memory.

about.h: How it enters AMAT and CPI
about.p: Average memory access time (AMAT) is hit time + miss rate × miss penalty. With a 2-cycle hit time, a 4% miss rate and a 150-cycle penalty, AMAT is 2 + 0.04 × 150 = 8 cycles, four times the hit time. In CPI terms, an ideal CPI of 1.0 with 1.3 memory accesses per instruction, a 2% miss rate and a 100-cycle penalty gains 1.3 × 0.02 × 100 = 2.6 stall cycles, giving a CPI of 3.6. A large penalty turns even small miss rates into large slowdowns.

about.h: Why miss rate alone can mislead
about.p: Larger or more associative caches reduce the miss rate but may lengthen the hit time, and larger lines exploit spatial locality but raise the miss penalty because each miss transfers more data. Designs must therefore be compared by AMAT, not miss rate. With a 20-cycle penalty, a cache with a 1-cycle hit and 5% miss rate averages 1 + 0.05 × 20 = 2.0 cycles, while one with a 2-cycle hit and 4% miss rate averages 2 + 0.04 × 20 = 2.8 cycles, so the cache with the lower miss rate is slower.

about.h: Techniques that cut the effective penalty
about.p: Adding cache levels shortens the trip for most misses. Critical word first sends the word the CPU requested before the rest of the line, and early restart lets execution resume as soon as that word arrives. Non-blocking caches keep serving hits while a miss is outstanding, and out-of-order cores overlap several misses so their latencies partly hide one another. Prefetching hides the penalty by fetching ahead; a useful rule of thumb sets the prefetch distance to roughly the miss penalty divided by the time per loop iteration.

faq.q: How do you calculate miss penalty in a two-level cache?
faq.a: The L1 miss penalty equals the L2 average access time: L2 hit time plus L2 local miss rate times the main memory access time. For example, 10 ns + 0.2 × 100 ns = 30 ns.

faq.q: What is the difference between miss rate and miss penalty?
faq.a: Miss rate is the fraction of accesses that miss in the cache, while miss penalty is the extra time each miss costs. Average access time depends on their product plus the hit time.

faq.q: Does a larger cache line increase the miss penalty?
faq.a: Yes. Each miss must transfer more bytes, so the transfer part of the penalty grows, even though larger lines can reduce the number of misses for code with good spatial locality.

ループブロッキング.desc: An optimization that processes large arrays in small blocks that fit in the cache so loaded data is reused many times before eviction. Very effective for matrix multiplication.

ノンブロッキングキャッシュ.desc: A cache that keeps servicing other accesses while a miss is outstanding. It can handle multiple misses at once, overlapping and hiding memory latency.

特権モード.desc: A CPU operating mode reserved for the OS kernel, in which dangerous operations such as setting page tables and controlling I/O are allowed. It is distinguished from user mode, where applications run.

システムコール.desc: The mechanism by which applications ask the OS for services such as file I/O or memory allocation. A dedicated instruction raises an exception that switches to privileged mode and invokes the kernel.

割り込みハンドラ.desc: The routine a CPU runs when an interrupt or exception occurs. It saves the interrupted state, handles the cause and returns. Handlers should be kept as short as possible.

about.h: What happens when an interrupt is accepted
about.p: When a device signals an interrupt, the CPU finishes the current instruction, saves the address it would have executed next along with state such as the operating mode and flags, and jumps to the interrupt handler, also called an interrupt service routine (ISR), usually found through an interrupt vector table. The handler saves any registers it uses, services the cause, clears the device's interrupt flag, restores state and executes a return-from-interrupt instruction. The interrupted program then resumes exactly where it stopped; it is neither discarded nor restarted.

While a handler runs, other interrupts of the same or lower priority are typically held off and the main code is stalled, so a long handler increases latency for everything else. Slow calls such as printf are especially risky because they take time and may themselves depend on interrupts. A good handler does the minimum, such as moving received data into a buffer or setting a flag, and leaves heavy processing to the main loop or a task. Operating system kernels formalize this by splitting work into an immediate part and a deferred part.

Variables shared between a handler and the main program cause classic bugs. If main spins on a flag that only the handler sets, an optimizing compiler may load it into a register once and never see the update; declaring it volatile forces every access to go to memory. A read-modify-write such as reg |= mask can be interrupted between the read and the write, wiping out a change the handler made to another bit. Briefly disabling interrupts or using hardware set and clear registers avoids this, and multi-byte variables need protection against torn reads.

A periodic timer interrupt is what lets an operating system take back the CPU from a program that never yields, enabling preemptive scheduling and context switches. Interrupts are asynchronous events from hardware, whereas exceptions such as page faults or divide-by-zero arise synchronously from the instruction being executed, though both enter the kernel through similar handlers. One common mistake is kicking a watchdog timer unconditionally inside a timer interrupt: the interrupt keeps firing even if the main loop has hung, so the watchdog never detects the failure.

faq.q: What is the difference between an interrupt handler and an ISR?
faq.a: There is no real difference: interrupt service routine (ISR) is another name for the interrupt handler, the code the CPU runs in response to an interrupt.

faq.q: Why should a variable shared with an interrupt handler be declared volatile?
faq.a: Without volatile, the compiler may assume the variable cannot change inside a loop and keep it in a register, so the main code never sees the handler's update. Volatile forces each access to read or write memory.

faq.q: What is the difference between an interrupt and an exception?
faq.a: An interrupt is an asynchronous signal from hardware such as a timer or peripheral, unrelated to the current instruction. An exception is raised synchronously by the instruction being executed, for example a page fault or an illegal operation.

割り込みベクタテーブル.desc: A table listing, for each type of interrupt or exception, the start address of its handler. The CPU indexes it by the cause number to find where to begin handling.

about.h: How the CPU uses the table
about.p: When an interrupt or exception is accepted, hardware determines a number, called the vector, that identifies its cause: a timer, a particular peripheral, a page fault, an illegal instruction or a system call. The CPU saves the address of the next instruction and status such as the operating mode, then uses the vector as an index into the interrupt vector table, typically reading the entry at base + vector × entry size. That entry holds the handler's start address. The handler saves the registers it uses, services the event and executes a return-from-interrupt instruction.

Architectures differ in detail. On Arm Cortex-M microcontrollers the table sits at the start of the code memory: its first word is the initial stack pointer, the second is the reset handler address, and later words point to fault and peripheral handlers; on most cores a vector table offset register (VTOR) lets software move it. In x86 real mode the table occupies the first 1 KB of memory with 256 four-byte entries, while protected and long modes use an interrupt descriptor table (IDT) located by the IDTR register. RISC-V uses the mtvec register, which can send all traps to one handler or vector interrupts to separate addresses.

about.h: Setting it up in embedded firmware
about.p: On a microcontroller with no operating system, the vector table must be at the address the hardware expects from the moment of reset. The startup code defines it as an array of function pointers in its own section, and the linker script places that section at the required flash address. Typical startup files give every entry a weak default handler, often an infinite loop, so the application overrides only the interrupts it uses by defining functions with matching names. A misspelled handler name therefore compiles cleanly but silently routes the interrupt to the default loop.

A vectored scheme sends each cause straight to its own handler, so the CPU does not need to read status registers to discover what happened, which shortens interrupt latency. The alternative is a single entry point whose handler reads a cause register and dispatches in software, as RISC-V's direct mode does. On a general-purpose operating system, the kernel fills the table at boot so timer ticks, device interrupts, page faults and system calls each reach the correct kernel routine.

faq.q: What is an interrupt vector?
faq.a: An interrupt vector is the number assigned to an interrupt or exception source, used as an index into the vector table. The term is also used loosely for the table entry itself, which holds the handler address.

faq.q: Where is the vector table on an ARM Cortex-M microcontroller?
faq.a: By default it is at the start of the boot memory, usually flash. Its first entry is the initial stack pointer value and its second is the reset handler, and on most cores the vector table offset register (VTOR) can relocate it, for example to RAM.

faq.q: What is the difference between the IVT and the IDT on x86?
faq.a: The interrupt vector table (IVT) is the real-mode table of 256 segment:offset addresses at the bottom of memory. The interrupt descriptor table (IDT) replaces it in protected and long modes, holding descriptors with privilege information, and can be placed anywhere via the IDTR register.

ページテーブル.desc: A table recording the mapping from virtual page numbers to physical page numbers. The OS builds one per process, and the CPU's MMU walks it to translate addresses. Each entry also holds protection bits.

about.h: How translation uses the page table
about.p: A virtual address is split into a virtual page number (VPN) and a page offset; with 4 KB pages the low 12 bits are the offset. The memory management unit (MMU) looks up the VPN in the page table to obtain the physical frame number, then appends the unchanged offset. Each page-table entry (PTE) also holds a valid or present bit, read, write and execute permissions, a user or kernel flag, and accessed and dirty bits used by the operating system. A register points to the current process's top-level table and is switched on each context switch.

A flat table must have an entry for every possible page. With 32-bit addresses, 4 KB pages and 4-byte entries that is 2²⁰ entries, or 4 MB per process, mostly describing unused space. Multilevel tables form a tree in which an absent upper-level entry means a whole region is unmapped, so no lower table is needed. A typical 64-bit design translates 48 address bits with four levels of 512 eight-byte entries, each table filling exactly one 4 KB page. Ending the walk one or two levels early yields large pages, such as 2 MB.

The page table lives in ordinary memory, so a full walk can cost several dependent memory accesses: up to four in the four-level case, and many more under virtualization, where guest and host tables are both walked. The translation lookaside buffer (TLB) is a small cache of recent translations inside the CPU that avoids most walks. On a TLB miss, a hardware page walker in most modern processors reads the table, helped by caches of upper-level entries. Large pages increase how much memory each TLB entry covers.

about.h: What the OS does with it
about.p: If a PTE is not present, the access raises a page fault and the operating system decides what to do: load the page from storage, allocate a zero-filled page, or kill the process for an illegal access. Pointing several processes' entries at the same frame enables shared libraries, and marking shared pages read-only enables copy-on-write after a fork. When the OS revokes or changes a mapping on a multicore system, it must also invalidate stale TLB copies on other cores, an operation known as a TLB shootdown.

faq.q: Why are multilevel page tables used instead of a single table?
faq.a: A single table needs an entry for every possible virtual page, which is megabytes per process even for 32-bit addresses. A multilevel tree only allocates lower-level tables for regions actually in use.

faq.q: What is the difference between a page table and a TLB?
faq.a: The page table is the complete mapping kept in memory by the operating system. The TLB is a small hardware cache in the CPU that holds recently used translations so most accesses avoid walking the table.

faq.q: What happens when a page table entry is not present?
faq.a: The MMU raises a page fault and the operating system handles it, for example by reading the page in from storage and updating the entry, then restarting the faulting instruction.

ページフォルト.desc: An exception raised when an accessed page is not mapped to physical memory or the access type is not permitted. The OS either supplies the page and retries the instruction or treats it as an illegal access.

about.h: What happens during a page fault
about.p: When the memory management unit (MMU) translates a virtual address, it checks the page-table entry. If the entry is not valid or the access type is not allowed, the MMU raises a page fault, a synchronous exception tied to the faulting instruction. The OS handler checks whether the address belongs to a region the process may use. If so, it finds a free physical frame, evicting another page if necessary, fills it from disk or with zeros, marks the entry valid and restarts the faulting instruction. If not, the process receives a segmentation fault.

Not every page fault touches the disk. A minor (soft) fault is resolved without I/O, for example when a page is already in memory in the file cache, needs only a fresh zero-filled frame, or must be copied for copy-on-write. A major (hard) fault must read the page from storage and costs milliseconds. The difference matters enormously: with a 100 ns memory access and an 8 ms fault service time, a major fault rate of just one per million accesses raises the average access time from 100 ns to about 108 ns.

Operating systems rely on faults as a lazy-evaluation tool. Demand paging maps a program without loading it, then loads each page on first touch. Memory-mapped files (mmap) read file contents in the same way. Copy-on-write lets fork share pages read-only and copy only the pages that are later written. Guard pages with no access rights sit beyond the stack so runaway recursion faults instead of corrupting data. On NUMA systems, Linux places a page on the node of the thread that first writes it, so initialization order affects performance.

about.h: Page fault vs. TLB miss vs. cache miss
about.p: These three are often confused. A cache miss is handled entirely by hardware, which fetches the line from a lower memory level. A TLB miss means the translation is not cached in the translation lookaside buffer; on most modern CPUs a hardware page-table walker fetches it, and if the entry is valid, no exception occurs. Only when the page-table entry itself is invalid or forbids the access does a page fault reach the OS. When faults become so frequent that the system spends most of its time paging, the condition is called thrashing.

faq.q: Is a page fault an error?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Most page faults are normal events used for demand paging, copy-on-write and memory-mapped files; only a fault on an address the process is not allowed to access becomes an error such as a segmentation fault.

faq.q: What is the difference between a minor and a major page fault?
faq.a: A minor fault is resolved without disk I/O, for example by mapping a page already in memory, while a major fault must read the page from storage and is thousands of times slower.

faq.q: Why does a page fault restart the instruction instead of skipping it?
faq.a: The faulting access never completed, so the OS fixes the mapping and re-executes the instruction from the start, letting the program continue as if nothing had happened.

デマンドページング.desc: Loading a program's pages into physical memory only when first accessed and a page fault occurs, rather than all at once. It speeds startup and saves memory for unused parts.

コピーオンライト.desc: Sharing duplicated memory with the original at first and copying a page only when either side tries to write it. It speeds process creation and saves memory.

about.p: When a process is duplicated, the kernel copies only the page tables. Parent and child entries point to the same physical frames, and every writable private page is temporarily marked read-only while the kernel keeps a reference count per frame. Reads proceed at full speed. The first write by either process causes a protection fault; the kernel recognizes a copy-on-write page, allocates a new frame, copies the page, maps the copy as writable for the writer and restarts the faulting instruction. If the reference count shows the page is no longer shared, it can simply be made writable again without copying.

about.h: Why it pays off for process creation
about.p: A common pattern on Unix-like systems is fork followed almost immediately by exec, for example when a shell starts a command. Exec throws away the entire address space and loads a new program, so eagerly copying the parent's memory would be pure waste. With copy-on-write, fork costs roughly the time to duplicate page tables, and only pages that are actually modified before exec, typically a few stack and data pages, are ever copied. Memory is saved too, because pages that neither side writes, such as code and read-only data, remain shared for the lifetime of both processes.

about.h: Where else you will meet it
about.p: The same idea appears whenever data is logically duplicated but usually left unmodified. Private file mappings use it: a shared library's writable data section starts out shared with the file cache and each process gets its own copy of a page only when it writes. Many kernels map freshly allocated anonymous memory to a single shared zero page until it is written. Copy-on-write file systems and storage snapshots write modified blocks to new locations instead of overwriting, and virtual machine snapshots and some language runtimes apply the principle to disk images and strings.

Copy-on-write moves cost rather than eliminating it. Each first write to a shared page takes a fault, a trap into the kernel and a page copy, which is far slower than an ordinary store. If a large process forks and the parent keeps writing to most of its memory, nearly every page is eventually copied and memory use can approach double. Marking pages read-only at fork also requires invalidating stale TLB entries on other cores. Copy-on-write must not be confused with shared memory: with shared memory both processes see each other's writes, while copy-on-write gives each writer a private copy.

faq.q: Does fork copy all of the parent's memory?
faq.a: Not on modern systems. Fork duplicates the page tables and shares physical pages marked read-only; a page is copied only when one of the processes first writes to it.

faq.q: What happens when a child process writes to memory after fork?
faq.a: The write triggers a page fault, the kernel copies that single page into a new frame and maps it writable for the child. The parent keeps the original, so neither process sees the other's change.

faq.q: Is copy-on-write the same as shared memory?
faq.a: No. Shared memory is deliberately visible to both processes after writes, whereas copy-on-write only shares pages until someone writes, at which point the writer gets a private copy.

スラッシング.desc: A state in which physical memory is so short that pages are constantly evicted and reloaded, and little useful work gets done. It is relieved by running fewer processes or adding memory.

コンテキストスイッチ.desc: Switching the process or thread running on a CPU. Registers, the program counter and other state are saved and restored, and switching processes also switches address spaces.

ASID(アドレス空間識別子).desc: A number tagged onto each TLB entry indicating which process's address space the translation belongs to. The TLB need not be flushed on a process switch, reducing TLB misses afterward.

TLBシュートダウン.desc: On a multiprocessor, the procedure for making other cores discard stale translations from their TLBs after a page table is modified. It uses inter-processor interrupts or instructions that broadcast the invalidation to all cores, and is costly.

メモリマップドI/O.desc: Assigning peripheral registers to specific addresses in the same address space as memory and accessing them with ordinary load and store instructions. That region is configured as uncached.

デバイスドライバ.desc: An OS component that operates a specific peripheral. It handles the device's registers and interrupts and lets applications use the device through a common interface.

IOMMU.desc: A unit that translates and protects the addresses peripherals use for DMA. It keeps devices from writing to unauthorized memory and is also used when assigning devices to virtual machines.

ハイパーバイザ.desc: Software that runs multiple virtual machines on one computer, allocating CPU, memory and devices to each guest OS and isolating them from one another. Also called a virtual machine monitor.

about.h: How it keeps control of the CPU
about.p: A hypervisor, or virtual machine monitor, runs at a higher privilege level than the guest operating systems. Guest kernels believe they control the hardware, but when one executes a privileged instruction or touches a protected resource, the CPU traps to the hypervisor, which reproduces the effect on that virtual machine's state and resumes the guest. This is trap-and-emulate. Hardware virtualization extensions add a dedicated mode and save and restore guest state quickly on each transition; RISC-V, for example, adds hypervisor modes to its machine, supervisor and user modes.

Each guest manages page tables that map guest virtual addresses to what it believes are physical addresses. Those guest physical addresses must in turn map to real host memory. With nested paging, hardware performs both stages automatically: guest virtual to guest physical through the guest's tables, then to host physical through the hypervisor's tables. Earlier systems used shadow page tables maintained in software, forcing the hypervisor to intervene whenever a guest edited its tables. The cost of two-stage translation is a longer page-table walk on TLB misses, which larger pages help reduce.

Emulating a real device register by register is fully transparent but slow, since every register access exits to the hypervisor. Paravirtualization instead installs virtualization-aware drivers in the guest that exchange batched requests with the hypervisor through queues in shared memory, which is the common choice for virtual disks and network cards. For the highest performance, a physical device can be assigned directly to one guest, with an I/O memory management unit (IOMMU) restricting its DMA to that guest's memory so isolation is preserved.

A type 1 hypervisor runs directly on the hardware, as in cloud servers, while a type 2 hypervisor runs as an application on a host OS. Containers are different again: they share one kernel and only partition processes, file systems and resources, so they are lighter but isolate less strongly than virtual machines, each of which boots its own kernel. Hypervisors also partition mixed-criticality software on automotive SoCs. Normally the hypervisor can read all guest memory; confidential-computing features encrypt VM memory so even the host cannot.

faq.q: What is the difference between a hypervisor and a virtual machine?
faq.a: The hypervisor is the software layer that creates and runs virtual machines and divides hardware among them; each virtual machine is one isolated guest environment running its own OS.

faq.q: What is the difference between type 1 and type 2 hypervisors?
faq.a: A type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor runs directly on hardware, while a type 2 (hosted) hypervisor runs as an application on top of an ordinary operating system.

faq.q: Are containers the same as virtual machines?
faq.a: No. Containers share the host kernel and are lightweight, while virtual machines each run their own kernel on a hypervisor, giving stronger isolation and the ability to run different operating systems.

入れ子ページング.desc: Hardware that walks two levels of page tables in succession, one managed by the guest OS and one by the hypervisor. It reduces hypervisor intervention and speeds up virtualization.

about.h: Two translations in one hardware walk
about.p: A guest operating system inside a virtual machine manages page tables that map guest virtual addresses to what it believes are physical addresses, called guest physical addresses. That memory actually lives wherever the hypervisor placed it. With nested paging, also known as two-stage translation, the hardware walks the guest's page tables and then the hypervisor's own tables, translating guest virtual to guest physical to host physical automatically. The common implementations are Intel's Extended Page Tables (EPT), AMD's Nested Page Tables (NPT) and Arm's stage-2 translation.

about.h: What it replaced: shadow page tables
about.p: Before hardware support, hypervisors used shadow page tables: software-maintained tables mapping guest virtual addresses directly to host physical addresses, which the real MMU used. To keep them correct, the hypervisor had to trap the guest's page-table writes and address-space switches, causing frequent and expensive exits from the virtual machine. Nested paging lets the guest edit its own tables freely, removing most of those exits and simplifying the hypervisor. The trade-off moves to the cost of a TLB miss.

about.h: Why a TLB miss can cost 24 memory accesses
about.p: Each entry the guest walker needs is located by a guest physical address, which must itself be translated through the host's tables before it can be read. With four-level tables on both sides, each guest level costs four host reads plus one guest-table read, five in all, for 20 across four levels, and translating the final data address through the host adds four more: (4 + 1) × (4 + 1) − 1 = 24, versus four for a native walk. Page-walk caches, TLBs that cache the final combined translation and large pages on the host side keep the average cost far lower.

faq.q: What is the difference between nested paging and shadow paging?
faq.a: Shadow paging has the hypervisor maintain combined guest-virtual-to-host-physical tables in software and trap guest page-table updates. Nested paging lets the hardware walk the guest and host tables in succession, so the guest updates its own tables without hypervisor intervention.

faq.q: How many memory accesses does a nested page walk need?
faq.a: With four-level page tables in both guest and host, a TLB miss can require up to 24 memory accesses in the worst case, compared with four for a non-virtualized walk.

faq.q: Is nested paging the same as nested virtualization?
faq.a: No. Nested paging is two-stage address translation for ordinary virtual machines, while nested virtualization means running a hypervisor inside a virtual machine.

NMI(マスク不可能割り込み).desc: An interrupt that is always accepted regardless of interrupt masking. It is used to report uncorrectable memory errors, serious hardware faults and watchdog events.

字句解析.desc: The first compiler phase, which splits the characters of source code into tokens such as identifiers, numbers, operators and keywords. Whitespace and comments are removed here.

構文解析.desc: The compiler phase that checks whether the token sequence follows the language grammar and builds the program's structure as a tree. Grammar errors are detected here.

about.h: Where parsing sits in a compiler
about.p: A compiler front end works in stages. Lexical analysis turns the character stream into tokens such as identifiers, numbers and symbols, discarding whitespace and comments. Syntax analysis, or parsing, then checks whether that token sequence forms a valid program according to the language grammar and records how the pieces nest: which statements form a loop body, which operands belong to which operator. Errors such as a missing semicolon or unbalanced parentheses are reported here. Semantic analysis follows, checking types and whether names are declared, before the program is lowered to an intermediate representation for optimization and code generation.
