faq.a: The == operator returns X if either operand contains X or Z bits, like a hardware comparator. The === operator compares X and Z literally and always returns 0 or 1, so testbenches use it to detect unknown outputs.

参照モデル.desc: A separate model, often in C, implementing the same function as the circuit. Its results for the same inputs serve as expected values for the design's outputs.

制約付きランダム検証.desc: Verification that generates random input values within constraints allowed by the specification, broadly exercising cases people might not think of.

回帰テスト.desc: Re-running existing tests after each design change to confirm that previously working features still work.

Lint.desc: A tool that checks HDL or other code against rules without simulation, flagging problem-prone constructs such as width mismatches and unintended latches.

ゲートレベルシミュレーション.desc: Simulation of the post-synthesis or post-layout netlist, optionally with delay information, to catch problems invisible at RTL.

generate文.desc: A Verilog construct that expands hardware descriptions by loops or conditions, used for example to instantiate a module repeatedly in a regular pattern.

組み合わせループ.desc: A structure in which combinational output feeds back to its own input without a flip-flop. It can oscillate or fail to settle and defeats timing analysis, so it is avoided.

VCD.desc: A standard file format recording signal value changes during simulation, viewed in waveform tools for debugging.

サイドチャネル攻撃.desc: An attack inferring secrets such as keys from physical information other than the intended output, such as processing time, power consumption or electromagnetic emissions.

タイミング攻撃.desc: A side-channel attack exploiting processing time that varies with secret values, prevented by constant-time implementation.

定数時間実装.desc: A way of writing cryptographic code so that branch directions, loop counts and memory addresses accessed do not depend on secret values.

投機的実行.desc: A CPU technique that executes instructions ahead based on predictions, such as branch outcomes, before they are known. Wrong results are discarded, but traces such as cache state may remain.

about.h: Why CPUs execute ahead of time
about.p: A high-performance CPU has a deep pipeline and executes instructions out of order, so waiting for every branch to resolve would leave it idle for many cycles. Instead, a branch predictor guesses the outcome and the core keeps fetching and executing along the predicted path. These speculative results are held in internal buffers and committed, or retired, only once the guess is confirmed. If the prediction was wrong, the core discards the speculative work and restarts on the correct path, so the program's visible results are always correct.

Rolling back a misprediction restores the architectural state, meaning the registers and memory a program can observe directly. It does not undo changes to microarchitectural state such as which lines are in the cache, TLB contents or predictor history. Those changes are normally harmless because programs cannot read them directly, but timing can reveal them: an access to a cached line is measurably faster than one to main memory. This gap between what is rolled back and what is not is the root of speculative-execution vulnerabilities.

about.h: How Spectre and Meltdown exploit it
about.p: In Spectre, disclosed in 2018 along with Meltdown, an attacker trains the branch predictor so that a path which should never run, such as code past a bounds check, executes speculatively, reads a secret, and uses its value to touch a particular cache line. The results are discarded, but timing which line is cached reveals the secret through a cache side channel. Meltdown abused CPUs that let a speculative load return data from kernel memory before the permission check took effect. Nearly all high-performance CPUs were affected by at least one variant.

Mitigations span every layer: operating systems separated kernel and user page tables, compilers insert speculation barriers or use indirect-branch sequences that avoid poisoned predictions, microcode updates add controls over predictor behavior, and newer CPUs build in hardware fixes. Each restriction on speculation, prediction or shared caches reduces leakage but can cost performance, so designers choose how far to go based on what data is at stake. The episode showed that performance features can become security weaknesses even when software is bug-free.

faq.q: Is speculative execution the same as out-of-order execution?
faq.a: They are related but different. Out-of-order execution reorders instructions whose inputs are ready, while speculative execution runs instructions before it is known that they should execute at all, such as those after an unresolved branch; modern cores do both.

faq.q: What is the difference between Spectre and Meltdown?
faq.a: Spectre tricks the branch predictor into speculatively running legitimate code paths that leak data the victim program can access. Meltdown exploited CPUs whose speculative loads could read kernel memory before the permission check took effect, and it was largely fixed by kernel page-table isolation and later hardware changes.

faq.q: Why can discarded speculative results still leak data?
faq.a: The CPU discards register results but does not restore the cache, so data loaded during speculation leaves a trace that can be detected by measuring access times.

Spectre.desc: A class of vulnerabilities, disclosed in 2018, that induces mispredicted speculative execution to read secret data and infers its value from traces left in the cache.

Meltdown.desc: A vulnerability in some CPUs where kernel memory could be read speculatively before the permission exception took effect, with values inferred from cache traces. Mitigated by KPTI and other measures.

KPTI.desc: An OS countermeasure to Meltdown that removes most kernel memory from the page tables while user programs run.

電力解析攻撃.desc: A side-channel attack inferring secrets from a chip's power consumption traces. Differential power analysis (DPA), which processes many traces statistically, is especially powerful.

故障注入攻撃.desc: An attack that deliberately makes a chip malfunction with voltage or clock glitches, lasers and the like to bypass authentication or infer keys.

コールドブート攻撃.desc: An attack reading DRAM contents that persist briefly after power-off to extract keys and other secrets; cooling extends persistence. Prevented by memory encryption.

セキュアブート.desc: A mechanism that verifies the digital signature of the next software at each boot stage and starts only authentic software, forming a chain of trust.

about.h: How the chain of trust works
about.p: At power-on, boot code in the chip's ROM loads the first bootloader and checks its digital signature: it hashes the image and verifies the vendor's signature over that hash. Only if the check passes does it run the bootloader, which in turn verifies the next stage or the OS kernel before handing over control. Each link vouches for the next, forming a chain of trust. If any signature fails, boot stops, so malware that rewrites the bootloader or OS boot code cannot run. Smartphones, PCs and many embedded devices use this scheme.

about.h: The root of trust in silicon
about.p: The chain is only as strong as its first check, so the root of trust must be immutable: boot code in mask ROM, fixed at manufacture, plus the public key used to verify signatures, often stored as a hash in eFuses (one-time programmable fuses) to save space. Public-key cryptography matters here. With a symmetric scheme, the key that verifies could also sign, so extracting it from one device would allow fake firmware for all devices. With public-key signatures, devices hold only a verification key and the signing private key never leaves the vendor's secure facility.

Signature checks alone still accept old firmware, because the vendor legitimately signed it. After a vulnerability is fixed, an attacker could reinstall the vulnerable version, so images carry a version number and the chip stores a minimum allowed version in write-once storage such as eFuses, advancing it with each update. Debug ports such as JTAG and SWD can read and write memory and halt the processor, which would bypass secure boot entirely, so shipped products disable them with fuses or open them only after cryptographic authentication.

Secure boot enforces: unverified code does not start. Measured boot records: each stage hashes the next and extends the result into TPM (trusted platform module) platform configuration registers, where a new value can only be formed by combining the old value with a new hash. Boot continues regardless, but the record lets software or a remote server later verify exactly what ran. Note also that a signature proves authenticity, not confidentiality; keeping firmware secret needs encryption. Secure boot protects only the start-up path, so it is one layer in defense in depth alongside memory protection, trusted execution environments and tamper resistance.

faq.q: What is the root of trust in secure boot?
faq.a: Immutable code in the chip's mask ROM together with the public key, or its hash in eFuses, used to verify the first bootloader. Everything later in the chain depends on it being unchangeable.

faq.q: What is the difference between secure boot and measured boot?
faq.a: Secure boot refuses to run software whose signature fails. Measured boot lets everything run but records hashes in a TPM so the boot state can be checked or attested later.

faq.q: Why does secure boot need anti-rollback protection?
faq.a: Older firmware versions carry valid signatures too, so without a minimum-version counter an attacker could reinstall a version with a known vulnerability.

ルートオブトラスト.desc: The component unconditionally trusted as the starting point of security checks, such as immutable ROM boot code and a public key inside the chip.

ロールバック防止.desc: A mechanism recording a minimum version number in unchangeable storage so software cannot be reverted to older vulnerable versions.

TPM.desc: A security chip or function that generates and stores keys, records measurements of booted software and attests to platform state.

測定ブート.desc: A mechanism that cumulatively records hashes of each boot stage's software in a TPM or similar so the boot state can be verified later.

リモートアテステーション.desc: A mechanism in which a device signs the state of its running software with an on-chip key and presents it to a remote server for trust verification.

TEE(信頼できる実行環境).desc: A hardware-protected execution environment isolated even from the normal OS, used for critical work such as key handling and authentication, for example Arm TrustZone.

TrustZone.desc: Arm's processor security architecture, switching between secure and normal worlds and using bus signals to distinguish and restrict access to memory and peripherals.

about.p: TrustZone gives an Arm core two security states: the secure world and the normal world. The rich operating system and ordinary applications run in the normal world, while a small trusted OS and its trusted applications run in the secure world. On Cortex-A processors, switching between them passes through a secure monitor entered with the SMC (secure monitor call) instruction, which saves one world's context and restores the other's. The same core, caches and memory system are time-shared between the two, so a secure area is created inside a single system on chip (SoC) without adding a separate security processor.

Security state is not just a software convention. Every transaction the core places on the on-chip bus carries a signal marking whether it is secure or non-secure. Address space controllers in front of DRAM, on-chip SRAM and peripherals check that signal and reject non-secure accesses to regions assigned to the secure world. Peripherals such as a fingerprint sensor interface or a crypto engine can likewise be reserved for secure software, and caches tag lines by world. As a result, even a fully compromised normal-world kernel cannot read secure memory, because the hardware blocks the access itself.

about.h: TrustZone as a trusted execution environment
about.p: A trusted execution environment (TEE) is a small, hardware-isolated environment for work that must survive a compromise of the main OS. TrustZone is the most widely used basis for a TEE on smartphones and similar devices. Typical secure-world tasks are biometric matching, payment credential handling, storage of digital rights management (DRM) keys and verification steps during secure boot. Keeping the trusted code base small is the point: a large OS cannot be made free of vulnerabilities, but a compact trusted OS with a narrow interface is much easier to review and harden.

about.h: TrustZone vs. a separate secure element
about.p: TrustZone isolates software logically but shares physical resources such as cores, caches and power rails with the normal world. That keeps cost low but leaves exposure to side-channel and fault-injection attacks that a dedicated chip can resist better. A secure element is a separate, tamper-resistant chip with its own processor and memory, often used alongside a TEE for the most valuable keys. Microcontroller-class Armv8-M cores implement a lighter TrustZone variant in which secure and non-secure code call each other directly through defined entry points, without a monitor.

faq.q: What is Arm TrustZone used for?
faq.a: It is used to run security-critical code such as biometric matching, payment processing, key storage and secure boot checks in a hardware-isolated secure world. Even if the normal operating system is compromised, the secure world's memory and keys remain inaccessible.

faq.q: What is the difference between TrustZone and a TEE?
faq.a: A TEE is the general concept of an isolated execution environment protected by hardware. TrustZone is Arm's hardware mechanism that provides the isolation on which a TEE's trusted OS and applications are built.

faq.q: How does TrustZone stop the normal world from reading secure memory?
faq.a: Each bus transaction carries a signal indicating whether it came from the secure or normal state. Controllers in front of memory and peripherals check that signal and refuse normal-world accesses to secure regions.

エンクレーブ.desc: A TEE approach in which part of an application runs in a region whose memory the CPU encrypts and protects, hidden even from the OS and hypervisor.

PUF(物理的複製困難関数).desc: A mechanism using per-chip manufacturing variation to produce values unique to each chip and hard to clone, allowing keys to be regenerated without storing them.

about.h: Where the chip-unique value comes from
about.p: No two transistors come out of a fab identical: threshold voltages, gate dimensions and wire delays vary randomly from chip to chip. A physically unclonable function (PUF) amplifies these differences into bits. An SRAM PUF reads which way each cell settles at power-up, decided by the stronger of its two cross-coupled inverters. A ring-oscillator PUF compares the frequencies of nominally identical oscillators. An arbiter PUF races a signal down two paths whose routing is set by a challenge and records which arrives first. Because the variation is random and uncontrollable, even the manufacturer cannot build a chip with a chosen response.

about.h: From noisy bits to a stable key
about.p: A PUF response is not perfectly repeatable. Cells or paths whose two options are nearly balanced can flip with temperature, supply voltage, noise and aging, yet a cryptographic key must be bit-for-bit identical every time. At enrollment the chip therefore records the response and computes helper data, public information for an error-correcting code. At each use the PUF is read again, the code corrects the flipped bits with the help of the helper data, and a hash or key-derivation step produces the final key. This construction, often called a fuzzy extractor, is designed so the helper data does not reveal the key.

about.h: PUF versus eFuse and OTP key storage
about.p: The conventional approach writes a per-device key into one-time-programmable eFuses or OTP memory, ideally readable only by the crypto engine. Such bits exist permanently and can be targeted by opening the package and probing or imaging the storage. With a PUF the key is regenerated only when needed and exists nowhere while power is off, and invasive probing tends to disturb the very variation that defines it. A common hybrid stores keys in flash encrypted with a PUF-derived key. Whatever the approach, restricting the read paths to the key is essential.

PUFs are judged by uniqueness, the Hamming distance between responses of different chips, ideally 50 percent; reliability, how few bits change between readings of the same chip; and uniformity, an even balance of zeros and ones. Weak PUFs, such as SRAM PUFs, offer few challenge-response pairs and suit key generation. Strong PUFs, such as arbiter PUFs, offer very many pairs for authentication, but their responses can often be learned with machine-learning modeling attacks from observed pairs. Side-channel leakage and helper-data manipulation are further attack surfaces.

faq.q: What is a PUF used for?
faq.a: PUFs provide chip-unique values for device authentication and for deriving cryptographic keys without storing them permanently in non-volatile memory. They are used in secure microcontrollers, FPGAs and other chips that need a hardware root of trust.

faq.q: Is a PUF the same as a random number generator?
faq.a: No. A true random number generator must produce fresh, unpredictable bits every time, whereas a PUF must reproduce the same chip-specific value on every reading. Some designs do harvest the unstable SRAM cells as an additional entropy source.

faq.q: Why does an SRAM PUF need error correction?
faq.a: A fraction of SRAM cells are nearly balanced and power up differently depending on temperature, voltage and noise. Error correction with helper data fixes these flipping bits so the derived key is identical every time.

真性乱数生成器.desc: A circuit generating random numbers from unpredictable physical phenomena such as thermal noise or oscillator jitter, serving as the source for cryptographic keys.

ハードウェアトロイ.desc: Malicious circuitry inserted during design or manufacturing to leak information or disable operation. It activates only under rare conditions, making it hard to detect.

偽造チップ.desc: A used, defective or lower-grade chip relabeled and sold as genuine, leading to failures and safety problems.

耐タンパ性.desc: The ability to withstand physical attacks such as opening a chip or probing it, protecting internal secrets, for example by erasing keys on detection.

about.p: Security chips in smart cards, secure elements and hardware security modules hold keys that must never leave the device. Attackers may decapsulate the package, remove layers one by one, and place microprobes on internal buses to read data directly, or use a focused ion beam to cut and reconnect wires. Semi-invasive attacks shine lasers or light on the exposed die to induce faults, and non-invasive attacks glitch the supply voltage or clock or measure power and electromagnetic emissions. Tamper resistance is the ability to withstand these attempts to extract secrets.

A fine metal mesh over the top of the chip acts as an active shield: if a probe or deprocessing step cuts or shorts it, the chip detects the change. Sensors watch for abnormal light, temperature, supply voltage and clock frequency. Internal buses and memories are encrypted or scrambled, and the layout can be scrambled so that functional blocks are hard to identify. When an anomaly is detected, the chip can erase its keys, often called zeroization, so that an attacker who succeeds in opening it finds nothing useful.

Tamper evidence only makes an intrusion visible afterward, for example through seals, coatings or labels that break when opened. Tamper resistance makes the attack harder in the first place, and tamper response actively reacts, for example by erasing secrets. Security evaluations of chips examine not only physical probing but also resistance to side-channel analysis and fault injection, because a chip with a perfect shield can still leak keys through its power consumption if the cryptographic implementation is not protected.

about.h: One layer of defense in depth
about.p: No countermeasure is absolute; tamper resistance aims to raise the cost, time and equipment an attack requires beyond the value of the secret. It is therefore combined with other layers such as secure boot, memory protection, trusted execution environments, encryption and side-channel countermeasures, so that breaching one does not expose everything. Designers also avoid sharing a single key across many devices, since a key extracted from one chip should not unlock the whole product line.

faq.q: What is tamper resistance in a security chip?
faq.a: It is the ability of a chip to resist physical attacks such as opening the package, deprocessing layers or probing internal wires to extract secrets, often combined with detecting such attacks and erasing keys in response.

faq.q: What is the difference between tamper-resistant and tamper-evident?
faq.a: Tamper-evident designs only show that an intrusion happened, for example through broken seals. Tamper-resistant designs make the attack itself difficult and may respond by destroying secrets.

faq.q: Does tamper resistance protect against side-channel attacks?
faq.a: Only partly. Shields and sensors stop physical probing, but leakage through power or electromagnetic emissions requires separate countermeasures in the circuit and the cryptographic implementation.

eFuse.desc: One-time-programmable storage written bit by bit by blowing thin wires with current, used for per-device keys, settings and anti-rollback counters.

動的消費電力.desc: Power consumed in CMOS circuits charging and discharging capacitance when signals switch, expressed as αCV²f with activity factor α, capacitance C, voltage V and frequency f.

about.p: Every CMOS gate output drives a load capacitance made of wire and the gates it feeds. When the output rises, the supply delivers CV² of energy: half is stored on the capacitor and half is dissipated in the pull-up transistors. When the output falls, the stored half is dumped to ground through the pull-down. Multiplying by how often this happens gives dynamic power, P = αCV²f, where α is the activity factor, the fraction of the capacitance switching per clock cycle. Some texts write ½αCV²f and count each edge as a transition, so check the convention before comparing α values.

Because of the V² term, voltage is the strongest lever: a 10% supply reduction cuts dynamic power by about 19%, and halving it leaves a quarter. Frequency is different. Halving f halves power, but a fixed task takes twice as long, so the energy for the task is unchanged; energy per switching event is set by CV². Lowering f is valuable because it lets the circuit run correctly at a lower voltage. If voltage can fall in proportion to frequency, halving both cuts power to one-eighth and task energy to one-quarter, which is the basis of dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS).

Since logic that does not toggle consumes no dynamic power, reducing α is a major design tool. The clock network switches every cycle, so clock gating, which stops the clock to registers and blocks whose values will not change, removes switching in both the flip-flops and the clock wiring. Capacitance falls with smaller transistors, shorter wires and low-k dielectrics. A worked example: α = 0.1, C = 1 nF, V = 1 V and f = 1 GHz gives 0.1 W.

Dynamic power is only part of the total. Short-circuit, or crowbar, current flows while both transistors are partly on during an input transition; with sharp edges it is roughly a tenth of dynamic power or less. Leakage, or static power, flows whenever the circuit is powered, so clock gating does not reduce it and power gating, which cuts the supply to idle blocks, is needed instead. Leakage also explains why lowering voltage stops paying off: near or slightly below threshold, circuits slow so much that leakage energy per operation rises, creating a minimum-energy voltage.

faq.q: What is the formula for dynamic power in CMOS?
faq.a: Dynamic power is P = αCV²f, where α is the activity factor, C the switched capacitance, V the supply voltage and f the clock frequency. It comes from repeatedly charging and discharging load capacitance.

faq.q: Why does lowering voltage save more power than lowering frequency?
faq.a: Power depends on the square of voltage but only linearly on frequency, and reducing frequency alone does not change the energy needed to finish a task. Reducing voltage lowers the energy of every switching event, so it saves both power and energy.

faq.q: What is the difference between clock gating and power gating?
faq.a: Clock gating stops the clock to idle logic, which removes its dynamic power but leaves leakage. Power gating disconnects the block from its supply with a switch transistor, eliminating nearly all leakage as well, at the cost of losing state and needing time to wake up.

活動率.desc: The fraction of a circuit's signals that switch per clock cycle, the α in the dynamic power formula αCV²f. It can be reduced by clock gating and similar.

about.p: The activity factor α measures how often a node actually switches, relative to the clock. A clock net that rises and falls every cycle is the reference case, while a data bit that changes only occasionally has a small α. Conventions differ: many texts define α as the probability of a 0-to-1 transition per cycle, because each rising transition draws CV² from the supply, so P = αCV²f and a clock has α = 1. Others count every toggle and write P = ½αCV²f. Both describe the same physics, so check which definition a tool or textbook uses.

With α = 0.1, switched capacitance C = 1 nF, V = 1 V and f = 1 GHz, the dynamic power is 0.1 × 10⁻⁹ F × (1 V)² × 10⁹ Hz = 0.1 W; the nano and giga prefixes cancel conveniently. The product αC is often called the effective switched capacitance, because only the capacitance that actually toggles costs energy. Power estimation tools obtain α for every net from simulation, using switching-activity files recorded while running realistic workloads, since a guessed average activity can be badly wrong for a specific block.

Clock gating is the most widely used technique: it stops the clock to registers whose contents will not change, which removes the switching of both the registers and the local clock tree, a large consumer because the clock toggles every cycle. Operand isolation holds the inputs of an idle arithmetic unit steady so it does not compute useless results. Encoding helps too, for example Gray-code counters or bus-invert coding that limit how many wires toggle. Balancing path delays reduces glitches, spurious transitions that add activity without doing useful work.

Reducing α lowers only dynamic power. Leakage power flows through off transistors whether or not anything switches, so a clock-gated block still leaks. Cutting static power requires different tools such as power gating, which disconnects the supply of idle blocks, or higher-threshold transistors. Supply voltage affects both: dynamic power scales with V² and leakage also falls at lower voltage, which is why dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) complements activity reduction rather than replacing it.

faq.q: What is the activity factor of a clock signal?
faq.a: Under the common convention where α is the probability of a rising transition per cycle, a clock has α = 1 because it rises once every cycle. Ordinary data signals usually have much lower activity.

faq.q: How does clock gating reduce power consumption?
faq.a: Clock gating stops the clock to registers that do not need to update, so those registers and the clock wiring feeding them stop switching. This lowers the activity factor α in P = αCV²f, but it does not remove leakage power.

faq.q: Why is it called the activity factor?
faq.a: It describes how active a circuit's signals are, that is, what fraction of nodes switch per clock cycle on average. Highly active circuits charge and discharge more capacitance per cycle and therefore consume more dynamic power.

静的消費電力.desc: Power consumed continuously by leakage currents through off transistors even when signals do not switch, also called leakage power. It rises steeply with temperature.

about.p: An ideal CMOS gate draws no current at rest, because one transistor between the supply and ground is always off. Real transistors leak. The largest component is usually subthreshold leakage: below threshold, drain current falls exponentially with gate voltage, at best by a factor of ten for every 60 mV or so at room temperature, so lowering the threshold voltage for speed raises off-state current sharply. Gate leakage tunnels through very thin gate dielectrics and was reduced by switching to high-k materials, and junction leakage and gate-induced drain leakage add smaller contributions.

about.h: Why it rises steeply with temperature
about.p: Higher temperature increases the thermal energy of carriers, so more of them surmount the source barrier, and it also lowers the threshold voltage. Both effects multiply subthreshold leakage, so a chip running hot can leak several times more than the same chip when cool. This creates a feedback loop: leakage generates heat, and heat raises leakage. Power budgets and thermal design must therefore be checked at the worst-case junction temperature, and in extreme cases the loop can lead to thermal runaway if cooling is insufficient.

Dynamic power is spent charging and discharging capacitance when signals switch, P = α·C·V²·f, so it falls when activity or clock frequency falls and responds strongly to voltage. If dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) halves both voltage and frequency, dynamic power drops to one-eighth and energy for a fixed task to one-quarter. Static power behaves differently: it flows whenever the circuit is powered, even with the clock stopped, and since a slowed task runs longer, leakage energy grows. In scaled technologies with billions of transistors, static power is a substantial fraction of the total, especially in standby.

Because clock gating cannot stop leakage, the most effective tool is power gating: header or footer sleep transistors disconnect idle blocks from the supply entirely, with retention registers or memories keeping essential state. Multi-threshold libraries place high-threshold, low-leakage cells on non-critical paths and reserve fast low-threshold cells for critical ones. Reverse body biasing raises the threshold during idle periods, and lowering the supply in standby reduces leakage further. At the device level, FinFETs and gate-all-around transistors cut off-state leakage through stronger gate control and a steeper subthreshold slope than late planar devices.

faq.q: What is the difference between static and dynamic power?
faq.a: Dynamic power is consumed when signals switch and charge or discharge capacitance, so it depends on activity, frequency and voltage squared. Static power is the leakage current through transistors that are nominally off and flows continuously whenever the circuit is powered.

faq.q: Why does leakage power increase with temperature?
faq.a: Higher temperature lets more carriers overcome the source barrier and also lowers the threshold voltage, both of which raise subthreshold leakage exponentially. As a result, leakage can multiply between a cool and a hot chip.

faq.q: Does clock gating reduce static power?
faq.a: No. Clock gating stops switching and so saves dynamic power, but leakage continues as long as the supply is connected; power gating is needed to remove static power from an idle block.

パワーゲーティング.desc: A low-power technique that switches off the supply to unused blocks, eliminating nearly all their leakage. State saving and wake-up time must be considered.

about.p: Power switches, also called sleep transistors, are placed between a block and its supply: header switches are PMOS devices between the main supply and the block's local virtual supply rail, and footer switches are NMOS devices on the ground side. They use high-threshold transistors so they leak little when off, and they are distributed in large numbers across the block to keep resistance low. When the block is off, isolation cells clamp its outputs to defined logic levels so floating signals do not disturb the blocks that remain powered.

Switching off the supply erases flip-flop and memory contents. Designs either accept losing state and reinitialize, save important state to memory in an always-on domain before shutdown, or use retention flip-flops whose small extra latch stays powered from an always-on supply while the main flip-flop is off. SRAMs may instead use a retention mode with lowered voltage that keeps data but cuts most leakage. The power controller that sequences isolation, state saving and switch control must itself sit in an always-on domain.

Switches add series resistance, so the block sees some voltage drop and runs slightly slower, and they take area. Turning on causes inrush current as the block's capacitance charges, so switches are enabled gradually, typically weak ones first and then the strong ones, to avoid sagging the shared supply. Waking up therefore takes far longer than resuming from clock gating. Each off-on cycle also costs energy, so shutting down only pays off when the idle period exceeds a break-even time over which the saved leakage energy outweighs that overhead.

about.h: Power gating vs. clock gating and DVFS
about.p: Clock gating stops the clock so a block stops switching, removing dynamic power and resuming within a cycle, but leakage continues because the supply is still connected. Power gating removes leakage too, at the price of state handling and wake-up latency. DVFS lowers voltage and frequency for blocks that keep working. Real chips combine all three: clock gating for idle periods of a few cycles, power gating for idle CPU cores, GPUs and accelerators in deep sleep states, and DVFS for running blocks.

faq.q: What is the difference between power gating and clock gating?
faq.a: Clock gating stops the clock to cut dynamic power and resumes almost instantly, but leakage continues. Power gating disconnects the supply, removing leakage as well, but loses state unless it is saved and takes longer to wake.

faq.q: What is an isolation cell in power gating?
faq.a: It is a gate on the outputs of a switchable domain that forces them to a fixed logic value while the domain is off, so undefined floating signals do not reach powered logic.

faq.q: Why is power gating not used for short idle periods?
faq.a: Each shutdown and wake-up spends energy on recharging the block and saving and restoring state, and it takes time. If the idle period is shorter than the break-even time, the leakage saved does not repay that overhead.

リテンションレジスタ.desc: A flip-flop that keeps its state in a small always-powered storage element while the block is power-gated, allowing operation to resume where it left off.

アイソレーションセル.desc: A cell placed at a boundary that passes a fixed value to running logic even when the outputs of a powered-off block are undefined.

レベルシフタ.desc: A circuit that converts signal voltages between blocks running at different supply voltages to suit the receiving side.

電源ドメイン.desc: A region of a chip sharing the same supply voltage and power on/off control, allowing voltage and power to be managed per block.

突入電流.desc: The large transient current that flows to charge capacitance the instant power is connected to an unpowered circuit, which can sag the supply voltage.

損益分岐時間.desc: The idle duration needed for the energy saved in a power-saving state to exceed the energy spent entering and leaving it.

C-state.desc: CPU idle states describing sleep depth. C0 is active; higher numbers use less power but take longer to wake.

P-state.desc: Performance levels of a running CPU defined by frequency and voltage combinations, switched by DVFS to match load.

レーストゥアイドル.desc: The strategy of finishing work quickly at high performance and entering deep sleep early, often advantageous when static power or other components' power is large.

ターボ動作.desc: Operation in which a CPU or similar automatically raises frequency above its rated value when power and thermal headroom allow.

サーマルスロットリング.desc: Control that lowers frequency and voltage when a chip gets too hot, reducing heat to protect it.

パワーキャップ.desc: Setting and enforcing an upper limit on server or CPU power, used in data centers to stay within power and cooling limits.

ACPI.desc: Advanced Configuration and Power Interface: the standard mechanism by which an OS manages device power states, power saving and thermals.

適応電圧スケーリング.desc: A technique that measures each chip's speed and temperature on chip and approaches the minimum voltage at which it works, trimming wasted margin.

エネルギー遅延積.desc: A metric multiplying energy per operation by its duration, used to evaluate the balance between energy efficiency and speed.

セルフリフレッシュ.desc: A low-power DRAM state in which the DRAM refreshes itself to retain contents without commands from the memory controller, used during system sleep.

PMIC.desc: An IC that generates multiple voltages from a battery or similar and manages power-up sequencing and voltage changes.

パワーシーケンス.desc: The specified order for applying and removing multiple supply voltages to a chip; violating it can cause malfunction or latch-up.

ニアスレッショルド動作.desc: Operating with supply voltage near the transistor threshold, greatly cutting energy per operation at the cost of speed and greater sensitivity to variation.

PUE.desc: Total data center power divided by IT equipment power; values closer to 1 indicate higher efficiency.

ティックレスカーネル.desc: An OS kernel that stops the periodic timer tick on idle CPUs so they can sleep until the next work.

CPI.desc: The average number of clock cycles per instruction, one factor in execution time = instruction count × CPI × cycle time, and the reciprocal of IPC.

about.p: CPU execution time equals instruction count × cycles per instruction (CPI) × cycle time, or instruction count × CPI ÷ clock frequency. Each factor has a different owner: instruction count depends mostly on the algorithm, compiler and instruction set architecture (ISA); CPI on the microarchitecture and memory system; and cycle time on circuit design and process technology. CPI is the reciprocal of instructions per clock (IPC). A program of 1 billion instructions at CPI 2 on a 2 GHz processor takes 2 billion cycles, or 1 second.

about.h: Average CPI from an instruction mix
about.p: Different instruction classes take different numbers of cycles, so average CPI is a weighted sum. With 50% ALU instructions at CPI 1, 30% loads and stores at CPI 2 and 20% branches at CPI 5, the average is 0.5 + 0.6 + 1.0 = 2.1. Breaking CPI down this way shows where time goes: branches are only a fifth of the instructions yet contribute nearly half the cycles. The same idea underlies CPI stacks in performance analysis, which attribute cycles to base execution, cache misses, branch mispredictions and other stalls.

Stall cycles add directly to the ideal CPI. If a core with a perfect cache achieves CPI 1.0 but each instruction makes 1.3 memory accesses with a 2% miss rate and a 100-cycle miss penalty, memory stalls add 1.3 × 0.02 × 100 = 2.6 cycles, giving CPI 3.6. Branch mispredictions add frequency × miss rate × penalty in the same way. Superscalar, out-of-order cores push base CPI below 1: a 2 GHz processor averaging CPI 0.5 completes about 4 billion instructions per second.

Optimizing one factor often worsens another, so only the product counts. Raising frequency 1.5× while CPI rises 1.2× gives a 1.25× speedup, not 1.5×, and deeper pipelines typically show exactly this pattern through larger misprediction penalties. A compiler change that removes 20% of instructions but raises CPI 10% still wins, at 0.88 of the original time. CPI is also not comparable across different ISAs, because the instructions do different amounts of work; for the same reason, raw instructions-per-second ratings can mislead.

faq.q: How do you calculate CPI?
faq.a: Divide total clock cycles by the number of instructions executed, or compute a weighted average of each instruction class's cycle count by its share of the instruction mix.

faq.q: What is the relationship between CPI and IPC?
faq.a: They are reciprocals: IPC is instructions completed per clock cycle and CPI is cycles per instruction, so a CPI of 0.5 means an IPC of 2.

faq.q: Does CPI mean something else in semiconductor packaging?
faq.a: Yes. In packaging, CPI usually means chip-package interaction, the cracking or delamination of fragile low-k interconnect layers caused by packaging stresses, which is unrelated to cycles per instruction.

速度向上率.desc: Execution time before an improvement divided by the time after; a value of 2 means twice as fast.

about.p: Speedup is time before divided by time after: a task that drops from 10 s to 4 s has a speedup of 2.5, the same change as "60% less time", and the two phrasings are easily confused. Because execution time equals instruction count × cycles per instruction (CPI) ÷ clock frequency, a single factor can mislead. Raising frequency 1.5 times while CPI rises 1.2 times, for example because a deeper pipeline pays larger branch penalties, gives a real speedup of only 1.5 ÷ 1.2 = 1.25.

If a fraction p of the run time is accelerated by a factor s, the overall speedup is 1/((1 − p) + p/s). Making half the program 4 times faster gives only 1.6, and no amount of acceleration on that half can exceed 2. To double overall speed by improving a 60% portion, that portion must become 6 times faster. For parallel computing, s becomes the processor count N: with 90% parallel code the limit is 10 regardless of N, and 10 processors give only about 5.3. The lesson is to attack the largest share of time first.

Amdahl's law assumes a fixed problem size, called strong scaling. Gustafson's law assumes the problem grows with processor count, as when a simulation grid is refined, so the parallel part grows, the serial fraction shrinks and speedup stays close to N; this is weak scaling. Parallel efficiency is speedup divided by core count: 6 times on 8 cores is 75%. Losses come from serial code, lock and barrier waits, load imbalance, cache-line bouncing from shared or falsely shared data, and memory bandwidth. Occasionally speedup exceeds N because each core's share of data fits in cache.

A speedup is only as meaningful as its baseline. The fair reference for parallel scaling is the fastest serial version, not the parallel code run on one core, and comparisons must use the same data size, accuracy and measurement scope, such as whether data transfer time is included. Algorithmic changes often dwarf hardware gains: replacing an n² method with n log n at a million elements cuts work by a factor of about 50,000. Conversely, removing operations does not guarantee speedup, as with unstructured pruning whose scattered zeros hardware cannot exploit efficiently.

faq.q: How do you calculate speedup?
faq.a: Divide the execution time before the change by the execution time after it. For parallel programs, divide the best single-core time by the time on N cores.

faq.q: What is the difference between Amdahl's law and Gustafson's law?
faq.a: Amdahl's law fixes the problem size, so the serial fraction caps speedup no matter how many processors are added. Gustafson's law lets the problem grow with the processor count, so speedup can scale nearly linearly.

faq.q: Can speedup be greater than the number of processors?
faq.a: Yes, occasionally. Superlinear speedup can happen when splitting the data lets each core's portion fit in its cache, though most programs fall below linear scaling because of serial work and synchronization.

グスタフソンの法則.desc: The observation that when processors are added and the problem is enlarged, the parallel fraction grows, giving gains nearly proportional to processor count.

強いスケーリング.desc: Parallel performance evaluation that fixes problem size and measures how much time drops as processors are added.

弱いスケーリング.desc: Parallel performance evaluation that fixes problem size per processor while growing the total and checks whether time stays constant.

ベンチマーク.desc: A representative program run under fixed conditions to compare computer or program performance. Choosing ones close to actual use is important.

SPEC CPU.desc: A standard CPU benchmark suite of many programs based on real applications, reporting ratios against a reference machine combined by geometric mean.

幾何平均.desc: The nth root of the product of n values, used to average performance ratios because the comparison does not depend on the reference chosen.

調和平均.desc: The reciprocal of the mean of reciprocals, used to average rates over equal amounts of work.

マイクロベンチマーク.desc: A benchmark timing a tiny isolated operation; beware pitfalls such as the compiler optimizing the computation away.

壁時計時間.desc: The actual elapsed time from start to finish, including I/O waits and time when other programs ran.

CPU時間.desc: The total time the CPU spent executing a program's instructions, excluding waits; with parallel execution it can exceed wall-clock time.

スループット.desc: The amount of work, requests or data processed per unit time, a different metric from latency, which describes how fast one task completes.

about.p: Throughput counts how much work finishes per unit time; latency measures how long one piece of work takes from start to finish. The two often trade against each other. A five-stage CPU pipeline ideally completes one instruction per clock, raising throughput about fivefold, even though each instruction's latency grows slightly. Batching requests in a server or AI inference engine raises throughput but makes each request wait. CPUs spend circuitry on making one thread fast, while GPUs run thousands of simpler threads to maximize total throughput.

Peak memory throughput is transfer rate times bus width. DDR memory transfers on both clock edges, so DDR4-3200 runs a 1600 MHz clock at 3200 MT/s, and a 64-bit channel peaks at 25.6 GB/s. Multiple DRAM banks overlap activate and precharge operations to keep data flowing. Link encoding also matters: PCI Express 3.0 moved from 8b/10b (80% efficient) to 128b/130b (about 98.5%), nearly doubling effective throughput while the signaling rate rose only from 5 to 8 GT/s.

The roofline model shows which kind of throughput limits a program. Plotting performance against arithmetic intensity, in operations per byte moved from memory, gives a slanted ceiling set by memory bandwidth and a flat ceiling set by peak compute. With 1 TB/s of bandwidth and 100 TFLOPS of compute, any kernel below 100 FLOP per byte is memory-bound, so improving data reuse helps more than adding arithmetic units.

Manufacturing uses the same idea. Tool throughput is quoted in wafers per hour, and choices often trade it against other goals: batch cleaning of about 50 wafers per bath is fast but risks cross-contamination, higher EUV dose reduces stochastic defects but lowers scanner throughput, and thermocompression bonding is slower than mass reflow. At factory level, Little's law states WIP = throughput × cycle time, so a fab shipping 50,000 wafers a month with a three-month cycle time holds about 150,000 wafers in process.

faq.q: What is the difference between throughput and latency?
faq.a: Throughput is the amount of work completed per unit time, such as requests per second or GB/s. Latency is the time a single request takes to complete; a system can have high throughput and still high latency, for example when it batches work.

faq.q: How do you calculate memory bandwidth?
faq.a: Multiply the transfer rate by the bus width in bytes. For example, DDR4-3200 on a 64-bit (8-byte) channel gives 3200 MT/s × 8 B = 25.6 GB/s peak; sustained throughput is lower because of refresh, bank conflicts and turnarounds.

faq.q: What is Little's law?
faq.a: Little's law says average work in progress equals throughput multiplied by average time in the system. It applies to fabs, queues and processors alike, so cutting cycle time at constant throughput requires less WIP.

テールレイテンシ.desc: The slow end of the response-time distribution, such as the 99th percentile, which governs overall latency when a task waits on many components.

リトルの法則.desc: The relationship that the average number in a system equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends there: L = λW.

about.p: Little's law relates three long-run averages of any stable system: L, the average number of items inside; λ, the average rate at which items arrive, which equals throughput in steady state; and W, the average time each item spends inside. Its power is its generality: it holds regardless of the arrival distribution, the service-time distribution or the order in which items are served, as long as the system is stable and units are consistent. It needs no assumption of Poisson arrivals, which is why it applies equally to factories, servers and memory systems.

about.h: Work in progress and cycle time in a fab
about.p: In manufacturing the law reads WIP = throughput × cycle time. A fab completing 50,000 wafers a month with a three-month cycle time always holds about 150,000 wafers in process. At fixed throughput, shortening cycle time requires holding less WIP, and releasing more wafers than the line can process only lengthens cycle time without raising output. Little's law does not by itself explain why cycle time explodes as tools approach full utilization; queueing models that account for variability address that part.

Applied to memory, the law says bandwidth equals data in flight divided by latency. If each cache miss fetches a 64-byte line and memory latency is 100 ns, one outstanding miss at a time yields 64 B ÷ 100 ns = 0.64 GB/s, while ten concurrent misses yield 6.4 GB/s. Saturating a memory system therefore requires many outstanding requests, not just lower latency. This is why cores track multiple pending misses, why hardware prefetchers issue requests early, and why the same reasoning sets network window sizes as the bandwidth-delay product.

A server receiving 100 requests per second, each taking 0.2 seconds on average, holds 100 × 0.2 = 20 requests in progress on average. That figure sizes thread pools, connection limits and queue buffers. The law also works backward as a sanity check: if measured concurrency and throughput imply a response time different from the one observed, the measurements or the assumption of steady state are wrong. Averages are all it gives, though; tail latency needs a fuller model of the system.

faq.q: What do L, λ and W mean in Little's law?
faq.a: L is the average number of items in the system, λ is the average arrival rate (equal to throughput in steady state) and W is the average time an item spends in the system. The law states L = λW.

faq.q: Does Little's law require Poisson arrivals?
faq.a: No. It holds for any stable system in steady state, whatever the arrival and service time distributions or the queueing discipline.

faq.q: How does Little's law relate to memory bandwidth?
faq.a: Bandwidth equals the number of bytes in flight divided by latency, so reaching high bandwidth with a fixed latency requires many outstanding memory requests at once.

プロファイラ.desc: A tool that measures which functions or parts of a program consume execution time, using sampling or instrumentation.

about.p: A sampling profiler interrupts the running program at regular intervals, using a timer or a hardware performance-counter overflow, and records the current instruction address and often the call stack, perhaps thousands of times per second. Functions that consume more time are caught more often, so the sample counts estimate where time goes statistically, with little overhead and an unmodified program. An instrumenting profiler instead inserts code at function entries and exits or in basic blocks, giving exact call counts but adding overhead that can distort timing, especially for small, frequently called functions.

Profilers usually report self time, spent in a function's own code, and inclusive time, which also counts the functions it calls. A flat profile ranks functions by self time, while a call graph or flame graph shows which call paths lead to the cost. The typical finding is a hotspot: a few percent of the code, often an inner loop, consuming most of the run time. Many profilers also read hardware performance counters, such as cache misses or branch mispredictions, which help explain why a hotspot is slow, not just where it is.

Amdahl's law states that if a fraction f of run time is sped up by factor s, overall speedup is 1 / ((1 − f) + f/s). Making code that takes 1% of the time infinitely fast gains only about 1%, while doubling the speed of code taking 80% gives about 1.7 times overall. Because intuition about where time goes is often wrong, the reliable workflow is to measure, optimize the biggest contributor, then measure again under the same conditions to confirm the gain and check that nothing else regressed.

about.h: GPU profiling, and a naming caution
about.p: For GPU programs, a timeline view first shows how total time divides among kernel execution, CPU–GPU data transfers and CPU-side work, and whether transfers overlap computation. Only if kernels dominate is it worth examining memory access patterns or occupancy, and higher occupancy is not automatically faster. In semiconductor metrology, "profiler" can mean something else entirely: a stylus profiler drags a fine stylus across a wafer to measure step heights, etch depth and planarity over millimeter distances, with coarser resolution than an atomic force microscope (AFM).

faq.q: What is the difference between a sampling profiler and an instrumenting profiler?
faq.a: A sampling profiler periodically records where the program is executing and estimates time statistically with low overhead. An instrumenting profiler adds measurement code to functions or blocks, giving exact counts but slowing and possibly distorting the program.

faq.q: What is a hotspot in profiling?
faq.a: A hotspot is a small region of code, often a loop or a few functions, that accounts for a large share of execution time. Optimizing hotspots gives the most benefit per effort.

faq.q: Does using a profiler slow down my program?
faq.a: Somewhat. Sampling profilers usually add little overhead, while instrumentation can add a lot, especially when it wraps many short functions.

フレームグラフ.desc: A profiling visualization stacking call chains vertically, with each function's width showing its share of time.

性能カウンタ.desc: A hardware counter in the CPU that tallies events such as instructions executed, cache misses and branch mispredictions.

トップダウン分析.desc: A method using performance counters to divide CPU issue slots into frontend bound, backend bound, bad speculation and retiring, narrowing down bottlenecks.

STREAMベンチマーク.desc: A benchmark that copies and adds large arrays to measure the memory bandwidth actually achievable.

並列効率.desc: Parallel speedup divided by the number of processors, indicating how effectively the cores are used.

プローブ効果.desc: The phenomenon in which adding a measurement mechanism changes the behavior of the program being measured.

絶対最大定格.desc: Limits on voltage, current, temperature and so on that may damage or degrade the device if exceeded even momentarily. Staying within them does not guarantee correct operation; normal use is within the recommended operating conditions.

推奨動作条件.desc: The range of conditions, such as supply voltage and ambient temperature, under which an IC is meant to operate. The min/max values in the electrical characteristics table are guaranteed only within this range. For a 3.3 V part, for example, the supply might be specified as 3.0 to 3.6 V.

ディレーティング.desc: Using parts with margin below their ratings for voltage, current, temperature and so on, rather than at the full rating, to improve reliability. Typical guidelines are voltage at no more than 70 to 80% of rating, or junction temperature at no more than 125 °C against a 150 °C maximum.

about.h: Why parts are run below their ratings
about.p: Most failure mechanisms accelerate with stress: chemical degradation and diffusion speed up exponentially with temperature, dielectrics wear out faster at higher field, and electromigration worsens with current density and temperature. Running parts with margin therefore lowers failure rates and also absorbs real-world effects that the nominal operating point hides, such as component tolerances, transients, ambient extremes and aging. Typical guidelines keep applied voltage at about 70 to 80% of the rating and junction temperature at about 125 °C against a 150 °C maximum, with exact numbers set by company or industry rules.

In power electronics, switching a current through stray inductance produces voltage spikes of L·di/dt above the DC bus, and sustained high voltage makes devices vulnerable to single-event burnout triggered by cosmic-ray neutrons, a risk that rises steeply with voltage and with altitude. Designers therefore pick devices rated around 1.5 times the working voltage, such as 650 V parts on a 400 V bus. Ceramic and electrolytic capacitors are derated too, since capacitance, leakage and lifetime all depend on applied voltage and temperature.

Datasheets often show a power derating curve: full rated dissipation up to a reference temperature, then a straight-line decrease to zero at the maximum junction temperature. It follows from Tj = Ta + P·θJA, where θJA is junction-to-ambient thermal resistance. With Tj(max) = 125 °C, θJA = 50 °C/W and Ta = 85 °C, allowable power is (125 − 85)/50 = 0.8 W. Because θJA depends strongly on board layout and airflow, designs keep further margin below this calculated value.

In chip design the word has a related meaning. On-chip variation (OCV) derating in static timing analysis multiplies path delays by factors to cover local differences in transistors, wires, voltage and temperature. For setup checks the launch clock and data paths are made slower and the capture clock faster; for hold checks the factors are reversed. Common path pessimism removal (CRPR) then credits back the impossible pessimism on clock buffers shared by both paths. Advanced OCV variants scale the factors with path depth or distance.

faq.q: What does derating mean in electronics?
faq.a: It means operating a component below its maximum ratings for voltage, current, power or temperature to increase reliability and absorb transients and tolerances. A common rule is 70 to 80% of rated voltage and a junction temperature well below the absolute maximum.

faq.q: How do you read a power derating curve?
faq.a: The curve gives allowable dissipation versus ambient or case temperature: flat up to a reference point, then falling linearly to zero at the maximum junction temperature. Its slope is the inverse of the thermal resistance.

faq.q: What is OCV derating in static timing analysis?
faq.a: It applies multiplying factors to cell and wire delays so that launch and capture paths are evaluated at pessimistic, different speeds, covering location-dependent variation within one chip.

ノイズマージン.desc: The difference between the voltage level an output guarantees and the level an input is guaranteed to interpret correctly. The low-level margin is VIL(max) − VOL(max) and the high-level margin is VOH(min) − VIH(min); noise smaller than this causes no misreading.

5 Vトレラント.desc: An input that can accept 5 V without damage and without current flowing into the supply, even when the IC runs from 3.3 V or similar. It only tolerates 5 V at the input; it does not mean the IC can output a 5 V signal.

オープンドレイン.desc: An output that brings out only the drain of the output transistor, actively driving only the low level. The high level comes from an external pull-up resistor, so several outputs can share one line or connect to circuits on a different supply voltage. It is used on I2C buses, for example.

エラッタ.desc: A document listing known defects found after shipment, such as behavior that differs from the specification, together with the affected chip revisions, the conditions under which they occur, and workarounds. It is provided for complex ICs such as microcontrollers and should be checked early in design.

静止電流.desc: The current consumed by an IC's own internal circuitry, such as a regulator's, separate from the current delivered to the load; written IQ. It dominates standby consumption in battery-powered equipment and ranges from under 1 µA to several mA depending on the product.

伝搬遅延.desc: The time from an input change to the resulting output change. For logic ICs it is measured between the points where input and output cross 50% of their swing, and is specified separately as tPLH (output low to high) and tPHL (output high to low). It grows with load capacitance.

許容損失.desc: The maximum power a package may dissipate, written Pd. It is set by the maximum junction temperature and the thermal resistance, and above a certain ambient temperature (often 25 °C) it must be reduced in proportion to temperature.

安全動作領域.desc: The range of voltage and current combinations in which a power transistor can be used without damage, abbreviated SOA. It is shown on a log-log graph, with boundaries set by on-resistance, current rating, power (thermal) limits and breakdown voltage. The thermal limit relaxes for shorter pulse widths.

入力オフセット電圧.desc: The small voltage that must be applied between an op amp's inputs to bring its output to zero, caused by mismatch among internal devices. It is multiplied by the circuit's gain into an output error: 2 mV at a gain of 100 shifts the output by up to 200 mV.

ドロップアウト電圧.desc: The minimum input-to-output voltage difference a linear regulator needs to hold its output voltage. It increases with output current and, usually, with temperature; for LDOs it is typically tens to hundreds of mV.

MSL(吸湿感度レベル).desc: A rating of how readily a surface-mount part absorbs moisture, defined by JEDEC's J-STD-020. It sets the floor life allowed between opening the moisture barrier bag and reflow: 168 hours at or below 30 °C/60% RH for MSL 3. Parts past their floor life are baked dry before mounting.

露出パッド(エクスポーズドパッド).desc: A large metal area on the underside of packages such as QFN, connected to the die pad. Soldered to the board, it is the main path for removing heat and is usually tied to inner-layer planes with thermal vias.

レール・ツー・レール.desc: Describes an op amp or similar whose input or output range extends close to both supply rails. It allows large signal swings in single-supply, low-voltage circuits, although the output still saturates some tens of mV short of the rails depending on load current.

スラック.desc: A value expressing timing margin. For setup it is required time minus arrival time, and for hold it is arrival time minus required time; a negative value means a violation.

about.p: Static timing analysis (STA) compares when data arrives with when it is required. For setup, the data launched at one clock edge must arrive before the next capture edge minus the setup time, so slack = required − arrival. With a 2.0 ns period, 0.2 ns clock-to-output, 1.4 ns of logic and 0.1 ns setup, arrival is 1.6 ns, required is 1.9 ns and slack is +0.3 ns. Clock uncertainty for jitter and unbuilt clock trees is also subtracted from the required time, and a multicycle path of 2 moves the capture edge one extra period later.

about.h: Hold slack and why frequency does not help
about.p: Hold asks the opposite question: does new data launched by an edge arrive so early that it corrupts the value the same edge is capturing? Here slack = arrival − required, using minimum delays and required = capture clock arrival + hold time. Because both checks refer to the same edge, the clock period does not appear, so slowing the clock never fixes a hold violation; in silicon it is usually fatal. Hold problems appear on short paths such as shift registers and are normally fixed by inserting delay cells on the data path.

Clock skew moves the two checks in opposite directions. If the capture clock arrives later than the launch clock (positive skew), setup slack grows by that amount and hold slack shrinks by the same amount; negative skew does the reverse. On-chip variation (OCV) derating makes the analysis pessimistic, for setup slowing the launch clock and data paths and speeding the capture clock. Where both clock paths share buffers from the root, that shared section cannot be fast and slow at once, so common path pessimism removal (CRPR) adds the difference back.

Reports summarize slack per endpoint. WNS (worst negative slack) is the single worst value and indicates how far the clock is from closing; TNS (total negative slack) sums the negative slacks of all violating endpoints and indicates how much work remains. Three endpoints at −0.1 ns give WNS −0.1 ns and TNS −0.3 ns. Both are reported separately for setup and hold, and per clock group. Setup violations are attacked by shortening logic, upsizing cells or restructuring; a multicycle exception is legitimate only if the logic really captures every other cycle.

faq.q: What does negative slack mean in timing analysis?
faq.a: It means the path violates its constraint: for setup the data arrives too late for the capture edge, and for hold it arrives too early and could overwrite the value being captured. The magnitude tells how much delay must be removed or added.

faq.q: What is the difference between WNS and TNS?
faq.a: WNS is the slack of the single worst path, while TNS is the sum of all negative endpoint slacks. A design can have a small WNS but a large TNS when many paths fail by a little.

faq.q: How do you fix a hold violation?
faq.a: Add delay to the short data path, typically with buffer or delay cells, or reduce the skew that pushes the capture clock late. Lowering the clock frequency does not help because the hold check does not involve the period.

WNS(ワーストネガティブスラック).desc: In STA, the worst (smallest) slack among all paths. Together with TNS (total negative slack), the sum of negative slack over violating endpoints, it indicates how large and how widespread the timing violations are.

クリティカルパス.desc: The path with the largest delay in a circuit, which sets the maximum clock frequency. In STA it is the path with the smallest slack, and speeding up a design starts by reducing its delay.

クロックの不確かさ.desc: A margin subtracted from the available time in timing analysis to account for jitter and for clock skew not yet known. It is set with set_clock_uncertainty in SDC, and before the clock tree is built it is set larger to cover skew as well.

OCV(オンチップばらつき).desc: Variation in transistor and wire delay from place to place within a single chip. STA applies separate factors to launch and capture paths (for example 1.1× and 0.9×) to analyze the most pessimistic combination.

CRPR(共通パスの悲観性の除去).desc: A correction in OCV-based STA that adds back to the slack the difference caused by applying both slow and fast factors to the shared portion of the launch and capture clock paths. The shared portion is physically the same, so it cannot be both slow and fast within one clock edge.

マルチサイクルパス.desc: A timing exception telling STA that a path may take several clock cycles to transfer data. When setup is set to N cycles, hold is usually set to N − 1 to move the hold check edge back to its original position.

フォールスパス.desc: A path that exists structurally but along which no signal actually propagates in operation. It is excluded from STA as a timing exception, specified with set_false_path in SDC.

SDC.desc: A format for timing constraints that describes clock periods and waveforms, input and output delays, timing exceptions and so on. Written as Tcl commands, it is shared by logic synthesis, place-and-route and STA tools.

リカバリーチェック.desc: A timing check that the release of an asynchronous reset or similar does not come too soon before a clock edge; it corresponds to setup. It is paired with the removal check, which verifies that release does not come too soon after the edge and corresponds to hold.

クロックドメイン.desc: A group of flip-flops driven by the same clock, or by clocks with a fixed frequency and phase relationship. Passing a signal between clock domains that are asynchronous to each other requires a synchronizer.

about.h: What makes two clocks the same domain
about.p: Flip-flops belong to one domain when they share a clock, or clocks whose frequency and phase relationship is fixed, such as divided clocks from the same PLL. Static timing analysis (STA) can then check every path for setup and hold. Clocks from independent sources, or with no known phase relationship, are asynchronous: a data edge can arrive at any point relative to the capturing edge, so timing cannot be guaranteed. Such paths are excluded from normal timing checks, for example by declaring the clocks as asynchronous groups in the constraints, and must instead be made safe by design.

If data changes inside a flip-flop's setup and hold window, the output can hover between 0 and 1, a metastable state, before resolving. The standard single-bit synchronizer adds a second flip-flop in the receiving domain, giving the first one a full cycle to settle. The probability of failure falls exponentially with that settling time, so two stages usually give a mean time between failures far beyond the product lifetime, and three are used at high frequencies. A synchronizer lowers the probability; it does not remove it, and it decides only when a change is seen, not whether it was valid.

about.h: Crossing with multi-bit data and pulses
about.p: Synchronizing each bit of a bus separately fails because different bits may be captured on different edges: a change from 0111 to 1000 can arrive as 1111 or 0000 for a cycle. Counters crossing domains are therefore Gray-coded so only one bit changes at a time, and arbitrary data is held stable while a single valid or request bit is synchronized, through a handshake or an asynchronous FIFO. Pulses also need care: a 2 ns pulse from a 500 MHz domain can fall between 10 ns edges of a 100 MHz clock and vanish, so it is stretched or converted to a toggle.

Signals entering a synchronizer must come straight from a flip-flop in the sending domain, because combinational logic can glitch and an asynchronous edge may capture the glitch. Toggle synchronizers need a minimum spacing between events, several receiving cycles, or two toggles can cancel out. Ordinary RTL simulation does not model metastability and rarely exposes these bugs, so dedicated clock domain crossing (CDC) tools check structurally for missing synchronizers, logic in front of them and unsafe multi-bit crossings. Resets crossing domains need the same care, typically asserted asynchronously and released synchronously.

faq.q: What is a clock domain crossing?
faq.a: A clock domain crossing is any path where a signal launched by one clock is captured by another clock that is asynchronous to it. Such paths need synchronizers, handshakes or asynchronous FIFOs because timing analysis cannot guarantee them.

faq.q: Why does a synchronizer use two flip-flops?
faq.a: The first flip-flop may go metastable when its input changes near the clock edge; the second gives it a full clock period to settle before the value is used. This makes the failure probability extremely small, though never zero.

faq.q: Are clocks with different frequencies always in different clock domains?
faq.a: No. If they are derived from the same source with a fixed ratio and phase, such as a clock and its divide-by-two, timing analysis can check paths between them, so they can be treated as synchronous.

同期化回路.desc: A circuit that aligns an asynchronous signal to the receiving clock. The basic form is two flip-flops in series, which raises the probability that metastability in the first stage resolves before the next edge.

about.p: When an asynchronous input changes inside a flip-flop's setup–hold window, the flop can go metastable, its output hovering between 0 and 1 for an unpredictable time. This cannot be prevented, but the probability that it is still unresolved falls exponentially with waiting time. A two-flop synchronizer exploits this: the first flop may go metastable, and the second samples it a full clock period later, by which time it has almost certainly settled. The rest of the receiving domain only ever sees the second flop's clean output.

Synchronizer reliability is expressed as mean time between failures, approximately MTBF = e^(t_r/τ) / (T_0 × f_clk × f_data), where t_r is the time available to resolve and τ and T_0 are flip-flop constants. Because t_r sits in an exponent, small changes matter enormously: with τ = 20 ps, one extra nanosecond multiplies MTBF by e^50. Adding a third stage adds roughly one clock period of resolution time. Raising the receiving clock frequency hurts twice, by adding more sampling events and by shrinking the period, which is why very fast domains often use three stages.

Connect the first and second flops directly, with no combinational logic or buffering between them, and place them close together; any delay there is subtracted from t_r. Never fan the first-stage output out to other logic, since different loads could interpret a metastable level differently. The signal entering the synchronizer must come straight from a flip-flop in the sending domain, not from combinational logic, because an asynchronous edge can catch a momentary glitch as a valid pulse. Clock-domain-crossing (CDC) verification tools check these rules automatically.

A synchronizer handles one bit at a time. If each bit of a bus has its own synchronizer, bits can resolve in different cycles, so a change from 0111 to 1000 may briefly read as 1111 or 0000. Signals synchronized separately and recombined, called reconvergence, show the same hazard. Short pulses are another trap: a 2 ns pulse can fall entirely between edges of a 100 MHz clock and vanish. Remedies include Gray-coded counters, holding data while a single valid bit is synchronized, handshakes, asynchronous FIFOs, and stretching level signals to about 1.5 receiving periods or more.

faq.q: Is a two flip-flop synchronizer enough?
faq.a: For most designs at moderate clock rates, yes: a two-stage synchronizer typically pushes MTBF to thousands of years or more. At very high receiving frequencies or with flops having a large τ, a third stage is added to gain another clock period of resolution time.

faq.q: Can I synchronize a multi-bit bus with one synchronizer per bit?
faq.a: No, not for arbitrary data, because different bits may be captured in different cycles and produce values that never existed. Use Gray code for counters, or hold the data stable and synchronize a single control bit through a handshake, or use an asynchronous FIFO.

faq.q: Why does a pulse get lost when crossing from a fast to a slow clock?
faq.a: If the pulse is shorter than the receiving clock period it can start and end between two receiving edges and never be sampled. Stretch it to well beyond one receiving period, or convert it to a toggle that is then synchronized and edge-detected.

MTBF(平均故障間隔).desc: The average interval between failures. For a synchronizer it is the average time between metastable events that fail to resolve and propagate onward, given by MTBF = e^(t_r/τ) ÷ (T_0 × f_clk × f_data). Adding stages lengthens the resolution time t_r and increases it exponentially.

about.p: Mean time between failures (MTBF) is the average operating time between successive failures of a repairable system. For parts that are not repaired, the matching figure is mean time to failure (MTTF), and the average time to restore service is mean time to repair (MTTR). With a constant failure rate λ, MTBF = 1/λ, and since 1 FIT is one failure per 10⁹ device-hours, 100 FIT corresponds to 10⁷ hours. An average is not a guaranteed life: under a constant failure rate about 63% of units have failed by the time t equals MTBF.

Quality describes whether a product meets specification at shipment, tracked with figures such as DPPM (defective parts per million) or controlled by sampling with an acceptable quality level (AQL). Reliability is the time-dependent ability to keep working under stated conditions, expressed with FIT, MTTF and MTBF. Quality can be checked by testing finished parts, but reliability has to be predicted, usually from accelerated stress tests at elevated temperature or voltage whose results are extrapolated to use conditions.

In digital design MTBF has a special meaning: the average time between metastable events that fail to resolve before the next stage samples them. It is approximated by MTBF = e^(t_r/τ) / (T_0 × f_clk × f_data). Here t_r is the resolution time available, roughly a clock period minus overheads; τ is the flip-flop's regeneration time constant; and T_0 relates to the width of its metastability window. More sampling events from a faster clock or a busier data input reduce MTBF linearly, while t_r acts exponentially.

Because t_r sits in the exponent, adding one synchronizer stage, which adds roughly one clock period, typically multiplies MTBF by an astronomical factor; with τ = 20 ps, one extra nanosecond gives e^50, more than 10^21. Doubling the receive clock from 500 MHz to 1 GHz halves the period and cuts MTBF by far more than two. Failure rates add for parts in series, so a chip with many synchronizers has a system MTBF lower than any single one, and well-designed crossings aim for thousands of years or more.

faq.q: Does an MTBF of 1,000,000 hours mean a device will last 114 years?
faq.a: No. MTBF describes a population's failure rate during its useful life, not the lifetime of a single unit. With a constant failure rate, about 63% of units would have failed by one MTBF, and wear-out mechanisms usually end life much earlier.

faq.q: How do you convert FIT to MTBF?
faq.a: Under a constant failure rate, MTBF in hours equals 10⁹ divided by the FIT value. For example, 50 FIT corresponds to 2×10⁷ hours.

faq.q: What is the difference between MTBF and MTTF?
faq.a: MTBF applies to repairable systems and measures average operating time between failures, while MTTF applies to non-repairable parts and measures average time until their single failure. For a chip that is replaced rather than repaired, MTTF is the appropriate term.

非同期FIFO.desc: A FIFO written and read on separate clocks, used to pass multi-bit data between clock domains. Its pointers are converted to Gray code before being synchronized into the other domain to decide full and empty. The pointers have one more bit than the address to distinguish wrap-around.

about.h: How an asynchronous FIFO is built
about.p: An asynchronous FIFO is a dual-port memory written on the sender's clock and read on the receiver's clock. The write pointer lives in the write domain and the read pointer in the read domain. Each pointer is passed through a synchronizer into the opposite domain: the write side compares its own pointer with the synchronized read pointer to generate full, and the read side compares its pointer with the synchronized write pointer to generate empty.
